Averages/Simple moving average.summary: All checks follow from ranged subtypes, bounded arrays and guards, but the loop-carried window sum and the bounded-buffer decimal formatting require careful shaping because no invariants can be written.

effects.explanation: Prints the in-order balance factors of the tree after inserting the keys 1 to 10.

risks.explanation: Nodes live in a fixed array indexed by a ranged subtype (0 is the null sentinel), so every loop-carried node index is in range by its type, and a full table is rejected by an explicit capacity guard before allocation.

Heights and balance factors are ranged subtypes, so each height increment and balance computation needs a guard just before it (reject when the height limit would be exceeded), and the rotation code must be written so that each stored balance is clamped by guarded branches rather than by an invariant.
Insertion descent, upward rebalancing and in-order printing are written as while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, and no recursion or function loops are used.
Keys are a bounded integer range and comparisons and height sums stay within small ranged types, so arithmetic overflow follows from types and guards.

Rotation correctness (that a child needed for a rotation is non-null) is not a proof obligation with a sentinel node at index 0, but the code should test the child before use so no later check depends on a tree-shape invariant.

AVL tree.approach: Represent the tree as a fixed-capacity array of node records (key, left, right, parent, balance, height) addressed by a ranged index type with 0 as the null sentinel, avoiding access types and recursion. Insert iteratively in a procedure by descending with a while loop, reject duplicates and a full table with a visible outcome, then walk up the parent links to recompute heights and balances and apply single or double rotations chosen by explicit guards. Insert keys 1..10 in a for loop and print the balance factors in order using an iterative in-order walk with a bounded explicit stack, guarded against overflow.
AVL tree.summary: The pointer-based, recursive, generic Ada solution can be recast as an array-indexed tree with iterative procedures, so index and range checks follow from types and guards, but the many loop-carried heights, balances and parent links make discharge depend on careful program shape rather than being routine.

effects.explanation: The rendered text-art plot of the curve and control points is printed line by line.

risks.explanation: The cubic basis products (t cubed times 6-scaled weights times coordinates up to 400) are bounded by small ranged subtypes for the step index and coordinates, so they fit in Integer by type ranges alone.

The computed grid cell is derived from a sum of nonlinear weighted terms that the prover cannot bound without an invariant, so an explicit guard just before the write skips points outside the grid, which is safe because coordinates are in range by construction and the guard is visible in the code.
Control point indices i to i+3 inside the segment loop are covered by a for loop over 0 .. 8 on a 12-element array, so they are static bounds.

B-spline.approach: Embed the 12 control points in a constant array of coordinate records, and evaluate a uniform cubic B-spline in pure integer arithmetic: for each of the 9 segments and each of 16 integer sub-steps, the four basis weights are cubic polynomials in the step scaled by 6 times 16 cubed, then summed per axis and divided by the scale. Mark the curve and control points in a fixed 2D Character grid (about 60 by 40, coordinates scaled down), then print each row through a bounded String buffer with Put_Line, with a guard before each grid write.
B-spline.summary: All loops are for loops over static ranges and arithmetic is integer with ranged operands, so most checks follow from types, with only the computed grid index needing a guard before the write.

effects.explanation: Prints the found integer (or a not-found message) with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The square of a candidate up to 99_736 reaches about 9.95e9, so it is computed in a declared 64-bit-range type whose range type bounds make the multiplication provably safe.

Babbage problem.approach: Declare a candidate subtype 1 .. 99_736 and a 64-bit square type, then loop over the candidates with a for loop, converting each to the wide type, squaring it and testing the square mod 1_000_000 = 269_696, exiting on the first hit and recording it in a Boolean-guarded result. After the loop, print the image of the answer if found, otherwise print a fixed not-found message.
Babbage problem.summary: The loop index is bounded by its declared range so the square fits in the wide type and the only loop-carried state is a Boolean and a ranged result, so every check follows from types; the not-found branch gives a visible outcome rather than narrowing behavior.

effects.explanation: The first 40 coordinates are printed as text lines.

risks.explanation: Cross and dot products of candidate vectors are nonlinear but discharge because vector components are subtypes bounded to a small window, so every product fits Integer.

The loop-carried position and previous squared length know only their subtype ranges, so each update is preceded by an explicit guard that rejects the run (visible outcome) if the new value would leave the declared range.
The nearest-longer-vector search uses a fixed-size window, so if no candidate is found the program rejects visibly, a documented resource limit that is never hit for 40 points.

Babylonian spiral.approach: Use pure integer arithmetic instead of floating point: keep the previous step as (dx, dy) and its squared length, and for each of 40 steps scan a bounded window of candidate vectors with nested for loops. Choose the smallest squared length strictly above the previous one, among those the smallest clockwise bend, ordered by the sign of cross products and a half-plane test, excluding collinear same-direction candidates. Then update the position behind a range guard, print the coordinates with 'Image text, and skip the optional 10000-point plot.
Babylonian spiral.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic in nested for loops inside a procedure, with no recursion or floats, so checks follow from subtype ranges and a few guards on the carried position and length; the nonlinear products stay within Integer because the window is small.

effects.explanation: The program prints the cipher text and the decoded hidden text with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The bit-stream position counter is loop-carried, so each write into the fixed-capacity bit buffer and each read of a 5-bit group is guarded by an explicit comparison against the buffer capacity just before use.
Counters are declared with bounded subtypes and incremented only after a guard, so the +1 and the 5*k+offset arithmetic cannot overflow.
The output buffer is a fixed-length String assigned by element with a message length known as a constant, so no slice or concatenation length check depends on loop state.

If the message holds fewer letters than 5 times the plaintext length, the program prints a specified rejection line instead of silently truncating, and a plaintext character outside a-z or space is encoded as a space.

Bacon cipher.approach: The program embeds the 27-symbol Bacon table (a-z plus space) as a constant String of 5-character groups, the plaintext and a longer carrier message as constants, and a fixed-capacity Boolean or Character bit buffer sized from the plaintext length times 5. Encoding is a for loop over the plaintext that looks up each symbol's group and fills the buffer, then a for loop over the carrier that upper-cases letters where the bit is B, guarded by the buffer count and a capacity check that rejects a too-short carrier with a printed message. Decoding counts case bits over the cipher text, then for each 5-bit group scans the table with a bounded for loop to find the matching symbol, and both results are printed with Put_Line.
Bacon cipher.summary: Every loop is a for loop over a constant or array range in the main procedure, and the only loop-carried values are bounded counters guarded by capacity comparisons, so the checks should discharge with careful program shape and no annotation.

effects.explanation: Each generated bracket string and its OK or NOT OK verdict is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The generator state is a ranged subtype and each update is reduced by mod, so the multiply-add cannot overflow.

The nesting depth counter is loop-carried and the prover knows only its type, so a guard before the increment rejects depth beyond a declared limit, which a string of at most 8 characters never reaches.
Swap positions come from a mod of the string length plus one, guarded against a zero length, and the checker loops over the buffer's own range.
Slicing a bounded buffer to the current length and concatenating with the verdict text needs the length provably within the buffer capacity.

Balanced brackets.approach: Use a fixed 8-character String buffer filled with N opening then N closing brackets for N from 0 to 4, shuffled by a Fisher-Yates style loop driven by a small ranged linear congruential generator held in a procedure. A separate function scans the string with a for loop over its range, keeping an Open counter and returning False when a closing bracket appears at depth zero or the final depth is nonzero. Main prints each bracket string with its verdict through Put_Line.
Balanced brackets.summary: Everything is a bounded for loop or a mod-bounded index over a small fixed buffer with embedded N values, so checks come from types and local guards and no invariant is needed. The only care points are the loop-carried depth counter and the generator arithmetic, which need range-bounded types or a guard.

effects.explanation: Prints a, b, c in decimal and the product in ternary and decimal.

risks.explanation: Trit sums and carries are computed in a small Integer range and checked against -1..1 after reduction, so they follow from the types and a guard before each narrowing.
Product positions I+J-1 are guarded against the fixed capacity and any excess nonzero trit sets a visible overflow flag instead of indexing out of range.
Conversion to a native integer accumulates value and place weight through a loop with no invariant, so each step is guarded by an explicit magnitude limit that reports overflow rather than wrapping.
Integer-to-trit conversion repeatedly divides a loop-carried value by 3 using mod and rem, which is nonlinear but stays within the Integer type and loops over a fixed trit count.
Arbitrary size is replaced by a documented fixed capacity (for example 40 trits) with overflow reported explicitly, which Oracle rule 7 permits.

Balanced ternary.approach: Represent a number as a record of a fixed-capacity array of 40 trits (a -1..1 subtype, least significant first) plus a length and an overflow flag. Procedures implement parse from text, from Integer, to Integer, to text, negate, add (carry loop), and multiply (shift-and-add using for loops with guarded indexes), and the main procedure embeds the test case and prints the results with Put_Line. All conversions use for loops over the fixed capacity, and overflow produces a visible rejection message rather than wrapped values.
Balanced ternary.summary: All loops are bounded for loops over a fixed capacity and every narrowing or index is protected by a local guard, so no annotation should be needed, though carry chains and guarded integer accumulation require careful shape. The arbitrary-size requirement is met with a documented fixed capacity and explicit overflow reporting.

effects.explanation: Prints the available resources, each process as it runs, and the safe or unsafe verdict.

risks.explanation: Summed and updated resource counts are loop-carried, so they use a small ranged subtype (0..1000) with each addition guarded by a comparison against the bound just before it, and an over-limit total rejects the input.
The outer scheduling loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and it also ends because each pass either marks a process finished or exits.
All indexing is by for-loop variables over the fixed constrained array ranges, so index checks follow from the loop ranges.

Banker's algorithm.approach: The program embeds the example (4 resource types, 3 processes) as constrained arrays: a Total vector plus Allocation and Maximum matrices indexed by enumeration or small ranged subtypes. A main procedure sums each allocation column, validates that the totals fit within Total and that Allocation does not exceed Maximum (rejecting with a visible message otherwise), derives Available and Need, then loops in a procedure: pick an unfinished process whose Need fits within Available, add its allocation back, and print it, or report an unsafe state if none fits. Counts are subtypes bounded to a small range so every addition is guarded by a bound comparison before use.
Banker's algorithm.summary: The task is bounded array arithmetic on embedded data with nested for loops and one while loop in a procedure, so every check follows from ranged subtypes and explicit guards, and nothing needs a variant or invariant.

effects.explanation: The fern is rendered as text art rows written with Put_Line, which meets the task without a display.

risks.explanation: X and Y are loop-carried, so they are declared with a subtype range of -100.0 .. 100.0 which the four affine maps provably map into itself (largest result about 90.6), letting range and overflow checks discharge without an invariant.

Converting scaled coordinates to grid column and row indexes needs a guard that tests the computed values against the grid bounds just before indexing, so a point outside the grid is visibly skipped rather than checked by proof.
The pseudo-random generator uses a 32-bit modular type so wraparound is defined behavior, and the percentage is derived by mod 100 on the modular value.

Barnsley fern.approach: The program keeps a fixed grid of rows (for example 40 by 60 characters) initialised to spaces, iterates a fixed 100000 times with a modular linear congruential generator choosing one of the four affine maps by percentage thresholds in an if/elsif chain, and marks the grid cell for each point after guarding the scaled indexes against the grid bounds. Coordinates are floats in a bounded subtype closed under all four maps. Afterwards a for loop prints each row with Put_Line.
Barnsley fern.summary: Every check follows from a closed float subtype range, a modular generator and explicit index guards, with no annotations, but floating-point range reasoning and float-to-integer conversion make discharge depend on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints each qualifying decimal number and the total count with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried Count is declared with a range and incremented only under a guard just before the increment, so the range check discharges.

Base 16 numbers needing a to f.approach: Main loops N over 1 .. 500 with a ranged-subtype copy C, and an inner for loop of three iterations (500 needs at most three hex digits) tests C mod 16 >= 10 then sets C := C / 16, setting a Boolean Found. Each qualifying N is printed with Put_Line using a trimmed 'Image string (one per line rather than 24 columns), Count is incremented behind a guard, and the final "Total count: " line is built by bounded concatenation with the Count image.
Base 16 numbers needing a to f.summary: All arithmetic is on small ranged integers with a fixed three-iteration for loop instead of a while loop, so no termination or invariant facts are needed and only the Count increment needs a guard.

effects.explanation: Prints each example input and its base58 encoding with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The carry (remainder times 256 plus byte) is declared in a subtype 0 .. 14847 and the remainder in 0 .. 57, so range checks on the loop-carried values follow from types, but the prover must show the quotient fits a byte, which needs 14847/58 <= 255 and is a small nonlinear fact.
The digit buffer is sized for the longest example (the 24-byte input needs at most 33 digits, so 40 slots) and a guard before each write rejects the input visibly if the count would exceed capacity.
The output String is built in a fixed buffer by reversing digits with for-loop indexes over the buffer range, so slice lengths follow from the guarded count.

Base58Check encoding.approach: Embed each example checksum as a fixed-size array of bytes (subtype 0 .. 255) with a length, copy it into a work array, and repeatedly divide the whole number by 58 in a for loop over the array, collecting each remainder as a digit index into the 58-character alphabet constant until the number is zero. Digits are stored least-significant first in a bounded buffer with a guard before each write that rejects on overflow, leading zero bytes are mapped to the first alphabet character, and the buffer is then reversed into a String for Put_Line. The outer repeat-until-zero loop lives in a procedure so it needs no termination proof, and all carried values are range-typed.
Base58Check encoding.summary: Base conversion by repeated division of a fixed-size byte array needs only range-typed carries and a guarded digit count, so no annotations are needed, though the nonlinear carry arithmetic and the while loop's buffer guard require careful shape.

effects.explanation: The decoded text is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Each 4-character group is read at indexes computed from the for-loop variable over a length that is checked to be a multiple of four, and output positions are guarded against buffer capacity before each write.

Each Base64 character maps through a case or if chain to a 0..63 subtype or an invalid flag, so the byte arithmetic (v1*4 + v2/16, and so on) stays within 0..255 by type ranges and Character'Val is only applied to a value already in range.
The decoded output goes into a fixed-capacity buffer sized for at most three quarters of the input length, and the final Put_Line prints only the filled prefix, so no slice can exceed bounds.

Base64 decode data.approach: The program embeds the encoded sample as a String constant and defines a procedure that checks the length is a multiple of four and that padding appears only at the end. It then runs a for loop over the groups, mapping each of the four characters to a 0..63 value, computing up to three bytes with integer division and mod, and storing them as Characters in a fixed buffer with a count. It prints the encoded input and the decoded prefix, and on any invalid character or bad padding it prints a specified rejection message instead of output.
Base64 decode data.summary: Every check follows from the 0..63 value subtype, for-loop indexes over groups of a length-checked input, and a guarded fixed buffer, with no loop-carried accumulator wider than its type. The task needs nothing an annotation would supply, and the only dependence is careful program shape around padding and index arithmetic.

effects.explanation: Prints the base64 text with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Each 6-bit group is computed with mod and / on a Natural byte value, giving 0..63 that indexes a constant 64-character alphabet string, so the index check follows from the arithmetic bounds.

Combining up to three bytes into a 24-bit Natural and the output position (3-byte group index times 4) are bounded by the fixed embedded array length, so the loop-carried output offset is a for-loop index expression with static bounds.

Base64 encode data.approach: Embed a fixed-length constant array of byte values (type 0..255) as the data, since the favicon download is not required to be fetched live, and a constant 64-character alphabet string. A for loop over full 3-byte groups computes the 24-bit value and writes four alphabet characters into a fixed-size output String buffer at offsets derived from the loop index, then a guarded tail handles the 1- or 2-byte remainder with '=' padding, and Put_Line prints the buffer.
Base64 encode data.summary: All arithmetic is on bounded byte values with mod and division by literals and a for loop over a static array range, so every check follows from types and static bounds with no loop-carried unbounded values.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 15 Bell numbers and the first ten Bell triangle rows as text.

risks.explanation: Triangle elements are a subtype bounded well below the 64-bit limit so a sum of two elements cannot overflow, and an explicit guard rejects any sum above the subtype bound before storing it.
The stored sum is range-checked against the element subtype, which the guard before the assignment discharges even though loop-carried array contents are known only by type.
Indexes come from for loops over the array's own bounds, with the previous row and next column computed from loop variables that are provably within range.

Bell numbers.approach: Use a constrained 2D array (rows 1..15, columns 1..15) of a bounded integer subtype, set the first element to 1, and for each later row copy the previous row's last entry into column 1 and fill each next column with the left neighbour plus the above-left entry inside for loops. A guard rejects any sum exceeding the subtype bound, then the program prints the first column of each row with 'Image and the first ten rows with Put. The optional 50th element is omitted since it needs big numbers, and the 15 numbers (up to the 15th row's last entry, 1382958545) fit easily.
Bell numbers.summary: All values stay far below 2**61 so a guard before each addition discharges overflow and range checks with only for loops and fixed array bounds, though loop-carried array contents need that guard to be placed carefully.

effects.explanation: Prints the actual versus expected first-digit table with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The digit-array addition carries through loops, so each digit sum is bounded by the 0..9 digit subtype (at most 19) and a leftover carry out of the top digit is rejected visibly by a guard, since the 1000th Fibonacci number needs only 209 of 220 digits.
The per-digit counters are incremented in a loop with no invariant, so each increment is guarded by a comparison against the counter subtype's upper bound with Reject as the visible outcome.
The first-digit scan walks a for loop over the digit array's own range and keeps the highest nonzero digit found, so every index is within bounds by construction.
Avoided by embedding the expected Benford percentages as integer hundredths constants instead of computing log10, and computing actual percentages with integer division.

Benford's law.approach: Two fixed-capacity little-endian decimal digit arrays (220 digits, each element a 0..9 subtype) hold consecutive Fibonacci numbers and are advanced 1000 times by a for loop whose inner for loop does ripple-carry addition. After each step a for loop over the array finds the most significant nonzero digit, which increments a guarded count in a nine-element array. The table of count, expected count, actual percent and expected percent (embedded integer constants, integer division for the actual values) is printed by a for loop over digits 1..9 using 'Image and bounded concatenation.
Benford's law.summary: Every check follows from declared digit and count ranges plus a carry-out guard, and no loop needs an invariant, but the nested carry loops and guarded counters need careful shape; floating point is avoided with embedded expected constants.

effects.explanation: Prints the resulting connection polynomial coefficients as text lines.

risks.explanation: Coefficient indices like i-1-j and i-L-1 are loop-carried, so each array access is guarded by an explicit range test just before use, with C and B held in fixed-capacity arrays of ranged index subtypes.
The linear complexity L and shift m change inside the loop without an invariant, so they are typed as subtypes bounded by the sequence capacity and each update is guarded to stay within that bound.
All coefficients and discrepancies are GF(2) values in 0..1 with mod 2 applied, so sums of at most capacity-many products stay far below the Integer limit.

Berlekamp\u2013Massey algorithm.approach: The 7-element binary sequence is embedded as a constant array, and C, B and a temporary copy are fixed-capacity arrays of 0..1 coefficients with a capacity of 16. A for loop over the sequence computes the discrepancy with an inner for loop with guarded indices, updates C from B using shifted for loops, and adjusts L, m and B per the standard algorithm in a procedure. The result is printed as a line built from the coefficients up to L.
Berlekamp\u2013Massey algorithm.summary: The algorithm is bounded nested for loops over fixed arrays with GF(2) arithmetic, so every check follows from types and index guards, though the loop-carried L and shift offsets need careful guards without invariants. The optional nth-term computation is omitted.

effects.explanation: Prints one line per nonzero Bernoulli number B0 through B60.

risks.explanation: Fixed-capacity digit arrays use small limbs (for example base 10000 in 64-bit integers) so every limb product and carry is bounded by type ranges, and the digit capacity is sized above the largest intermediate Akiyama-Tanigawa value with an explicit overflow-reject path for results that do not fit.
Schoolbook multiply, subtract, divide and gcd loops index limb arrays through for loops over the array range or with a guard just before each access, since carried positions have no invariant.
Gcd and normalisation use while loops, which are only safe because they live in procedures that get no termination check; functions must be limited to for loops.
Signed rational subtraction and long division carry loop-carried quotient and remainder values that are bounded only by their declared subtypes, so each step needs explicit guards before narrowing.
Output lines are assembled in a fixed-size buffer whose width is sized for the 43-digit numerator, with right alignment computed from digit counts under guards.

Bernoulli numbers.approach: Represent signed rationals as numerator and denominator arrays of base-10000 limbs with a length, and implement add, subtract, multiply by small integer, divide by small integer and gcd reduction as procedures with for and while loops over the fixed arrays. Run the Akiyama-Tanigawa double loop over a 61-entry array of such rationals for each n from 0 to 60, reducing after every step, then for even n and for n=1 build the line "B(n) = numerator / denominator" with aligned solidi into a fixed string buffer and print it with Put_Line. Any capacity overflow is rejected with a visible outcome rather than clamped.
Bernoulli numbers.summary: The task needs only console output and bounded big-rational arithmetic with no recursion, heap use or annotations, so it is feasible once a fixed-capacity big number facility exists, but the multi-limb carry, gcd and division loops make proof discharge depend on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints the 15 rows of the triangle to standard output.

risks.explanation: Stored sums come from array elements known only by their type range after the first iteration, so each sum is guarded against the 16384 limit with a visible Reject outcome that never fires for 15 rows.
Row and column indexes are for-loop variables over the array's own ranges, with the k-1 neighbour only used when k is at least 1, so index checks follow from the loop bounds and a guard.
Image conversion and spacing for values up to five digits need a bounded output buffer or Put of 'Image, whose length checks must be provable from the element range.

Bernoulli's triangle.approach: Use a 15 by 15 array of a ranged subtype 0..16384 filled row by row with for loops: column 0 is 1, interior entries are the sum of the two entries above, and the last entry of each row is twice the previous row's last entry. Each sum and doubling is guarded against the subtype limit with Reject, then rows are printed with Put of each value's image followed by a space and a final Put_Line. All loops are for loops over constant ranges in the main procedure, so no termination obligations arise.
Bernoulli's triangle.summary: The program is bounded integer array filling with for loops over static ranges, so almost every check follows from types and loop bounds, with only the loop-carried sums needing explicit guards. The 15-row limit keeps all values at most 16384, so the guards are unreachable but cheap.

effects.explanation: The program prints the coefficient and evaluation tables to standard output.

risks.explanation: Every Float add and multiply needs a finite-result check, which discharges only if inputs are range-subtyped (coefficients within a few thousand, t within 0.0 .. 10.0) so the provers can bound each intermediate de Casteljau value.
Chained products such as s*b01 + t*b12 are nonlinear, so the subtype bounds must be tight enough that interval reasoning proves the results stay inside the Float range.

Results of tobern and bern2to3 are assigned to range-constrained out parameters, so the subtype bounds must be wide enough for all in-range inputs or the program needs a visible guard that rejects out-of-range coefficients.
Formatted float text is built in a fixed bounded buffer, so a clamp or fixed-width formatter must show the length can never exceed the buffer.

Bernstein basis polynomials.approach: Define a bounded Float subtype for coefficients and for t, then write five small procedures and functions (tobern2, evalbern2, tobern3, evalbern3, bern2to3) as straight-line code with no loops, using the embedded example polynomials and the points 0.25 and 7.50. The main procedure calls them in the task's order and prints each result as a rounded two-decimal value through a fixed-width formatter built on a bounded buffer. Inputs are all constants inside the declared ranges, and any generic entry point would reject out-of-range coefficients with a visible message.
Bernstein basis polynomials.summary: All code is loop-free and recursion-free with literal data, so the only non-routine checks are floating-point overflow and range on a handful of products, which declared subtype bounds should let the provers discharge. The heavier part is the new surface (floating point, float formatting), so discharge depends on careful range choices rather than any annotation.

effects.explanation: Prints one line per test case in the form original, shuffled, (score).

risks.explanation: The score counter is loop-carried, so its increment is guarded by a comparison against the fixed maximum length, which never fires for valid data.
Swap indexes come from nested for loops over the buffer's own range, so every index check follows from the loop bounds.
The output line is concatenated from bounded pieces whose maximum lengths are statically below the buffer capacity, with the Image of a small ranged score.

Best shuffle.approach: Each embedded test string is copied into a fixed-capacity Character array with a length; a deterministic double for loop swaps positions I and J when both characters would land in a differing spot, as in the existing greedy swap, over the array's own index range. A second for loop counts unchanged positions into a ranged score, and the result line is built with concatenation and the score's Image, then printed with Put_Line.
Best shuffle.summary: Every check follows from for-loop ranges over a fixed-capacity buffer, with only the loop-carried score needing a guard, and no recursion, annotations or exceptions are required. The greedy swap is deterministic and acceptable under the task, so the outlook is plausible rather than likely because of the guarded accumulator and string assembly.

effects.explanation: Prints each message, its ciphertext and the decrypted text with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Coordinate indexes 2*I-1 and 2*I into a fixed 80-element buffer are safe because a guard rejects any message longer than 40 letters before the loop, and the offsets derive from the string's own range.
Square lookup returns a 0..24 position from a for loop over the 25-letter key, with a Boolean found flag so unknown characters give a visible rejection instead of an unchecked index.
Offset arithmetic on an unconstrained String's 'First is bounded by the 40-character length guard, so no sum can exceed Integer'Last.

Bifid cipher.approach: Each Polybius square is a 25-character String constant; a lookup function scans it with a for loop to give a row/column pair in 0..4 (J mapped to I when the square lacks J). Encrypt writes all rows then all columns into a bounded 80-element Integer array, re-pairs consecutive entries to index back into the square, and decrypt reverses this, with messages up to 40 letters guarded and an unknown letter producing a printed rejection. Main embeds the four test messages and squares, uppercases the January sentence by hand, and prints plaintext, ciphertext and round-trip result.
Bifid cipher.summary: All loops are for loops over bounded ranges inside procedures with a length guard, so every index and range check follows from types and guards without invariants; the only mildly delicate part is coordinate index arithmetic over unconstrained strings.

effects.explanation: The enlarged image is written as plain-text PPM (P3) lines through Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Source indexes x*(W-1)/NewW and the +1 neighbour are nonlinear, so the program clamps the neighbour index with an explicit if guard just before use.
Weighted sums multiply four 0..255 samples by products of weights up to the bounded output dimensions, which fit in Integer because dimensions are ranged subtypes capped at small constants.
Divisors are the output width/height, declared as subtypes of positive range, so non-zero follows from types.
Each PPM output line is built in a fixed bounded buffer sized for three 3-digit samples per pixel, with the pixel count capped.

Bilinear interpolation.approach: The program embeds a small constant RGB image (for example 8x6) as a two-dimensional array of ranged samples, computes the output size as size*16/10, and for each output pixel and channel finds the source cell with integer arithmetic, clamps the neighbour indexes with guards, and blends with integer-weighted bilinear sums divided by the weight total. It prints a P3 PPM header and one text line per output row using Put_Line with integer-to-text conversion into a bounded buffer.
Bilinear interpolation.summary: All loops are for loops over fixed ranges with no loop-carried values, and every index, overflow and division check follows from ranged subtypes plus a clamp guard, but the nonlinear integer interpolation arithmetic needs careful bounding so the outlook is plausible rather than likely. The embedded image and text PPM output stand in for opening and saving an image file, which keeps it free of file effects.

effects.explanation: Prints the two bin tables line by line to standard output.

risks.explanation: The per-bin counter is loop-carried and only its type is known after the first iteration, so each increment is guarded by a test against the counter subtype's maximum, with overflow giving a visible rejection.
Padded output lines are assembled in a fixed-size buffer whose length is bounded by the digit counts of the Integer-range limits and counts, so each append is guarded against the buffer capacity.
The bin index is computed in a reverse for loop over the limits' own range with a bin-index subtype one larger, so each count access is within bounds from types alone.

Bin given limits.approach: The two limit lists and two data lists are embedded as constant Integer arrays, and a procedure first validates that the limits are strictly ascending (rejecting otherwise), then loops over the data, scanning the limits in a reverse for loop with exit to pick a bin and incrementing a bounded-range counter array guarded against its maximum. A print procedure walks the bins with a for loop, formats each limit and count with padding into a bounded string buffer, and emits the line with Put_Line (or Put for the segments); the whole thing is plain iteration with no recursion or heap.
Bin given limits.summary: Every check follows from array ranges, bounded subtypes and guards just before the operation, and all loops are for loops in procedures, so nothing needs an annotation. The only care is the guarded counter increment and the bounded text formatting.

effects.explanation: The program prints each test case's decimal and hexadecimal result lines with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Subtraction digit Diff + 10 - Right stays in 0..9 only through the branch condition Diff < Right, which is a linear fact the guard provides just before the use.
Carry and borrow are a 0..1 subtype and digit sums are at most 19, so loop-carried values are bounded by their types alone.
Text rendering indexes a fixed buffer with the loop index and a length counter, which needs a guard that the counter stays within the buffer capacity.
A carry out of the top digit is reported as an explicit overflow outcome rather than dropped, though the three test cases never reach it.

Binary coded decimal.approach: Digits are stored little-endian in a fixed 4-element array of a 0..9 subtype for unpacked BCD, and in a 2-element array of bytes of two nibbles (mod 256 type with divide and mod by 16) for packed BCD. Procedures Add and Subtract run a for loop over the array range carrying a 0..1 carry or borrow, with an overflow flag if a carry leaves the top digit. The three embedded test cases are printed by building decimal text, with leading zeros stripped, and hex text from digit characters into a bounded buffer, then calling Put_Line.
Binary coded decimal.summary: Every operation is bounded digit arithmetic in for loops over fixed arrays whose carry, borrow and digits are limited by subtypes or an immediate guard, so no annotation is needed. The only care is subtraction digit range and string-buffer indexing, both handled by guards just before use.

effects.explanation: Prints each binary string followed by a newline using Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Character'Val(48 + N mod 2) is routine because N mod 2 is provably 0 or 1, so the position stays in 48..49.
Slicing from the first '1' position to the buffer end needs a guard that the position lies in the buffer, supplied by the for-loop index range and an explicit zero-value branch.

Binary digits.approach: A procedure Show takes a value of a subtype Natural range 0 .. 2**31-1, fills a fixed 31-character buffer by a reverse for loop, taking N mod 2 as the digit character and halving N each iteration. It then finds the first '1' with a second for loop, and prints either that slice or the single string "0" when the value is zero. Main calls Show on the embedded values 5, 50 and 9000 (plus 0 optionally).
Binary digits.summary: All loops are for loops over static ranges and every arithmetic result is bounded by the subtype, so overflow, range and index checks follow from types and the loop index, with no loop invariant needed. Only the slice bounds need a small guard, which the loop index and the zero branch provide.

effects.explanation: Prints a found or not-found line for each embedded search value.

risks.explanation: Low and High are loop-carried so the prover knows only their type range 0..N+1, and Array(Mid) discharges only because an explicit guard just before the access sends out-of-range Mid to a visible not-found outcome (a guard that is dead in practice but not provable as dead without an invariant).
Low, High and Mid are declared as a small ranged subtype (0..N+1) so Low + High and Mid - 1 cannot overflow, and Mid is computed as Low + (High - Low) / 2.
The while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is required.
Result text built with 'Image and concatenation must fit a fixed-size bounded String buffer sized for the longest line.

Binary search.approach: An embedded constant sorted Integer array (for example 2 4 6 8 9) is searched iteratively by a procedure with out parameters Found and Position, using Low and High as a ranged subtype 0..N+1 and a while Low <= High loop with Mid = Low + (High - Low) / 2 and a guard on Mid before indexing. A main loop over an embedded array of search values calls the procedure and prints "contains X at I" or "does not contain X" through Put_Line with 'Image concatenation into a bounded String; the recursive variant and insertion-point variants are optional and omitted.
Binary search.summary: Everything follows from small declared ranges and a guard before the array access, but the loop-carried Low/High bounds mean the in-range index fact must come from an explicit guard rather than an invariant, so success depends on careful shape; no annotations are needed.

effects.explanation: The demo prints each operation's result (lengths, equality, byte values) to standard output.

risks.explanation: Append, join and replace could exceed the fixed capacity, so each checks remaining room just before writing and sets a visible Overflow outcome instead of truncating.
Substring and replace use loop-carried read and write positions, which discharge because they are Natural subtypes bounded by the capacity and guarded immediately before each array access.
Replace scans with a while loop, so it is a procedure with a position that always advances; functions use only for loops, so no variant is needed.

Binary strings.approach: Represent a binary string as a record holding a Length in 0..Capacity and a fixed array of Octet (Integer subtype 0..255) of size Capacity. Creation, assignment, cloning, emptiness, comparison, append, substring and join are small procedures and for-loop functions with explicit capacity and range guards that report Overflow or invalid-range outcomes; replace-all is a procedure with a while loop that scans the source and writes to the output only after checking remaining capacity. A main procedure runs embedded example data through every operation and prints the results.
Binary strings.summary: Every operation is a bounded array scan whose indexes are range-typed and guarded just before use, with capacity overflow producing a visible outcome, so no annotation is needed. The loop-carried positions in replace-all and join make discharge depend on careful guard placement rather than being routine.

effects.explanation: Prints each sequence and its forward, inverse and round-trip transforms as text lines.

risks.explanation: Each transform accumulator is loop-carried and only known by its type after the first iteration, so each addition is guarded against a declared bound and rejects otherwise, which the 64-bit values for 15 terms (under 1e11) never reach.
Pascal-triangle entries are built by adding two previous row entries held in a ranged subtype, so a guard before each store is needed and the maximum C(14,7)=3432 stays far below the bound.
Number-to-text conversion into a fixed output buffer needs a capacity sized for 15 values of at most 12 digits plus sign and separator, with guards on the write position.

Binomial transform.approach: Embed the four 15-element sequences as constant Long_Long_Integer arrays and build a 15x15 Pascal triangle table in a nested for loop with a bounded-sum guard. Procedures apply the forward and inverse transforms with for loops over the array range, choosing the sign by parity of n-k, and guard the accumulator before every add, rejecting on failure. A formatting procedure appends each value's image to a bounded String buffer and prints it with Put_Line, covering forward, inverse and round-trip lines.
Binomial transform.summary: All loops are for loops over fixed array ranges with small embedded data, so indexes are routine and only the loop-carried accumulators and Pascal sums need explicit range guards with a visible reject outcome, which makes automatic discharge plausible rather than certain.

effects.explanation: Prints the pretty-printed sequence lines and the per-base and total counts.

risks.explanation: The four loop-carried counters are discharged by a guard before each increment (counter below its type's upper bound, otherwise reject), since without an invariant only the type range is known after the first iteration.
Line slices use a for loop over line numbers with start and end computed from constants and clamped by a guard against the sequence length, so slice bounds follow from static bounds.
Each output line is built in a fixed-size bounded buffer (position prefix of width 3 plus up to 70 characters), sized statically so no length check can fail.

Bioinformatics/Base count.approach: The 500-base sequence is embedded as a constant String, printed 70 bases per line with a for loop over line numbers, each line prefixed by padded start..end positions built from 'Image into a bounded buffer. A second for loop over the sequence's own index range uses a case statement on each Character to bump one of four bounded counters, rejecting any other character, then prints A, C, G, T and the total (the sequence length).
Bioinformatics/Base count.summary: All checks follow from the constant string's static bounds, for-loop indexes over its own range, and a guard before each counter increment, so no annotation is needed. The only care is the loop-carried counters and the fixed-width text formatting.

effects.explanation: Prints each superstring, its length and its A, C, G, T counts with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Overlap and substring scans index two bounded buffers with loop-carried offsets, so each access needs a guard on offset plus length against the buffer's stored length just before use.

Appending a non-overlapping tail to the candidate must be guarded by a check that the new length fits the 1200-character capacity, with a visible rejection otherwise (the true total of the examples is at most about 1170).
Length sums and the best-length minimum are held in subtypes bounded by the capacity, so additions stay within range once guarded.

Heap's iterative permutation uses a while loop with loop-carried index state, which is acceptable only in a procedure (no termination check) and with its swap indexes typed by the sequence-count subtype.

Exhaustive permutation of the roughly nine surviving strings in the last example is about 362880 candidates, which is a runtime cost rather than a proof obligation, and a subset DP would avoid it at the price of more indexed arithmetic.

Bioinformatics/Global alignment.approach: Each sequence is a record holding a Length and a Character array of capacity 100, with the four examples embedded as aggregates in an array of at most 13 sequences. Procedures remove duplicates and contained sequences using for loops with guarded comparison, then enumerate orderings with an iterative Heap's algorithm in a while loop, merging each ordering by a longest-overlap function into a 1200-character bounded buffer and keeping the shortest. A reporting procedure counts A, C, G and T with a case statement and prints the sequence, its length and the counts via 'Image.
Bioinformatics/Global alignment.summary: Every array access is bounded by declared capacities and guards on stored lengths, with no recursion, so checks follow from types and local guards, but several loop-carried offsets and the while-loop permutation need careful shaping.

effects.explanation: Prints the pretty-printed sequences, base counts and mutation log lines.

risks.explanation: The LCG state update is nonlinear loop-carried arithmetic, discharged by using a modular-type generator or a state range small enough that the multiply cannot overflow, with mod keeping it in range.

Insert and delete shift elements in a fixed-capacity array with a separate length, so each shift index needs a guard against capacity and the length, and insert is rejected visibly (or capacity sized at 210) when full.

The length counter changes by plus or minus one in a loop, so it must be kept within its subtype by guards (length greater than zero before delete, below capacity before insert) which are provable with guards just before use.
Random position is a mod of the generator output by current length, so it needs a guard that length is nonzero to avoid division by zero and out-of-range indexing.
All loops are for loops or while loops inside procedures, so no termination check arises.

Bioinformatics/Sequence mutation.approach: The sequence is a fixed-capacity array of a four-value Nucleotide enumeration (or Character) of capacity 256 plus a length, and a deterministic LCG with a fixed seed drives position, operation and base choices. Procedures handle generation, mutation (case on operation, with shifting for insert and delete guarded by length and capacity) and pretty printing in 60-wide rows with position prefix and per-base counts via a count array, with output through Put_Line and Put with 'Image text for numbers. Ten mutations run in a for loop and each logs its operation, position and base.
Bioinformatics/Sequence mutation.summary: Everything uses bounded arrays, for loops and procedures with guards before each shift or index, so no annotation is needed, but the LCG arithmetic and length-tracking shifts need careful shape, hence plausible.

effects.explanation: Prints the generated sequence, the four-letter subsequence and each match position with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The LCG step State * 48271 mod 2147483647 is discharged because State is declared in a subtype 0 .. 2147483646, so the product stays below 2**47 inside a 64-bit type even though State is loop-carried.
The scan uses for I in 1 .. 197 with Sequence (I .. I + 3) and Sequence (I + k) accesses, which are in range of the 200-element string from the loop bounds alone.
Output lines are built by concatenating fixed-width pieces with bounded Image text, so a static length bound must be visible, which needs the image of a bounded Natural range padded to a known width.

Bioinformatics/Subsequence.approach: A 200-character String is filled in a for loop from a deterministic Lehmer generator whose state is a ranged subtype, mapping State mod 4 to one of A, C, G, T via a constant 4-character lookup string; a 4-character pattern is generated the same way. A for loop over start positions 1 .. 197 compares the four characters at each offset with and then, and every match prints "Found at position: N..N+3" with Put_Line, printing a "none found" line when the count is zero.
Bioinformatics/Subsequence.summary: All checks follow from fixed array bounds, for-loop index ranges and a ranged generator state that bounds the one multiplication, so no invariant or variant is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the day count and the three biorhythm values with descriptions via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The day-number computation uses year, month and day subtypes with small ranges so every intermediate product and sum fits in Integer without any loop-carried value.
Each cycle position comes from mod 23, 28 or 33 into a subtype equal to the table's index range, so table lookups are statically in bounds.
The target date must not precede the birth date, so the program checks this just before subtracting and prints a specified rejection message otherwise.

Biorhythms.approach: Embed the birth and target dates as constants of ranged year, month and day subtypes, convert each to a day number with integer-only civil-calendar arithmetic, and reject the pair with a message if the target precedes the birth. Take the difference mod 23, 28 and 33, look up each sine value in a constant integer-percent table sized to the cycle, so no floating point or Sin is needed, and derive the trend text from the position with if statements. Build each output line by concatenating fixed text with 'Image of the day and the percent into a bounded buffer.
Biorhythms.summary: All arithmetic is integer over small declared ranges, mod results index tables of matching size, and there are no loops or recursion, so every check follows from types and one date-order guard. Floating point is avoided by tabulating the sine percentages, which keeps the output faithful to the task's example values.

effects.explanation: Prints the estimated group size for each of multiplicities 2 to 5 with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The linear congruential generator multiplies a state bounded by a declared 31-bit range by a literal constant, so the product stays under 2**63 and the check discharges from the type range.
Day indexes come from a mod 365 on a non-negative ranged value and group-size histogram indexes come from a for loop bounded by the pigeonhole limit 4*365+1, so both discharge from types.
Per-day counters and histogram tallies are loop-carried, so they are declared with ranges wide enough for trials times people and incremented under a guard just before use.

Birthday problem.approach: For each multiplicity m in 2..5, run a fixed number of trials; each trial resets a 365-entry day-count array, then adds people one at a time with a for loop up to 4*365+1 using a deterministic LCG for the birthday, exiting once any day count reaches m, and tallies the group size in a histogram array. A final for loop accumulates the histogram until the cumulative count passes half the trials and prints that size via 'Image concatenated into Put_Line; the simulation lives in procedures with the seed passed in out and a fixed documented trial count.
Birthday problem.summary: All data are fixed-size arrays and ranged integers with loops bounded by constants, so every index and overflow check follows from types and no loop needs a variant or invariant; the only care needed is declaring ranges on several loop-carried counters.

effects.explanation: The address to validate comes from the first command-line argument, defaulting to the task's example address.
The program prints whether the address is valid, or why it was rejected.

risks.explanation: The base58 decode keeps the carry in a 0..255 subtype and computes Temp := Carry + Byte * 58 (at most 15045) fresh in each inner iteration, so every bound follows from types without an invariant.
Assigning Temp / 256 to the carry and Temp mod 256 to a byte, and converting digest words to bytes with mod 256 on the modular type, discharge from the just-computed values.
The SHA-256 message schedule reads W(I-2), W(I-7), W(I-15) and W(I-16) for I in 16..63, which follows from the static loop bounds, and the argument is scanned with a for loop over its own 'Range.

Bitcoin/address validation.approach: Main reads the address with First_Or_Default, defaulting to the task's example. It rejects with a message any argument that is empty, longer than 35 characters or contains a non-base58 character, using a constant Character-indexed digit table. It then decodes the address into a 25-element byte array with a multiply-by-58 carry loop, rejecting it if a carry is left over. The program computes a single-block SHA-256 twice over arrays of Unsigned_32-style modular words, using constant round tables and for loops only. It reports the address valid only when byte 1 is zero and bytes 22..25 match the first four digest bytes.
Bitcoin/address validation.summary: Every check comes from byte and carry subtypes, from modular arithmetic that cannot overflow, or from static for-loop bounds. There are no while loops or recursion, so nothing needs a variant or invariant.

effects.explanation: The program prints the computed Base-58 address with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: In the Base-58 long division the remainder is held in a 0..57 subtype, so Rem * 256 + Byte stays at or below 14847 and its quotient by 58 fits a byte, which needs the solver to bound a division by a constant but no invariant.
Narrowing 32-bit words to bytes in the digest serialization uses mod 256 before conversion, so the result range follows from the mod operator.

The RIPEMD-160 word-selection and rotation tables are constant arrays whose element subtypes are 0..15 and 5..15, so indexing the 16-word block and the shift amounts discharge from the declared types.

Padding uses one 128-byte buffer and a message-length parameter of subtype 0..119, so the copy loops and the 64-bit length field have static bounds; the 65-, 32- and 21-byte inputs all lie in that range.

Bitcoin/public point to address.approach: The public point is embedded as a constant 65-byte array (prefix 4, then X and Y) of a mod-256 byte type. SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 run as procedures over a 32-bit modular word type, using rotations built from modular shifts, fixed padding into a 128-byte buffer and for loops over static block, round and schedule ranges. The 25-byte payload is version 0, then the RIPEMD-160 digest, then the first four bytes of a double SHA-256. It is Base-58 encoded by 34 passes of byte-wise long division into a fixed 34-character String indexed from the alphabet constant, then printed.
Bitcoin/public point to address.summary: Every hash operation uses modular arithmetic that cannot overflow, and every index comes from a for-loop range or a constant table with a ranged element type. The only non-routine check is the Base-58 division bound, which follows from the declared 0..57 remainder subtype. No annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: A text-art dump of the image is printed to check the fill, set and get results.

risks.explanation: Set_Pixel and Get_Pixel take X and Y as Positive and test them against the fixed Width and Height with an explicit guard that reports out-of-range coordinates, so every array access is provably in bounds.

The Image array is fully assigned by Fill (or an aggregate) before any read, which is easy for flow analysis on a whole-array aggregate but would be less routine if left uninitialised, so Allocate returns an all-black aggregate.

Bitmap.approach: The image is a fixed-capacity two-dimensional array (for example 16 by 8) of Pixel records whose R, G and B components are an integer subtype 0..255, with an Allocate function returning an all-black aggregate and a Fill procedure using nested for loops over the array's own ranges. Set_Pixel and Get_Pixel guard Positive coordinates against the fixed bounds (Set_Pixel returns a Boolean success flag; Get_Pixel returns black when out of range and the caller checks first), and Main fills white, sets and copies a few pixels, then prints a text-art rendering with Put and Put_Line. All control flow is straight-line code plus for loops, so there are no loop-carried values.
Bitmap.summary: Every check is an array index or a subtype range, discharged by for-loop bounds over the array's own ranges or by a guard just before the access, and nothing needs a loop invariant, recursion or heap, so the proofs should discharge routinely.

effects.explanation: The 16x16 text picture is printed row by row to standard output.

risks.explanation: Loop-carried error terms would only be known by type, so the program computes each step's minor-axis coordinate directly from the loop index with operands bounded by a 1..16 coordinate subtype, keeping products far below the Integer limits.

Converting the computed minor-axis coordinate back to the 1..16 subtype needs the prover to show it lies between the endpoints; an explicit clamp guard that cannot trigger for valid inputs, or interpolation bounded by DY, covers it.
The division by twice the major-axis delta is guarded by a test that the delta is nonzero, with a single-point case handled separately.
Pixel stores use Coord-typed indexes over the array's own ranges so they discharge by type.
All loops are for loops inside procedures, so no variant is needed.

Bitmap/Bresenham's line algorithm.approach: The program declares a Coord subtype 1..16 and a 16x16 Character array filled with a blank, and a Line procedure that picks the major axis, then loops with a for loop over the major-axis offset, computing the minor-axis coordinate with integer rounding arithmetic instead of a carried error term. It draws the four-line diamond from the task's sample into the grid and then builds and prints each row as a 16-character String with Put_Line.
Bitmap/Bresenham's line algorithm.summary: Integer Bresenham on a small fixed grid has all indexes and arithmetic bounded by 1..16 subtypes and for loops, so checks should discharge without annotations, though the nonlinear rounding division and subtype conversions need careful shaping. Silver today lacks arrays, loops, procedures, characters and integers, which are needed.

effects.explanation: The rendered 16x16 text-art bitmap is printed row by row to standard output.

risks.explanation: The Bezier numerator sums four products of at most 20^3 times a coordinate of at most 16, which fits easily in Integer, and the discharge relies on coordinates and the sample index being declared range subtypes.
Each interpolated pixel is computed with a fresh value per for-loop iteration (no loop-carried error term), and a guard that rejects out-of-bitmap points keeps the 2D array index in range.

Bitmap/B\u00e9zier curves/Cubic.approach: The program holds a 16x16 array of Character initialised to blanks, computes 21 curve points with integer-only Bernstein arithmetic (sample index 0..20, numerator divided by 8000) from embedded control points, and joins consecutive points with a Draw_Line procedure. Draw_Line steps a for loop over the longer axis and computes the other coordinate directly with rounded integer division from the loop index, so nothing is carried between iterations; the bitmap is then printed row by row through a String buffer.
Bitmap/B\u00e9zier curves/Cubic.summary: Every value is a function of a for-loop index over subtypes with small declared ranges, so all overflow, division and index checks follow from types and static bounds with no loop-carried state, though nonlinear integer arithmetic needs the ranges to be tight.

effects.explanation: The 16x16 text-art bitmap is printed row by row to standard output.

risks.explanation: The weighted sums (N-I)^2*P1 + 2*I*(N-I)*P2 + I^2*P3 are nonlinear but discharge because coordinates are subtypes of 1..16 and I is a for-loop index in 0..20, so the maximum is a few thousand.

Each computed pixel coordinate must be shown to lie in 1..16 after integer division, which the provers may not derive from the convex-combination structure, so an explicit visible range guard before each store (skipping out-of-range points) is used.
Line interpolation divides by the step count, which is guarded to be at least 1 immediately before the division, and the curve division is by the constant 400.
Line points are computed as x0 + (x1-x0)*k/steps with no loop-carried state (rather than Bresenham error accumulation) so each value is bounded by types and guards without an invariant.

Bitmap/B\u00e9zier curves/Quadratic.approach: The program holds a 16x16 Character array filled with spaces, computes 21 curve points with integer Bernstein weights (parameter I over N=20, divided by 400) into an array of coordinates, and joins consecutive points with a stateless interpolated line routine in a for loop that sets pixels to a mark character under range guards. It then copies each row into a fixed 16-character String by index and prints it with Put_Line.
Bitmap/B\u00e9zier curves/Quadratic.summary: Everything uses bounded integer ranges, for loops and fixed arrays, with no loop-carried accumulators, so checks follow from types and local guards, though the nonlinear integer arithmetic and the need for explicit pixel-range guards make careful shape necessary.

effects.explanation: The filled image is printed as text art, one row per line.

risks.explanation: Neighbour coordinates are computed only after explicit guards (X > 1, X < Width and so on) and stored in range-typed subtypes, so the array accesses discharge.
The stack top counter has a declared range equal to the capacity and is incremented only after a guard that the stack is not full, so the increment cannot overflow.
The worklist loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and each cell is pushed at most once because it is marked as filled when pushed.
Stack capacity equals the number of cells, so a push can never find the stack full, and a guarded visible reject path covers it regardless.

Bitmap/Flood fill.approach: The image is a fixed 2D Character array (for example 16x16) embedded as aggregate rows, with a start point and fill character as constants. An iterative four-neighbour flood fill uses an explicit stack array of coordinates and a while loop in a procedure, marking cells when they are pushed and checking each neighbour's bounds with guards before indexing. The result is printed row by row with Put_Line, building each row string in a fixed-length buffer.
Bitmap/Flood fill.summary: The iterative worklist fill needs only range-typed coordinates, boundary guards before each neighbour access and a stack sized to the cell count, so every check follows from types and guards and the while loop sits in a procedure. Discharge depends on careful program shape (a guarded stack top and loop-carried coordinates), but nothing needs an annotation.

effects.explanation: The thresholded black-and-white image is printed as text art, one row per line.

risks.explanation: Histogram counts and the running cumulative total are loop-carried, so the program guards each increment and addition against a declared count limit and rejects with a visible outcome rather than relying on an invariant.
Pixel values are of a ranged Luminance subtype so histogram indexing and for-loops over the array's own ranges discharge from types.
Each output row is built in a fixed-length String buffer filled by a for loop over the image width, so slice and assignment lengths are static.

Bitmap/Histogram.approach: An embedded small grayscale image is a constant two-dimensional array of a 0..255 Luminance subtype, and a procedure fills a Histogram array indexed by Luminance with counts guarded against exceeding a declared count limit. The median is found by a for loop over Luminance accumulating a cumulative count until it reaches half the pixel total, then each pixel is compared with the median and written as a '#' or ' ' character into a fixed-width row buffer that is printed with Put_Line.
Bitmap/Histogram.summary: Everything is fixed-size arrays and for loops whose indexes follow from declared ranges, with the only non-routine checks being the loop-carried counts, which explicit guards with a visible rejection outcome can bound without an annotation.

effects.explanation: The finished bitmap is printed row by row as text art with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried decision value F (and Y) only has its type range after the first iteration, so each update is preceded by a range guard on F with Reject on failure, and the 2*X+3 and 2*Y terms are recomputed from bounded X and Y rather than carried.

Pixel coordinates Center plus or minus X or Y are checked by a single up-front test that the circle lies inside the 16x16 image (Reject otherwise), but the prover must relate the loop-carried X and Y to the bounds, so each plot is also guarded by a coordinate range test before the array write.
Y := Y - 1 is guarded by Y > 0 and X := X + 1 by X < Y, so the subtype ranges of X and Y hold without an invariant.

Bitmap/Midpoint circle algorithm.approach: The program holds a 16x16 constrained 2D array of Character initialized to blanks, a Fill-equivalent loop, and a Circle procedure running the midpoint algorithm with small ranged-subtype X, Y and F inside a while loop in a procedure, plotting eight symmetric pixels through a guarded plot step. Center and Radius are embedded constants validated up front (circle must fit the image, otherwise Reject), and the image is printed by copying each row into a 16-character String and calling Put_Line.
Bitmap/Midpoint circle algorithm.summary: Every check follows from small declared ranges and guards just before each update or array write, with no annotation needed, but the loop-carried F, X and Y require careful guarding so the outlook is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The task requires delegating JPEG encoding to an external utility (cjpeg, ppmtojpeg or convert) by writing PPM data through a pipe to a spawned process.
The converter's JPEG output goes to a file or the process's standard output, so the program needs file output unless the pipe is read back.

Bitmap/PPM conversion through a pipe.summary: The task needs a bounded in-memory bitmap (an array of RGB pixels) written as PPM to a pipe feeding an external JPEG converter. That is a process and pipe effect Silver lacks today, but no fixed Oracle rule forbids it, so there is no conflict.

effects.explanation: Reads a binary P6 PPM file by name and writes the grayscale result as a PPM file.
The input file name is taken from the first command-line argument.
Reports success or the specific rejection reason for malformed or oversized input.
A rejected or unreadable file yields a nonzero exit status.

risks.explanation: Header number parsing accumulates digits in a loop, so each step is guarded by a digit-count and value limit that rejects oversized dimensions rather than clamping them.
Pixel indexes are computed from row, column and channel, so they are held in ranged subtypes bounded by the fixed maximum image size and for loops run over the array's own ranges.
Header scanning uses while loops, which is acceptable only because they live in procedures that get no termination check.
The header and pixel data are read through a library file operation that reports how many bytes were obtained, and a short read is rejected before any pixel is used.
The luminance weighted sum is nonlinear but bounded by 0..255 channel subtypes and a fixed divisor, so overflow checks discharge from types.

Bitmap/Read a PPM file.approach: The program takes a file name from the first argument, reads bytes through a bounded file-read operation into a fixed buffer, and parses the P6 magic, width, height and maxval in a procedure with a while loop that skips whitespace and comments and rejects anything malformed or beyond the fixed maximum dimensions. Pixels are stored in a two-dimensional array of RGB record components with 0..255 subtypes, converted to gray by an integer weighted sum, and written back as a P6 file built in a bounded output buffer. Every invalid or truncated input produces a specified message and nonzero exit status.
Bitmap/Read a PPM file.summary: All checks follow from ranged subtypes, fixed maximum dimensions and guards in the header parser, with no annotation needed, but the loop-carried parse state and computed pixel indexes require careful program shape and an admitted binary file-read and file-write library.

effects.explanation: The task requires running a delegate tool (cjpeg or ImageMagick convert) and reading its PPM output through a pipe.
The foreign image file is read by the delegate tool; PPM data may be read from the pipe or an intermediate file.
The input image file name is most naturally supplied as a command-line argument.

Bitmap/Read an image through a pipe.summary: The task needs a delegate process to convert a foreign image to PPM, whose output is parsed into a bounded bitmap array (header validation, bounded dimensions, pixel records). That is a process/pipe effect plus ordinary SPARK data handling, so no fixed Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: Writes a binary P6 PPM file through an admitted file-output operation with a specified failure outcome for unwritable paths.
Reports success or the rejection of a failed write with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The row buffer index 3*J+k is bounded because J is a for-loop index over the fixed image width and the buffer is sized three times the width.
Character'Val of a color channel is safe because channels are a 0..255 subtype and the conversion target covers it.
The header text is built in a bounded buffer whose capacity covers the fixed width, height and 255 digits, so concatenation lengths are statically bounded.

Bitmap/Write a PPM file.approach: The program declares a fixed-size pixel array (e.g. 16 by 16) of records with 0..255 Red, Green and Blue components, fills it with an embedded gradient via nested for loops, and builds the P6 header from the constant dimensions using 'Image. A procedure then writes the header followed by each row, packed into a fixed-size byte buffer indexed by the for-loop variables, through an admitted binary file-write operation, and reports or rejects on a write failure.
Bitmap/Write a PPM file.summary: All indexes and conversions follow from constant dimensions, for-loop ranges over the array's own bounds and 0..255 channel subtypes, so only the missing binary file-output library operation stands between Silver and this program.

effects.explanation: The packed 7-bit byte sequence is written to a named binary file and read back to test the bit reader.
The program reports whether the decompressed text matches the original and may print the packed bytes in hexadecimal.

risks.explanation: The bit accumulator is a Byte modular type or an Integer range 0..255 updated with a shift and an OR, so wraparound is defined and the range subtype for the used-bit count 0..8 is guarded by a flush-when-full test before each shift.
Loop-carried output and input positions are indexes into fixed-capacity byte arrays and each is guarded by a capacity check just before use, with overflow of capacity giving a visible failure result.

Extracting a bit from a byte via division by a power of two and conversion to a 0..1 subtype is safe because the byte type bounds the quotient, and a read past end of data returns a visible failure flag.
Only for loops over fixed ranges are used in functions and any while loop (for example reading until end of file) lives in a procedure, so no variant is needed.

Bitwise IO.approach: A bit writer and bit reader are records holding a fixed-capacity Byte array, a byte position, and a bit-count subtype 0..8, with procedures Write_Bit, Flush (zero-padding the last byte), and Read_Bit that returns an out success flag. The test embeds a short ASCII string, rejects any character with code above 127, writes each character as 7 bits MSB first, flushes, writes the bytes to a file, reads them back through the reader, and compares to the original. Each position and count update is preceded by an explicit capacity or end-of-data guard that leads to a printed failure outcome.
Bitwise IO.summary: All arithmetic is on small bounded byte and bit-count types with guards before each increment, and the loops are for loops or procedure while loops, so checks should discharge without annotations; the main uncertainty is the library file read/write operations that Silver does not yet have.

effects.explanation: Each operation's result is printed with Put_Line.

Bitwise operations.approach: Declare 8-bit modular constants A, B and a shift amount N as embedded example data, and print AND, OR, XOR, NOT, shifts and rotates using the standard Interfaces operations with 'Image concatenated into Put_Line strings. An if on N being below 8 guards the shift and rotate section, with a printed rejection message otherwise; no loops are needed.
Bitwise operations.summary: Modular operations never raise overflow checks and the shift amount is guarded, so every check is straight-line and follows from types; the only new needs are modular types, 'Image and bounded text building.

effects.explanation: Prints the beam result (H, R or the exit number) for each of the 32 edge entry points.

risks.explanation: The beam position and direction are loop-carried values updated in a while loop, so each step is guarded by an explicit test that the next cell is within the 0..9 border box before the position subtype is assigned.
Atom lookups go through a function that returns False for coordinates outside 1..8 before indexing the 8 x 8 Boolean array, so no index check depends on loop-carried facts.
The beam-tracing loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed (the beam always exits in the real game).
The exit-numbering counter is a small ranged integer incremented at most once per entry point, bounded by a guard against its subtype maximum.

Black box.approach: Embed the four atoms of a fixed 8 x 8 board in a Boolean array and trace a beam from each of the 32 edge entry points with a while loop inside a procedure, keeping position and direction in small ranged subtypes. Each step applies the hit, reflection and deflection rules via bounds-checked Atom_At lookups, then records H, R or a pair exit number in a fixed result array that is printed with Put_Line using scalar image and bounded concatenation. The interactive guessing, scoring and board drawing are replaced by a deterministic non-interactive run that reports every entry's outcome.
Black box.summary: All indexes and positions are bounded by subtypes and guards placed before each step, and the only loop carrying state is a while loop inside a procedure, so no annotation is needed, though the loop-carried beam state needs careful guard placement.

effects.explanation: The strategy tables, per-hand results and the yearly win/loss summary are printed as text lines.

risks.explanation: Win and loss probabilities are accumulated through loops, so they use a wide ranged Long_Float subtype and divide only after guarding that the remaining card total is positive, so no float overflow or range check can fail.
The explicit depth-first stack replacing recursion needs a guard before every push and pop on the stack index, and a full stack must give a specified rejection rather than a silent change of result.
Money totals over 365 days of 50 hands, and the generator state, are held in ranged integers or modular types sized well within 64 bits so the arithmetic is bounded by the types.
Enumeration and simulation loops live in procedures (no termination check) and the only functions use for loops over fixed ranges.
Every probability division by the cards remaining is guarded by a test that the count is nonzero, which holds for a single deck since at most 11 cards are drawn from 52.

Blackjack strategy.approach: Cards are ranks 1..10 held as a 10-element array of remaining counts; hand totals, soft flags and pair status are small ranged integers, and dealer and player continuations are enumerated by an iterative depth-first search over an explicit bounded stack in procedures, accumulating exact-as-floating win, lose and push probabilities per dealer upcard. The hard, soft and pair tables are stored in 2D arrays of an action enumeration chosen by comparing expected values against a double threshold, printed as text lines, and then a deterministic LCG deals 50 hands for each of 365 days using the table to track daily and yearly totals, biggest win and biggest loss.
Blackjack strategy.summary: Everything can be bounded by types (single deck, at most a handful of cards per hand, 365*50 hands) and the recursion is replaced by an explicit stack in procedures, but float probability accumulation, the stack-index guards and split and double rule handling make the proof shape demanding though annotation-free.

effects.explanation: Prints membership results for sample words and the byte sizes of the filter versus a hash set.

risks.explanation: The hash step h*31+c is computed on a hash subtype bounded below 2**20 and a Character position of at most 255, so the product fits in Integer and is reduced with mod before storing.
