Each bit index is the result of mod by the fixed bit count, so it is statically within the bit array's range.
The k-th probe index (h1 + k*h2) mod M uses h1 and h2 bounded below 2**20 and k at most 7, so the sum stays in range before the mod.

Bloom filter.approach: The filter is a fixed-capacity array of 8192 Boolean bits with a deterministic polynomial hash over the characters of each embedded dictionary word, split into two ranged hashes and combined by double hashing for K=4 probes via a for loop. Add is a procedure and Contains a function over a String parameter indexed by its own 'Range, and Main adds an embedded word list, tests one present and one absent word, then prints the filter size in bytes against the hash-set size (count times 4 bytes plus table overhead) using Integer'Image.
Bloom filter.summary: Every operation is a bounded for loop over ranged integers with mod reduction, so all checks follow from types and static bounds with no unbounded loop-carried value, and no annotation is needed. The memory comparison is computed arithmetic on declared sizes, which avoids files, floats and system memory queries.

effects.explanation: Prints the matching size and matched pairs for the embedded example graph.

risks.explanation: The BFS queue loop, the LCA parent-walk loops and the path-flip loop are while loops, so they live in procedures (the LCA walks return their result through an out parameter) and procedures get no termination check.

Vertex ids and -1 sentinels are carried through match, parent and base arrays in loops, so every array read of a loop-carried value needs an explicit guard against the no-vertex sentinel (a Vertex_Or_None subtype with a branch on None), with the not-found case rejected visibly.
The circular queue head, tail and count are loop-carried, so they are kept in subtypes with a capacity of N*N and updated with explicit wrap guards instead of mod on unbounded values.
Flattened adjacency indexing v*N+i and the matching-size counter stay within small declared ranges, so the arithmetic is bounded by types with fixed N.

Blossom algorithm.approach: The program embeds the 5-cycle example (and possibly one more graph) as a constant edge array, builds a fixed-capacity N-by-N adjacency matrix, and runs Edmonds' BFS blossom search with array-based match, parent, base, used and blossom-flag tables plus a circular queue. All loops that cannot be for loops are while loops inside procedures, vertex indices use a ranged subtype with an explicit none value, and every parent or match dereference is guarded by a test for the none value. It then prints the matching size and the matched pairs with Put_Line.
Blossom algorithm.summary: Every check follows from fixed vertex bounds, ranged subtypes and sentinel guards, and the loops are while loops in procedures, so no annotation is needed; the plausible rating reflects the many loop-carried indices that each need a guard just before use.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 50 Blum integers, the selected Nth values and the last-digit percentages as text.

risks.explanation: Candidate, divisor and counter variables are declared with ranged subtypes (candidate bounded by a fixed 10,000,000 limit, divisor by 4000), and every increment is preceded by a guard, so D*D and the percentage product count*100000 stay within Integer.
The 50-entry result array and 4-entry digit-count array are indexed only after a guard on the running count or by a digit mapping from N mod 10 that the case statement confines to 1, 3, 7 or 9.
The trial-division while loop lives in a procedure (no termination check) and also exits when D exceeds the fixed bound, while the outer scan is a for loop.

If the fixed search limit is reached before 400,000 Blum integers are found, the program must print a specified failure message rather than silently truncating, which an explicit guard on the count provides.

Blum integer.approach: The program scans candidates N in a for loop up to a fixed limit, and a procedure with a bounded while loop finds the smallest prime factor by trial division with a ranged divisor. It accepts N when the smallest factor P and the cofactor Q differ, both are 3 mod 4, and Q has no smaller divisor (checked by a second bounded trial-division procedure), then records the first 50 in an array, prints the requested Nth values, and tallies final digits in a 4-element array. Percentages are computed in integer arithmetic as count*100000/400000 and printed with three decimals built into a bounded string.
Blum integer.summary: Everything is integer arithmetic over ranged subtypes with fixed-size arrays and loops whose bounds are guarded, so every check follows from types and guards without annotations; the only demands are a modest set of new surface features and explicit handling when the search limit is exceeded.

effects.explanation: The textual simulation prints each frame of the framed board with walls and boids to standard output.

risks.explanation: Neighbour cells (x+1, y-1, y+1) are indexed only after explicit guards that the coordinates lie inside the declared 16x86 grid, with the frame cells also being walls so moves never leave the board.
Frame counters and coordinates are subtypes bounded by the grid size and a fixed frame count, so loop-carried values stay in type range without invariants.
All iteration is for loops or while loops inside procedures with a fixed frame count, so no function needs a variant.

Boids.approach: The program stores the cave as a constant 16x86 Character grid of walls and free cells and keeps up to 18 boids as bounded x/y coordinate arrays, all initialised from embedded data. For a fixed number of frames a procedure moves each boid right if the target cell is inside the grid, not a wall and not occupied, otherwise tries up or down with the same guards, and another procedure prints the framed board using a bounded row buffer with Put_Line. Boids that cannot move simply stay in place, which is a specified visible outcome.
Boids.summary: The simple rule-based textual boids simulation uses only bounded integer coordinates, a fixed grid and for loops with explicit bounds guards before each array access, so every check follows from types and guards. The optional vector-based flocking with floating point is left out, and the task accepts the textual simulation.

effects.explanation: The program prints lines showing the Boolean values and the results of conditionals.

Boolean values.approach: Declare Boolean constants and variables set to True and False, then use if statements on them and on comparison results to print which branch ran with Put_Line. Use the Boolean literal names directly as text, and use a plain if statement to show that only Boolean-typed expressions are valid conditions, so no other object stands for true or false. There are no loops, arrays or arithmetic.
Boolean values.summary: The program only needs Boolean declarations, if statements and string output, so every check is trivial and no loop or arithmetic is involved.

effects.explanation: Prints each MST edge with its weight and the total MST weight.

risks.explanation: Vertex and edge indexes are subtypes of fixed ranges (for example Vertex range 0..3), so array accesses follow from types and for-loop ranges over the arrays' own bounds.

Edge weights are a small range subtype and the total is accumulated in a loop, so the accumulator's type must be wide enough (for example a range of 0..10_000_000 with weights capped at 1000 and at most 16 edges), or a guard is needed.
The outer stage loop is a while loop kept in a procedure and is replaced by a for loop over at most the vertex count, with each stage merging at least one tree or exiting, so no variant is needed.

Find with path compression is recursive, so the program uses an iterative find in a procedure with a for loop bounded by the vertex count and no path compression, which still discharges without a variant.
Facts like 'num_trees stays at least 1' are not known to the prover after loop iteration, so the tree counter must be a range subtype (1..V) with a guard before each decrement.

Bor\u016fvka algorithm.approach: Embed the 4-vertex, 5-edge example graph as a constant array of edge records with subtype-ranged vertex and weight fields, and keep a parent array of Vertex values with an iterative, for-loop-bounded find in a procedure. Run at most V stages in a for loop, each stage scanning edges to record the cheapest edge per component in arrays with a sentinel flag, then merge components with guards, accumulating the weight in a wide ranged integer. Print each included edge and the final weight using Image-based string building and Put_Line.
Bor\u016fvka algorithm.summary: All indexes and values come from small declared subtypes and for-loops over fixed bounds, so checks mostly follow from types, but the loop-carried parent links, counters and weight accumulator need careful subtype and guard shaping. No annotations are required once recursion and while loops are replaced by bounded for loops.

effects.explanation: Prints the 15 transformed values for each of the six sequences as text lines.

risks.explanation: Each triangle sum T(k,n-1)+T(k-1,k-n) is a loop-carried value, so the program stores values in a bounded subtype (about 10**15) and guards each addition with a visible reject when the sum would exceed the bound, which keeps the true results (max about 3e11) in range.
The index k-n is within 0..k-1 because the for loops run n in 1..k and k in 1..14 over the array's own bounds, which provers discharge from the loop ranges.
Generating factorial inputs by multiplication needs a guard before each product (or the factorial sequence is embedded as constants) so that the loop-carried accumulator stays within the subtype.
Each output line is built in a fixed-size buffer sized for 15 numbers of up to 20 characters, with an explicit guard before each append.

Boustrophedon transform.approach: Keep a 15-element sequence array of a bounded integer subtype and a 15x15 triangle array, and a procedure fills T(k,0)=a(k) then for k in 1..14 and n in 1..k sets T(k,n) from the recurrence after a bound guard, with b(n)=T(n,n). The six sequences (ones, all 1s, alternating, primes, Fibonacci, factorials) are built by short for loops or embedded as constant aggregates, and each result is formatted with 'Image into a bounded line buffer and printed with Put_Line. The 1000-digit stretch is omitted as optional.
Boustrophedon transform.summary: Every check is a bounded-range array index or a guarded addition in for loops, so nothing needs an annotation, but the loop-carried triangle sums depend on careful bound guards and the 2D array and text formatting are beyond today's Silver.

effects.explanation: The program prints a header, a separator and 33 table rows to standard output.

risks.explanation: Writing the expanded name into a fixed 32-character buffer needs a guard that the next append fits, and the abbreviations are 4 characters expanding to at most 18, so a length guard before each append discharges it.
Computing the point index from hundredths of a degree uses division and mod on an integer bounded by the declared heading range, so the result stays within 0..32 and mod 32 gives a valid array index.
Heading arithmetic in hundredths (at most 35999 times 2 plus 1125) is tiny against Integer, so the nonlinear products are bounded by the heading subtype.

Box the compass.approach: Headings are held as integer hundredths of a degree (i*1125 plus or minus 562 by i mod 3) in a ranged subtype, so no floating point is needed; the point index is (2*h+1125)/2250 mod 32, which rounds exactly as the task's 5.62/5.63 boundaries need. A constant array of 32 four-character abbreviations is expanded by a for loop over its characters into a bounded buffer with a length guard before each append, and each row is printed with Put, a hand-formatted decimal angle (whole part and two-digit fraction from / and mod) and the 'Image of the index.
Box the compass.summary: Every value is a small bounded integer and every loop is a for loop over fixed ranges, so all checks follow from subtype ranges and a few length guards; the only care needed is the string-building buffer and fixed-width number formatting.

effects.explanation: Prints needle, haystack and a marker line for each search case.

risks.explanation: The shift-table lookup indexes by Character'Pos into a 256-entry array, which is safe by type, and the haystack index start+j is guarded by start + needle length <= haystack length before each comparison.
Start position and shift values are loop-carried, so they are held in bounded subtypes and each advance is guarded against the haystack length before the add.
The scanning while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and each iteration advances start by at least one.

Boyer-Moore string search.approach: Embed the texts and needles as String constants and write one procedure that builds a bad-character shift table (array of 256 bounded shifts) from the needle, then scans the haystack right-to-left at each alignment with a while loop and guarded indexes. Matches are recorded in a fixed-length marker String of the haystack's length, set to '^' over each match, and the procedure prints the needle, haystack and marker line, or a not-found line when there is no match.
Boyer-Moore string search.summary: Every index and shift is bounded by array types and explicit guards before use, and the loops sit in procedures, so no annotation is needed, though loop-carried positions need careful bounded subtypes.

effects.explanation: Each expanded string is written to standard output, one per line, using Put_Line (and Put for quoting or markers if wanted).

risks.explanation: Scan positions, comma-position tables and stack slots are loop-carried, so each access is guarded by an explicit bound test (or the table is sized to the maximum string length) just before use.
Building prefix & option & suffix into a bounded buffer is preceded by an explicit check that the total fits the capacity, otherwise the input is rejected with a visible message.
Brace depth and counters are ranged subtypes bounded by the maximum input length, with guards before each increment so the loop-carried values cannot exceed their ranges.
The expansion worklist is a fixed-capacity array of bounded strings with an explicit full check, so exponential blow-up yields a specified rejection instead of unbounded growth.
Recursion is replaced by a worklist loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed.

The paired-brace and innermost-comma rules (escapes, unmatched braces, nearest-opener association) require careful scanning code whose correctness is not proved but whose run-time safety follows from guarded indexes.

Brace expansion.approach: Represent a string as a record holding a fixed-capacity Character array and a ranged length, and keep a fixed-capacity worklist array of such records. A procedure scans the top item with an escape flag and depth counter to find the outermost brace pair with at least one comma, builds one new item per branch as prefix, branch and suffix (checking capacity first), and pushes them in reverse order so output order is preserved, while items with no alternation are printed; the four test inputs are embedded and run in sequence.
Brace expansion.summary: The task needs only bounded string buffers, array scanning and a worklist loop in a procedure, so every check follows from ranged types and explicit capacity guards with overflow of capacity rejected visibly, but the brace and comma association logic makes the program shape delicate.

effects.explanation: Prints each test pattern followed by its indented expansions.

risks.explanation: Scanning for braces, dots and digits uses for loops over the pattern's own range with a guard before every look-ahead character access, and output buffers are written only after a capacity guard.
Numeric endpoints are parsed digit by digit with a cap on digit count (for example at most 6 digits) and rejected otherwise, so the stepping accumulator stays inside a declared Integer range.
Stepping loops live in procedures (no termination check), and the step is made positive by rejecting a zero increment before the loop.

Every expansion is appended to a fixed-capacity bounded buffer with an explicit check that the output length and the product of counts for multiple ranges fit, with a specified rejection or literal outcome if not.
Zero-padded formatting computes digits into a fixed-width buffer with width bounded by the parsed digit limit, so character positions stay in range.

Brace expansion using ranges.approach: The program embeds the ten test patterns as String constants in a fixed table and, for each one, scans bounded Character data to find the first complete brace pair, validates the contents as numeric or single-character ranges with an optional increment, and treats anything else as literal text. Counts and endpoints are held in bounded integers with digit-count caps, expansions are generated by a stepping loop into fixed-capacity line buffers (handling the minus-sign reversal and zero-padding), and several ranges are handled by iterating a nested index over the per-range counts rather than recursing. Emoji endpoints are treated as a bounded run of bytes compared as a unit, with each range's multi-byte endpoints expanded through a small fixed byte-sequence table, and all output goes through Put_Line.
Brace expansion using ranges.summary: Everything is bounded string scanning and integer stepping that guards and declared limits can cover, but the many loop-carried indexes and the capacity and overflow guards make the shape delicate, with no need for annotations.

effects.explanation: Prints three lines of 20 numbers each.

risks.explanation: The digit-peeling loop and trial-division prime test are while loops so they live in procedures (or become for loops over a bounded digit count), since a function would need a variant.
Numbers are held in a declared range subtype (e.g. 1 .. 10000) and the divisor loop variable is bounded by for-loops, so d*d and n+2 are guarded by range checks before use.
The search for the next candidate is bounded by a fixed maximum (the 20th prime Brazilian is 757) and exits with a visible reject if the bound is reached, so counters and n+1 stay in type range.
Result storage is a fixed array of 20 entries indexed by a counter guarded with Count < 20 before each store.

Brazilian numbers.approach: Use a bounded subtype for candidates, procedures Same_Digits and Is_Brazilian returning Boolean via out parameters, with for loops over bases 2 .. N-2 and a for loop over a fixed maximum digit count to peel digits by mod and /. Three passes (all, odd, prime) each scan candidates upward under a fixed upper bound, printing numbers via 'Image into bounded buffers with Put_Line, with primality tested by for-loop trial division up to a fixed small bound.
Brazilian numbers.summary: All loops are bounded by declared ranges and every arithmetic value fits a small range subtype, so proofs should discharge with careful guards and without any invariants, provided digit-peeling and trial division are written as for loops or in procedures.

effects.explanation: Prints the recovered password with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Break OO privacy.approach: A package declares a private record type holding a fixed-length 8-character String password with a default value, and a child package of it exposes a non-dispatching function returning that password through the parent's private view. Main declares an object, calls the child function, and prints the result inside quotes using bounded concatenation. There are no loops, no tagged types, no unchecked conversion and no input.
Break OO privacy.summary: The child-package "friend" mechanism is ordinary Ada that bypasses privacy without reflection or unchecked conversion, and every check is a static fixed-length String operation, so proofs discharge trivially.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 100 brilliant numbers and the order-of-magnitude table to standard output.

risks.explanation: The brilliant-number counter and the products i*j in the sieve are bounded by a capped counter type with a guard before each increment and by the loop ranges i<=100 and j<=10_000/i, so no overflow check needs a loop invariant.
The divisor p comes from a for-loop index starting at 2 and the found-factor variable is only used for n/p behind a guard p /= 0, so the division check follows from the guard.
The sieve index q is checked to be at most 10_000 by the digit-count test before use as an array index, so the index check follows from a guard just before the lookup.

Brilliant numbers.approach: Embed a sieve of primes up to 10_000 as a Boolean array built with nested for loops (i in 2..100, j in 2..10_000/i), then a single for loop over n in 4..1_100_000 in a procedure that scans a candidate factor p in 2..1_010 for the smallest divisor, requiring the cofactor q=n/p to be a sieve-prime below 10_000 with the same digit count as p (digit counts via comparison against powers of ten). Each brilliant number is counted behind a guard on a capped Natural counter; the first 100 are printed six per line and the first at or above each of 10^1..10^6 is printed with its position using scalar images and unterminated Put.
Brilliant numbers.summary: All arithmetic stays within small declared ranges (n up to about 1.1 million, divisors up to about 1,010, a sieve to 10,000) using only for loops and guards in procedures, so every check follows from types and guards and no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: Each maximal clique is printed as a comma-separated line of vertex letters via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The explicit stack depth is a loop-carried value, so every push is guarded by depth < capacity (capacity = vertex count + 1) with a visible Reject outcome, since without an invariant the prover cannot derive that depth stays below the bound.
Pivot degree counts, clique sizes and output-buffer positions are carried through loops, so they use small ranged subtypes or are guarded before each increment.
The recursion is replaced by a while loop in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the inner loops are for loops over the fixed vertex range.
Recursive Bron-Kerbosch is avoided entirely by an explicit fixed-size stack of R, P, X Boolean-array sets, so no input-dependent stack depth exists.
Output lines and the stored clique list use fixed-capacity buffers sized for the required output, with a guard before each append and a visible rejection if capacity were exceeded.

Bron\u2013Kerbosch algorithm.approach: The graph is a constant edge list for vertices a to f embedded in the program and loaded into a symmetric Boolean adjacency matrix indexed by a small vertex subtype, with R, P and X as Boolean arrays held in a fixed-depth explicit stack frame array. A while loop in a procedure walks the stack: at each frame it picks the max-degree pivot from P union X by for loops, takes the next candidate in P not adjacent to the pivot, pushes the child frame with intersected sets, and on pop moves the vertex from P to X; maximal cliques of size over two are stored in a bounded list in index order, then printed in sorted order as comma-separated characters.
Bron\u2013Kerbosch algorithm.summary: Every check follows from small ranged vertex indexes, for loops over fixed ranges and a guarded explicit stack that replaces recursion, but the loop-carried depth and counters need careful guard placement rather than being routine.

effects.explanation: The tree is drawn as text art on standard output, which meets the task without a display.

risks.explanation: The generator state is a modular type (for example a linear congruential generator in a 32-bit modular type), so wraparound is defined and a range-reduction mod gives a result inside the field bounds by its type.

Walker coordinates are subtypes of the field range and a guard that keeps the walker off the border runs just before each neighbour access and each step, so the +1 and -1 index and range checks discharge.

All loops live in procedures, which get no termination check, and the walk is bounded by a for-loop step budget per particle so the program also finishes; a particle that exhausts its budget is discarded in a specified way.

Each particle walk reassigns the coordinates in a loop, so the border guard is re-tested every iteration and the range check on the stepped coordinate relies on that guard rather than on an invariant.

Brownian tree.approach: A constrained 2D Boolean array (for example 40 by 24) holds the tree, with a fixed seed in the centre and a modular-type LCG supplying the coordinates and directions. A for loop over a fixed particle count launches each particle at a pseudo-random cell; a bounded walk loop checks the border, stops when a neighbour is set, and otherwise steps by a case on a random direction. The field is then printed as rows of characters built in a fixed-length string with Put_Line.
Brownian tree.summary: Every index and range check follows from the field's subtypes and a border guard placed before each neighbour access and step, and no loop-carried fact needs an invariant, but the walk and generator arithmetic need careful shaping. It is plausible rather than likely because of the nested loop-carried coordinates and the modular arithmetic.

effects.explanation: The raw and simplified regular expressions are printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: Node-pool allocation, explicit-stack pushes and output-buffer writes are each guarded by a capacity test that rejects with a visible message instead of overrunning.
The raw expression expands to a large tree string, so the output buffer is sized for it and every append is guarded by remaining capacity with a specified overflow outcome.
Printing and simplification are iterative while loops in procedures (no termination check), using an explicit stack and a bottom-up pass over children-before-parent node indices instead of recursion.
Loop-carried counters (node count, stack top, output position) are subtypes bounded by the pool and buffer capacities, with a guard before each increment.

The fixpoint repetition of simplification is replaced by a fixed bounded number of for-loop passes with hash-consed node ids so equality is an index comparison, which must still produce the same final result as the task's fixpoint.

Brzozowski algebraic method.approach: Expressions live in a fixed-capacity node pool (arrays of kind, left, right and character) where children always have lower indices, with the 3x3 example matrix and final-state array embedded; the Brzozowski loop uses for loops over the matrix indices that allocate Star, Concat and Union nodes with capacity guards. Simplification is a bottom-up for-loop pass over node indices applying the identity, zero, star and duplicate-union rules using canonical ids for equality, and printing is a while-loop procedure with an explicit stack that appends into a bounded String buffer before Put_Line.
Brzozowski algebraic method.summary: Everything reduces to bounded arrays, for loops and explicit-stack while loops in procedures with capacity guards, so no annotation is needed, but many loop-carried indices and buffer positions require careful guarding.

effects.explanation: Prompts, rejection messages and bull/cow scores are printed to standard output.
Each guess is read as a line from standard input, with a specified outcome at end of input.

risks.explanation: The bull and cow counters are loop-carried in nested loops, so each increment sits behind a guard against the counter's declared maximum, or the counts are derived from per-position Boolean flags, since no invariant can be written.
The deterministic generator keeps its state in a ranged subtype and uses a multiply-add followed by mod, with constants chosen so the product fits in 64 bits.
The secret digit is picked by state mod remaining-size plus one, which lies within the 1..9 digit array, and removal is done by a for-loop shifting elements over the array's own range.
The guess loop is a while loop inside a procedure, so no termination check applies, and end of input must exit the loop with a specified outcome.
The input line must be checked to have length exactly 4 before indexing, with the line read into a bounded buffer whose overlong input is rejected as malformed.

Bulls and cows.approach: Fixed-seed linear congruential generator over a ranged state picks four distinct digits from a 9-element array by removing each chosen digit, stored in a 1..4 array of digit values. A while loop in the Main procedure reads a line through an admitted stdin operation, rejects it with a message unless it has length 4, all characters are in '1'..'9' and no two are equal, then counts bulls and cows with nested for loops over 1..4 and prints the score or a win message.
Bulls and cows.summary: All indexing, arithmetic and validation follow from small constant ranges and guards placed just before use, and the only loop-carried counters are small and guardable, so no annotation is needed; the program does depend on a stdin-line operation with a defined end-of-input outcome and on bounded-buffer string handling that Silver lacks today.

effects.explanation: Prints the introduction, each guess, prompts, and the final answer or give-up message.
Reads the user's bulls and cows score lines after each guess.
Signals rejection of malformed or inconsistent score input with a specified failure status.

risks.explanation: Bull, cow and candidate counters are loop-carried so the prover knows only their subtype range; each increment is preceded by a guard against the subtype maximum that can never trigger on real data.
The pool is a fixed array of 3024 candidates filled by four nested digit for-loops with distinctness checks, and the fill counter is guarded against capacity before each store.
The guess loop is a while loop in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and is also bounded by at most 3024 guesses.
Parsing the typed bulls and cows into 0..4 digits requires explicit validation of length and character range, with invalid or inconsistent input (bulls+cows above 4) rejected visibly.

Bulls and cows/Player.approach: Candidates are 3024 four-digit records with distinct digits 1..9 held in a fixed array with an alive flag, generated by nested for loops. A while loop in a procedure picks the first alive candidate (deterministic rather than random), prints it, reads a two-character bulls and cows line from stdin, validates it, and prunes candidates whose score against the guess differs via nested for loops. It ends on 4 bulls, on a single candidate remaining, or with a give-up message when none remain.
Bulls and cows/Player.summary: All checks follow from fixed array bounds, small ranged subtypes and guards before each increment or parse, with no annotation required, but many loop-carried counters need careful guarding and stdin parsing support is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints each embedded test string, its transform and the recovered original, plus a rejection message for input containing the STX or ETX markers.

risks.explanation: Rotation indexing (start + k) mod n is discharged by a ranged subtype for n with n at least 1 and by mod yielding a value below n, and each test string is checked against the buffer capacity before use.
All counters and rotation offsets are subtypes capped at the small buffer capacity, so sums such as start + k stay within Integer.
The inverse follows the rank-permutation chain for exactly n steps in a for loop, and every stored index is of a range subtype bounded by the buffer length, so no loop invariant is needed.
Output strings are assembled in a fixed-capacity buffer with explicit length guards, and over-long or marker-containing input is rejected with a visible message rather than truncated.

Burrows\u2013Wheeler transform.approach: Each test string is copied into a bounded Character buffer of capacity 64 with a length, after being checked for STX or ETX (rejected with a printed message), and then wrapped as STX, text, ETX. A rotation-start index array is sorted with a bounded bubble sort of for loops whose comparison function scans two rotations with (i+k) mod n indexing, and the last characters of the sorted rotations form the output. The inverse builds a stable rank mapping from the transformed buffer by counting, walks it for n steps in a for loop to rebuild the text, and prints it.
Burrows\u2013Wheeler transform.summary: Everything is bounded for loops over fixed-capacity arrays with range-subtype indices and mod-based wraparound, so checks follow from types and guards, though the sort comparison and inverse mapping need careful shaping. No annotations are required, and the nested loops carry no facts beyond types.

effects.explanation: Prints the four intersection points' (x,y) coordinates.

risks.explanation: Polynomial evaluation of the curve difference must not overflow or produce infinities, discharged by declaring x and y as a bounded float subtype (about -100.0 to 100.0) so every intermediate product stays within range.
The bisection midpoint and the stored root must stay inside the declared subtype, which holds because the midpoint of two in-range bounds is in range given the bounded subtype.
Bisection uses a for loop over a fixed iteration count inside a procedure, so no variant is needed.
Float-to-text formatting of the coordinates must come from an admitted library operation, since 'Image on floats is not yet available.

B\u00e9zier curves/Intersections.approach: Reduce the two parabolas analytically to y = 5(1-x^2) and x = 2 - 20s + 20s^2 with s = (y-1)/2, giving a quartic residual f(x) in x alone. Search x in [-1,2] with a fixed table of sub-intervals (sampled by a for loop) to find sign changes, then refine each by a fixed-count (e.g. 60) bisection for loop in a procedure on a bounded float subtype, storing the roots in a 4-element array and printing x and y for each. If the number of sign changes found is not four, print a specified failure message.
B\u00e9zier curves/Intersections.summary: Everything is a fixed-count for loop over bounded floats with no loop-carried values beyond bracket endpoints whose subtype range keeps arithmetic safe, so it should prove without annotations, but floating-point range bounding and float output make it need careful shaping.

effects.explanation: Prints the plaintext, ciphertext and decrypted text with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Character'Val needs its argument in 0..255, which follows because (x mod 26) + 65 lies in 65..90 or (x mod 26) + 97 lies in 97..122.
Character'Pos values are at most 255 and the key is a constant 1..25, so the sum before mod cannot overflow Integer.

Caesar cipher.approach: A constant message String and a constant Key (a subtype range 1..25) are embedded; a pure function Shift(C, K) uses case or if on 'A'..'Z' and 'a'..'z' to apply ((Pos(C) - Pos(Base) + K) mod 26) + Pos(Base) and leaves other characters unchanged. Two fixed-length String variables of the message's length are filled by for loops over their own index range, encrypting with Key and decrypting with 26 - Key, and the three results are printed with Put_Line and concatenation.
Caesar cipher.summary: Every check is an index over the loop's own range or a Character'Val/mod computation bounded by constant types, with no loop-carried values, recursion or reading of input, so proofs should discharge routinely.

effects.explanation: The program prints the computed value of e as a line of text.

risks.explanation: The scaled sum is loop-carried, so a guard against a declared bound just before each addition is needed to make the add and the range check provable.
The term shrinks each iteration but the prover only knows its subtype range, so division by the positive loop index is assigned back into the same subtype, which is routine.

Digit extraction into a fixed 15-character buffer uses a for loop over the buffer's own range with the remainder converted to a character via 'Val on a 0..9 value, which discharges from the mod bound.

Calculating the value of e.approach: Compute e as a fixed-point integer scaled by 10**15 using the series sum of 1/k!, with a term variable divided by the for-loop index k (1..20) and added to a sum guarded by a declared bound. Then split the sum into integer part and 15 fraction digits, filling a fixed-length String buffer with a for loop using mod and div by 10, and print "e = " plus the digits via Put_Line concatenation. No floating point, recursion or while loops are used.
Calculating the value of e.summary: Integer fixed-point series over a bounded for loop keeps every operand within declared ranges, so all checks follow from types and one guard, giving a plausible outlook; floating point is avoided since the task only asks for the value of e, not a specific method.

effects.explanation: The calendar lines for 1969 are written to standard output with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Row and column positions for each day are computed from the weekday offset and day number, and the 0..5 row and 1..20 column bounds follow from constant-divisor arithmetic on ranged subtypes, which the provers should discharge without a loop invariant.
The day-of-week calculation uses the year, so Year is a subtype limited to 1..9999 (a documented resource limit) and the intermediate products stay far inside Integer.

Calendar.approach: Embed the twelve centered 20-character month names and the weekday header as constants, and compute each month's 6x20 character grid in a three-dimensional or array-of-String buffer using a closed-form weekday (Zeller-style, Gregorian only) and a case-based days-in-month with the leap-year rule. Print the year heading, then for each of four rows of three months build each output line in a fixed 72-character String by slice assignment and emit it with Put_Line; the digits of each day are written directly as characters, so no 'Image is needed. All loops are for loops over fixed ranges with no loop-carried state, and the year is a range-limited subtype whose test value is 1969.
Calendar.summary: Every check follows from ranged subtypes, constant loop bounds and constant-divisor arithmetic, and the task needs no recursion, while loops, input, or exceptions, so only the String slice index bounds need careful shaping. The optional Julian-to-Gregorian transition and arbitrary page widths are left out, with the 80-column device chosen.

effects.explanation: Prints the 132-column 1969 calendar with the Snoopy placeholder and title lines via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Column positions in the 132-character line buffer and month-name slices are computed from for-loop indexes with small declared ranges, so the bounds follow from types and static ranges.
Day-number arithmetic (row*7 + column - start offset) uses small ranged subtypes and a guarded 1..days test before digit conversion, so no overflow or range check is left open.

Calendar - for \"REAL\" programmers.approach: The year is fixed at 1969 (not a leap year), with embedded constant arrays for month lengths, Jan-1-weekday-derived start offsets per month, and one fixed-width month-name text. Nested for loops over month group (3), week row (6) and month in group (4) with day columns (7) fill a String(1..132) buffer with blanks, day-number digits via mod/div on Character'Val/'Pos, and then call Put_Line per line, after the centered placeholder and the NINETEEN-SIXTY-NINE title. All code is written in uppercase, which Ada's case-insensitivity permits.
Calendar - for \"REAL\" programmers.summary: Every check follows from for-loop indexes over small constant ranges and a guard that the day number lies in 1..month length before it is converted to digits, with no loop-carried values or recursion. The only effect is console output of fixed-size text.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 20 terms and the position of 83116/51639.

risks.explanation: The next-term denominator (2*floor(a/b)+1)*b - a is loop-carried, so it is computed in a wider range and guarded to be within 1..limit with a visible rejection otherwise.

The index accumulator Index*2+bit is loop-carried through nested loops over up to 83116 repetitions, so it needs a guard rejecting values above a fixed cap before each doubling, and the cap must still admit 123456789.
The continued-fraction term array is capped at 64 entries and the Euclid while loop guards Count < 64 before each store, rejecting otherwise.
The parity fix Terms(Count)-1 needs a guard that the last term exceeds 1 so the result stays positive, which Euclid guarantees but the prover must see from a visible test.

Calkin-Wilf sequence.approach: Rationals are held as numerator and denominator in ranged subtypes (small bound for part 1, up to 100000 for part 2), and part 1 loops for I in 1..20 applying next = b/((2*(a/b)+1)*b - a) with a guard that the new denominator is positive and bounded. Part 2 runs a while-loop Euclid in a procedure filling a 64-entry term array with a count guard, makes the count odd, then walks the terms in reverse with nested for loops doubling a capped accumulator and adding the parity bit. Lines are assembled with Integer'Image concatenation into bounded strings and printed with Put_Line.
Calkin-Wilf sequence.summary: Everything is small bounded integer arithmetic with iteration, so checks follow from ranged types and explicit guards with visible rejection, though several loop-carried values (denominator, term count, index accumulator) each need a guard placed just before use.

conflicts.explanation: The whole point of the task is to call a function written in another language (for example C's strdup) through a foreign function interface. Rule 8 lists foreign-language calls among the constructs that are never available, and the C side cannot be proved free of run-time errors (Rule 2). So no Silver program can do what the task requires.

effects.explanation: The program must print the string that the foreign function returns.

Call a foreign-language function.summary: Not a candidate. The task exists to demonstrate calling a foreign-language (C) function, and foreign-language calls are permanently outside Silver under the Oracle's fixed rules. Printing the result is the only other part, and that is just console output.

effects.explanation: Each call demonstration prints its returned value or an explanatory line with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The variadic-style Sum over an unconstrained array of small-range items carries an accumulator through a for loop, so each addition is preceded by a guard against Integer'Last minus the item that sets an out Ok flag to False, which Main reports visibly.
Functions with fixed, optional (defaulted) and named parameters take operands of a declared small subtype so their sums and products fit Integer by type alone.

Call a function.approach: Main declares a parameterless function, a function with a fixed parameter list and a defaulted optional parameter over a small ranged subtype, a procedure with in, out and in out parameters, and a Sum procedure over an unconstrained array type standing in for variadic calls via aggregates of different lengths. Main calls each positionally, with named and mixed associations, in statement context (procedure) and expression context (function results in expressions), uses Integer'Image as a built-in call, and prints lines stating parameter-passing modes and that partial application is not directly available. The Sum loop guards each addition and reports overflow through an out Boolean that Main prints.
Call a function.summary: Every check follows from small declared operand ranges, for-loop indexes over the array's own range, and one overflow guard placed just before the accumulator update, so no annotation is needed. First-class functions and partial application are optional items and are covered by printed statements rather than access-to-subprogram types.

conflicts.explanation: The task's whole point is to load a shared library at run time and call one of its functions at the ABI level. That means a foreign-language call through an entry-point address that is only known at run time, which in Ada needs pragma Import or Convention and an unchecked conversion from System.Address to an access-to-subprogram. Rule 8 never allows this, and rule 6 rules out an admitted library operation for it, because an arbitrary foreign function's behavior cannot be specified.

effects.explanation: Uses the operating system's dynamic loader (dlopen/dlsym or LoadLibrary/GetProcAddress) to load a library and look up a symbol at run time.
Prints the result of the call, or the result of the internal fallback when the library is missing.

Call a function in a shared library.summary: Excluded: the task requires loading a shared library at run time and calling a function in it through its address at the ABI level. That needs foreign calls and an unchecked Address-to-subprogram conversion, which SPARK and the Oracle rules exclude, and no admitted library operation could give it a specified, provable behavior.

effects.explanation: Each method prints a greeting line with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Call an object method.approach: Declare a package My_Class with a tagged null-record type Object, a static procedure Static with no parameters, and an instance procedure Primitive taking an Object, each printing a fixed string with Put_Line. Main declares one Object, calls My_Class.Static, then calls the instance method both as Primitive (Obj) and as Obj.Primitive. There are no loops, arithmetic or input, so there are no guards.
Call an object method.summary: The program has only straight-line calls of procedures that print constant strings, so there are no run-time checks beyond initialization and flow, which discharge trivially. The only growth needed is Silver support for packages, tagged types and user procedures, and the task does not require dispatching or overriding.

effects.explanation: Prints each Calmo number found below 1000.

risks.explanation: Triple sums are computed fresh from three array elements each bounded to 0..999 (at most 2997), so no loop-carried accumulator exists and the addition discharges from types alone.
The slot index is a subtype 0..2 that is reset by a guard just before it would pass 2, so indexing the three-element array is checked locally.

Calmo numbers.approach: A single Main procedure loops n from 2 to 999 with a for loop, scans d from 2 to n-1 counting divisors, then rescans, storing each divisor in a 3-element array of range 0..999 and, when the third slot fills, summing the three elements and testing primality by trial division in a for loop (a Boolean flag, no accumulators). Calmo numbers are printed one per line with 'Image, and an n with zero eligible divisors or a count not divisible by 3 is simply skipped.
Calmo numbers.summary: All loops are bounded for loops with small ranged types and the divisor sums are recomputed from bounded array elements, so every check follows from types and local guards.

effects.explanation: The program prints the longest sequence, its sum and its length to standard output.

risks.explanation: Prefix sums and window sums are loop-carried, so each is held in a ranged subtype (0 .. 1060, the sum of all primes below 100) and every addition or subtraction is computed in Integer and guarded before narrowing, with out-of-range falling to a visible Reject.
Window start and end indexes come from for loops over the prime array's own range, and the prefix-sum lookup before the first prime is guarded by a Tail = 1 test rather than relying on an invariant.
The output text is assembled in a fixed-size buffer sized for 25 primes with up to 3 digits each plus separators, and each append is guarded by remaining capacity.

CalmoSoft primes.approach: Fill a constant-size array with the 25 primes below 100 using a trial-division Is_Prime function built on a for loop (no exit statements), then build a prefix-sum array with guarded additions. Two nested for loops over head and tail indexes test each window's sum with Is_Prime, keeping the longest prime-sum window, and a procedure prints the primes, the sum and the length through scalar image text. The p(n) less than fifty million stretch is omitted as optional.
CalmoSoft primes.summary: Every bound follows from the fixed p(n) < 100 limit, with sums at most 1060 and a for-loop-only trial division, so checks follow from subtypes and guards placed just before the arithmetic.

effects.explanation: Prints each embedded sample and its snake case and camel case conversions with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The output write position advances by up to two per input character, so each write is preceded by a capacity guard on a Natural-range position that rejects overlong input visibly instead of relying on an invariant.
Position counters are subtypes bounded by the buffer capacity and are incremented only after a guard, so no overflow or range check depends on loop-carried facts.
Input length is checked against a fixed maximum before conversion, and the result is shown as a slice 1 .. Len of the buffer, whose bound follows from the guarded type of Len.
Trimming uses while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, and the conversion loops are for loops over the input range.

Camel case and snake case.approach: Samples are String constants embedded in the program (the non-ASCII sample is kept as its bytes, treated as ordinary characters outside the upper-case, digit and separator classes). A procedure Show takes an unconstrained String, finds the trimmed bounds with while loops, then two conversion procedures fill a fixed 128-character buffer through a guarded position counter and return a length, with the guard rejecting input longer than 64 characters. Character classification uses small Boolean functions with plain comparisons and lower/upper conversion uses 'Pos and 'Val arithmetic, and results print via Put_Line of concatenated slices.
Camel case and snake case.summary: Everything is bounded character-by-character string processing in procedures with for loops and explicit capacity guards, so all index, range and overflow checks follow from types and guards just before use. The main work needed is Silver growing character, string indexing, slices, unconstrained String parameters and procedures.

effects.explanation: Prints a text-art rendering of the detected edges (or a summary) to the console.

risks.explanation: Gaussian blur and Sobel sums are accumulated over fixed 3x3 or 5x5 windows of pixels typed 0..255, so the sum ranges are static and bounded, but the prover must bound each loop-carried sum by its declared subtype.
Neighbour accesses are kept in range by running the loops only over interior coordinates (2..W-1, 2..H-1), so the offsets stay inside the fixed image bounds.

The program avoids sqrt and atan2 by using integer gradient magnitude (|Gx|+|Gy|) and comparing Gx and Gy with integer ratio tests to choose one of four directions, which keeps the arithmetic integer-only.

Hysteresis tracing is done as a bounded number of full-image for-loop passes that promote weak pixels next to strong ones, instead of a stack-based while loop or recursion, so termination is automatic.
The embedded input is a small synthetic image of fixed size, such as 16x16, and the result is printed as text art; this is a documented resource limit rather than a silent narrowing of the task.

Canny edge detector.approach: The program embeds a small grayscale image as a constant 2D array of a 0..255 subtype, then runs Gaussian blur, Sobel gradients, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis as separate procedures over fixed-size 2D arrays of bounded integer subtypes. All loops are for loops over interior coordinates, direction is picked by integer comparisons, and hysteresis repeats a fixed number of propagation passes. The final edge map is printed row by row as characters using Put_Line and Put.
Canny edge detector.summary: Every check follows from fixed array bounds, bounded pixel subtypes and for-loop ranges, with no recursion or floating point needed, but the nested stencil sums and many bounded integer subtypes require careful program shape to discharge. The task does not require file or window I/O, so text art on a small embedded image is faithful.

effects.explanation: Prints each input CIDR and its canonical form to standard output.

risks.explanation: The parser advances a loop-carried position through the padded input string, so every read is preceded by an explicit Pos <= S'Last guard, and failure yields a printed rejection line.
Octet and mask accumulation of decimal digits is capped by guards (stop after three digits, reject values above 255 or mask above 32) so the loop-carried values stay within their subtype ranges.
Masking divides by a power of two taken from a constant table indexed by the bit count 0..8, so the divisor is statically nonzero.
Scanning uses while loops only inside procedures, which get no termination check.

Canonicalize CIDR.approach: The five example CIDR strings are embedded as an array of fixed-length padded Strings, and a procedure parses each into four octets (subtype 0..255) and a mask (subtype 0..32) with digit-by-digit guarded accumulation, reporting invalid text as a rejection line. Canonicalization is done per octet: the number of network bits falling in that octet (0..8) selects a constant divisor table entry, and the octet becomes (octet / d) * d. The result is printed with 'Image-style conversion of each octet and mask joined by dots and a slash.
Canonicalize CIDR.summary: Every operation is bounded integer arithmetic on small subtypes with guards before each string index and digit accumulation, so no annotation is needed, but the hand-written parser's loop-carried position and value need careful guard placement.

effects.explanation: Prints the five rows of the Cantor set as text art with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried value J is a subtype 0 .. 80 and each update (J mod 27) * 3 is at most 78, so the range check discharges from the type and arithmetic alone.
The row index comes from a for loop over 1 .. 81, which is the String's own range, so indexing is routine.

Cantor set.approach: One 81-character String buffer is reused for five rows (levels 0 to 4). For each level and each column I, a subtype 0 .. 80 variable J starts at I-1 and, for each of the Level leading base-3 digits, a column is blanked if J / 27 equals 1, and J then becomes (J mod 27) * 3; the cell is set to '*' or ' ' and the row is printed with Put_Line.
Cantor set.summary: All loops are for loops with static bounds and the only loop-carried value has a declared range that the update provably stays within, so every check follows from types and no annotation or recursion is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the shuffled deck orderings as text lines.

risks.explanation: Pile cursors in the riffle merge are loop-carried, so each array access is guarded by an explicit bound check just before use, with the pile sizes fixed by the constant deck size.
The deterministic LCG state is kept in a modular or range-bounded type and reduced with mod before each use, so no arithmetic overflows.
The overhand while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and each pass takes at least one card so it ends anyway.
Remaining-card counts are loop-carried and must stay inside 0..52 and be guarded before subtraction, and the group size is clamped to at least 1 and at most the remaining count.

Card shuffles.approach: The deck is a constant-size array of 52 card indices with a second output array, and a seeded LCG in a procedure supplies pseudo-random numbers. Riffle splits at a fixed point and merges by comparing a random draw against the remaining pile proportions, guarding both cursors; overhand repeatedly takes a random group of 1 to a fifth of the remaining cards and places it on the new pile, using a while loop in a procedure. Each shuffle runs for a fixed n iterations and the result is printed as card-name text lines, with a simple built-in-style Fisher-Yates comparison optional.
Card shuffles.summary: All arithmetic is small bounded integer work on a fixed 52-element array, so checks reduce to types and guards before each index, but loop-carried cursors need careful shaping without invariants.

effects.explanation: Prints each Carmichael triple and product line by line.

risks.explanation: The products (H3+P1)*(P1-1), P1*P2 and P1*P2*P3 are nonlinear but every operand has a small subtype range (P1 up to 61, P2 up to 7261, P3 up to about 443000), so interval reasoning keeps them below 2**40.
Assigning P2 and P3 into ranged subtypes needs the provers to bound quotients using D>=1 and H3>=1, which follows from the loop-index ranges but depends on careful typing.
The divisors D, H3 and P1-1 are nonzero because loop indexes start at 1 and P1 is at least 2.

Carmichael 3 strong pseudoprimes.approach: Use a ranged integer type (0 .. 2**40) and a function Is_Prime doing for-loop trial division, then nested for loops over P1 in 2..61 (prime only), H3 in 1..P1 and D in 1..H3+P1-1 following the pseudocode. Each candidate P2 and P3 is computed from bounded operands, tested with Is_Prime and the mod condition, and qualifying triples are printed with Put_Line using 'Image concatenation into bounded strings.
Carmichael 3 strong pseudoprimes.summary: Every check follows from loop-index ranges and small declared subtypes, with only nonlinear products and quotients needing interval propagation, and all loops are for loops so no variant is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the lambda and iteration table for 1 to 25 and the lowest n for each iteration count.

risks.explanation: The lcm product of two lambda values and the (p-1)*p**(k-1) totient term are nonlinear, and are discharged by computing in a 64-bit type with subtype bounds on n (at most 5,000,000) plus a visible reject guard if a result exceeds the bound.

Loop-carried values such as the running lcm, the remaining cofactor and the iteration counter have only their type range after the first iteration, so each is bounded by a subtype and a guard just before assignment.
The gcd, prime-dividing and iteration-counting while loops are placed in procedures, which get no termination check, and the lambda and iteration helpers are procedures rather than functions.
The first-occurrence array is indexed by the iteration count, which is guarded by a comparison against the array bound before each use.

Carmichael lambda function.approach: Use subtype-bounded Integer/Long_Long_Integer values (n up to 5,000,000) with procedures: factor by trial division using a for loop over candidate primes with an inner while dividing out each prime, combine lambda of prime powers via a Euclid gcd while-loop procedure and lcm, and count iterations in a bounded while loop with an explicit cap. A single for loop over n from 1 to 5,000,000 records the first n for each iteration count 0..15 in a fixed array guarded by index checks, and results print through Put_Line with 'Image concatenation; the stretch part (i 16 to 25, n near 3^24) is left out as optional.
Carmichael lambda function.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic in procedures with explicit guards and no recursion or annotations, but loop-carried lcm and counter values need careful subtype bounds and guards, so discharge depends on program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints each product as a line of text such as {(1,3),(1,4),...}.

risks.explanation: Odometer-style indexing of lists by loop-carried positions needs each index held in a subtype bounded by the fixed list capacity, so the type range discharges the check.
Loop-carried odometer positions and output-buffer lengths are bounded by their subtype ranges and guarded before each increment, with the buffer sized for the largest product (24 tuples).
Appending numbers to a bounded text buffer needs a guard that remaining capacity covers the digits, with a visible reject outcome otherwise.
All iteration is done in procedures with for loops or one while loop over a bounded odometer, so no function termination check arises.

Cartesian product of two or more lists.approach: Lists are fixed-capacity arrays (a 2D array of values plus an array of lengths, bounded subtypes) holding the embedded example data. A procedure prints the n-ary product by walking an odometer of index positions (a for loop over the total tuple count, deriving each position by integer division and mod), appending 'Image digits into a bounded line buffer and printing with Put_Line. An empty list gives product count zero, so the output is {}.
Cartesian product of two or more lists.summary: The task only needs bounded arrays, nested for loops and integer-to-text output, all of which have types or guards bounding every index and length, and no recursion or heap is required. Plausible rather than likely because the n-ary odometer and text-buffer building carry loop-carried values that need careful range-bounded subtypes.

effects.explanation: Prints the single result line with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Case-sensitivity of identifiers.approach: Declare one String constant Dog := "Bernie" and print "There is just one dog named " & DOG & "." through Silver_IO.Put_Line, referring to the identifier in a different letter case to show Ada's case insensitivity. There are no loops, inputs or arithmetic, so only a bounded concatenation of constant-length strings is involved.
Case-sensitivity of identifiers.summary: The program uses only constructs Silver already supports (String constant, concatenation, Put_Line), and every check is static, so proofs discharge trivially.

effects.explanation: Prints the filtered numbers and the proportion summary lines.

risks.explanation: The digit-sum accumulator is kept in a subtype 0..8 by subtracting 9 whenever it reaches 9, so each addition is bounded by types alone and needs no invariant.
k*k is computed only for k in a declared range of at most 10000 (and Base in a small declared range), so the square fits in Integer by types.
Digit extraction uses a for loop over a fixed maximum digit count (10 iterations) rather than a while loop, so no variant is needed even if co9 is a function.
Division by Base-1 is safe because Base is a subtype declared as 2..16 so Base-1 is at least 1, and the percentage divides by a count that is guarded to be nonzero.

Casting out nines.approach: Embedded constants set the range 1..100 and bases 10 and 16; function Co9 (value in a bounded subtype, base in 2..16) peels digits with a fixed-count for loop, adding each digit to a running residue kept in 0..Base-2 by conditional subtraction (repeated digit addition, 0 reported as Base-1). A for loop over k prints those k with Co9(k) = Co9(k*k) via Put and Image-style conversion into a bounded buffer, counts them, then prints the count and an integer percentage saving, and a second pass with the mod (Base-1) shortcut for Part 3 compares equal results.
Casting out nines.summary: All values are bounded by declared subtypes, the accumulator is reduced each step so no loop invariant is needed, and loops are for loops over fixed ranges, so every check follows from types and simple guards.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 15 Catalan numbers, one per line.

risks.explanation: The product Result*2*(2*I-1) is safe only because Result has a ranged subtype (up to 2**40) in a 64-bit intermediate type, so the bound comes from the type rather than from a loop invariant.

Assigning the quotient back to the ranged accumulator would fail the range check without an invariant, so the program computes the quotient in a wide temporary and guards it against the subtype maximum, with a visible Reject branch that never fires for N up to 15.
The divisor I+1 is at least 2 because I is a for-loop index in 1..15, which is routine.
Building the 'N = value' output line needs a bounded buffer sized for the largest Image text, which is routine once the lengths are statically bounded.

Catalan numbers.approach: Use the iterative recurrence C_n = C_(n-1)*2*(2n-1)/(n+1) in a single for loop over 0..15 inside Main, keeping the running value in a ranged subtype and printing each index and value with Put_Line of concatenated 'Image text. The next value is computed in a wide temporary type, guarded against the subtype maximum with a Reject branch, then assigned, so no check depends on a loop invariant.
Catalan numbers.summary: The task is plain bounded integer arithmetic with 15 iterations, and the overflow and range checks discharge from the wide temporary type plus an explicit guard before the assignment. Nonlinear multiply and divide on loop-carried values make it depend on careful program shape rather than being routine.

effects.explanation: Prints the 15 Catalan numbers, one per line, via Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Pascal row entries are loop-carried values whose sum has no invariant bound, so each addition is guarded by a comparison against Integer'Last that leads to Reject, and the true values (at most 155117520) never trigger it.
Row indexes and the Catalan extraction indexes come from for-loop ranges over the array's own bounds, so they discharge routinely.
Element subtype Natural makes the subtraction of adjacent central entries safe, though the prover must see that both operands are non-negative from the type alone.
Integer'Image results are bounded by the type, so appending them to a fixed-size line buffer or printing directly is routine.

Catalan numbers/Pascal's triangle.approach: Keep one Pascal row as an array of Natural indexed 0..30, initialised to row 0, and update it in place with a reverse for loop for each of the 30 rows, guarding every addition against overflow with a Reject outcome. After building row 2n, the n-th Catalan number is Row(n) - Row(n+1), printed with Integer'Image through Put_Line, for n from 1 to 15 (Catalan numbers C(n) from rows 2n requires snapshotting at each even row inside a single loop).
Catalan numbers/Pascal's triangle.summary: All values stay below 2**31 and every index comes from for-loop ranges, so only the loop-carried row additions need explicit overflow guards, which makes discharge plausible rather than trivially likely.

effects.explanation: The four fold results (min, max, sum, product) are printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: The product accumulator is loop-carried so the prover knows only its subtype; the program uses a bounded accumulator subtype and a guard before each multiplication that reports a visible rejection message rather than clamping.
The accumulator assignment must fit its subtype for Add and Mul, which the same pre-operation guard on the bound discharges.

Catamorphism.approach: Declare a small element subtype, a fixed array of four embedded values (1,2,3,4), and an enumeration of fold operations (Min, Max, Add, Mul); a Fold procedure takes the operation and array, seeds the accumulator from the first element, then runs a for loop over the remaining indexes applying a case on the operation. Before Add and Mul the loop tests the accumulator against a declared limit and, on exceeding it, sets an overflow-rejected status that is reported in the output. Main calls Fold for each operation and prints each result with Put_Line using 'Image.
Catamorphism.summary: Higher-order function parameters are not available in SPARK, so reduce is expressed with an operation enumeration, and all indexes come from the array's own range while the only loop-carried arithmetic is bounded by subtype limits and explicit guards. Discharge depends on careful guard placement for the accumulator but needs no annotation.

effects.explanation: The surface is rendered as a text-art depth map printed line by line to the console.

risks.explanation: cosh(u), Cos(v) and Sin(v) need an admitted bounded math library, or a hand-written Taylor series over a range-limited Float (u in -2..2), so that no overflow or NaN check can fail.
Projected coordinates are converted to grid indices only after explicit guards that skip points falling outside the fixed 60x30 character grid, so the index checks discharge.
Every float operand is bounded by the range of its subtype, so products and sums stay finite without needing a loop invariant.

Catenoid surface.approach: The program fixes an angle grid (41 by 41) over u in -2..2 and v in 0..2*pi, computes each surface point with a bounded cosh and table-driven or series sin and cos, and projects it with a fixed rotation onto a 60x30 constrained character grid. Each point is written to the grid only after an explicit bounds guard, using a depth character chosen by height, then the grid rows are printed with Put_Line in a procedure. All loops are for loops over constants, so no loop-carried invariant is needed.
Catenoid surface.summary: The task asks only to draw a catenoid and the text-art rendering meets it, so there is no Oracle conflict. The floating-point trigonometry and hyperbolic functions are the only non-routine proof burden, which a range-limited library or series keeps dischargeable without annotations.

effects.explanation: The program prints the refined mesh's vertex coordinates and face index lists as text, which satisfies the render requirement without a display.

risks.explanation: Averages and the m1/m2/m3 weighting must stay finite, which discharges only if coordinates are a bounded float subtype and the embedded cube data is small, though provers handle float range reasoning weakly.
Dividing by a face's vertex count or a vertex's face count n is guarded by a visible check that skips or rejects vertices with n = 0, and the counts are also typed as at least 1 where known.

Edge lookup, edge-point numbering and new-face writes index fixed-capacity arrays with loop-carried counters (edge count, next point number, next face), so each increment needs an explicit capacity guard just before use.

The edge count and new-vertex numbers grow across loop iterations with no invariant, so they must be typed to the capacity range and guarded before each increment, with overflow of capacity giving a specified rejection outcome.
Arrays of points, edges and face tables must be fully initialized by aggregate before the loops fill them, since partial fills cannot be proven by flow analysis.

Catmull\u2013Clark subdivision surface.approach: The program embeds the cube (8 vertices, 6 quad faces) in constrained arrays of a point record with bounded Float components, then in procedures computes face points, a deduplicated edge table (with a second adjacent-face slot and a hole check), edge points, new vertex positions, and the new quad face table, all with for loops over fixed-capacity arrays. It prints coordinates and faces as text for one or two rounds, and guards n = 0 and capacity overflows with explicit rejection outcomes.
Catmull\u2013Clark subdivision surface.summary: Every check can be tied to array bounds, ranged counters and pre-use guards with no annotation, but the bounded floating-point arithmetic and several loop-carried counters make discharge depend on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints the centre coordinates and radius as text lines.

risks.explanation: Squares, products and the divisions cannot overflow only if the coordinate type is a bounded float subtype, and the sqrt argument must be shown nonnegative by an explicit guard.
The two determinant denominators are guarded against zero with an explicit collinear-points rejection that prints a visible outcome.
Float-to-text formatting to two decimals needs an admitted library routine with a bounded input range, since 'Image on floats is not provable to a fixed format.

Provers must bound intermediate products of nonlinear float expressions, so subtypes with small ranges (such as plus or minus 1000.0) are needed and the guard on the sqrt argument may not be provable by simple range reasoning.

Centre and radius of a circle passing th.approach: Define a bounded float subtype for coordinates, a Point record, and a procedure Find_Circle computing the centre with the determinant formula on embedded sample points, rejecting collinear points when the denominator is zero. Compute the radius with a square root guarded by a nonnegative test, then print centre and radius with a bounded fixed-decimal formatting routine.
Centre and radius of a circle passing th.summary: Everything is straight-line code with no loops, so the only difficulty is floating-point overflow, division by zero and sqrt-domain checks, which range-bounded subtypes and explicit guards can address, though float formatting and sqrt need admitted library support.

effects.explanation: Prints each point set and its centroid to standard output.

risks.explanation: The per-dimension sum is a loop-carried accumulator, so it is held in a wide Long_Long_Integer with coordinates in a bounded subtype and a guard just before each addition that rejects out-of-bound running sums.
The division by the point count is guarded by an explicit check that the count is at least 1 before dividing, with a visible rejection otherwise.
Loops run over the arrays' own index ranges up to the declared maximum point and dimension counts, with the actual count and dimension parameters checked against those maxima before use.
Text for numbers is built in a fixed-capacity buffer sized for the worst-case digits, signs, point and separators, with a guard before each append.
Fractional output (e.g. 3.1, -1.475) uses thousandths-scaled integers split into whole and fraction parts with mod and rem on bounded values, so conversions stay within declared subtypes.

Centroid of a set of N-dimensional point.approach: Coordinates are stored as integers scaled by 1000 in a bounded subtype inside a constrained two-dimensional array (max points by max dimensions) with separate count and dimension values. A procedure sums each dimension with a for loop into a wide accumulator guarded before each add, rejects a zero point count, divides by the count, and then formats each value as decimal text in a bounded buffer and prints each embedded test set with its centroid. The 3D plot stretch is skipped as optional.
Centroid of a set of N-dimensional point.summary: Every check follows from bounded subtypes, array index ranges and guards before the sum and division, though the loop-carried sum and the decimal formatting need careful shape. Scaled-integer arithmetic avoids floating point and nothing requires an annotation.

effects.explanation: The dictionary unixdict.txt (about 25,000 words) is too large to embed, so the program must read it line by line from a named file.
Each qualifying pair is printed as a line of text.
The dictionary path is taken from the first command-line argument, with a default of unixdict.txt.
A missing, oversized or over-capacity dictionary is rejected with a specified failure status.

risks.explanation: Words are stored in a fixed-capacity array of fixed-length padded strings with a length array, and a guard rejects the input when the word count or a word length exceeds the capacity before each store.
The word count and binary-search bounds are range-typed subtypes bounded by the capacity, with a guard before each decrement so the midpoint arithmetic and Mid-1 cannot leave their range.
The reading loop and the binary search are while loops placed in procedures, which get no termination check, and the per-word translation uses for loops.
Translated words are built in a bounded buffer whose length is checked against the stored word length before comparison, so slices stay within bounds.

Change e letters to i in words.approach: The program reads unixdict.txt line by line into a fixed-capacity array of padded 32-character words with a length array, rejecting input that exceeds the word count or word length capacity. For each word of length at least 6, a for loop builds a copy with each e or E replaced by i or I, and if it differs from the original, a binary search procedure over the sorted dictionary (guarded Low/High range types) reports whether the copy is present and the pair is printed with Put_Line.
Change e letters to i in words.summary: Every check follows from fixed array bounds, range-typed indexes and explicit capacity guards, with the loops in procedures so no variant is needed, but it needs file input, string slicing and ordering that Silver lacks and careful guards on the search indexes.

effects.explanation: The program reads the named dictionary file unixdict.txt line by line, with a specified outcome when it is missing or unreadable.
Each matching word pair is printed as one line on standard output.
An unreadable dictionary or one exceeding the stated capacity is rejected with a visible failure status.

risks.explanation: Reading each line into a fixed 32-character buffer with a stored length needs explicit guards rejecting lines longer than 32 and a full table of 1024 entries, after which all indexing follows from the declared ranges.
The count of differing letters is a loop-carried value, so it is kept in a small ranged subtype and saturated at 2 by a guard, which preserves the exactly-one-difference test.
The line-reading while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the pairwise comparison uses only for loops.
Output slices Word(1..Len) depend on the stored length, which is bounded by its subtype range, and Len is compared for equality between the two words before characters are compared.

Changeable words.approach: Read unixdict.txt line by line in a procedure with a while loop, keeping only words of 12 or more characters in a fixed array of records holding a 32-character buffer and a length, rejecting overlong words or a full table with a visible failure. Then a pair of nested for loops over table indexes compares words of equal length, counting differing characters with a saturating counter, and prints each pair with Put and Put_Line using slices of the stored length.
Changeable words.summary: Every check follows from declared ranges, for-loop indexes and guards on line length and table capacity, and nothing needs an annotation, but the file-reading procedure and the loop-carried counter need careful shape, so the outlook is plausible.

effects.explanation: Prints the plaintext, the alphabets after each step, the ciphertext and the recovered plaintext with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Rotation indexes are computed as ((I + Index - 2) mod 26) + 1 with Index in a 1..26 subtype, so the result is statically within 1..26 without any invariant.
The output buffer and the found-index variable are initialized before their loops so no loop-carried uninitialized read remains.
The letter lookup uses a found flag and an explicit rejection path for characters outside the alphabet, so the position never leaves 1..26 and the case is not silently altered.

Chaocipher.approach: Both alphabets and the 28-letter plaintext are fixed-length String variables or constants, with a subtype for 26-character alphabets and a Positive subtype 1..26 for positions. A step procedure finds the letter's position with a for loop and found flag (printing a rejection message if absent), maps it to the other alphabet, then rebuilds the left and right alphabets into temporary strings using for loops with mod-based rotation and a shift of the nadir-adjacent letter. The main procedure encrypts, prints each alphabet pair, then decrypts the ciphertext with the same procedure and prints both results.
