risks.explanation: Interpreted +, -, * and negation run on a wide ranged type and a guard rejects any result outside the interpreter's value range, so the check discharges and overflow has a visible outcome.
A guard rejects a zero divisor before / and mod, and truncation toward zero matches Ada's native semantics.
Node, string-pool, variable and stack indexes are range-typed and every load or push is guarded against the fixed capacities, with overflow rejecting the input.

Recursion is replaced by an explicit work stack inside procedures with while loops, which get no termination check, and a non-terminating guest program simply runs forever, which is not a proved property.
Input lines, identifiers and string literals are copied into fixed-size bounded buffers with length guards that reject over-long tokens.
All node, variable and pool arrays are initialized by whole-array aggregates or for loops before use.

Compiler/AST interpreter.approach: The program reads the AST lines from stdin into a fixed-capacity array of node records (kind enumeration, left and right indexes, value) using a loader that parses with an explicit stack instead of recursion, then interprets it with an iterative explicit-stack evaluator in a procedure over a bounded variable table and string pool. Every arithmetic result, index and capacity is guarded and violations reject the input with a specified message; output goes through Put-style procedures and integer text conversion.
Compiler/AST interpreter.summary: Nothing needs an annotation because recursion is replaced by explicit stacks in procedures and all arithmetic, indexes and buffers are bounded by types and guards, but the many guarded loop-carried indexes and the text parsing make discharge depend on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: The task requires reading the flattened AST text produced by the syntax analyzer, which the program reads line by line from standard input.
The header, string pool and virtual assembly listing are written to standard output.

risks.explanation: Node, instruction, string-pool, variable and explicit-stack indices are loop-carried counters, so each push or append is preceded by a capacity guard that rejects the input, and stored child links use a ranged Node_Index subtype so indexing through them follows from the type.

Integer literals are parsed digit by digit with a guard against the 32-bit limit before each multiply-add, and code addresses and jump offsets are sums and differences of capacity-bounded positions, so their ranges follow from declared subtypes.
Tokenizing lines that respect double quotes and copying identifiers and strings into fixed buffers needs explicit length guards before each slice copy and each assembled output line.

Replacing recursive AST loading and code generation with explicit stacks of pending-child slots and phase-tagged work items for If and While must still produce exactly the reference byte offsets and backpatched jumps, which is a correctness burden rather than a proof one.
The line-reading, tree-building, generation and listing loops are while loops kept inside procedures, and the pool lookups in functions use for loops, so no variant is needed.

Compiler/code generator.approach: The program reads the flattened AST from standard input into a fixed-size node pool of records (kind enumeration, left and right Node_Index links, value buffer). It builds the tree without recursion by keeping an explicit stack of parent slots still waiting for children. It then generates code with an explicit work stack of phase-tagged items into a bounded array of instruction records, backpatching jz/jmp targets and computing byte addresses as 1 or 5 bytes per instruction. Finally it prints the Datasize/Strings header, the string pool and the formatted listing. Unknown node names, malformed lines, early end of input, integer literals over 32 bits and exceeded capacities each lead to Reject with a message.
Compiler/code generator.summary: Every check can follow from ranged index subtypes plus capacity and digit-overflow guards placed just before each push, append or multiply. Nothing needs an annotation, but the many loop-carried counters and explicit stacks make discharge depend on careful program shape, so the outlook is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Source text is read from standard input.
The task allows reading the source from a named file given as the first argument.
Token lines with line, column, name and value are written to standard output, and diagnostics are reported with a specified message.
Optional first argument selects the input file.
Lexical errors end the run with a nonzero status after a diagnostic.

risks.explanation: A scan position is carried through a while loop in a procedure, so each lookahead and buffer access is guarded by an explicit position-less-than-length test just before use.

Line, column, token length and integer-literal value counters are loop-carried, so they use bounded subtypes with guards, and over-long input or integer literals beyond the limit are rejected with a specified diagnostic.
Input buffer, token text buffer and string values have fixed capacities, and input exceeding the capacity is rejected visibly rather than truncated.
The scanner is a procedure with a while loop, so no termination check applies, and the position advances on every state transition.
The buffers and the output token fields are fully initialized by declaration, and every case branch sets them before use.

Compiler/lexical analyzer.approach: Read the whole source into a fixed-capacity Character array with a length, rejecting over-capacity input, then scan it in a procedure with a while loop and a position index, tracking line and column in bounded subtypes. A case statement on the current character classifies tokens, with guarded one-character lookahead for two-character operators, comments, identifiers, integers, character and string literals, and keywords recognized by comparing the token buffer. Each token is written as a line with Put and scalar image, and the eight lexical errors are reported through a specified message and nonzero exit status, never an exception.
Compiler/lexical analyzer.summary: Every check follows from bounded buffers, subtype-ranged counters and an explicit guard before each lookahead, and the scanner is a procedure so termination is not checked, but the many loop-carried positions, counters and buffers need careful guard placement. Nothing requires an annotation, and the exception-based error reporting of the existing solution is replaced by specified diagnostics.

effects.explanation: Reads the optional debug flag, input file name and output file name from the command line.
Reads source lines from standard input when no input file is named.
Reads the source file and each included file, and optionally writes the output file.
Writes the processed text to standard output when no output file is named, and reports rejected input.
Signals failure for a missing include, an include nesting deeper than five, an illegal macro redefinition or an over-capacity input.

risks.explanation: Every scan position into a bounded line buffer is guarded by a comparison against the current line length just before use, and macro and stack tables are indexed by counters typed to their capacity.
Expanded lines are appended into fixed-capacity buffers only after a guard checks the remaining room, and overflow is rejected with a visible error rather than truncated.
Loop-carried scan cursors and counters are subtypes bounded by the buffer capacity and are advanced only under guards, since there is no invariant to carry the bound.
All scanning and expansion loops live in procedures (no termination check), and include nesting uses an explicit five-entry file stack instead of recursion.
Substitution can grow a line, so output length is checked against capacity before each append and macro expansion is performed in a single non-nested pass over the definition.

Compiler/Preprocessor.approach: Lines are held in fixed-capacity character buffers with explicit lengths, macros live in a bounded table of records (name, parameter list, body), and includes are handled by an explicit stack of at most six open files driven from a while loop in a procedure. Each line is classified as an include, a define or ordinary text; ordinary text is scanned character by character for a hash-delimited usage, which is parsed, looked up, and expanded by a single substitution pass into a bounded output buffer, with unmatched text copied through unchanged. Every capacity, depth, redefinition and file-open failure is an explicit rejection with a specified message and exit status.
Compiler/Preprocessor.summary: All checks reduce to bounded buffer indexing and length guards placed before each append, and recursion is avoided by an explicit include stack and fixed capacities, so nothing needs an annotation; the heavy loop-carried cursor state and string building make discharge depend on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Reads the main source file and each included file by name, and writes the combined output file.
Takes the input and output file names (and could take a nesting option) from the command line.
Reports completion or an open-failure message to the console.
Signals failure to open a file or an over-deep nesting with a nonzero status.

risks.explanation: Line buffers are fixed-capacity strings, so the directive scan, trim and quote search need guards before each indexed read and slice, and over-long lines must be rejected with a visible outcome.
Extracting the quoted file name into a bounded buffer needs the computed slice length checked against the capacity before copying.
The line-reading and scanning loops are while loops, so they must live in procedures (no termination check) and nesting is done by an explicit bounded stack of open files rather than recursion.

Compiler/Simple file inclusion pre proce.approach: The program takes input and output file names from the arguments, then processes lines in a procedure with an explicit fixed-depth stack of open input files (say 8 levels) instead of recursion, which gives bounded nested includes. Each line is read into a bounded buffer, trimmed, tested for a leading #include followed by a quoted name, and either replaced by pushing the named file or copied to the output; unopenable files, over-long lines, over-deep nesting and malformed directives each reject with a specified message and nonzero status.
Compiler/Simple file inclusion pre proce.summary: Everything is bounded text processing over fixed buffers with an explicit file stack, so no annotations are needed, but the many index and slice guards and the file-library dependency make careful program shape necessary.

effects.explanation: The lexer's token listing is read line by line from standard input.
The flattened AST and any rejection message are written to standard output.

risks.explanation: The recursive descent and precedence climbing are replaced by one while loop inside a procedure driven by an explicit bounded stack of pending states, and procedures get no termination check.
Nesting depth of parentheses, blocks and operators is limited by a fixed-size stack array, and exceeding it rejects the input visibly, so no recursion depth depends on input.
Every write to the token table, node table, stack or line buffer is guarded by a capacity test just before the access, and over-capacity input is rejected with a message.
Identifier and string token text is copied into fixed-length buffers with a guard that rejects over-long tokens, and the AST dump walks the node array with an explicit stack of the same bounded kind.
Integer literals stay as text and are never converted to numbers, so no arithmetic can overflow, while line and node counters are ranged subtypes bounded by their capacities.
Token and node arrays are fully initialized by aggregate before use, and record fields are set before any read.

Compiler/syntax analyzer.approach: Read the lexer output from stdin into a bounded token table of records holding an enumeration kind and fixed-length text, then parse with a single while loop in a procedure that uses an explicit bounded stack of parse states and an operator stack for precedence climbing, building the binary tree in a fixed-capacity node array with integer child indices (0 for null). Print the flattened tree by a second loop with an explicit stack of node indices, and reject malformed tokens, unexpected tokens or any exceeded capacity with a specified message and Reject.
Compiler/syntax analyzer.summary: All checks follow from fixed-capacity arrays, ranged indices and capacity guards, but the explicit-stack parser replacing recursion is a large loop-heavy program whose index and loop-carried bounds need careful guarding, so it is plausible rather than likely.

It prints "true", or "false" followed by an error message.

risks.explanation: The scanner advances a position through a bounded line buffer, so each character access is guarded by a position <= length test just before use.
Scanning loops are while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, and each iteration advances the position.
The paren-depth counter and position index are bounded by guards, and exceeding the documented maximum nesting or line length yields a specified "false" rejection message.
The grammar's nesting is handled by an explicit fixed-size array of per-depth flags in an iterative state machine instead of recursion, so no input-dependent stack depth arises.
Building the error message with the numeric position uses bounded concatenation in a buffer sized for the maximum line length plus the position digits.

Compiler/Verifying syntax.approach: The program reads each line of the input file into a bounded String buffer, then scans it with a while loop in a procedure that classifies tokens (identifier, integer, keyword or, and, not, true, false, operators, parentheses) by Character comparisons. Grammar checking is an iterative pushdown state machine: an enumeration state expects an operand or an operator, a fixed-capacity array indexed by paren depth records whether a comparison has been used in the current level, and "not" is only admitted at the start of a comparison operand. Over-long lines or over-deep nesting are rejected with a specified "false" message, and every failure prints "false" plus the position and reason.
Compiler/Verifying syntax.summary: The recursive-descent grammar can be recast as an iterative bounded-stack automaton, so every check follows from array bounds and guards just before indexing, with no annotation needed. The outlook is plausible rather than likely because of the tokenizer's loop-carried position, the bounded-depth stack, and the needed file-reading library.

effects.explanation: Reads the assembly listing (header, string pool, instruction lines) line by line from standard input.
prtc, prti and prts write characters, integers and pooled strings to standard output without line terminators.
Malformed listings, limit overruns and VM faults must end with a specified rejecting exit status.

risks.explanation: Stack pointer, data index, string index and pc are loop-carried, so each use is preceded by an explicit bounds guard that ends the run with a rejecting fault outcome.

32-bit signed arithmetic on stack words is held in a range-limited subtype, and add, sub, mul and neg compute in a wider 64-bit type and fault with a visible outcome if the result leaves the 32-bit range.
div and mod test for a zero divisor and for the minus-2^31 by minus-1 case just before the operation and fault visibly.
Jump targets and operand values parsed from text are range-checked while parsing and again before pc is assigned, and parsing digit accumulators are guarded against exceeding the limit on each digit.
String-pool entries and input lines live in fixed-capacity buffers with explicit lengths, and over-long lines or escape expansions are rejected at append time.
All loops are in procedures, which get no termination check, so the interpreter loop needs no variant, though a guest program that loops forever simply runs forever by specification.

Compiler/virtual machine interpreter.approach: The listing is read from stdin line by line into fixed-capacity tables: a string pool of bounded buffers with lengths, and parallel code arrays of opcode, operand and address, with the data area and a 32-bit-ranged word stack as constrained arrays. A hand-written scanner parses the header, quoted string literals with the escapes backslash-n and double backslash, and each instruction line, rejecting anything malformed; then a while loop in a procedure dispatches by case on the opcode, guarding stack depth, indexes, division and 32-bit overflow before each operation and ending in a specified fault outcome when a guard fails. Output goes through Put of characters, a hand-built decimal conversion for prti, and pooled strings for prts.
Compiler/virtual machine interpreter.summary: No Oracle rule is broken and no annotation is needed because every stack, index, arithmetic and parsing check can be guarded just before use with a visible fault outcome, but the many loop-carried values (sp, pc, accumulators) and the wide-type overflow handling make careful program shape necessary.

risks.explanation: The factor counter is a small ranged subtype that saturates at 2 (only 'more than one factor' is tested, so results are unchanged), while k, v and f*f stay within 99,999,999 and 10,000-squared by type ranges.
The substring function indexes the image strings only after a guard that offset plus pattern length does not exceed the text length, so the loop-carried index is bounded by the for-loop range.
The inner division while loop and the outer search live in procedures (the substring check is a function with only for loops), so no variant is needed.
Divisions by f are safe because f starts at 11, and v only shrinks by exact division, so its subtype range holds without an invariant.

Composite numbers k with no single digit.approach: Main iterates odd k from 11 over a bounded Integer range with an early exit once twenty hits are printed, trial-dividing by f from 11 up to 10,000 with an exit when f*f exceeds the remaining cofactor v. Each prime factor found is checked as a substring of k's decimal image by a Boolean function using nested for loops with explicit length guards, and the cofactor greater than one is checked likewise; hits are printed with Put_Line of the image.
Composite numbers k with no single digit.summary: All arithmetic is bounded by declared ranges and for-loop bounds, and the only while loops are in a procedure, so no annotation is needed. The risk is limited to a few loop-carried counters and image-string indexing that need careful guards.

Trial division uses a function over N in 2..9999 with a for loop of divisors 2..99, so the mod operand is never zero and no loop-carried value needs an invariant.

Nested for loops over P1 and P2 test both for primality, compute the concatenation as P1*10 or P1*100 plus P2 depending on whether P2 < 10, mark a Boolean array indexed by Full, then a final for loop prints each marked value with 'Image trimmed via a small bounded digit buffer, and the guarded count, using Put_Line.
Concatenate two primes is also prime.summary: Every check follows from declared subtypes, for-loop ranges and a counter bounded by a visible guard, with no while loops or recursion, so proofs should discharge without annotations. The only extra surface is integer-to-text formatting for output.

effects.explanation: Each of the three tasks prints its word on its own line.
The clock supplies a per-run seed and the start time for each task's absolute delay, so the order differs between runs.
Each task waits a pseudo-random interval (delay until, the form Ravenscar/Jorvik allows) before printing, which produces the random order.

risks.explanation: The task requires real concurrency, and SPARK admits tasks and protected objects only under a Ravenscar or Jorvik profile pragma, which Silver source cannot contain, so admission would need a toolchain-supplied configuration rather than a proof.

Three tasks calling Put_Line on the same output are concurrent access to shared state, so Silver_IO would need to be an admitted synchronized operation, or output would need to go through a protected object, before flow analysis accepts it.
Turning the clock's seconds count into a delay in milliseconds is safe if the value is reduced with mod to a small ranged subtype before any multiplication.

Concurrent computing.approach: A library-level package declares three tasks, one per word, as Ravenscar/Jorvik requires; each task reads Ada.Real_Time.Clock and derives a small bounded delay from the clock value and its own index, using mod into a ranged subtype. It then does delay until on the start time plus that many milliseconds, and prints its word through a synchronized output operation, while the Main procedure body is null.
Concurrent computing.summary: The arithmetic is trivial and would prove, but the task requires tasks or threads, which SPARK allows only under a Ravenscar/Jorvik profile pragma that Silver source cannot contain, and output from several tasks also needs synchronized I/O; for these reasons tasking makes the outlook unlikely.

effects.explanation: Each conditional structure reports which branch it took with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Conditional structures.approach: Main declares an enumeration type Day and an embedded example constant Today, then shows each conditional structure Ada/SPARK offers in turn: an if/elsif/else chain, a case statement with an alternation choice and a when others default, a full-coverage case statement without others, an if expression and a case expression. Each one passes a String literal to Put_Line. No arithmetic, indexing or loops are involved, so the only checks are the trivial ones on discrete choices that the compiler has already shown to be complete.
Conditional structures.summary: The program only branches on a constant of an enumeration type and prints literal strings, so it has no run-time check that could fail beyond what types and static case coverage already settle. The task's "select" demonstration needs tasking, which the task does not require, so it is left out.

effects.explanation: Prints the six conjugated forms of each example verb, one per line.

risks.explanation: Stem slicing and bounded-buffer appends are guarded by the verb length checks and by a buffer sized for the longest stem plus the longest ending.
Assembling stem plus ending into a fixed buffer needs a length guard before each copy, which the program supplies via a bounded stem length and a Last counter.

Conjugate a Latin verb.approach: Embed four example infinitives (amare, monere, regere, audire) in a constant array of fixed-length strings with recorded lengths, plus constant arrays of six present-tense endings per conjugation. A procedure takes a conjugation number and an infinitive, checks the length exceeds the 3-character suffix, copies the stem into a bounded buffer, and a for loop over 1..6 appends each ending and prints the line. A too-short verb prints a specified rejection message instead of conjugating.
Conjugate a Latin verb.summary: All work is bounded string assembly over fixed-size buffers with for loops and constant ending tables, so every index and length check follows from static bounds and a single guard before the copy.

effects.explanation: Prints each matrix, its conjugate transpose and the three classification results with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Every real component is a subtype bounded to about +-1.0e3 and products and sums of at most three terms stay below Float'Last, so finiteness checks discharge from ranges alone.

Matrix-product sums are accumulated in a loop-carried value, so the program either unrolls the fixed 2x2 and 3x3 sums or guards the accumulator against a bound before each addition and rejects out-of-range input visibly.
Assigning a computed product or difference back into the bounded component subtype needs an explicit conversion guarded by a bound test, which nonlinear float reasoning may need extra care to prove.
Nested for loops run over the matrix's own constrained index ranges, so index checks for M(i,j) and its transpose M(j,i) follow from the declared square bounds.
Formatting floats to four decimals for output needs a bounded-buffer float-to-text routine whose own internal checks must be provable (an admitted library operation would be ideal).

Conjugate transpose.approach: Represent a complex number as a record of two bounded Float components and matrices as constrained 2-D arrays of that record (fixed 3x3, with the 2x2 case padded or handled by a second constrained type). Procedures compute the conjugate transpose, the products M*M^H and M^H*M, and tolerance-based comparisons for Hermitian, normal and unitary (M^H*M close to identity, avoiding a general inverse), using for loops over the arrays' own ranges. The embedded example matrices are printed together with Boolean results using Put_Line and a bounded float formatter.
Conjugate transpose.summary: All data is fixed-size with bounded float components and for-loop indexing, so index and finiteness checks follow from types and no recursion, while-loop or inverse is needed; the plausible rating reflects floating-point accumulation in matrix products that needs range guards or unrolling.

effects.explanation: Prints the two longest prime sequences and their differences.

risks.explanation: The sieve's inner while loop and the prime-list append rely on a guard before each write (j <= 999_999 and Count < capacity), with a visible rejection if capacity were exceeded.
Loop-carried streak, best-length and start-index counters are bounded by subtypes limited to the prime-list capacity, and differences of values below 10**6 fit in Integer.
The while loops live in the Main procedure, which has no termination check, and every loop advances a bounded counter.

Consecutive primes with ascending or des.approach: Sieve of Eratosthenes over a constant-bounded Boolean array up to 999,999, then collect primes into a fixed-capacity array of 78,498 entries with a guarded append. A single linear pass tracks the current ascending and descending run lengths from consecutive differences, records the first longest run of each, and then prints each prime and its difference with one Put_Line per element using Integer'Image.
Consecutive primes with ascending or des.summary: All arrays have static bounds, all loops are in a procedure, and every index and counter is bounded by a subtype or a guard just before use, so no annotation is needed. The only non-routine parts are the sieve step index and the counters, which are handled by guards and bounded subtypes.

effects.explanation: Prints each example's hex input, encoded and decoded forms, and any decode error message.

risks.explanation: Output buffer indexes (encoder write position, code-byte position) are loop-carried, so each write is guarded by an explicit capacity check that rejects over-long input with a visible outcome.
The run-length code counter is a subtype 1..255 and is reset or flushed by a guard when it reaches 255, so increments never leave the range.

Length arithmetic (position plus code byte versus packet length) uses Natural-bounded types small enough that sums cannot overflow, and the decoder checks the milestone against the remaining length before copying.
All loops are for loops or while loops inside procedures, so no termination check is generated.
Xor with a non-zero marker needs a modular Byte type with conversions, which is routine once the byte type is a modular 8-bit type.

Consistent overhead byte stuffing.approach: Bytes are a modular 8-bit type stored in fixed-capacity arrays (about 600 bytes) with a length record, and the eleven example packets are built by for loops into embedded arrays. Encode and decode are procedures that walk the input with a running code counter and a code-byte position, flush at zero bytes or at 255, apply Xor with the marker, and the decoder rejects a milestone pointing past the packet end or a missing trailing marker with a printed error and an empty result. A hex-printing procedure writes the first and last five bytes of each array.
Consistent overhead byte stuffing.summary: Everything is bounded array and counter logic that types and just-before guards can discharge, but several loop-carried indexes and the hex formatting need careful guard placement, so it is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The program prints lines confirming that the example eatable items were stored in their food box.

risks.explanation: The box's array of a formal private element type has no default value, so the generic takes an Empty formal object to initialize every slot by aggregate, and flow analysis then sees it fully initialized.
Add writes Items (Count + 1) only after testing Count < Capacity, with Count declared in 0 .. Capacity, so the index and range checks follow from that guard.

Constrained genericity.approach: A generic package Food_Boxes takes a private Food type, a formal procedure Eat (Item : in out Food) that is the eatable constraint and is never called, an Empty filler value and a static capacity, and declares a Box record holding a fixed array of Food plus a count ranged 0 .. Capacity. Add stores an item only when Count < Capacity and reports the outcome through a Boolean out parameter, so a full box is a visible rejection. Main declares an example record type Banana with its own Eat procedure, instantiates Food_Boxes for it, adds a few bananas and prints a line for each accepted or rejected add.
Constrained genericity.summary: Ada's generic formal subprogram expresses the eatable constraint directly without tagged types, and GNATprove analyses each instance, where the only checks are a count increment and index guarded by Count < Capacity, so proof should discharge without annotations.

effects.explanation: The fuzzy circle is printed as 31 lines of text art, with an asterisk at each chosen point.

risks.explanation: The pool counter carried through the nested precalculation loops is bounded only by its type, so a guard such as 'if Pool_Count < Pool_X'Last' before each increment and store discharges it; the guard never fires because the pool has room for all 961 grid points.
The random index uses 'Seed mod U32 (Pool_Count)' inside an 'if Pool_Count > 0' guard, so the divisor is provably nonzero, and the result plus 1 stays within 1 .. Pool_Count.
x*x + y*y is nonlinear, but with both operands in -15 .. 15 the sum is at most 450, and the generator uses a modular type that wraps by definition, so neither can overflow.

Constrained random points on a circle.approach: A subtype Coordinate covers -15 .. 15, and nested for loops collect every grid point with 100 <= x*x + y*y <= 225 into two fixed arrays of 961 entries; the pool counter is guarded before each increment. A 32-bit modular linear congruential generator then picks 100 pool indexes with 'mod Pool_Count + 1', under a guard that Pool_Count is positive. Each chosen point sets an asterisk in an array of 31 blank 31-character String rows, which are printed with Put_Line.
Constrained random points on a circle.summary: Using the precalculated pool avoids an unbounded rejection loop, every operand comes from small declared ranges or modular wraparound, and the only loop-carried value (the pool counter) is made safe by a guard placed just before its use, so all checks should discharge without annotations.

effects.explanation: Prints the three approximations, one per line.

risks.explanation: The backward loop Fraction := B/(A+Fraction) divides by a loop-carried float, so the program must keep Fraction in a bounded float subtype (all coefficients are positive so A+Fraction >= 1) and guard the denominator before dividing, which provers handle only with range guards.
Pi's B(N) = (2N-1)**2 at N up to 10000 is about 4e8, so N is a ranged subtype capping steps and B is computed in a 64-bit integer range so the product cannot overflow.

Float conversion of the integer coefficients and the Fraction result must stay inside the declared float subtype range, which needs explicit bounds such as 0.0 .. 1.0 for the tail since each tail value is at most B/A.
Printing a float needs an admitted float-to-text library operation (or integer scaling to fixed decimals via integer-division digit emission), since Silver has no float formatting yet.

Continued fraction.approach: Write one procedure per series (or a single procedure with a selector) that runs a for-loop in reverse over 1 .. Steps with constant step counts, computing the coefficients A and B from N in ranged integer subtypes and converting them to a bounded float subtype. The accumulator Fraction is declared in a subtype 0.0 .. 1.0 (or 0.0 .. 2.0) and the denominator A + Fraction is guarded to be at least 1.0 before each division. Results are printed with a library float-to-text operation or by scaling to an integer and emitting 14 decimal digits, using Put_Line.
Continued fraction.summary: The task is a fixed-step reverse for-loop with positive coefficients, so termination is trivial and checks follow from ranged subtypes. The nonroutine part is bounding the float accumulator so the division and conversions discharge, and Silver lacking float formatting.

effects.explanation: Prints each test label and its list of convergents as text lines.

risks.explanation: Convergent numerators and denominators, and the quadratic recurrence terms P, Q and P*P, are loop-carried, so each update is preceded by a guard against a fixed bound (for example 10**9 in 64-bit Long_Long_Integer), and exceeding it ends the sequence with a visible 'limit reached' line.
The quadratic recurrence divides by the loop-carried Q, so the loop tests Q /= 0 immediately before each division and reports a visible failure otherwise.
The Euclid loop and the integer square root are while loops, so they live in procedures (which get no termination check), and the convergent loop is a for loop over k.
Partial quotients come from division and are stored in a bounded array indexed by a for-loop counter, with the term count capped at a declared maximum such as 16.
Output text is assembled in a fixed-size bounded buffer with explicit remaining-capacity guards before each append, sized well above the longest line printed.

Continued fraction convergents.approach: Embed the five test cases as constants; rationals use a Euclid while loop in a procedure that stores partial quotients in a fixed array, and quadratic numbers are normalised to (P+sqrt(D))/Q and expanded by the integer recurrence a=(P+isqrt D)/Q, P'=aQ-P, Q'=(D-P'^2)/Q for k=8 terms using an integer-only square root. Convergents h=a*h1+h2 and k=a*k1+k2 are computed in Long_Long_Integer with explicit bound guards before each multiply-add, then formatted with 'Image into a bounded line buffer and printed with Put_Line.
Continued fraction convergents.summary: Everything is integer arithmetic in procedures with for loops or procedure-only while loops, and the loop-carried overflow and zero-division risks are handled by visible guards, so no annotation is needed, but it takes careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints each fraction and its continued fraction terms to standard output.

risks.explanation: The expression (N1 - r) / N2 is discharged because both operands are bounded by a declared 64-bit subtype range of about plus or minus 10**9, so no overflow or range check on the quotient can fail.
mod and / are discharged by the while M2 /= 0 loop condition, which holds just before each division.

Loop-carried M1 and M2 are assigned only values within their declared subtype range (the remainder lies within the bounds of the divisor's range), so the type alone covers them after the first iteration.

Continued fraction/Arithmetic/Construct.approach: Embed the 18 numerator/denominator pairs in a constant array of records with a declared integer range wide enough for them, and loop over it with a for loop. A procedure copies each pair into two range-typed variables and runs a while loop, which is allowed in a procedure, that divides while the denominator is nonzero. It prints the terms with Put and 'Image, using a separator that depends on the term position.
Continued fraction/Arithmetic/Construct.summary: Every check follows from declared integer ranges and the while M2 /= 0 guard immediately before mod and division, and there is no recursion, function loop or annotation need, so proofs should discharge. The remaining effort is Silver surface (integers, ranged types, arrays, loops, Put and 'Image) rather than proof difficulty.

effects.explanation: Prints each expression and its bracketed continued fraction terms.

risks.explanation: The matrix entries are loop-carried through the input and output steps, so each iteration guards that every entry and term stays within a declared bound of 10^9 before computing the products in a 64-bit type, and rejects with a printed message otherwise.
The divisions a/b and a1/b1 are each guarded by a test that the divisor is nonzero immediately before use, and the bounded range excludes the First/-1 overflow case.
Narrowing the computed 64-bit results back to the bounded entry subtype follows from the guard checks made just before, which the provers handle as linear bounds on the products of bounded operands.
The only while loops are in procedures, which get no termination check, and an explicit iteration cap with a visible reject outcome keeps the infinite sqrt(2) source finite.

Continued fraction/Arithmetic/G(matrix n.approach: The state is four bounded integer variables for the matrix, and the source is either a rational (a fixed-capacity array of terms precomputed by Euclid's algorithm with a count) or sqrt(2) (term 1 then repeating 2), selected by an enumeration or record tag with no heap or pointers. A procedure loops: if both denominators are zero it stops, otherwise it outputs a term when the integer quotients agree and both denominators are nonzero, and otherwise ingests the next source term or injects infinity by copying the first column over the second. Output is capped at 20 terms and written by a procedure that formats the integers with 'Image and brackets, and composed cases (such as the nested 1/sqrt(2) then +1, then /2) are run by chaining the transform over a bounded term buffer.
Continued fraction/Arithmetic/G(matrix n.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic with guards just before each product and division, and the embedded demo data stays far below the bounds, so the proofs should discharge but only with carefully placed range guards on loop-carried matrix entries.

effects.explanation: Prints the resulting continued-fraction terms for the example operations.

risks.explanation: The eight matrix coefficients grow with every input term, so they are held in fixed-capacity big integers, or in a 64-bit range with a guard that stops processing with a visible 'term limit reached' outcome when any coefficient exceeds a threshold.
Non-terminating products such as sqrt(2)*sqrt(2) are bounded by a fixed term budget in a for loop or a procedure-only while loop, so no variant is needed.
Floor division of a by b and the comparison of a1/b1, a2/b2 and a/b are each guarded by an explicit b /= 0 test before use, with zero denominators treated as infinity.
Choosing between N1 and N2 by comparing fractions needs cross-multiplication, which stays bounded only if the coefficients are capped by the same threshold guard.

Continued fraction/Arithmetic/G(matrix n.approach: Each continued fraction is a fixed-capacity array of Integer terms (sqrt(2), 1/2 style examples are embedded), and the eight-coefficient NG state is a record of bounded integers updated in a procedure-based main loop with a fixed iteration budget. Each step checks whether the four floor quotients agree (guarding b /= 0), emits a term if so, and otherwise ingests a term from N1 or N2, injecting infinity when a source is exhausted. After each update a magnitude guard stops with a printed outcome if any coefficient would exceed the limit, and terms are printed with Put_Line and 'Image.
Continued fraction/Arithmetic/G(matrix n.summary: The algorithm is iteration over a bounded state with explicit zero-denominator and magnitude guards, so no annotations are required, but the coefficient growth needs careful range guards or fixed-capacity big numbers, which makes discharge plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Each embedded test record and its TSV conversion is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Every read of Line(Pos) and write of Buf(Len) is immediately preceded by an explicit bound guard on the loop-carried Pos or Len, so the check does not depend on an invariant.
The output buffer is fixed-capacity, and a guard before each append (up to two characters) sets an overflow flag that ends the record with a visible rejection message instead of silently truncating.
Pos+1 and Len+2 on loop-carried Integer values need guards (Pos < Line'Last, Len <= Capacity-2) or ranged subtypes so the increments cannot overflow.
The field-scanning while loops live in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and each iteration advances Pos.

Convert CSV records to TSV.approach: The program embeds the thirteen test records as String constants (building the TAB, CR and NUL ones by concatenating Character'Val values) and passes each to a Convert procedure that scans it with a Pos index in a state-machine loop (skip spaces, quoted field with doubled-quote handling, or unquoted field up to a comma, stopping at nonsense). Each output character goes through an Append procedure that guards the fixed-capacity buffer and applies the escape rules (TAB to \t, LF to \n, CR to \r, NUL to \0, backslash doubled before n, r or t), after which the record is printed as input => output via a buffer slice. Over-long input is rejected with a printed message rather than truncated.
Convert CSV records to TSV.summary: The task is pure string scanning with character-level rules and no conflicts, and every index and buffer length is guarded just before use, though several loop-carried positions need careful guards because there are no invariants.

effects.explanation: Prints the DD/MM/YYYY triplet for each of the three embedded example day counts.

risks.explanation: The remaining-days accumulator is a ranged subtype of 0..146096 and is only decremented inside a guard comparing it with the current year or month length, so subtraction stays in range without an invariant.
Year, month and day outputs are initialized to defaults before the search loops, and a found flag guards each assignment so no path leaves them unset.

Month-length table lookups use a for-loop index over the table's own range, and zero-padded digit output indexes a fixed two- or four-character buffer by constants derived from values bounded by subtypes.

Convert day count to ordinal date.approach: Embed the three example day counts in a constant array of a ranged subtype 0..146096; a function decides leap years by mod 4/100/400 on a year subtype 0..399, then a for loop over years subtracts each year's length from a remaining-days variable under a guard and a found flag, followed by a for loop over a month-length table. Digits for DD, MM and the zero-padded YYYY are built in a fixed-length String from division and mod of bounded values, and printed with Put_Line.
Convert day count to ordinal date.summary: All values are bounded by declared subtypes (day count 0..146096, year 0..399, month 1..12), and loops use for-loop indexes with guards before each subtraction, so every check follows from types and local guards with no variant or invariant needed.

effects.explanation: Prints each decimal with its reduced fraction, one line per example.

risks.explanation: Digits are accumulated into a 64-bit value and the parser rejects any input with more than 17 digits, so Value*10+Digit stays in range via a guard before each step.
Euclid's gcd loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and its mod divisor is guarded to be nonzero by the loop condition.
The loop-carried accumulator and scale carry no invariant, so they are typed with ranged subtypes (digit count 0..17, value 0..10**17) and guarded before each update.
Output text is built in a fixed-size buffer sized for two 18-digit numbers plus separators, with the scalar image lengths bounded by the ranged types.

Convert decimal number to rational.approach: Embed the three example decimals as String constants ("0.75", "0.9054054", "0.518518"), and a parsing procedure scans each character, rejecting anything other than digits and one point, accumulating the digits into a ranged integer numerator and counting fraction digits (at most 17) with a guard before each multiply-add. The denominator is built as a power of ten by a for loop over the digit count, a procedure computes the gcd by Euclid's while loop, and both numerator and denominator are divided by it and printed as "N / D" in a bounded buffer, with invalid input printed as a specified rejection line.
Convert decimal number to rational.summary: Every check follows from ranged types and guards before each accumulation, and the only loops with loop-carried state are for loops or a gcd while loop inside a procedure, so no annotation is needed, though the guarded parse and string building need careful shape.

effects.explanation: Prints one formatted duration line per embedded test case with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The output buffer length is loop-carried through appends, so each append is guarded by a capacity test against a 64-character buffer sized well above the longest possible output, with a visible truncation-free reject path otherwise.
The 'Image of the quantities is bounded by a ranged Seconds subtype (for example up to 100_000_000), so the digit count and the slice bounds are statically small.

Convert seconds to compound duration.approach: A ranged Seconds subtype holds each embedded test value (7259, 86400, 6000000), and a procedure splits it with mod and / into a five-element array of quantities (weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds). A for loop over the array index appends, for each non-zero quantity, a separator, the trimmed 'Image digits and the unit suffix into a fixed 64-character buffer with a length counter, guarded before each append, and the main procedure prints the buffer slice with Put_Line.
Convert seconds to compound duration.summary: Every division is by a non-zero literal, quantities are bounded by the ranged input subtype so no overflow can occur, and the only loop-carried value (buffer length) is guarded by capacity tests before each append, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: The hull points are printed as text lines.

risks.explanation: The cross product multiplies coordinate differences, which is discharged by declaring coordinates as a small subtype (about -100..100) so every product and difference fits in Integer.

The hull stack top is a loop-carried counter, so every push is preceded by a guard comparing it to the capacity (2 * point count) with a specified reject outcome, and every Top - 1 or Top - 2 access is preceded by a Top >= 2 test.
The insertion sort's shifting while loop is in a procedure and guards its index with J > 1 before each access, so no invariant is needed.
The output line is assembled with 'Image of each coordinate into a bounded buffer whose size covers the worst case, with a guard before each append.
All while loops live in procedures, which get no termination check, and the cross product is a plain non-recursive function.

Convex hull.approach: The 20 example points are embedded as a constant array of a Point record with coordinates in a small integer subtype, copied into a working array and sorted by X then Y with an insertion sort procedure. Andrew's monotone chain builds the lower and then upper hull on a fixed-capacity array used as a stack, with a Cross function and guarded while loops that pop while Top >= 2 and the turn is not counter-clockwise. The hull is printed one point per line with Put_Line (or a bounded line buffer), rejecting visibly if the stack capacity guard ever fails.
Convex hull.summary: All arithmetic is bounded by a declared coordinate subtype and all array accesses are protected by guards just before use, but several loop-carried stack indices need careful guard placement, so discharge is plausible rather than certain.

effects.explanation: Prints each generation of the blinker as text rows.

risks.explanation: Neighbour reads at I+-1 and J+-1 are discharged by looping only over the interior of a grid with a one-cell dead border, so for-loop bounds make every access static.
The neighbour count is a sum of eight 0..1 cells (at most 8) held in a Natural or 0..8 subtype, so no overflow or range check can fail.

Conway's Game of Life.approach: Use a constant-size two-dimensional array of 0..1 cells with a dead border, embed the blinker as the initial state, and compute each next generation into a second array with for loops over the interior, summing the eight neighbours and applying the rule with if/elsif. A procedure prints each generation row by row using Put for one character per cell and Put_Line to end each row, for three generations, and no input is read.
Conway's Game of Life.summary: All indexing and arithmetic are bounded by static array ranges, for-loop indexes and a 0..1 cell subtype, so no invariant or variant is needed and the work lives in procedures using only for loops.

effects.explanation: Prints the term count and the sequence terms to standard output.

risks.explanation: Euclid's gcd uses a while loop, so it is a procedure with out parameter (procedures get no termination check), keeping the loop out of any function.
The term counter is a ranged subtype 0..50 and is incremented only under an explicit guard count < 50, with a visible stop otherwise.
Sequence array is indexed 1..50 and the predecessor lookups count-1 and count are guarded by count >= 2, and the used-flag array is indexed by values in 1..49 by type.
The mod in gcd is guarded by the while condition b /= 0, so the divisor is provably nonzero.

Coprime triplets.approach: Keep Seq as an array (1..50) of Candidate (subtype 1..49) plus a Used Boolean array indexed 1..49, seeded with 1 and 2; an outer while loop in the main procedure scans candidates 1..49 with a for loop, computing gcd against the last two terms via a gcd procedure (while b /= 0 with mod), appends the first unused coprime candidate, and exits when none is found. After the loop it prints the count and each term by building the line in a bounded String buffer using 'Image-style digit conversion and Put_Line.
Coprime triplets.summary: Every check follows from ranged subtypes, 1..49 bounded loops and a guard before each increment, and the only while loops sit in procedures, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints one result line per input pair with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The Euclid while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed.
The mod by N is guarded by the loop condition N /= 0, which is visible just before the operation.

Coprimes.approach: A Report procedure takes two Natural parameters, runs Euclid's algorithm in a while loop on local Natural variables M and N (T := M; M := N; N := T mod N), then prints "Are A and B coprime? TRUE/FALSE" using Integer'Image and an if on M = 1. Main calls Report five times with the embedded pairs; no input is read, so every execution path is covered by the Natural parameter type.
Coprimes.summary: Euclid's gcd on Natural values with the mod guarded by the loop condition has no overflow, range or division risk, and as a procedure loop it needs no variant.

effects.explanation: The program prints the source and the copied string with Silver_IO.Put_Line to show the copy holds the same contents.

Copy a string.approach: A Main procedure declares a String constant Src ("Hello") and a fixed-length String variable Dest of the same length, assigns Dest := Src to copy the contents, then overwrites Dest with another equal-length literal and prints both to show the source is unaffected. Ada value semantics make every String assignment a content copy, so the "additional reference" case does not apply without access types, which the task only asks to distinguish "where relevant".
Copy a string.summary: Today's Silver already covers this program (String constants, equal-length fixed String assignment and Put_Line), and its only check is a static length check that the declared lengths settle, so it should prove automatically.

effects.explanation: The program reads every character of standard input until end of input.
Each character read is written unchanged to standard output.

Copy stdin to stdout.approach: The Main procedure holds one Character variable and loops with a while loop until an admitted end-of-input test reports no more input. Each iteration reads one character through an admitted stdin operation and writes it with Put, so the copy is exact and needs no buffer or length limit. Read failures have a specified outcome in the library operation (for example end of input or rejection).
Copy stdin to stdout.summary: The only state is one Character with no arithmetic, indexing or accumulator, and a while loop in a procedure gets no termination check, so nothing needs an annotation. The proof burden lies in the admitted stdin and output library contracts, not in the program.

effects.explanation: Prints the cosine results for the four angles.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried x, y and z values are known only by their subtype range after the first iteration, so each update is computed in Long_Long_Integer from a wide-margin subtype and guarded with an explicit range test that rejects out-of-range results.

Range reduction of -9 and 6 into [-pi/2, pi/2] uses a fixed-point constant for pi and a guarded for-loop or while-loop in a procedure that subtracts pi, with the angle subtype bounding every intermediate.
Scaled integer fixed-point arithmetic avoids floating-point provers entirely, at the cost of the shifts being written as division by a power of two from a table.
Iterations use a for loop over a constant count, and any range-reduction while loop lives in a procedure so no variant is required.

CORDIC.approach: Angles and arctangent constants are embedded as integers scaled by 10^9 in a constant array, and a procedure runs a fixed 24-iteration for loop doing the rotate step on x, y, z subtype-bounded Long_Long_Integer values using division by powers of two in place of shifts. Inputs -9, 0, 1.5 and 6 are first reduced into [-pi/2, pi/2] by a guarded loop that tracks a sign flip, then the scaled cosine is converted to a decimal string by integer division and 'Image into a bounded buffer and printed with Put_Line.
CORDIC.summary: All arithmetic is bounded scaled-integer work with for loops and guards before each update, so the checks follow from types and guards, but the carried x, y and z values need careful subtype and guard shaping and the decimal formatting adds string-building effort.

effects.explanation: Prints the string and the vowel and consonant counts.
The string to analyze is taken from the first command-line argument, with invalid input rejected.

risks.explanation: Counters are Natural subtypes bounded by the string's fixed maximum length, so a range subtype capped at that length (or a guard before the increment) discharges the increment checks.
The input is rejected if longer than a documented bound (e.g. 1024), so the output buffer is sized from the bound and concatenation lengths are statically known.

Count how many vowels and consonants occ.approach: Take the first argument via First_Or_Default, reject it if it exceeds a documented maximum length, then a for loop over the string's own index range classifies each character with a case statement on letters (A, E, I, O, U and lowercase as vowels, other letters as consonants), incrementing two counters typed to the length bound. Print the quoted string and the counts using integer 'Image into a bounded line.
Count how many vowels and consonants occ.summary: Every check follows from the for-loop index range over the string, a counter subtype bounded by the documented maximum length, and a length guard on the input, with no loop invariants needed.

effects.explanation: Prints one line per number with its factor product to standard output.

risks.explanation: The trial divisor squared and the divisor increment are bounded by a subtype range and a guard before the increment, so no overflow can occur.
The remaining cofactor is only divided by a divisor of at least 2, so it stays within its subtype after each division.
The divisor is declared in a subtype starting at 2, so division by zero is excluded by type.

Count in factors.approach: An outer for loop counts N over a subtype 1..10_000 (an explicit documented limit in place of the unbounded count), and a procedure factors N by trial division in a while loop with divisor D of subtype 2..101 and a remaining value R. Each prime factor is printed with Put of Integer'Image separated by " x ", with 1 shown as itself, and the while loop exits when D*D exceeds R or the guard on D fails, in which case the leftover R is itself prime.
Count in factors.summary: Every check follows from subtype ranges and guards just before the operations, since trial division with a bounded divisor and a halving cofactor needs no invariant, and the loops sit in procedures so no termination check applies. The only extras are Put and 'Image output, which are not yet in Silver.

effects.explanation: Prints one octal number per line to standard output.

risks.explanation: Each digit is Character'Val (48 + N rem 8) where N is a Natural, so the digit is bounded to 0..7 by the type and the Character range check discharges.

The digit buffer is a fixed 11-character String indexed by a for loop over its own range, and the start-of-number index is found by a for loop over the same range, so index checks follow from the loop bounds.

Count in octal.approach: Loop I over 0 .. Integer'Last (the maximum of the numeric type in use, as the task allows); for each I copy it into a Natural, fill an 11-character String buffer from the right with the octal digits using rem 8 and / 8 over a fixed for loop, and record the first nonzero position (defaulting to the last digit so zero prints as 0). Then print the slice from that position with Silver_IO.Put_Line, one number per line.
Count in octal.summary: Every check follows from Natural and Integer types and for loops over fixed ranges with no loop-carried value needing an invariant, and the digit buffer of 11 characters holds Integer'Last in octal (17777777777), so the program should prove without annotations.

effects.explanation: The program prints the two example counts, 3 and 2, as text lines.

risks.explanation: Each window comparison index (Pos + K - 1) is guarded by an explicit Pos + Pat'Length - 1 <= Text'Length loop condition inside a procedure with fixed-length String parameters, so it discharges.
The match counter and position are subtypes bounded by the fixed text length, and the count increment is guarded by the position bound, so the increment does not overflow.

Count occurrences of a substring.approach: A procedure Count_Substring takes a text String, a pattern String and an out Natural count, and scans left to right with a while loop (allowed in procedures) that keeps a Natural position, comparing the pattern characters by index in an inner for loop with an explicit guard that the window fits and the pattern is non-empty (an empty pattern gives count 0 as a specified outcome). On a full match it increments the count and jumps by the pattern length, otherwise it advances by one; Main calls it on the two embedded examples and prints the results with Integer'Image through Put_Line.
Count occurrences of a substring.summary: All checks are index and range checks on a bounded left-to-right scan guarded by the window-fits test, and since the loop sits in a procedure no termination check is needed, so discharge should be routine.

effects.explanation: Prints only "Ways to make 100 cents with 25, 10, 5 and 1: 242" followed by LF; the optional $1000 result is not produced.

risks.explanation: Total is at most 300 from the static loop ranges. Ways is bounded 0 .. 1155 and the immediate Ways < 1155 guard makes Ways + 1 fit; at most 1155 triples exist, so the guard is harmless to the required count.

Count the coins.approach: Main enumerates Quarters in 0 .. 4, Dimes in 0 .. 10 and Nickels in 0 .. 20. It computes Total := Quarters * 25 + Dimes * 10 + Nickels * 5 with explicit grouping. When Total <= 100 and Ways < 1155 it increments Ways; the remaining cents uniquely determine the number of pennies. It prints the resulting count for 100 cents.
Count the coins.summary: The 5 * 11 * 21 = 1155 triples include every affordable quarter/dime/nickel choice exactly once, so the counter guard cannot skip an iteration that should count. The independently derived required result is 242. The optional $1000 case with two additional denominations is excluded. effects.explanation: Prints the unordered and ordered counts for the three embedded examples.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried DP counts are unbounded by type after the first iteration, so each addition is guarded against a documented cap with a visible overflow outcome, and the count-times-factorial products are guarded the same way against a 64-bit range.
The index sum minus coin value is guarded by an explicit comparison just before each table access, and the subset-size dimension is bounded by the fixed 16-coin capacity.
The target and coin values are declared as bounded subtypes and the example data are embedded, so the DP table bounds are static.

Count the coins/0-1.approach: Embed each example as a fixed-capacity coin array (16 slots) plus a count, and run a 0/1 knapsack DP in a procedure over a table ways(size, sum) with descending sum for-loops, avoiding the exponential recursion. The unordered answer is the total over sizes at the target, and the extra ordered answer is the sum of ways(size, target) times a constant factorial table, with every addition and product guarded against a cap that yields a printed overflow message. Results are printed with 'Image via Put_Line.
Count the coins/0-1.summary: All indices and bounds come from static array ranges and for loops with no recursion or while loops, but the loop-carried counts and factorial products need explicit cap guards to discharge overflow without invariants, so it is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints the ten digit counts to standard output.

risks.explanation: The carry c is loop-carried with no invariant, so a guard before each c + v(i)*10 rejects the run if c exceeds a fixed bound, which a Long_Long_Integer type makes provable at the guard.
The digit index dcount(c) depends on the loop-carried carry, so an explicit guard that c is in 0..9 (otherwise Reject) precedes the increment.
The divisor a is computed as N+1-i from the for-loop index rather than carried, so its range 1..N+1 follows from the loop bounds.

Storing c mod a into the digit-state array needs the element subtype to cover 0..N, which follows from a's bounds, and the incremented counters need a bounded subtype with a guard against exceeding it.

Count the occurrence of each digit in e.approach: Port Ken Thompson's spigot with a constrained Integer array v of fixed size (say 2000, all 1s) and a ten-element counter array pre-seeded with the leading 2; nested for loops compute each digit with the divisor derived from the inner index, guarding the carry before the multiply-add and before indexing the counters. Counts are printed in a procedure with Put and 'Image, rejecting visibly if a guard ever fails.
Count the occurrence of each digit in e.summary: Every check follows from fixed array bounds and loop indexes except the loop-carried carry, which needs two visible guards but no annotation, so discharge depends on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints each puzzle's numbers, target and the found calculation steps, or a no-solution message.

risks.explanation: Stored values are a ranged subtype capped at 10**9 and products are computed in a 64-bit type so the multiply cannot overflow, then a visible guard checks the result against the cap before storing it.

The iterative depth-first search keeps stack depth, pair indices and value counts in ranged subtypes with guards just before each array access, since loop-carried indices have only their type range after the first iteration.
The search is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed; recursion is avoided by using an explicit bounded stack of states.
Division is attempted only after guards that the divisor is nonzero and the remainder is zero, and subtraction only when the result stays positive.

Countdown.approach: Embed three example games (six numbers and a target each, plus one from a deterministic LCG), and run a brute-force search over pairs of the remaining values with +, -, *, / using an explicit fixed-capacity stack of states (value arrays of up to six entries, current pair and operation indices) in a while loop inside a procedure. Each step records the operation in a bounded step array; when a result equals the target the steps are printed using 'Image text, otherwise a no-solution line is printed.
Countdown.summary: Everything is bounded by six numbers and values below 10**9, so overflow, index and division checks follow from subtypes and local guards, but the explicit-stack search with many loop-carried indices needs careful program shape. Nothing requires an annotation, and the unbounded-recursion and heap problems are avoided.

effects.explanation: Prints each cousin prime pair and the final pair count to standard output.

risks.explanation: The pair counter is a loop-carried value, so it is declared as a subtype with range 0 .. 1000 and incremented only under a guard that it is below 1000, which the 995 candidates can never reach.
Is_Prime uses only a for loop over the fixed divisor range 2 .. 31, so the function termination check discharges without a variant.

Cousin primes.approach: An Is_Prime function takes a subtype Natural 0 .. 1003 and tests divisors D in 2 .. 31 with a for loop (31 squared is below 1000, 32 squared is above), returning False on D*D < N with N mod D = 0. The main procedure loops N in 1 .. 995, prints each pair using Integer'Image into Put calls, breaks the line when the guarded Count mod 8 = 0, and prints the final count with Put_Line.
Cousin primes.summary: Every check follows from small declared ranges, fixed for-loop bounds and a guard before the counter increment, so no loop invariant or variant is needed. The program is only a bounded trial-division loop with 'Image output, which is within reach once integers, for loops, functions and Put exist.

effects.explanation: Prints the four solved values w, x, y and z one per line with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Determinant products of four bounded entries are nonlinear, so entries are a declared range (for example -1000..1000) and sums are computed in Long_Long_Integer so the provers can bound every product and sum from types alone.
Each quotient is guarded by an explicit test that the determinant is nonzero, with a visible rejection message otherwise.
Cramer's rule gives a rational result, so the program checks the remainder is zero before dividing and otherwise prints the numerator and denominator, which avoids silently truncating results.
Minor extraction indexes a 4x4 array with for-loop variables over its own ranges, which is routine, but skipping a row or column needs guarded index arithmetic.

Cramer's rule.approach: Use a ranged Integer subtype for a constant 4x4 matrix and right-hand side vector embedded in the program, and compute 4x4 determinants with a function that expands along the first row into explicit 3x3 determinant functions (no recursion). For each column, copy the matrix into a local array, substitute the right-hand side with for loops, compute the numerator, and in a procedure guard the denominator being nonzero before dividing and printing each value via 'Image concatenation.
Cramer's rule.summary: Integer coefficients with ranged types make Cramer's rule a bounded straight-line computation with for loops only, so overflow and division checks should discharge from type ranges and a nonzero-denominator guard, though nonlinear products make provers need careful bounds.

effects.explanation: Prints the checksum as eight hexadecimal digits with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Hex digit lookup converts (crc / 16**k) mod 16 to a 0..15 index, which follows from the modular type range and the constant digit string's bounds.
Message bytes are read by a for loop over the constant string's own range, and the output buffer is filled by a for loop over its own fixed 8-character range.

CRC-32.approach: Embed the 43-character message as a String constant and keep the CRC in an Unsigned_32 modular variable initialised to 16#FFFFFFFF#. An outer for loop over the message range xors in Character'Pos of each byte, and an inner for loop of eight iterations either shifts right by dividing by 2 or does the same then xors 16#EDB88320#, chosen by testing the low bit with mod 2; the result is complemented and rendered into an 8-character buffer from a hex digit constant string.
CRC-32.summary: Every operation is on modular values or bounded for-loop indexes, so no overflow, range or index check can fail, and no loop-carried fact beyond type ranges is needed. The expected output 414FA339 is a fixed visible result.

effects.explanation: Creates an empty (0-byte) file named output.txt in the current directory and another in the filesystem root.
Creates an empty directory named docs in the current working directory and another in the filesystem root.

Create a file.summary: The task creates two empty files and two empty directories, in the current directory and in the filesystem root. That needs only admitted file-creation and directory-creation operations, with a specified outcome (for example a message and exit status) when creation fails, such as a permission error at the root. No fixed Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: Create a new file named TAPE.FILE on the tape device or a tape-mounted path, and write content to it.
The task requires the file to be on magnetic tape, a physical storage device.

Create a file on magnetic tape.summary: The task is to create a file named TAPE.FILE on magnetic tape, which needs a file-creation operation and tape hardware access. No Oracle rule is broken, so Silver could cover it once admitted library operations exist for file creation and tape hardware.

effects.explanation: The two dimensions are taken from the first and second command-line arguments.
The written element is printed, and invalid input gets a rejection message.
Invalid or out-of-range dimensions are rejected through Silver_Arguments.Reject, which sets a failure status.

risks.explanation: The digit-parsing accumulator is guarded before each step (Value > (Max_Dim - Digit) / 10 rejects), so its range check follows from the guard placed just before the update.
Writing one element does not make the whole matrix initialized for flow analysis, so the declaration takes an (others => (others => 0)) aggregate before the element is written and read.
The matrix lives on the stack with a size that depends on input, but a documented subtype Dimension is range 1 .. 100 caps it at a fixed size, which fits the sufficient-memory premise.
Indexing Matrix (Rows, Cols) is safe because Rows and Cols are the upper bounds of the block-declared array, and both have subtype Dimension.

Create a two-dimensional array at runtim.approach: Main reads two arguments and calls a Parse_Dimension procedure on each. The procedure checks every character for a digit with a for loop over the string's range, guards its accumulator against overflow, and returns a Valid flag with a value in subtype Dimension (1 .. 100); any invalid or out-of-range text is rejected with a message. A declare block then declares Matrix : Matrix_Type (1 .. Rows, 1 .. Cols) := (others => (others => 0)) from an unconstrained two-dimensional Integer array type, assigns Matrix (Rows, Cols), and prints it with 'Image; the block's exit releases the array.
Create a two-dimensional array at runtim.summary: Every check comes from the Dimension subtype, the array's own bounds, a static digit test, or an overflow guard placed just before the accumulator update, so no annotation is needed. The runtime-sized stack array stays within a fixed, documented size limit.

effects.explanation: Writes the embedded interpreted-language source to a temporary file and deletes it afterward.
Launches the external interpreter on the generated source (or a compiler/build command), as the task describes.

Create an executable for a program in an.summary: The task asks for an executable that embeds an interpreted program's source and runs it. In a Silver-friendly solution that means writing a constant string to a temporary file, spawning the interpreter and removing the file. That needs the files and processes effects but breaks no fixed Oracle rule.

effects.explanation: The program prints the HTML table text line by line to standard output.

risks.explanation: A deterministic linear generator (or plain sequential values) is kept inside a 0..9999 subtype by reducing with mod before each assignment, so the arithmetic is bounded by the types.
Each row is assembled into a fixed-capacity buffer sized for the worst case of four 4-digit numbers plus tags, so concatenations cannot exceed it.

Create an HTML table.approach: Store a 3-row by 3-column array of a 0..9999 subtype filled with sequential or LCG-derived values, then print the fixed header lines, and for each row loop over columns, appending the 'Image of the row number and each value to a bounded buffer and printing it with Put and Put_Line. The row number column is the for-loop index and every cell uses the same right-aligned td tags. All loops are for loops over the array's own ranges inside the Main procedure.
Create an HTML table.summary: Everything is a fixed-size for-loop over a small constant array with values bounded by a ranged subtype, so all checks follow from types and static bounds. The only new surface is arrays, integer image, bounded string building and non-newline Put.

conflicts.explanation: The task's whole point is to take a machine address, print it, and put a second object at that address so the two names refer to the same memory. That needs address arithmetic and conversion ('Address, System.Storage_Elements.To_Integer) plus an address clause that makes two objects share storage. That is the unrestricted aliasing and address manipulation the Oracle excludes.

effects.explanation: Prints the object's address and the aliased object's value before and after the original is changed.

Create an object at a given address.summary: Excluded. The task requires placing an integer at the address of another object and printing that address, which needs address operations and overlay aliasing. Silver's Oracle bans unsafe constructs such as address arithmetic and unrestricted aliasing.

effects.explanation: Prints the dictionary contents before and after assignment, reset and the rejected-key outcome.

Create an object/Native demonstration.approach: Keys are a fixed enumeration type (for example Key_A, Key_B, Key_C), so no key can be added or removed. The object is a constant array of initial Integer values plus a mutable array of current values, both indexed by the key enumeration. Procedures Assign (key, value) and Delete (key) write the current array, with Delete copying the initial value back, and a for loop over the key type prints the state after each step.
Create an object/Native demonstration.summary: Every index is of the key enumeration type and every value is a bounded Integer, so all checks follow from declared types and the for loop over the enumeration, and no loop-carried facts are needed. Ada has no magic methods, so the program only demonstrates the required fixed-key, reset-on-delete behavior, which the task treats as optional.

effects.explanation: The program prints the formatted result lines to standard output.

risks.explanation: The output buffer position is loop-carried, so each append is guarded by an explicit capacity test that rejects the run visibly instead of truncating.
The format-string scan index advances by one or two inside the loop, so a guard that the next character exists is placed before each lookahead after % or backslash.
Digit extraction and comma insertion use a constant embedded Integer value whose type range bounds the divisions, so the digit loop is a bounded for loop.

Create your own text control codes.approach: The program embeds a constant format string and the argument values (an integer and a text string), and a procedure scans it with a for loop, copying characters into a fixed-capacity output buffer with a length counter. Control codes %d, %s, the new %y (integer with thousands commas) and %z (reversed string) are handled by a case statement, with backslash-n producing a line break by emitting the buffer in separate Put_Line calls. Every append is guarded by a capacity check and unknown codes are copied literally, giving a specified outcome for every input.
Create your own text control codes.summary: The task is a self-written formatting routine over embedded data, which needs only bounded buffers, guarded indexing and simple integer arithmetic, so no annotation should be needed beyond careful guards on the loop-carried buffer position.

effects.explanation: The program prints the cross-compilation explanation as lines of text with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Cross compilation.approach: The task asks only for a prose explanation under a "baked in" or "third party" header, so the program is a parameterless Main that prints that explanation (the header, the toolchain needed, the target and architecture options, runtime and platform-specific notes) as a fixed sequence of Put_Line calls on String literals. There is no input, no loop and no arithmetic, so there is nothing to guard.
Cross compilation.summary: The program is a fixed sequence of Put_Line calls on literals, which Silver already supports, so no run-time check can arise. The task needs no new language surface and has no Oracle conflict.

effects.explanation: The task reads a named CSV file and writes the modified CSV to another file, with specified outcomes for a missing, unreadable or unwritable file.
The input and output file names come from command-line arguments.
Rejected input or I/O failure must be reported with a nonzero exit status.
Rejection reasons are printed to the console.

risks.explanation: Each row sum is a loop-carried accumulator, so each field is limited to a declared range (such as 0..999999999), the field count is capped, and a guard before each addition rejects the row if the sum would exceed a declared sum subtype.
Field scanning uses a loop-carried position in a while loop, so every character access is guarded by a comparison with the line length just before use.
