Queue head and tail are loop-carried values, so each enqueue is guarded by tail < capacity, and since each vertex is enqueued at most once the capacity guard never changes the result; adjacency indexes are ranged subtypes.
Distances and the matching size are subtypes bounded by the vertex count, and increments are guarded by comparisons so the checks discharge from the types alone.
The explicit-stack DFS with per-vertex edge cursors must carry stack depth and cursors as loop-carried values bounded by their subtype ranges, which needs careful program shape but no annotation.

Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm.approach: Represent the graph as a fixed-capacity adjacency matrix or edge array of Boolean/ranged indexes with vertex 0 as NIL, an integer distance array with a sentinel INF, and a fixed-size array queue. The BFS is a procedure with a while loop returning an out Boolean, and the DFS is an iterative procedure with an explicit stack of vertices and per-vertex neighbor cursors, all guarded against capacity. The main procedure runs phases until BFS finds no augmenting path and prints the matching size for the embedded 4x4 example.
Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm.summary: Every array index and counter is bounded by ranged subtypes and capacity guards, so checks are routine, but the recursive DFS must be restructured into an explicit-stack procedure whose loop-carried state needs careful guards, with no annotation required.

effects.explanation: The operator enters latitude, longitude and legal meridian, read as lines of text from standard input.
Prompts, the sine of latitude, the longitude difference and the 13 hour lines are printed.

risks.explanation: Sin, Tan and Arctan come from an admitted elementary-function library, and Tan has no bound the prover can use, so the program must test the Tan result against a fixed magnitude and print a visible 'vertical line' outcome otherwise.

Hour angle 15*H - (Lon - Meridian) and the degree-to-radian scaling stay bounded only because parsed latitude, longitude and meridian are validated to -180..180 (latitude -90..90) and invalid input is rejected.
Parsing decimal text into Float with validation (sign, digits, one point, length limit) needs loop-carried accumulators kept in range by guards or by a bounded digit count.
Float'Image output must fit a fixed-size buffer when building each report line.

Horizontal sundial calculations.approach: A procedure reads three lines from stdin, parses each into a Float with validation and range limits (latitude within -90..90, longitude and meridian within -180..180), and rejects invalid input with a message. It computes the sine of latitude once, then a for loop over H in -6..6 computes the hour angle and the dial line angle, guarding the Tan result by magnitude before multiplying, and prints each line as bounded text.
Horizontal sundial calculations.summary: No contracts or recursion are needed and every loop is a bounded for loop in a procedure, but floating-point trigonometry with no prover-visible bounds on Tan and hand-written decimal parsing make discharge depend on careful range guards.

effects.explanation: The program prints the evaluated polynomial value (128) with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried accumulator product Res * X is nonlinear, so it discharges only because a guard checks that Res is within a documented bound just before each step and declared ranges bound X and every coefficient; if the guard fails, the routine sets Ok to False instead of computing.

Assigning Res * X + Coeffs (I) back to the bounded accumulator subtype needs the guarded bound on Res combined with the coefficient and X ranges, so the bound constants must be chosen so the worst-case result fits the accumulator subtype.

Horner's rule for polynomial evaluation.approach: Coefficients are an unconstrained array of a bounded coefficient subtype (for example -1000 .. 1000), and the example data (-19, 7, -4, 6) with x = 3 is embedded. A Horner procedure walks the array's own range in reverse with a for loop and returns the value and an Ok flag through out parameters; before each multiply-add it checks that the accumulator is within a documented bound, and otherwise it sets Ok to False and leaves the accumulator unchanged. Main prints the value with 'Image, or prints a visible "result exceeds limit" message when Ok is False.
Horner's rule for polynomial evaluation.summary: Index checks discharge from the reverse for loop over Coeffs'Range. The only non-routine checks are overflow and range checks on the loop-carried accumulator's nonlinear multiply-add, and a guard on the accumulator placed just before each step makes them provable without an invariant.

effects.explanation: Prints the Race 4 result table and the winner's time to standard output.

risks.explanation: The bubble-sort inner loop reads element y+1, discharged by choosing for-loop bounds of the form 1 .. N-1 over a constrained array type with no loop-carried index.
Ratings are small integers in a declared subtype (about -1000..1000) updated only by constant offsets, so all additions stay within Integer.

Horse racing.approach: Embed the nine past-form ratings and the four adjustments as integer pound values (the 0.4 and 0.2 per-tenth-second terms are whole pounds), store ten horses in a constrained array of records (letter, rating, colt flag), and bubble-sort descending with for loops and a swap through a temporary. Print each row from integer data: positions with "=" for ties, weights chosen by sex, distances as half-length integers formatted as N.0 or N.5, and the winner's time computed in tenths of seconds and split into minutes and seconds with / and mod.
Horse racing.summary: All data is fixed and small, so every arithmetic result is bounded by declared ranges and every array index comes from for-loop ranges over the array, with no recursion, while loops or floating point needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the word size and the endianness.

Needs system information about the host: its word size and byte order. Ada gets these from the static constants System.Word_Size and System.Default_Bit_Order, so Silver would have to admit those as specified platform facts.

Host introspection.summary: Included. The task only prints two host properties, and Ada exposes both as compile-time constants in package System (Word_Size and Default_Bit_Order). SPARK allows reading these constants, and doing so needs no run-time introspection, unsafe code or annotations.

effects.explanation: The program has to ask the operating system for the host name, so it needs an admitted library operation that queries system information, with a specified outcome when the lookup fails.
The program prints the host name it finds.

Hostname.summary: The task asks only to find the name of the host the program is running on. A Silver program can do this by calling an admitted library operation that returns the host name as a bounded string and then printing it, so no Oracle rule is broken. What Silver lacks today is a system-information effect, not anything a fixed rule forbids.

effects.explanation: The accumulator is printed as text art, one line per rho row, so no image file or display is needed.

risks.explanation: Rho is computed as x*cos + y*sin with ranged coordinates and a scaled integer table, so the products and sum are bounded by types and fit in Integer.
The computed rho row index is guarded by an explicit range comparison just before the accumulator update, and the guard is never taken for in-image pixels because the table scale bounds rho.
Accumulator counts are ranged and incremented only when below the type maximum, which is at least the pixel count of the embedded image, so the saturation guard never changes a real result.

Hough transform.approach: Embed a small bitmap (for example 32 by 32 rows of '#' and '.') as a constant array of equal-length Strings, and a constant table of 180 integer cosine and sine values scaled by 1000 in place of floating point. Nested for loops over the image's own index ranges and the angle range increment a two-dimensional ranged-count accumulator for each dark pixel, guarding the computed rho row index before indexing. A final nest of for loops maps each accumulator cell to a density character in a fixed-length row buffer and prints each row with Put_Line.
Hough transform.summary: All loops are for loops over array ranges, and every arithmetic result is bounded by ranged types and scaled integer tables, so overflow and index checks follow from types plus one guard before the accumulator update. Floating point and image-file I/O are avoided, leaving bounded integer work whose discharge depends on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prompts, the elapsed and remaining sand state, and the final result are printed.
The one-player game reads the player's move lines (flip 4, flip 7, wait) from standard input.

risks.explanation: Elapsed time and sand counters are ranged integers with a capped move count, and each update is guarded by a comparison just before it.

Hourglass puzzle.approach: The program keeps elapsed time and the sand remaining in the upper bulb of each of the two hourglasses as bounded integers, and a procedure reads one command line at a time from standard input in a while loop capped at a fixed number of moves. Each command (flip 4, flip 7, or wait until the next glass runs out) advances time by a guarded amount and updates the sand state, while unrecognised commands or end of input print a rejection outcome. The game ends with a success message when exactly 9 minutes have been measured between a start and a stop command.
Hourglass puzzle.summary: All state is small bounded integers updated by guarded transitions inside a procedure-based while loop with a fixed move cap, so every check follows from types and guards without invariants.

effects.explanation: The program has to fetch a resource over HTTP from a URL, so it needs an admitted network/HTTP client operation with specified failure outcomes.
The fetched resource content is printed to the console.

HTTP.summary: The task only asks to fetch a URL over HTTP and print what comes back. A future Silver could do this through an admitted HTTP client library operation that specifies what happens on failure, so no fixed Oracle rule is broken. What is missing today is the network effect.

effects.explanation: The program has to send an HTTPS GET request over TLS to https://www.w3.org/ (certificate checking is recommended) and receive the response.
The program has to print the fetched resource to the console.

HTTPS.summary: The task asks for an HTTPS GET of a fixed URL and printing the response body. That needs network access plus console output. No fixed Oracle rule is broken: a future admitted HTTPS client library whose failure outcomes are specified, writing into a bounded buffer, would be enough. So this task is a candidate, waiting on a network effect.

effects.explanation: The task requires making an HTTPS GET request to a remote host, which needs network access through an admitted library operation with specified failure outcomes.
The task requires printing the response body to standard output.

HTTPS/Authenticated.summary: The task asks only for an authenticated HTTPS request and display of the response. A Silver-friendly version would use fixed host, path and credential constants, one HTTPS GET through an admitted network library, and a bounded buffer read in a loop that prints the bytes. Nothing in the task requires a run-time error, annotations, exceptions or unsafe code, so the only gaps are the network effect and the console output. The existing FreeBASIC solution uses WinINet, but that is evidence only and does not change the analysis.

effects.explanation: The program must open an HTTPS (TLS) connection to a web server and present a client certificate during the handshake, which needs an admitted TLS/HTTP client library operation with specified failure outcomes.
The client certificate and private key the program presents are normally loaded from named PEM/PKCS#12 files.
The program shows that the connection worked by printing the server's response or a status message.

HTTPS/Client-authenticated.summary: The task needs an HTTPS connection with a client certificate, and Silver does not have network access yet. That makes it an effect, not a fixed-rule conflict. A future admitted TLS client operation that takes the certificate and key files and has specified failure outcomes would let a Silver program connect, check the result and print the response, with no exceptions, annotations or unsafe code.

effects.explanation: The program prints one line per distinct character giving its Huffman code.

risks.explanation: Merged-node weights are loop-carried sums, so they are stored in a bounded Weight subtype and a guard before each addition rejects totals above the documented limit (far above the 39-character example).
Node count and the min-search indexes are loop-carried, so each is a ranged subtype with a guard before every increment or array access against the fixed node capacity.
The merge loop and the leaf-to-root walks are while loops, which is acceptable only because they sit in procedures, which get no termination check.
The code buffer is filled while walking leaf to root, so a guard on depth against the buffer capacity precedes each write and rejects the input if exceeded.
Parent, weight and active arrays are fully initialized with aggregates before the loops use them.

Huffman coding.approach: The program embeds the example string, counts character frequencies in a 256-entry weight array, and builds the tree in fixed arrays (weight, parent, bit, active flag) of capacity 2*256 nodes. A while loop in a procedure repeatedly scans for the two lowest-weight active nodes (deterministic tie-break by lowest index), creates a parent node with guarded weight addition, and finally for each used character walks parent links to the root into a bounded bit buffer, then prints the reversed code as a line. Capacity, weight limit and depth checks reject with a specified outcome rather than altering results.
Huffman coding.summary: Replacing the pointer tree and priority queue with index arrays and a linear-scan minimum search makes every check follow from ranged subtypes and guards, with only the loop-carried weights, counts and depths needing careful guarding and no annotations.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 50 humble numbers on one line and the per-digit-count table, one row per line.

risks.explanation: Candidate products 2h to 7h are computed on a 64-bit range type whose element bound is far below the type limit, so the multiplications by constants discharge, and a value is stored only after a guard comparing it to the digit limit.

The four merge pointers are loop-carried in a while loop with no invariant, so each is declared with the array's index subtype and its increment is guarded by a comparison with the array's last index, giving a visible stop outcome rather than a silent clamp.
Digit counting by repeated division by 10 and the per-digit counter increments rely on the digit-count array index type and counter types having ample range, with a guard before each increment.
All loops live in procedures, which get no termination check, so no variant is needed.

Humble numbers.approach: Compute humble numbers with the standard four-pointer merge (multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7) into a fixed-capacity array of a 64-bit range type, in a while loop inside a procedure, stopping once the next value exceeds 10^9 (about 5200 terms, with the array sized with margin). Then tally each value's decimal digit count into a small array indexed by digit count, using a bounded division loop. Finally print the first 50 numbers on one line and one row per digit count using integer-to-text conversion into bounded buffers, with guards before every pointer advance and array store.
Humble numbers.summary: Everything is bounded arrays, ranged integers and procedure while loops, so checks follow from types and guards just before each use; the main care is guarding the loop-carried merge pointers and the stored values without invariants.

effects.explanation: Prints room descriptions, sensed hazard messages, prompts and win or loss outcomes.
Reads the player's move or shoot commands and target room numbers line by line, with a specified outcome for invalid or ended input.

risks.explanation: Room numbers are a 0..19 subtype and the adjacency table is a constant 20x3 array, so lookups are safe, but typed player input must be parsed and range-guarded before conversion to a room.
The deterministic LCG multiplies a seed held in a bounded range subtype followed by mod, so a seed range small enough to keep the product within Integer discharges it by types alone.

The main game loop and the rejection-sampling placement loops are while loops, which are acceptable only inside procedures (no termination check), so placement and play stay in procedures and avoid functions with loops.
Game state (positions, arrow count, seed) is held in local variables of Main and every one is assigned before first use, passed as in out parameters to helper procedures.
Command lines and numeric tokens are read into bounded String buffers with explicit length guards, and over-long or non-numeric input is rejected with a printed message.

Hunt the Wumpus.approach: The program keeps the dodecahedron as a constant 20x3 array of room numbers and the game state (player, Wumpus, two bats, two pits, arrows) as ranged variables, with distinct hazard rooms chosen by a deterministic LCG and scan-or-resample loops in procedures. A while loop in a procedure reads one command per line from stdin, parses move or shoot and a validated room number, rejects non-adjacent or malformed targets with a message, and applies the rules (Wumpus or pit loss, bat transport to an empty room, shot hit or miss with a 75 percent LCG-driven Wumpus move, arrow exhaustion loss); end of input ends the game with a specified message.
Hunt the Wumpus.summary: Every array access is by a ranged room subtype, arithmetic is bounded by types, and all loops live in procedures, so checks should discharge from types and guards, but the pile of loop-carried game state, input parsing and the PRNG need careful shape. No annotation is required and the Ada solution's exception handlers are replaced by explicit input validation.

effects.explanation: The program reads the unixdict.txt word list from a named file line by line.
It prints the four counts and the plausibility verdicts.
Unreadable files, overlong lines or too many words are rejected with a visible failure status.

risks.explanation: The four counters are loop-carried across the line-reading loop, so each increment is preceded by a guard against a documented maximum word count and exceeding it rejects the input visibly.
Each line is held in a fixed-capacity buffer with a length, and the scan uses a for loop whose upper bound is the length minus 2, so the three-character window indexes stay in range.
Lines longer than the buffer capacity are rejected with a specified outcome rather than truncated.
The plausibility test compares ie against 2 times ei using counters bounded well below the integer limit so the multiplication cannot overflow.

I before E except after C.approach: A procedure reads unixdict.txt through an admitted line-reading library operation into a bounded String buffer plus length, lowercases via Character comparisons, and a for loop over window start positions tests each 'cie', 'cei', 'ie' and 'ei' occurrence, setting per-word Boolean flags so each word counts once. Counters are ranged-subtype Naturals with a guard-then-reject check before each increment, and a final procedure compares counts with integer multiplication by 2 and prints counts and verdicts using integer image conversion. The stretch goal is left out.
I before E except after C.summary: All checks follow from bounded buffers, for-loop indexes over the line length and guarded counters, with no annotation needed because the loop-carried counters are bounded by an explicit visible rejection limit.

effects.explanation: Prints the shortest routes, the Floyd routes, the longest shortest route and the unreachable and farthest cells.

risks.explanation: Floyd relaxation sums two distances held in a subtype capped at an Infinity sentinel and only relaxes when both are below it, so the sum fits in Integer and any improved value is below the cap.
Cell lookups use row and column subtypes 0..22, with explicit guards that x + n*dx and y + n*dy lie in 0..22 before indexing, which is nonlinear but bounded by the digit range 0..9.

Dijkstra with unit steps is done as a breadth-first search in a procedure over a fixed-capacity queue sized to the 529 cells, and path reconstruction follows predecessors with a step counter capped at the cell count, so no loop needs a variant.

The Floyd triple loop (about 12 million iterations over 23x23 cells squared) is for loops over array index ranges with loop-carried distance and next-hop arrays whose element subtypes keep every store in range.
Route text is built in a bounded buffer sized for the longest route, with a guard before each append that rejects or truncates visibly when capacity would be exceeded.
All distance, predecessor and next-hop arrays are filled by aggregate or full for loops before use, so flow analysis can see them initialized.

I'm a software engineer, get me out of h.approach: The map is embedded as 23 String constants decoded into a 0..22 by 0..22 array of digit subtype 0..9 (outside-disc cells marked blocked), with all-pairs data in distance and next-hop arrays over cell indices. Part 1 runs a unit-cost breadth-first search (Dijkstra with equal weights) from HQ in a procedure using a fixed ring queue and predecessor array, printing all shortest routes to zero cells; Part 2 runs a triple for-loop Floyd with a sentinel Infinity and saturation guard, then reconstructs routes with a bounded while loop and finds the longest shortest route and unreachable or farthest cells by scans.
I'm a software engineer, get me out of h.summary: Every check follows from bounded index subtypes, for loops and explicit range guards, with no recursion or function loops, but the loop-carried distances, bounded route-string building and nonlinear jump arithmetic need careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints a valid or not-valid line for each embedded IBAN via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The compacted buffer is a fixed 34-character array and the count is incremented only behind a guard Count < 34, with longer input rejected as invalid.
The running remainder is a subtype 0 .. 96 so Num * 100 + 35 is bounded and the mod 97 result restores the range without any loop invariant.

IBAN.approach: Embed the sample IBANs as String constants, and a procedure copies the non-space characters, upper-cased through a case statement on Character ranges, into a 34-character buffer with a guarded count, rejecting any other character or overflow of 34. It then checks the country code and length against a constant table of two-letter codes and lengths, rotates the first four characters to the end by index arithmetic, and folds each character into a remainder in 0 .. 96 with a for loop, accepting when the remainder is 1; the result is printed with Put_Line.
IBAN.summary: Every check follows from a fixed-size buffer, a guarded count, a bounded remainder subtype and for-loop indexes, so no annotation is needed; the 34-character limit is a documented resource limit that rejects longer input visibly.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 10 iccanobif primes, one per line.

risks.explanation: The Fibonacci recurrence a+b is loop-carried, so it is guarded by an explicit upper limit on both operands before each addition, with the loop stopping when the limit is hit.
The digit-reversal accumulator r*10+d is loop-carried and is guarded by checking r against a limit just before the multiplication, which cannot trigger for numbers up to about 10^17.
Trial division uses the divisor test d <= n / d instead of d*d <= n so no product can overflow.
Primality and reversal loops are while loops, so they live in procedures with out parameters rather than functions to avoid needing a variant.

Iccanobif primes.approach: Main iterates Fibonacci numbers F(1..) in a guarded for loop over a bounded index with two Long_Long_Integer-range variables, and for each value calls a reversal procedure (while loop over digits with a guarded accumulator) and a trial-division procedure returning a Boolean out parameter. Each hit is printed with Put_Line of the integer image and counted until 10 are found; the loop ends at the count, and the guard-limit exit has a visible outcome. The 10 required primes all come from Fibonacci numbers up to F(26), well inside 64 bits, and the stretch (digit counts of 15 more, needing thousands of digits) is treated as optional and omitted.
Iccanobif primes.summary: The required 10 primes need only Fibonacci values below 10^6 and plain 64-bit arithmetic, so every check follows from types and guards placed just before additions and multiplications. The loop-carried accumulators need explicit limit guards but no annotation, and the while loops sit in procedures, so the outlook is plausible.

effects.explanation: The matrix size is read from the first command-line argument, since the task says the size is known at run-time.
The resulting matrix is printed row by row to standard output.
An invalid or out-of-range size argument is rejected with a specified failure outcome.

risks.explanation: The parsed size must be checked against the fixed capacity 1..16 by an explicit guard before it is converted to the size subtype, with out-of-range input rejected visibly.
The matrix is fully initialized by an others => 0 aggregate before the diagonal loop, so flow analysis passes; the loop writes only in-range indexes of the for-loop variable.

Identity matrix.approach: Declare a bounded square array type Matrix (1..16, 1..16) of a 0..1 subtype, parse the first argument to a size N, and reject it with a visible message unless 1 <= N <= 16. Initialize the matrix to all zeros with an aggregate, set the diagonal with a for loop over 1..N, then print the top-left N-by-N block with nested for loops using Put per element and Put_Line at row ends.
Identity matrix.summary: Every check is an index or range check on for-loop variables bounded by a guarded N, with no loop-carried values or recursion, so proofs should discharge automatically. The only new library need is validated integer parsing of the argument, which the Oracle's admitted operations must supply.

effects.explanation: Prints the sets of characters valid in identifiers with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The write position in the fixed 64-character buffer is a loop-carried count, so each append is guarded by testing the count against the capacity just before the store and the increment.
The slice Buffer (1 .. Count) is safe because Count is declared Natural range 0 .. 64 and the buffer covers 1 .. 64.

Idiomatically determine all the characte.approach: A procedure loops with a for loop over every value of the Character type and classifies each one with plain comparisons (letters a-z and A-Z, digits 0-9, underscore) for the three sets (first, middle, last position). Each matching character is appended to a 64-character String buffer behind a guard on a bounded count, and the buffer slice is then printed with Silver_IO.Put_Line under a label that names the character set (ASCII/Latin-1 as the platform's Character type).
Idiomatically determine all the characte.summary: All checks come from the for-loop index range, the declared count range and a capacity guard before each append, with no while loops or recursion, so proofs should discharge automatically. The set of identifier characters is the fixed Ada rule applied to every Character value, which is a faithful, bounded program.

effects.explanation: Prints the lowercase and uppercase letter lines with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Each buffer index is computed from the loop character's position minus the position of the range's first letter, which is safe because the loop variable is typed to the subtype Lower or Upper so the index lies in 1..26.

Idiomatically determine all the lowercas.approach: Declare subtypes Lower and Upper as Character ranges 'a'..'z' and 'A'..'Z', and two 26-character String variables initialised to a placeholder. A for loop over each subtype's range stores each letter at index Character'Pos(C) - Character'Pos(range first) + 1, then Put_Line prints "Lower: " & Lower_Buffer and "Upper: " & Upper_Buffer. No input is read, so there is no invalid-input path, and the character positions are derived from the language's own Character type rather than hardcoded for ASCII.
Idiomatically determine all the lowercas.summary: Every check (loop bounds, buffer index, Character'Val-free arithmetic) follows from the subtype ranges and a for loop over a static range, so proofs should discharge without annotations. The only new Silver surface is Character subtypes, for loops and String indexing, with no recursion, no floating point and no loop-carried values.

effects.explanation: Prints the 65 idoneal numbers, one per line or several per line, to standard output.

risks.explanation: Products a*b and c*(a+b) are nonlinear, but a, b and c are subtypes of 1..1850 so the sum is at most about 10 million, well inside Integer, and the provers handle these bounded products.
The Boolean marker array is indexed by the sum only after an explicit guard that the sum is at most 1850, so the index check follows from the guard just before the store.

Idoneal numbers.approach: Declare a subtype N_Range is Integer range 1 .. 1850 and a Boolean array Representable indexed by it, initialized to False. Nested for loops over a, b and c (each N_Range, with guards skipping unless a<b<c) compute s = a*b + b*c + a*c in Integer, and only when s <= 1850 set Representable (s) to True; then a final for loop prints every n whose flag is False via Put_Line of the Image text. All loops are plain for loops in the parameterless Main procedure, so no variants or invariants are needed.
Idoneal numbers.summary: Every check follows from the 1..1850 subtypes, the bounded products and the explicit guard before the array store, and all loops are for loops in a procedure, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: The filtered grayscale image is printed as rows of numbers (text PGM-style) and optionally the original for comparison.

risks.explanation: Each output pixel is a nine-term sum written as one unrolled expression over Pixel (0..255) and Coefficient (-16..16) subtypes so the bound follows from types, avoiding a loop-carried accumulator that would lose its range.
Neighbor reads at the image border are guarded by explicit row and column comparisons before indexing (out-of-image neighbors count as zero), and row/column loops run over the array's own ranges.
The scaled sum is clamped to 0..255 by explicit if tests before conversion back to Pixel, so the narrowing conversion discharges.
The kernel divisor is a constant subtype of positive integers (1..64), so division by zero cannot occur.
The conversion of pixels and coefficients to a wider working range for the product relies on solver handling of small nonlinear products, which is routine given the tight type bounds.

Image convolution.approach: Embed a small constrained 2-D array of Pixel (0..255) as the test image and a 3x3 constant array of integer coefficients plus a positive divisor (for example sharpen and box blur), and write a Filter procedure that reads the input image and writes a separate output image. For each pixel, guarded neighbor reads (zero outside the image) feed one unrolled nine-term weighted sum, which is divided by the divisor, clamped to 0..255 by if statements, and stored; the result is printed row by row with Put and Put_Line.
Image convolution.summary: Every check follows from small declared ranges, border guards placed just before indexing, and an unrolled nine-term sum with no loop-carried accumulator, so no annotation is needed; the main care is keeping integer kernel coefficients (real-valued kernels replaced by scaled integers) tightly bounded.

effects.explanation: The task asks for a continuously generated 320x240 black and white noise image with a frame rate shown. It does not require a window. A Silver-friendly solution writes each frame (or a bounded number of frames) as a PBM/PGM image file.
The frames-per-second figure is printed as text.
FPS needs elapsed time measured against a clock.

Image noise.summary: The task needs a 320x240 bounded pixel array filled from a deterministic pseudo-random generator, written to an image file, with FPS measured from the clock and printed. No fixed Oracle rule is broken. Bounded loops, fixed-size arrays and modular-integer arithmetic suffice, and a bounded frame count can stand in for running forever.

effects.explanation: The conversion tables and round-trip results are printed as text lines.

risks.explanation: Real and imaginary parts are subtypes bounded to about plus or minus 1000, so the carry adjustment and the powers-of-2i weights (at most 2**12 times digit 3) stay within Integer, but the nonlinear multiplications need those type bounds for the provers.
The digit is the result of a mod-4 adjustment into 0..3 and is converted to a Character by 'Pos arithmetic, which the provers can discharge only with a guard or the declared digit subtype.
Digit positions are written by a for loop over a fixed number of positions (12) so the index always lies in the array bounds and no while loop with a computed index is needed.
Using for loops with a fixed digit count avoids any variant, and the conversion is a procedure, so no termination check arises.
Inputs outside the supported range or not representable in the fixed digit count must be rejected visibly with a printed message, which is a specified outcome and not a silent narrowing.

Imaginary base numbers.approach: Embed the 1..16 and negated integer and imaginary test values, represent each Gaussian integer as two bounded Integer subtypes, and encode it into a fixed array of twelve base-2i digits (0..3) using a for loop that repeatedly takes a mod -4 remainder with carry correction on the real and imaginary parts at alternating positions. A guard rejects values outside the range or with a nonzero residual after the digits are used up, then a decoding procedure sums digit times (2i)**k using a rotating weight, and the strings are built in a bounded buffer and printed with Put_Line. The fractional stretch goal is covered by allowing an odd imaginary part to produce a single digit after the point.
Imaginary base numbers.summary: All arithmetic is bounded-integer work in a procedure with fixed-count for loops, so every check follows from subtype ranges and a few input guards, though the carry and weight arithmetic need careful range shaping.

effects.explanation: Prints each converted value with a label to standard output.

risks.explanation: Narrowing explicit conversions between the declared integer types are applied only to constants or after an explicit if guard on the value's range, so each range check follows from the guard.

Implicit type conversion.approach: Declare a chain of integer subtypes of increasing size (for example 8-bit, 16-bit, Integer, 64-bit) plus a distinct derived type, then assign values up the subtype chain implicitly and across the derived type with explicit conversions, printing each with a label via 'Image. The user-defined conversion is a small function between two types, and any narrowing step is guarded by an if comparison before the conversion.
Implicit type conversion.summary: Ada has few implicit conversions (literals and subtype widening), so a faithful demonstration uses only constants, subtype ranges and guarded explicit conversions that GNATprove discharges from types and guards, with no loops or recursion.

effects.explanation: The included package's procedure prints a line to show that the other file's code was used.

Include a file.approach: A small package in its own source file declares one parameterless procedure that calls Silver_IO.Put_Line with a fixed message, and Main withs that package and calls the procedure. There are no loops, arithmetic or data, so control flow is a single call, and the only new capability needed is multi-file compilation units with user-defined packages.
Include a file.summary: The program only needs a with clause on a user package in another file and one call to a procedure that prints a literal, so every check is trivial. Silver needs user packages and procedures plus multi-file support, and nothing in the Oracle conflicts with this.

effects.explanation: Prints the first fifty inconsummate numbers and the one thousandth.

risks.explanation: The digit sum is zero only for N = 0, so the loop starts at 1 and a guard Sum > 0 precedes mod and / to discharge the check.

Counters and the digit sum are bounded by loop ranges and ranged digit subtypes, so no loop-carried unbounded value exists; the 400000 bound is documented as sufficient since sum is at most 54 and ratios are capped at 7000.
The array index N / Sum is guarded by a comparison with 7000 immediately before the assignment.

Inconsummate numbers in base 10.approach: Embed a Boolean array Consummate(0 .. 7000); a for loop over N in 1 .. 400000 computes the digit sum by six unrolled digit extractions (each (N / 10**k) mod 10 with a ranged subtype), so the sum is bounded without a loop-carried accumulator. When N mod Sum = 0 (Sum is at least 1 for N at least 1, guarded), the ratio N / Sum is marked if it is at most 7000. A second for loop scans 1 .. 7000 counting unmarked entries, printing the first 50 and the 1000th (6996) with Put_Line of a bounded image string.
Inconsummate numbers in base 10.summary: All checks follow from for-loop ranges, ranged digit subtypes and a guard before the array index, with no loop-carried unbounded values, so proofs should discharge automatically. The only extra needs are integer arithmetic, arrays, loops and number-to-text output.

effects.explanation: The program prints the table of increasing gaps.

risks.explanation: Counters and the gap sum are held in a 64-bit Long_Long_Integer with declared ranges far below its limits, and the counter increments are preceded by explicit limit guards.
The digit sum starts at zero but n >= 1 means the loop adds at least one digit, so a guard 'if sum > 0' just before the divisibility test makes the mod check discharge.
The digit-sum loop is a bounded for loop over at most 10 digits inside a procedure, and the outer search is a for loop, so no variant is needed.

Increasing gaps between consecutive Nive.approach: A main procedure runs a for loop over n from 1 to a fixed documented limit (about 150 million, enough for the ten millionth Niven number) in a 64-bit ranged subtype, computing each digit sum with a bounded inner for loop of 10 digit extractions using mod and /, and testing divisibility under a sum > 0 guard. It keeps previous, largest gap, gap index and Niven index as ranged variables, printing a row via Put plus a small digit-by-digit number formatter into a bounded buffer whenever a gap exceeds the previous maximum, with an explicit guard before incrementing counters.
Increasing gaps between consecutive Nive.summary: Every check follows from declared ranges, a bounded digit loop and for-loop indexes, with only simple guards before counter increments and the division, so proofs should discharge without annotations. The main new surface is integer arithmetic with mod and /, loops, and numeric text output.

effects.explanation: The incremented numeric string is written with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Character'Val(Character'Pos(C)+1) is only evaluated after an explicit guard that C is between '0' and '8', so the result stays a digit and the check discharges.
Loop indexes run over the string's own fixed range and the result buffer is one character longer, so every index follows from static bounds.

Increment a numerical string.approach: The numeric string "12345" is a fixed 5-character String constant copied into a 6-character result buffer, and a reverse for loop over its indexes adds one with a Boolean carry, turning '9' into '0' and otherwise stepping the digit. A leading-digit overflow such as "99999" is handled by writing '1' into the extra leading slot; a non-digit character takes a visible rejection branch that prints a message. The result is printed with Put_Line after trimming a leading blank.
Increment a numerical string.summary: Every check comes from fixed string bounds, a Boolean carry and a digit guard placed just before each character arithmetic step, so no loop invariant is needed. The program avoids Integer'Value, which would raise on bad text, and uses digit-wise increment instead.

effects.explanation: Prints each demonstrated list, its rank and the recovered list, plus unrank of 0 to 10.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried rank accumulator is only bounded by its type, so each step is preceded by an explicit guard (rank <= (Limit - x) / M) that rejects the list with a printed message instead of silently truncating.
Unrank's index into the output array needs a count guard against the fixed capacity, which a while loop in a procedure can supply with an explicit check that stops with a visible capacity message.
The unrank while loop is inside a procedure so no termination check is generated, and it is also bounded by the capacity guard.
Building output lines of computed length in a bounded buffer needs explicit capacity guards before each append.

Index finite lists of positive integers.approach: Lists are held as a fixed-capacity array of elements in 1..M plus a length, and rank uses bijective base-M numeration (rank := rank*M + x) in a for loop, with a guard before each step that rejects the list if the result would exceed a 64-bit limit, which is a documented resource limit. Unrank is a procedure with a while loop that repeatedly takes x := (n-1) mod M + 1 and n := (n-1)/M, filling the array in reverse under a capacity guard. The demonstration uses embedded example lists (random choice replaced by a deterministic pseudo-random or fixed data) and the extra-credit table of unrank(0..10), printed with Image-based text building.
Index finite lists of positive integers.summary: Bijective numeration needs only bounded integer arithmetic and loops, with every overflow and capacity check dischargeable by a guard just before the operation and a visible rejection outcome, but the loop-carried accumulator and output-buffer building make it depend on careful program shape. The "arbitrarily large" requirement is met only up to a documented fixed bound, which the Oracle permits as a resource limit.

effects.explanation: Prints the returned largest positive float with Put_Line.

Infinity.approach: A function Sup returns Float'Last, since SPARK floating point is proved finite and so has no infinity, which is the task's fallback branch of returning the largest positive float. Main calls Sup and prints "Supremum" followed by Float'Image of the result, with no loops, guards or input.
Infinity.summary: The task needs no arithmetic, loop or input, only returning and formatting the constant Float'Last, so every check is trivial once floating-point constants and float-to-text formatting exist.

effects.explanation: The Main procedure prints one confirmation line with Silver_IO.Put_Line so the program has a visible outcome.

Inheritance/Multiple.approach: Main declares Camera as a tagged null record, Mobile_Phone as an interface, and Camera_Phone as a type that derives from Camera and Mobile_Phone with a null record extension. The task needs no operations, so the program has no data and no control flow, and it prints one confirmation line with Silver_IO.Put_Line.
Inheritance/Multiple.summary: The task is satisfied by type declarations alone (a tagged type, an interface and a type extension of both), and SPARK supports these. No run-time checks arise, so Bronze and Silver proof is trivial once Silver admits tagged and interface types.

Inheritance/Single.approach: Main declares a tagged null record Animal, then extends it to Dog and Cat with null record extensions, and extends Dog to Lab and Collie. The body is a null statement, because the task asks only for the type tree and the declarations themselves show it. There is no data, arithmetic, input or output to guard.
Inheritance/Single.summary: The program only declares types, with null records, no operations and an empty body, so GNATprove has no run-time checks to discharge apart from trivial flow analysis. The only new surface Silver needs is tagged record types and type extension.

effects.explanation: The program prints a short explanation and the demonstration results with Put_Line.

Inner classes.approach: Ada has no classes nested inside classes, so the program substitutes the equivalent structure: an Inner record type with a bounded Integer field is declared inside the Main procedure's declarative part, beside an outer record that holds an Inner component. A constructor function returns an Inner aggregate, and a method procedure increments the field only after a guard against the range limit, with a visible outcome when the guard fails. Main instantiates the outer and inner objects, calls the method, and prints explanatory String literals and the field value via 'Image.
Inner classes.summary: The task is a small demonstration with records, a constructor function and one method on bounded integers, so every check follows from declared ranges and one explicit guard; no loops carry unbounded values and no annotations are needed.

effects.explanation: The program reads standard input line by line until end of data.
Each line read is written to standard output.

risks.explanation: An input line longer than the fixed buffer must have a specified visible outcome (for example splitting it across reads or rejecting it), which the admitted read operation's contract provides so the slice Line(1..Length) is always in range.
The while loop sits in the Main procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed even though the input length is unbounded.

Input loop.approach: Main declares a fixed-capacity String buffer, a Natural length and a Boolean end-of-input flag, then runs a while loop in the procedure that calls an admitted Silver_IO line-read operation (returning the length and the end flag) and echoes Line(1..Length) with Put_Line until end of input. The read operation's contract guarantees Length is within the buffer bounds and defines what happens to over-long lines, so the only loop-carried values are bounded by their types.
Input loop.summary: Every check follows from the buffer's declared bounds and the read operation's verified postcondition, and the unbounded stream is handled by a procedure-level while loop that needs no variant.

effects.explanation: Reads the count line and then that many text lines from standard input.
Writes each line to standard output.

risks.explanation: The parsed count is validated into a bounded subtype (for example 0 to 1000) before the for loop, with a visible rejection otherwise, so the loop bounds are type-safe.

Each line is read by an admitted library operation into a fixed-capacity buffer with a length and status, and over-long or missing lines (end of input) are rejected visibly so the echo procedure only sees valid lengths.

Input/Output for lines of text.approach: An admitted stdin library procedure reads the first line into a bounded buffer, a text-parsing operation converts it to a count in a ranged subtype, and invalid or missing input calls Reject. A for loop over 1 .. Count calls a small Echo procedure that reads one bounded line (with a status check) and writes it through Put_Line, with no loop-carried state besides the loop index.
Input/Output for lines of text.summary: Every check follows from a ranged count subtype, a fixed-capacity line buffer with library-reported length and status, and a for loop that needs no invariant, so proofs should discharge once Silver gains the stdin line-reading and number-parsing operations.

effects.explanation: Reads the count line and then one line per pair from standard input.
Writes each pair's sum on its own line to standard output.
Malformed or out-of-range input is rejected with a nonzero exit status.

risks.explanation: Parsed integers are accepted only within a declared range of plus or minus 10**9, so the sum of a pair always fits Integer, and digit accumulation is guarded before each multiply-add.
The line parser's while loop carries a position, so each character access is guarded by an explicit position-within-length test just before use.
Parsing loops live in procedures, which get no termination check, and the pair loop is a for loop over the parsed count.
Line buffers are fixed-capacity with a stated maximum, and over-long lines are rejected rather than truncated.

Input/Output for pairs of numbers.approach: A procedure reads the first line into a bounded line buffer and parses it as a count constrained to a declared maximum, rejecting anything else. A for loop over that count reads each line, a guarded scanner skips spaces and parses two optionally signed decimal integers within a bounded range, rejects trailing junk or missing fields, then prints the sum with scalar image text through Put_Line. Missing lines (end of input) and out-of-range values lead to a specified Reject outcome.
Input/Output for pairs of numbers.summary: Every check follows from bounded integer subtypes and guards before each buffer access and digit accumulation, but the hand-written parser with loop-carried values needs careful guard placement, and Silver needs stdin line reading plus text parsing first.

effects.explanation: The two integers are read from the first two command-line arguments.
The comparison messages, or a rejection message, are printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Converting argument text to Integer must reject out-of-range digit strings, which a validated parse operation (or a guard before each multiply-add) discharges, after which the three comparisons carry no checks at all.

Integer comparison.approach: Main reads two command-line arguments, parses each into an Integer with validation, and rejects the input with a specified message if either argument is missing or not a valid in-range integer. It then tests A < B, A = B and A > B in three separate if statements and prints the matching message for each case.
Integer comparison.summary: After validated parsing, the program only compares two Integer values, which raises no run-time checks, so every obligation follows from the parse operation's contract and explicit rejection of invalid input.

effects.explanation: Prints the decimal expansion with the repeating block marked and the period length via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The digit buffer and seen-remainder table are indexed by a loop-carried count and remainder, so the while condition requires count below the buffer capacity and the remainder is typed as a range 0 .. 148, making each index check follow from the loop guard and subtype.
The remainder times 10 and the position counter are bounded by their declared subtypes (remainder below 149, position at most the capacity), so no loop invariant is needed.

Assigning r*10 mod 149 back to a ranged remainder subtype and converting a digit 0..9 to Character via 'Val relies on solver reasoning about mod and division by constants, which should discharge without an invariant.
Assembling the output text in a fixed buffer with a computed fill index needs a guard before each append so the index never exceeds the buffer length.

Repeat detection through the seen table ends the loop by pigeonhole, which only a procedure (no termination check) allows, and the explicit capacity guard gives a visible outcome (reject) if a denominator ever exceeded the buffer.

Integer long division.approach: Embed numerator 1 and denominator 149 as constants and run a procedure with a while loop that records, for each remainder (a ranged subtype 0 .. 148), the position where it first appeared in a fixed seen-position array while appending the next digit character to a bounded digit buffer, stopping when a remainder repeats or the remainder becomes 0. The loop condition guards the buffer capacity, and the period is the digit count minus the stored first-seen position (0 when the remainder reached 0). A second pass copies the integer part, the pre-period digits and the repeating block in braces into a bounded text buffer and prints it and the period via Put_Line with Integer'Image.
Integer long division.summary: All indices and arithmetic are bounded by ranged subtypes and a capacity guard in the while-loop condition, and the loop lives in a procedure so no termination variant is needed; the arithmetic is only small integer mod/div by a constant, so the proofs should discharge with careful program shape.

conflicts.explanation: The task requires performing arithmetic "such that the result would overflow" and demonstrating what happens. Rule 2 requires every Silver program to be proved free of overflow and range check failures, so no admitted program can perform or observe an overflowing computation.

effects.explanation: The program prints the result of each expression, or the behavior it shows, for each integer type.

Integer overflow.summary: The task deliberately performs overflowing fixed-size arithmetic, whereas every admitted Silver program must prove its overflow checks; catching the resulting Constraint_Error cannot discharge those obligations.

effects.explanation: Prints the three example results (cube roots of 8 and 9, square root of 2*10^38) as text lines.

risks.explanation: Schoolbook big-by-big multiplication accumulates digit products and carries in loops, so digits are a small ranged subtype and each partial sum is kept below base*base*capacity+base, which fits Integer from the types alone.

Product positions i+j are checked against the fixed capacity by a guard before each write, and a product exceeding capacity sets an overflow flag that is reported as a visible rejection rather than dropped.
Each carry-derived digit is reduced with mod before storing into the ranged digit subtype, which provers handle given the bounded operands.
Only for loops and procedures are used (digit-by-digit search from the top position with trial digits 9 down to 0), so no variant is needed.

The task's no-arbitrary-limits clause is met only as an explicit documented fixed capacity (for example 64 digits for the 38-digit example), and the optional 2001-digit example would need a much larger capacity that makes the nested loops heavier for the provers.

Integer roots.approach: Represent numbers as fixed-capacity little-endian decimal digit arrays with a documented capacity, embed X for the three examples, and compute the root digit by digit from the most significant position, trying digits 9 down to 0 and keeping the largest whose N-th power (repeated big multiplication into a bounded result with an overflow flag) is at most X. Control flow is entirely for loops inside procedures, with guards on product indices and an explicit overflow outcome, and results are printed by converting digit arrays to a bounded String with leading zeros skipped.
Integer roots.summary: Nothing needs an annotation because all loops are for loops over fixed digit ranges in procedures and every arithmetic value is bounded by the digit type, but the nested big-number multiplication inside the search loops makes discharge depend on careful program shape. The needed big-number support (digit arrays, multiply, compare, print) is a sizeable new surface.

effects.explanation: Each integer in the sequence is written to standard output on its own line with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Integer sequence.approach: Main uses for Value in 1 .. 2147483647 loop and calls Silver_IO.Put_Line (Integer'Image (Value)). The explicit literal is the current signed 32-bit Integer maximum; Integer'Last is not admitted syntax. Successful execution emits exactly 2147483647 lines, one for every integer from 1 through 2147483647 inclusive. Each line is one ASCII space, the ordinary decimal digits of Value, then LF. No arbitrary precision example is claimed. Do not cap this source or treat a prefix execution as complete task execution; keep the full-run validation disposition explicit.
Integer sequence.summary: The current finite Integer-loop and standard Integer Image fragment can express the task's explicitly permitted implementation limit, 2147483647. This is language eligibility, not evidence that a complete 2147483647-line execution was performed; a normal sample-run disposition remains separate.

review.setting_evidence: Selected inherited reviewer setting; runtime setting not independently exposed
review.method: Targeted static task, current-language and scratch-source review; no native admission, proof, build, test or execution

effects.explanation: The help text and the pointer to further documentation are printed with Silver_IO.Put_Line.
The first command-line argument is read with Silver_Arguments.First_Or_Default to recognise a --help or -h request.

Interactive help.approach: Main reads the first argument with Silver_Arguments.First_Or_Default and compares it, using String equality guarded by 'Length comparisons, against "--help" and "-h". On a match it prints a fixed usage summary of the program's options and a line saying where the Silver/SPARK documentation can be found; with no argument it prints a short hint to run with --help, and any other argument is rejected with Silver_Arguments.Reject.
Interactive help.summary: The task asks only for command-line help or a message on where to find more information, and today's Silver can already do that with string literals, argument comparison, if/elsif and Put_Line. Every check is a static string length or equality, so proof is routine.

conflicts.explanation: The task requires starting the language implementation's interactive mode (a read-eval-print loop) and defining a function interactively, i.e. evaluating source code entered at run time. Ada/SPARK is a compiled language with no interactive mode, and the task explicitly says it is not about writing your own interpreter, so no Silver program can meet it.

effects.explanation: An interactive session reads lines the user types.
The session prints results such as 'Rosetta::Code'.

Interactive programming (repl).summary: The task asks how to start the language's built-in interactive mode (REPL) and how to define a function in it, which means evaluating code typed in at run time. Ada/SPARK has no such mode, and the task rules out writing your own, so it is excluded. The string function itself (s1 & sep & sep & s2) would be easy, but a compiled program like the FreeBASIC one does not do what the task asks.

effects.explanation: Prints each wheel group and its first twenty generated terms.

risks.explanation: Mapping a wheel-name character to a wheel index and reading the current character both need explicit range guards, which are placed just before each use and discharge directly.
Name-reference chains that could cycle forever are cut off by a bounded for loop inside a procedure, so no variant is needed and an over-deep chain is rejected visibly.

Intersecting number wheels.approach: Each wheel group is embedded as constant Strings (for example "1B2" and "34") with a small array of per-wheel positions of a ranged subtype and a lengths array. A procedure Next_Term runs a for loop of bounded depth: it reads the current character of the wheel, advances that wheel's position with an if-wrap, and either takes a digit as the result or maps a letter name to its wheel index after a range guard and continues. A for loop over 20 terms appends each digit to a fixed 39-character output String, which is written with Put_Line for each of the four groups, and a reference chain longer than the depth bound gives a specified Reject outcome.
Intersecting number wheels.summary: All checks follow from ranged position subtypes, for-loop indexes over the array ranges and guards placed just before character lookups, and the cyclic-reference risk is handled by a bounded loop in a procedure.

conflicts.explanation: The core task asks the program to check while it runs whether a variable named "bloop" and a function "abs" exist, and to call abs only if they do. That is introspection of the program's own structure. Ada/SPARK settles name resolution at compile time, so a program that names a missing entity is rejected instead of running and reporting it is missing. Ada also gives no portable way to ask for the version of the running compiler or runtime.

effects.explanation: The program must look up the version of the compiler or runtime it is running under.
The program must exit, with a failure status, when the version is too old.
The program prints the result of abs(bloop).

Introspection.summary: Excluded: the task needs a running program to test whether the variable bloop and the function abs exist, and to read its own compiler or runtime version. Both are introspection that Ada/SPARK cannot express, because names are resolved at compile time. The existing Ada solution admits this and prints target type limits instead.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 100 elements and the position and value of each threshold hit as text lines.

risks.explanation: Counts is indexed by the loop-carried inventory index i and by each element value j, so each use is preceded by an explicit guard against the array bound, with an overflow-limit outcome reported visibly rather than clamped.

The per-value count increment and the running position are loop-carried, so each is guarded just before the +1 and the position is held in a wide enough integer type, with a visible stop message if a limit were hit.
The main loops are while loops inside the Main procedure, which gets no termination check, and the sequence is known to keep growing so reaching the 10,000 threshold is not proof-relevant.
The line-formatting buffer for the first-100 display uses fixed-width text built from image conversions, so lengths must be bounded by the integer subtype ranges.

Inventory sequence.approach: Only the occurrence counts are needed to generate the sequence, so the program keeps a constrained array Counts indexed by value (0..10_000) plus a 100-element array holding the first elements for display. A while loop in Main restarts the inventory at i = 0, reads j = Counts(i), increments Counts(j), advances the position, records the element if among the first 100, and checks the 1000..10000 thresholds, with explicit guards on i, j and the counters before each indexing or increment. After the loop it prints the 100 elements as text rows and each threshold's position and value; the optional plot is omitted.
Inventory sequence.summary: Every check is an array index or counter increment that a guard immediately before it can discharge, and the loops live in a procedure so no variant is needed. It is plausible rather than likely because the index and counter values are loop-carried and the position of the first element at or above 10,000 may be large, requiring a wide integer type and a visible limit outcome.

effects.explanation: Reads the file-name line and each search query line interactively.
Reads the named text files to build the index.
Prompts and lists matching file names.

risks.explanation: Word tokenizing over bounded line buffers needs scan positions guarded just before each indexed access, since loop-carried positions have only type ranges.
Words, lines, file names and the word table have fixed capacities, and over-long input must give a specified rejection or skip outcome instead of silent truncation.
All scanning and search loops live in procedures or are for loops, so no variant is needed, provided the tokenizer is not written as a while loop inside a function.
Fixed-capacity word and posting tables must be fully initialized before use, and count variables must stay within the capacity range via guards.
File-read failure (missing or unreadable file) must be reported as a visible outcome through the admitted file library rather than an exception handler.

Inverted index.approach: Keep a fixed-capacity table of distinct words (bounded String buffers with lengths), each with a Boolean array marking which of a small fixed number of files contain it. A procedure reads each named file line by line via an admitted file library, tokenizes letters into words with guarded scan indexes, and inserts them with a linear search, reporting a visible message when a capacity is exceeded; a search loop reads query lines from stdin, looks up each word, ANDs the file marks, and prints the matching file names or a not-found message until an empty line.
Inverted index.summary: The program is bounded loops over fixed-capacity arrays with guards before each index, so it likely proves without annotations, but tokenizing, table capacity limits and loop-carried counters make it depend on careful program shape. It also needs a large new surface (file and stdin input, strings, arrays, records).

effects.explanation: The program prints a line for each traditional and inverted-style form it demonstrates.

risks.explanation: The loop counter is a 1..10 subtype incremented after an immediately preceding exit when Foo >= 10, so the increment's range check follows from that guard alone.

Inverted syntax.approach: The main procedure declares Boolean variables Raining and Need_Umbrella and a counter Foo of a 1..10 subtype, then shows the traditional conditional (if Raining then Need_Umbrella := True) and the traditional assignment, printing results with if and Put_Line. It then shows the only inverted-style form Ada has, a loop whose first statement is exit when Foo >= 10 before Foo := Foo + 1, and prints the final counter value as a literal-based message chosen by a comparison.
Inverted syntax.summary: The program uses only Booleans, a small ranged counter and a plain loop with exit when, and each check follows from declared ranges and the guard just before the increment. Ada has no true inverted assignment or trailing-if syntax, so the faithful demonstration is the traditional forms plus exit when, which needs no annotation.

effects.explanation: Creates and opens named pipes (FIFOs) on the file system and reads and writes them as files.
The pipes exist to communicate with other processes, which write to the 'in' pipe and read the 'out' pipe, so the program is a long-running server.
Creating a FIFO (mkfifo) and handling blocking open and read calls on it are operating-system services. The program must also stay responsive on both pipes by polling or multiplexing.
Polling the two pipes in a loop, instead of blocking on one, would sleep between polls.

IPC via named pipe.summary: The task is a server that tallies bytes written to an 'in' FIFO and reports the running total to readers of an 'out' FIFO. A Silver-friendly solution can poll both pipes in one sequential loop, with a bounded total and a visible outcome on overflow, so no Oracle rule is broken. It does need FIFO, file and inter-process effects that Silver lacks today and that would have to come from admitted library operations.

effects.explanation: The gateway must open network connections to an IRC server and to another IRC server or chat server, and send and receive messages over them.
Reporting connection status and relayed messages as text; relaying traffic itself is covered by network.

IRC gateway.summary: The task asks for a gateway that relays messages between an IRC server and another IRC server or chat server. That needs network sockets plus bounded IRC message parsing and a relay loop, all of which fit bounded strings, arrays and iteration. No fixed Oracle rule is broken, so the only gap is the network effect Silver lacks today.

effects.explanation: Prints each embedded ISBN with a Good or Bad verdict line.

risks.explanation: The running sum is a loop-carried value, so it is kept in a 0..9 subtype by reducing mod 10 after each addition, which preserves the final mod-10 result and makes every addition provably in range.
The digit value is computed from Character'Pos only after a guard that the character lies between '0' and '9', so it is provably in 0..9.

ISBN13 check digit.approach: The four test codes are embedded as constants of a fixed-length 14-character String subtype, and a Boolean function loops over indexes 1..14 of the constant. It requires a hyphen at position 4, checks each other character is a digit before converting it, applies weight 1 or 3 by digit position parity, and keeps the sum reduced mod 10 in a 0..9 subtype. A procedure prints each code with Good or Bad using bounded concatenation and Put_Line, and any non-digit or misplaced hyphen yields Bad.
ISBN13 check digit.summary: All checks follow from the fixed string length, the digit guard before Character'Pos, and the mod-10-reduced sum in a small subtype, so no loop invariant is needed. The loop is a for loop inside a function, which terminates by itself.

effects.explanation: Reads the word list unixdict.txt line by line, with a specified outcome if it is missing or unreadable.
Prints the two sorted result lists to standard output.
Reports a rejected file or an over-limit word or result count through a failure exit status.

risks.explanation: The count table is indexed by Character'Pos over a 0..255 subtype and result-array indexes are guarded by a capacity check before each insertion, so both discharge from types and guards.
Per-character counts are bounded by the maximum word length, which is a declared subtype range, so increments cannot overflow.
Words longer than the fixed buffer, or more results than the table holds, are rejected with a visible outcome rather than truncated, so buffer lengths are guarded before use.
Line reading and insertion-sort shifting use while loops, but they live in procedures, which get no termination check.
The count table and result arrays are fully initialized by aggregates or reset loops per word, so flow analysis is routine.

Isograms and heterograms.approach: Each line of unixdict.txt is read into a bounded buffer with a length (rejecting over-long lines), lowercased, and its characters tallied in a 256-entry count array; a for loop then checks that all nonzero counts are equal, giving n. Words with n>1, or n=1 and length>10, go into two fixed-capacity result tables (records of buffer, length, n), kept ordered by an insertion sort in a procedure comparing n, then length descending, then lexicographic ascending, and the tables are printed with scalar images.
Isograms and heterograms.summary: Every check follows from declared subtypes, fixed capacities with explicit reject guards, and loops in procedures, but it needs a file-reading library operation, string ordering and careful guard placement in the sort and the counting loops.

effects.explanation: Prints the horizontal table for 0..65 and the vertical table of odd powers of 7 with comma-grouped numbers.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried q, r and z values have no invariant, so they get bounded subtypes and an explicit guard (q at most 4**29) before q*4, with x limited to 7**21 which is below 2**60.
The 7**N value is built by repeated multiplication by 49 under a guard against exceeding the Int64 limit, which restricts output to N up to 21 as the task permits for smaller-integer languages.
The comma-grouped output is built into a fixed 32-character buffer whose write positions must be guarded against underflow below the first index.

Isqrt (integer square root) of X.approach: Use a bounded 64-bit integer subtype and a procedure Isqrt(X, Result) implementing the quadratic-residue algorithm with a for loop that grows q by 4 under a guard, then a for loop that shifts down and updates z and r. Print the 0..65 table in three rows via 'Image, then loop N over odd values 1..21 computing 7**N by guarded repeated multiplication and printing it and its Isqrt with commas inserted into a fixed buffer built from digit extraction by div and mod 10.
Isqrt (integer square root) of X.summary: The algorithm uses only integer arithmetic that bounded subtypes and guards can keep in range, and the 64-bit limit is explicitly allowed by the task (show what you can), but the 7**N values up to 7**73 would need fixed-capacity big numbers to be fully faithful.

effects.explanation: Prints the two counts (below 1_000_000 and below 100_000_000) with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The Count accumulator is loop-carried, so it is declared in a 64-bit integer range type (or guarded below its bound) so that Count + 1 cannot overflow after the first iteration.

The eight-term digit-square sum is written as one non-loop-carried expression of table lookups bounded by 81 each, so the 0..648 result range check is a linear fact over constant array values that the provers should discharge.
The chain-following while loop (until the value is 1 or 89) lives in a procedure that fills the 0..648 lookup table, so no termination check applies.

Iterated digits squaring.approach: A procedure fills a Boolean table Ends_89 over 0..648 by following each value's chain with a while loop and a three-digit square-sum step written as an explicit expression; the main loop then runs a for loop over 1..99_999_999, sums the squares of the eight digits with an unrolled expression using a constant squares array, indexes the table, and increments a 64-bit Count. It prints the count when A = 999_999 and again at the end using 'Image, with all loop-carried values held in ranged subtypes.
Iterated digits squaring.summary: Every check follows from ranged subtypes, array bounds and non-loop-carried digit expressions, with the only loop-carried values being a 64-bit counter and a range-typed chain value inside a procedure, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: The program prints each container's elements and the selected first, fourth, fifth and last, fourth-to-last and fifth-to-last elements to standard output.

risks.explanation: Following a cursor of type 0 .. Capacity into the node array is preceded by an explicit Cursor /= 0 guard, so the conversion to the 1 .. Capacity index subtype and the indexing discharge from that guard alone.

Each Name (1 .. Len) slice discharges because Len is a record component declared in 1 .. 9 and Name is String (1 .. 9), and the positional offsets (Count - K + 1) are computed with static K over a Count typed 0 .. Capacity and guarded with K <= Count before use.

Iterators.approach: The days are a constant array of seven records holding a padded String (1 .. 9) and its length, and the colors are an array-backed doubly linked list of node records with Next and Prev cursors of type 0 .. Capacity, where 0 means none. Separate cursor procedures (First, Last, Next, Previous) and an Element function give container-independent access, with all-element printing done by a for loop over the day array and a while loop over the list cursor inside a procedure. Positional access walks a for loop of K - 1 steps, guarding each step with Cursor /= 0 and printing a specified "no such element" line when the cursor runs off the end.
Iterators.summary: Every check follows from declared index and length ranges plus a Cursor /= 0 guard before each dereference, and the list's while loop lives in a procedure, so no termination check or invariant is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the 21 pairing lines to standard output.

risks.explanation: The intersection count is a loop-carried accumulator, so each increment sits behind an explicit guard (count below the set capacity) or uses a subtype bounded well below Integer'Last.
The union size is tested for zero before dividing, returning 1 for the empty/empty pairing exactly as the task's expected output shows.
Set sizes, element indexes and the scaled-decimal quotient (numerator at most 10 times 10**7) stay within declared subtypes, and the decimal digits are emitted by a fixed-count for loop.
Each output line is built in a fixed-capacity buffer sized for the longest line (e.g. J(B,C) = J(C,B) = 0.4285714) so concatenations cannot exceed it.

Jaccard index.approach: Each of the six sets is a row in a constant 6x5 Integer table with a parallel array of element counts (A has 0), and the sets contain distinct values so the union size is |A|+|B|-|A∩B|. Nested for loops over the index ranges count the intersection with a guarded increment, a function returns the index as a scaled integer (guarding union=0 to give 1), and a procedure prints "J(X,Y) = J(Y,X) = d.ddddddd" using integer division and mod for the seven decimal digits and Character'Val for the set letters, for X<=Y over A..F.
Jaccard index.summary: All checks follow from fixed array bounds, for-loop ranges over them and a zero-union guard, and the exact-decimal output via scaled integers avoids floating point; the only non-routine point is the loop-carried intersection counter, which a visible guard keeps in range.

effects.explanation: The program prints the Jacobi symbol table for odd n from 1 to 29 and a from 1 to 20.

risks.explanation: Loop-carried a, n and the sign result live in small declared subtypes (for example 0..1000 and -1..1), so negation and mod cannot overflow once types bound them.
Each mod or / is placed under an explicit n > 0 guard just before use, since no invariant can carry that fact across iterations.
The Euclid-style reduction loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed.
After the swap step the new n must be positive, which is guarded by testing a /= 0 immediately before the swap rather than relying on a loop invariant.

Jacobi symbol.approach: A procedure Jacobi (A, N in; Result out) uses the standard reduction loop: reduce a mod n, strip factors of two while flipping the sign when n mod 8 is 3 or 5, then swap using quadratic reciprocity (flip when both are 3 mod 4), and return 0 when the final n is not 1. The main procedure loops over the odd n and a ranges from the task table, converts each symbol to a width-3 field in a bounded String buffer, and prints each row with Put and Put_Line. All values are in small declared subtypes with explicit positivity guards before every mod.
Jacobi symbol.summary: The algorithm is pure bounded integer arithmetic with a while loop inside a procedure, so termination is not checked and range and division checks follow from subtypes plus local guards; only careful guard placement in the loop-carried a, n values keeps it from being routine.

effects.explanation: Prints the four sequences, one line per sequence or one value per line.

risks.explanation: The recurrence J(i-1) + 2*J(i-2) is loop-carried with no invariant, so each step is guarded by an explicit cap check that rejects with a visible message, or the arrays use a 64-bit type whose range is checked against the known 32-term bound.
The oblong product J(i)*J(i+1) needs both operands guarded below about 2**31 so the 64-bit product cannot overflow.
Trial division is written as a for loop over candidate divisors up to 30000 with an early exit, so no while-loop variant is needed in a function.
Array indexes come from for-loop ranges over the arrays' own bounds, with the prime search bounded by the 32-entry table so index checks are routine.
