effects.explanation: The year is read from the first command-line argument.
Twelve ISO date lines are written to standard output.
Invalid or missing year input is rejected with a specified failure status.

risks.explanation: The parsing accumulator is loop-carried, so each digit step is preceded by a guard that the value is at most 999, keeping value*10+digit within the Year range.
The weekday formula uses mod and division on values bounded by the Year subtype and month table, so intermediate sums stay far below Integer limits and results map into 0..6 and 1..31 subtypes.
Writing digits into the 10-character output buffer uses fixed literal positions and digit values proven 0..9 by mod and division of bounded numbers.

Last Friday of each month.approach: Parse the first argument into a Year subtype (1583..9999) with a digit-by-digit loop that guards the accumulator before each multiply, rejecting non-digit, empty or out-of-range input. For each month in a for loop over 1..12, take the month length from a constant array (February adjusted by a leap-year test using mod), compute the weekday of the last day with a Zeller-style integer formula bounded by the ranged types, subtract the offset back to Friday, and build the "YYYY-MM-DD" line in a fixed 10-character String from digit characters before calling Put_Line.
Last Friday of each month.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic over a validated year with a fixed 12-iteration for loop, so all checks follow from types and guards just before use, with only the argument parse loop needing a careful guard.

effects.explanation: The program prints the length of the longest chain and the names in one such chain.

risks.explanation: The explicit DFS stack depth is a loop-carried value, so the program guards each push with a test against the 70-element capacity and has a specified visible outcome if it were reached, with all other indexes typed as ranges of 1..70.
Candidate cursors and best-length counters are loop-carried, so they are declared with subtypes that include one-past-the-end values and incremented only after a guard just before the increment.

The search is an iterative while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed, though exhaustive backtracking over 70 names is a practical runtime concern rather than a proof one.
Reading first and last letters from fixed-width padded name buffers requires each stored length to be a typed range within the buffer width, so the last-letter index is safe by type.

Last letter-first letter.approach: Embed the 70 names as a constant array of fixed-width padded strings with a parallel array of lengths, and precompute first and last letters by indexing. A single procedure runs an iterative depth-first search with an explicit stack array of chosen indices and per-level cursors plus a used-flag array, copying the best chain whenever a longer one is found. After the search it prints the best length with Integer'Image and each name from its buffer using its length.
Last letter-first letter.summary: The task needs no recursion because backtracking can use an explicit bounded stack in a procedure, and all indexes are typed ranges or guarded before use, so no annotation is needed. The risk lies in loop-carried stack depth and cursor values needing careful subtypes and guards.

effects.explanation: Prints each step (the list, the two smallest items and their sum) and the final list as text lines.

risks.explanation: The sum of the two smallest items is checked against the element subtype's upper bound with a guard that rejects with a visible message, so the stored value and the addition both discharge from declared ranges.
The smallest-item search and the shift-down removal use for loops over the current length, with the length a ranged subtype of 0 .. 9, so every index stays within the array bounds.
The outer while loop sits in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and it strictly shrinks the length each pass.
Each printed line is assembled in a bounded buffer sized for nine items of the maximum digit width, and the line-building code needs guards before each append.

Last list item.approach: Keep the list in a nine-element array of a ranged integer subtype with a separate length variable, initialised from the task's data. While the length is at least 2, print the list, find the index of the smallest item by a for loop, remove it by shifting, repeat for the second smallest, guard the sum against the subtype's upper bound (rejecting on overflow), append it, and finally print the single remaining item. Output lines are built from integer images into a bounded buffer and written with Put_Line.
Last list item.summary: All checks follow from ranged subtypes, for-loops over the array's own range and one explicit sum guard, with the outer while loop in a procedure, but the text-building of each step line is the fiddly part. Nothing needs an annotation, so discharge is plausible rather than certain.

effects.explanation: Prints the four order-4 squares and the table of orders 1 to 6 with sizes and totals.

risks.explanation: The iterative backtracking cursor (cell position and candidate value) is loop-carried, so it is declared with a ranged subtype and every step and backtrack is guarded just before the array access.

The solution counter and the size times n! times (n-1)! products are bounded by range types sized for order 6 (9408 and 812851200), with an explicit guard that rejects counts above the documented cap.
The row, column and used-value arrays are fully initialized by aggregates or for loops before the search loop so flow analysis sees no uninitialized reads.
The unbounded-looking backtracking while loop lives in a procedure, which has no termination check, so no variant is needed.

Latin Squares in reduced form.approach: Use a fixed 6x6 Integer array with Boolean used-per-row and used-per-column arrays, and an iterative depth-first search in a procedure that walks cells row-major with an explicit cursor, trying values 2..n that are unused in the row and column and counting or printing each completed square (first row and column pre-set to natural order). A for loop over n=1..6 calls the counter, computes size*n!*(n-1)! in a bounded range type, and prints the table with the expected OEIS A002860 values embedded as a constant array, while the order-4 run prints each square with Put and Put_Line of 'Image text. All indices are ranged subtypes with explicit guards before each array access, and the counter is capped with a rejecting guard.
Latin Squares in reduced form.summary: The task fits an iterative bounded backtracking procedure over fixed-size arrays with small ranged integers, so every check follows from types and guards, though cursor and counter bookkeeping in the loop needs careful guarding.

effects.explanation: Prints the reduced order-4 squares with their counts, the 56 order-5 counts, the 750th order-42 square, and summary text.
Part 4 asks to confirm the approximate time taken for 1000 order-256 squares, which needs elapsed-time measurement.

Latin Squares in reduced form/Randomizin.summary: The task needs only integer and array computation: a bounded n*n*n incidence cube for n up to 256, a Jacobson-Matthews move loop driven by a deterministic pseudo-random generator, reduction to reduced form, and frequency counts over 4 or 56 reduced squares. It also needs text output and elapsed-time measurement, and nothing in it breaks an Oracle rule. The order-256 cube has about 16.7 million cells, which a fixed-capacity array can hold within documented resource limits.

effects.explanation: Prints the countdown numbers 5 to 0 and each ASCII-art rocket frame to standard output.
A one-second countdown and a frame-by-frame animation with shrinking frame intervals need sleeping between outputs.

Launch rocket with countdown and acceler.summary: The task needs bounded loops, integer-based position and velocity arithmetic (altitude grows by an integer accelerating step each frame) and fixed ASCII-art strings printed to stdout, with sleeps for timing. Nothing in it breaks an Oracle rule, so it is a candidate once Silver gains console loops, integer arithmetic and a delay operation.

effects.explanation: Prints each triple and the per-angle counts with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The per-angle counter is carried through nested loops and, with no invariant, its increment is proven safe only by a guard against its subtype maximum that rejects visibly, which is never reached for sides 1..13.
Computing A*A + B*B +/- A*B in an Integer-based expression is bounded by the side subtype 1..13 so it cannot overflow and the C*C comparison needs no guard.

Law of cosines - triples.approach: Declare a Side subtype 1..13 and a small bounded count subtype, then run three nested for loops (A in 1..13, B in 1..A, C in 1..13) once per angle (60, 90, 120) in a helper procedure or three loop blocks, testing A*A + B*B -/+ A*B = C*C. Each hit prints the triple with 'Image concatenation and increments a guarded counter, and the count is printed after each angle; the optional 1..10_000 extra credit is omitted.
Law of cosines - triples.summary: All arithmetic is bounded by the 1..13 side subtype and the loops are plain for loops, so only the loop-carried counter needs a visible guard; the result is plausible rather than certain because of that guard and the integer-to-text output.

effects.explanation: Prints twelve labelled leap/common verdicts, including leap for 1600, 2000 and 2400 and common for the other demonstrated century years.

Leap year.approach: Main iterates over a constant Gregorian_Year array bounded 1 .. 2400, containing 1600, 1700, 1800, 1900, 1996, 1999, 2000, 2004, 2100, 2200, 2300 and 2400. An inline condition tests divisibility by 400 or divisibility by 4 but not 100, then prints leap or common.
Leap year.summary: The inline Gregorian predicate covers ordinary leap/common years, common century years and century years divisible by 400. Only literal nonzero divisors are used; no function or computed String buffer is needed. The exact source passed admission, complete required application/library proof audit, build and manifest execution in integration run 20261107T164659-9f6192441d21; the linked assessment records the evidence scope. Independent closing review remains pending.

effects.explanation: Prints the LCM results for the embedded example pairs.

risks.explanation: abs(A)*(abs(B)/G) can overflow, so inputs are declared as a bounded subtype (for example -10**6 .. 10**6) so the product fits in Integer and GNATprove discharges it from type ranges.
The divisor G is the Euclid result for nonzero inputs, but without a loop invariant GNATprove cannot show G is nonzero, so the program must guard G /= 0 before dividing and reject otherwise.
The Euclid while loop must be inside a procedure (not a function) so no variant is needed, with the result returned via an out parameter.
Loop-carried M and N are known only by their subtype after the first iteration, so declaring them in the bounded subtype keeps mod and assignments in range.

Least common multiple.approach: Declare a bounded integer subtype and a procedure Gcd that runs Euclid's algorithm with a while loop on in-subtype variables, returning the result in an out parameter. A procedure Lcm returns 0 if either input is zero, otherwise takes absolute values, guards the gcd being nonzero, and computes abs(A)*(abs(B)/G) in the bounded range. The main procedure runs the three embedded example pairs and prints each result with Put_Line and 'Image.
Least common multiple.summary: Everything is integer arithmetic with bounded subtypes, and the only non-routine items are the nonzero-gcd divisor and the product bound, both handled by a guard and a range choice; the while loop sits in a procedure so no termination check applies. It is plausible rather than likely because the gcd's nonzero-ness is not inferable without an invariant and must be guarded.

effects.explanation: Prints the 50 terms and the first m greater than 1000 with its position as text lines.

risks.explanation: Limb products and carries in the fixed-capacity big-number add, subtract and multiply-by-small routines are bounded by limb subtypes held in 64-bit intermediates, and the factorial step rejects visibly if the final carry would exceed capacity.
Limb loops run over the array's own range, but shifted or carried positions need explicit guards just before the index to discharge.

The Miller-Rabin exponent-halving and candidate-search loops are while loops, so they live in procedures (no termination check), with the m search capped by a documented bound and a specified failure message.
Modular multiplication must use double-and-add with modular add rather than long division to avoid Knuth-D index arithmetic, costing run time but keeping every loop-carried value type-bounded.

Least m such that n! + m is prime.approach: Represent numbers as a record of a fixed-capacity array of 16-bit limbs (about 40 limbs, enough for 106!, ~565 bits, plus a documented rejecting capacity limit) with a length, and build procedures for compare, add, subtract, multiply by small, modular add, double-and-add mulmod and modpow. Loop n from 0 upward updating the factorial in place, search m from n+1 upward with a trial-small-prime filter then fixed-base Miller-Rabin as procedure while loops, store the 50 terms in an array and print them in rows with Put, then report the first m above 1000 and its position (106 factorial gives position 107 counting from 1) via scalar image conversion; stretch thresholds are optional.
Least m such that n! + m is prime.summary: Nothing needs an annotation, since every loop value sits in a bounded limb subtype or behind a guard, but the fixed-capacity big-number arithmetic carried through many nested loops makes discharge depend on careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints the left factorials for 0..10 and 20..110 by tens and the digit counts for 1000..10000 by thousands.

risks.explanation: Limb arithmetic limb*K+carry is nonlinear but bounded by range subtypes (limb 0..9999, K at most 10000, carry at most 10000), so it fits in 32-bit Integer without an invariant.
The limb count is a loop-carried value, so each increment is guarded by a visible capacity check that rejects (reports overflow) instead of writing beyond the fixed 9100-limb array.
Carry and limb values assigned in loops are kept within their subtype ranges by mod and / by the base, whose results the provers bound from the operand ranges.
All loops live in procedures (for loops over limb ranges, plus a while loop for digit counting), so no variant is needed.
Two fixed arrays of about 9100 integers each are local objects whose size is static and modest.

Left factorials.approach: Represent big numbers as a record of a fixed array of base-10000 limbs (about 9100 limbs) plus a bounded Natural length; procedures Multiply_Small and Add_Big update the factorial accumulator and the running sum in a for loop over k, with capacity guards that reject on overflow. Printing converts limbs to decimal text in a bounded buffer for the values up to !110, and digit counts are computed from the top limb and limb count, emitted at the required thousand steps while the sum is carried through a single pass to 10000.
Left factorials.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic over fixed-capacity limb arrays in procedures with for loops, so checks follow from subtype ranges and capacity guards, but the carry loops over roughly 9000 limbs and nonlinear limb products need careful typing to discharge without invariants.

effects.explanation: Prints pi(10^k) for k = 0 to 9 as text lines.

risks.explanation: The signed accumulator of the explicit-stack phi evaluation is loop-carried with no invariant, so each addition is preceded by a guard against a wide ranged subtype bound that Rejects visibly, which never triggers since partial sums stay within about 1e9 in magnitude.

The explicit stack top and the prime index a-1 are loop-carried, so each push is guarded by a capacity test (capacity 3500 exceeds the true maximum depth of about 3402) and each prime lookup by a range test on a, with Reject on failure.
The sieve's i*i start and the product loop use values bounded by the sieve limit 31623, so subtype ranges and a guard i <= 177 before squaring discharge it.
The divisor p_a is read from a prime array whose type is a subtype of 2..31623, so nonzero follows from the declared range.
All while loops live in procedures, which get no termination check, and the sieve and pi loops are for loops.

Legendre prime counting function.approach: A Boolean array sieves primes up to 31622 into a constrained prime array with a count; for each n = 10^k (computed by repeated multiplication in a ranged subtype) a procedure evaluates phi(n,a) without recursion using an explicit stack array of (x, a, sign) triples popped in a while loop, stopping branches at a = 0 or x <= p_a and pushing the two children otherwise. Every push, prime lookup and accumulator update is guarded with a Reject outcome, and the result phi + a - 1 is printed with 'Image-based text and Put_Line.
Legendre prime counting function.summary: All data is fixed-size arrays and ranged integers with explicit guards, and the recursion is replaced by an explicit stack in a procedure so no variant is needed, but the loop-carried stack top and signed accumulator need careful guard placement.

effects.explanation: Each test string is printed with its computed LZ76 complexity through Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Reads at offsets I+V and U+V are safe from the loop condition U+V <= N for the second, but I < U is a loop-carried fact, so the first needs an explicit guard I+V <= N (unreachable in practice) that reports an internal error rather than an invariant.

Updates V := V+1, U := U+Vmax and Vmax := V on counters typed 0..64 need guards just before each assignment (V+1 follows from U >= 1 and U+V <= N, but U+Vmax <= N+1 needs an explicit check with a visible rejection branch).

The result line concatenates the test string with an image, so the procedure first rejects strings longer than the documented 64-character limit, which bounds the concatenation and keeps every offset computation from overflowing.
The while loop sits in a procedure, so no termination check arises, and every iteration either advances V or I toward a bound fixed by N.

Lempel\u2013Ziv complexity.approach: Main calls a procedure Report(S : String) once for each of the 18 embedded test strings, including the empty one. Report rejects strings longer than 64 characters. It then runs the classic LZ76 scan in a while loop over the integer counters I, U, V and Vmax (subtype 0..64), comparing S(S'First+I+V-1) with S(S'First+U+V-1) and putting a guard before each index and counter update. It prints the string followed by Integer'Image of the complexity, and leaves out the optional phrase listing.
Lempel\u2013Ziv complexity.summary: The algorithm only needs bounded integer counters, character comparisons and a while loop inside a procedure, so no termination proof is needed. Several loop-carried relations (I < U, U+Vmax <= N+1) would normally need an invariant, so each must be replaced by an explicit guard just before its use. That makes discharge depend on careful program shape rather than being routine.

effects.explanation: Prints the computed arc length of about 43.6332 for the radius 10, 10 to 120 degree example.

risks.explanation: Scaled integer products such as 360 * 3141593 * Radius stay far below 2**63 because Angle (0..360) and Radius (0..1000) are declared subtypes, so the checks follow from the type ranges.
The absolute angle difference is at most 360 and the major angle 360 - diff is within 0..360 because the angle subtypes bound it, so no guard is needed.

Length of an arc between two angles.approach: Use ranged subtypes for angles in degrees (0..360) and radius (0..1000), and a function Major_Arc_Length that computes (360 - abs (A2 - A1)) * Pi_Scaled * Radius / 180 in scaled-integer arithmetic (Pi scaled by 10**6, result in millionths), avoiding floating point. The main procedure embeds the example (radius 10, angles 10 and 120), then prints the integer part, a decimal point and four fractional digits using integer division/mod and a small bounded text buffer, with no loops needed.
Length of an arc between two angles.summary: All arithmetic is bounded integer arithmetic over declared ranged subtypes with no loops or recursion, so every overflow, range and division check follows from the types; the only extra surface is decimal text formatting of a scaled integer.

effects.explanation: Prints the two 25-number sequences and their headings to standard output.

risks.explanation: The recurrence L(n-1)+L(n-2)+Add is loop-carried, so each step is preceded by a guard comparing the operands against the subtype's upper limit and rejecting visibly instead of altering results.

Leonardo numbers.approach: A procedure Show (First, Second, Add) fills a constant-size array of 25 values of a bounded integer subtype using a for loop over the array's indexes, guarding each sum against the subtype limit before computing it, then prints each value with Put and 'Image in a second for loop over the array's own range. The main program calls Show with (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 0), with the seeds embedded as literals, and the overflow guard emits a specified message and stops filling.
Leonardo numbers.summary: The task is a small bounded recurrence on a fixed-size array where the values fit comfortably in a ranged subtype and a guard before each addition removes the only loop-carried overflow risk, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: Reads the named text file character by character, with a specified outcome when it cannot be opened or read.
Prints one line per letter with its count.
Reports a rejected input (missing file or counter limit exceeded) through a failure status.

risks.explanation: Each counter is a bounded range type and the increment is guarded by an explicit test against the maximum just before it, rejecting the input rather than saturating.
The read loop is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the end-of-file test comes from the admitted library operation.
The array is indexed by a character subtype A to Z after a range guard on each character, so the index check is routine.

Letter frequency.approach: A 26-element array of bounded counts indexed by a subtype 'A'..'Z' is zeroed by aggregate; a procedure opens the file through an admitted library operation and loops with while not end-of-file, reading one Character at a time. Characters outside A..Z (after folding lower case by a guarded Pos offset) are skipped, and a counter already at its maximum rejects the input; a for loop over the array's own range then prints each nonzero count with Put_Line using 'Image.
Letter frequency.summary: Every check follows from the array's declared character-subtype index, a guard before each counter increment, and a for loop over the array's own range, with the only loop being a while loop in a procedure. The remaining dependence is on an admitted file-reading library with specified failure outcomes, which Silver lacks today.

effects.explanation: Prints the two distances for the example pairs.

risks.explanation: Matrix indices I-1 and J-1 are safe because for loops run over 1..Length of constant strings inside a matrix declared 0..Max.

Each cell is a ranged subtype wider than the longest string, and a loop-carried cell read after the first iteration is only known by type, so a guard before the +1 keeps the cell within range while still computing the true minimum.

Levenshtein distance.approach: Use a procedure Main with a fixed-size 2D array (0..16, 0..16) of a ranged subtype for the DP matrix, computing the distance for each embedded string pair with nested for loops over 1..Length of constant strings and if/elsif minimum selection. Print the results with Silver_IO.Put_Line after converting the small integer with 'Image. Strings are String constants, so lengths are static and every index is bounded by the loop range.
Levenshtein distance.summary: All loops are for loops over static ranges and every cell value is bounded by a ranged subtype, so index and overflow checks follow from types and guards without invariants.

effects.explanation: The two aligned rows are printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The traceback loop carries I, J and the output position through a while loop with no invariant, so each decrement and array access is preceded by an explicit guard (I > 0, J > 0, P > 0) and the indices have subtypes bounded by the string lengths.

Matrix cells are stored in a bounded subtype, so the DP recurrence needs a guard that rejects or clamps-free-checks a candidate value above the subtype limit before assignment because min of three sums is not provably small without an invariant.
The two output rows are filled backwards in fixed 24-character buffers and the used part is sliced, so the alignment length is guarded against the buffer capacity with a visible rejection outcome.

Levenshtein distance/Alignment.approach: Embed the two words as String constants, fill a 0..11 by 0..13 integer matrix with nested for loops over the constants' own ranges, then trace back from the corner in a procedure with a while loop that emits the aligned source and target characters (using '-' for gaps) into two fixed 24-character buffers from the end. Each step is guarded by explicit comparisons of I, J and the output position to zero, and the final rows are printed with Put_Line.
Levenshtein distance/Alignment.summary: All checks come from declared index subtypes, for-loop ranges and guards just before each decrement or write, but the traceback's loop-carried indices and the bounded matrix cell values make discharge depend on careful program shape rather than being routine.

effects.explanation: The program prints the intersection points for the embedded example lines, segments and circles.

risks.explanation: Intermediate products and the discriminant must be proven finite and within Float range, which works only if coordinates and radius are declared as tightly ranged subtypes such as -1000.0 .. 1000.0.
The quadratic coefficient is the squared length of the direction vector, so the program guards with an explicit check that the two defining points differ and reports a degenerate line otherwise.
Square root is called only in a branch guarded by discriminant >= 0.0, and segment membership is a plain comparison of the parameter t against 0.0 and 1.0.
Formatting float results into text needs a bounded buffer sized for the worst-case image, which depends on how float-image is admitted in the library.

Line circle intersection.approach: Use a ranged Float subtype for coordinates, a Point record, and a procedure Intersect(P1, P2, Center, Radius, Is_Segment) that solves the parametric quadratic with t along P1 to P2, rejecting coincident points and negative discriminants with visible outcomes, then keeping t within 0..1 for segments. The main procedure runs the task's embedded examples, including the stretch cases, by calling Intersect, which prints each result via Put_Line with text built from float images; there are no loop-carried values.
Line circle intersection.summary: The task is closed-form geometry with no loops or recursion, so the only non-routine checks are float range, sqrt domain and division, which tightly ranged subtypes and explicit guards should discharge, though floating-point keeps it at plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints the first ten values of the BSD and Microsoft sequences with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Linear congruential generator.approach: Declare a modular type with modulus 2_147_483_648 so that State * Multiplier + Adder wraps exactly as the task's mod 2^31 formula requires, and keep one state variable for each generator, seeded with an embedded constant. Two for loops over 1 .. 10 update each state and print it, BSD directly and Microsoft divided by the static constant 65_536, using 'Image.
Linear congruential generator.summary: Modular arithmetic cannot overflow and is never checked, and dividing by a static nonzero constant produces no division check, so every remaining obligation is routine initialization and flow.

effects.explanation: Reads the first line of /proc/stat, twice, to get cumulative CPU times.
Sleeps for a short interval between the two samples so the time deltas give real-time utilization.
Prints the computed CPU utilization percentage.

Linux CPU utilization.summary: The task reads one line from /proc/stat, parses unsigned counters, sums them, takes deltas across a sleep, and prints a percentage. Bounded integer arithmetic with a guard for a zero total delta and a defined outcome for malformed input fits the Oracle rules. It needs file reading, a delay and console output, which are effects Silver lacks today and are not conflicts.

effects.explanation: Prints the list of triples to standard output.

risks.explanation: A*A+B*B and C*C are bounded because A, B, C are subtype-ranged loop indexes with a constant Max of 20 so products stay far below Integer'Last.
Appending to the fixed-capacity result array is guarded by a Count < capacity test, with the capacity chosen above the number of triples (6 for n=20) and overflow reported visibly.
The output line is built in a bounded buffer whose size is sized for the maximum count of triples, with each append preceded by a length guard.

List comprehensions.approach: Embed n = 20 as a constant, declare a ranged subtype 1 .. 20 and an array of triple records (or three parallel arrays) with a Count variable, and fill it with three nested for loops (A in 1..N, B in A+1..N, C in B+1..N) testing A*A+B*B = C*C and appending only when Count is below capacity. Then loop over 1..Count in a procedure and print each triple with Put and 'Image text, so no recursion, access types or while loops are required.
List comprehensions.summary: The only loop-carried value is the Count, which is guarded against capacity, and all arithmetic is bounded by small subtype ranges so every check follows from types and local guards; the list comprehension itself is rendered as nested for loops since Ada has no such construct.

effects.explanation: The program prints each partition and the error outcome for an oversized n.
The task's error case for n greater than the list length is reported as a nonzero exit status alongside a message.

risks.explanation: Dividing by n is discharged by an explicit n = 0 guard that prints a specified rejection before the division.
Element indexes are computed from part-start offsets, so they are derived from bounded subtype ranges or guarded to stay within the array bounds.
The running start offset and the (part-1)*d product are nonlinear loop-carried values that discharge only because every operand is a small ranged subtype.
Part sizes d and d+1 must be proven within the capacity subtype, which follows from the guard n <= length and the bounded length.

List division.approach: Embed a fixed-capacity Integer array (capacity about 16) with a ranged length subtype, and a procedure Divide(Data, Length, N) that first rejects N = 0 or N > Length with a visible error message and nonzero exit status. Otherwise it computes d = Length / N and r = Length mod N, then uses a for loop over parts 1..N, computing each part's start offset and size from d, r and the part number, and a nested for loop that prints the elements via 'Image with Put, commas and brackets. Main calls Divide on the embedded example lists from the task, including the oversized-n error case.
List division.summary: All checks follow from ranged subtypes, for-loops and explicit guards on n, but the bounded offset arithmetic in nested loops needs careful shape so provers see the indexes stay in range, and no annotations are required.

effects.explanation: Each tree is printed as a parenthesis string on its own line.

risks.explanation: The successor step searches for the last level greater than 1 and indexes the level array and parent position with loop-carried values, so each access needs an explicit guard (position at least 1 and at most N) just before use, with a visible stop when none exists.
Level values are stored in a subtype 0..N-1 and the copy/increment steps are computed from neighbours, so each assignment is guarded by comparing against the bound before adding.
The parenthesis buffer position advances in a loop, which is discharged by a buffer of fixed size 2*N and a guard before each write, with the per-tree close count bounded by the level subtype.
Enumeration uses a while loop with an exit when no successor exists, which is safe because it lives in a procedure and so gets no termination check.

List rooted trees.approach: Fix N (for example 5, with the 9-tree output) and enumerate rooted trees as canonical level sequences held in a constrained array of a ranged subtype, starting from the path and applying the Beyer-Hedetniemi successor in a while loop inside a procedure until no successor exists. Each sequence is rendered into a fixed 2*N character buffer by emitting the needed closing parentheses and then an opening one per node, and printed as one line. Every index and level update is preceded by an explicit bounds guard.
List rooted trees.summary: The task is plain deterministic enumeration with small fixed bounds and no annotations are needed since loops live in procedures, but the successor algorithm's loop-carried indexes and levels need careful guards to prove automatically.

effects.explanation: The program prints each literal form next to the value it denotes, using Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: All values are static constants written as literals well within Float's range, so the compiler checks their range statically, no arithmetic happens at run time and the only operation is formatting them as text.

Literals/Floating point.approach: Main declares Float constants written in each literal form Ada allows: plain decimal (0.13), digit groups with underscores (3.141_592_6), exponent notation (1.0E-12, 6.022_140_76E+23) and based literals (2#1.1#E+1, 16#F.8#). For each one it prints the source spelling as a String literal, followed by Float'Image of the constant. There are no loops, no input and no guards.
Literals/Floating point.summary: This should prove automatically (outlook likely). The program only declares static floating-point constants and prints them, so no run-time check can fail and none needs an annotation. All it adds to today's Silver is floating-point types and float-to-text formatting.

effects.explanation: Prints the value of each based literal with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Literals/Integer.approach: Explain the complete parameterized syntax: B is a decimal base from 2 through 16; write B#digits# or B:digits: using digit values below B, with case-insensitive A through F for values 10 through 15. Single underscores may separate digits. A nonnegative E exponent multiplies a based numeral by B raised to that exponent, while a decimal numeral uses base 10; the current exponent resource bound is 4096 and the resulting signed value must fit Integer. Demonstrate representative bases 2, 8, 10 and 16, both delimiters, separators, 727E0, 7#1#E3 and the signed endpoints using literal Integer initializers, not parsing/conversion calls. The first seven examples denote 727; 7#1#E3 denotes 343. Unary minus forms the negative endpoint expression. Current Silver has one predefined signed Integer type; no additional integer type or unsigned suffix syntax is claimed.
Literals/Integer.summary: Current Integer numerals already cover decimal and every based literal base from 2 through 16, hash and colon delimiters, digit separators, nonnegative exponents and the signed Integer endpoints. Numeral interpretation is performed by the language, with Image used only to display the resulting values.

review.setting_evidence: Selected inherited reviewer setting; runtime setting not independently exposed
review.method: Targeted static task, current-language and scratch-source review; no native admission, proof, build, test or execution

effects.explanation: The program prints the literal values it declares with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Literals/String.approach: Main declares a Character constant from a character literal ('a' and the quote character '''), String constants from literals including the empty string and a literal with doubled quotes (""), and prints each, concatenating the Character onto a String literal for output. There are no loops, no input and no guards; because Ada has no verbatim strings, here-strings or variable interpolation, the program simply shows that the fixed literals print exactly as written.
Literals/String.summary: The only checks are static-length concatenations and assignments of literals to constants, which GNATprove discharges trivially, so proof is likely. The only addition beyond today's Silver is a Character constant built from a character literal and concatenated onto a String for output.

effects.explanation: The results of and, or, xor and not are printed with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Logical operations.approach: A nested procedure Print_Logic (A, B : in Boolean) evaluates A and B, A or B, A xor B and not A, and for each one an if/else chooses between two fixed String literals such as "A and B is TRUE" and "A and B is FALSE" to pass to Put_Line. Main calls Print_Logic four times with the embedded literal pairs (True, True), (True, False), (False, True) and (False, False), first printing a header line for each pair the same way.
Logical operations.summary: The only checks are Bronze-level initialization and data flow of two in-mode Boolean parameters; Boolean operators and literal output cannot raise a run-time error, so everything discharges trivially.

effects.explanation: Prints the fitted r and R0 to standard output.

risks.explanation: Exp of R*I can overflow unless R is clamped to a guarded range (for example -1.0 to 1.0, with I at most 95) before each Exp call, and the clamp must reject out-of-range candidates visibly rather than alter the result.
The squared-error sum over 96 terms and the division by 1 + N0*(Eri-1)/K need range guards on the operands so the provers can bound them and the denominator stays nonzero.
The search loop lives in a procedure and uses a fixed iteration cap so no variant is needed and the result is not altered.
Whether the elementary function library admits Exp with a verified contract is an assumption about future library operations.

Logistic curve fitting in epidemiology.approach: Store the 96 daily totals as a constant Integer array and implement the sum of squared errors as a function over a bounded Real candidate r, guarding r to a safe interval before calling Exp. A procedure runs the pattern search (step doubling or halving) in a for loop with a fixed iteration cap, then computes R0 = Exp(12*r) and prints both values with a fixed-decimal float image.
Logistic curve fitting in epidemiology.summary: Everything is bounded floating-point arithmetic over a fixed 96-element array with a capped search loop in a procedure, so no annotation is needed, but proving no overflow in Exp and the squares depends on careful range guards and an admitted Exp.

effects.explanation: The program prints the revision date, the element count and the last element name with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried word counter is not bounded without an invariant, so the increment is guarded by a test just before it (Count < Natural'Last), with an else branch that prints a specified, visible error that can never be reached.

The start of the last word is kept as Start := I + 1, with I drawn from Elements'Range, so Start is Positive and at most Elements'Last + 1, and the slice Elements (Start .. Elements'Last) is either within bounds or empty.

Long literals, with continuations.approach: Elements is a constant String built from about 16 string literals joined with &, each under 81 columns, with a comment explaining that & is the continuation mechanism; Revision is a constant String holding an ISO date. A single for loop over Elements'Range tests each character against ' ', adds one to a guarded Natural counter and records Start := I + 1 at each blank. Three Put_Line calls then print the date, Count'Image and the slice from Start to Elements'Last.
Long literals, with continuations.summary: Every check comes from a static constant string, a for-loop index over that string's own range, and one guard placed just before the counter increment, so no annotation is needed. The only new surface is integers, characters, string indexing and slicing, for loops and 'Image.

effects.explanation: Prints the decimal result of 2^64 * 2^64 to standard output.

risks.explanation: Result indexes i+j-1 and i+20 are bounded by for-loop ranges 1..20 over a 1..40 array, so they discharge from static bounds.
The accumulator is a small ranged integer built from digit-typed operands (at most 9+81+9=99) and the carry is a 0..9 subtype, so ranges follow from types without a loop invariant.

Long multiplication.approach: Represent each operand as a constant 20-element array of base-10 digits (2^64 embedded as data) and the product as a 40-element digit array initialised to zero; schoolbook long multiplication uses nested for loops with a carry per row and writes the final carry into the row's top cell. Output scans from the most significant cell with a for loop and a Boolean flag to skip leading zeros, printing each digit via Character'Val, so no while loops or recursion are needed.
Long multiplication.summary: Fixed-capacity decimal digit arrays with for loops keep every index and arithmetic check derivable from declared ranges, so no invariant is required.

effects.explanation: Prints the long primes up to 500 on one line and the eight counts, one per line.

risks.explanation: The residue update r*10 mod p is safe because r and p are subtypes bounded by 64000 so r*10 fits Integer, and the result stays below p.
The long-prime counter is loop-carried, so each increment sits behind an explicit guard against the capacity bound that rejects visibly if ever reached.
Sieve marking uses j in 2 .. Max/i so i*j <= Max is a mild nonlinear fact the provers should accept, or a while loop with a guard before j+i avoids it.
The order search is a for loop over 1 .. p-1 with an early exit, so no variant is needed even for p = 2 or 5 where the residue never returns to 1.

Long primes.approach: A Boolean composite array indexed 0..64000 is filled by a nested for-loop sieve, and a function computes the multiplicative order of 10 modulo p with a bounded for loop that exits when the residue is 1, with the residue and p as range-bounded subtypes. A main loop over odd primes counts those whose order equals p-1, printing those up to 500 on one line and the running count at each doubled limit (500 up to 64000), using Integer'Image for the numbers.
Long primes.summary: Every check follows from small declared ranges (values at most 64000, products at most 640000) and for-loop bounds, with only the counter needing a visible guard, so proofs should discharge without annotations. The main burden on Silver is surface growth: arrays, subtypes, for and while loops, functions, and number-to-text output.

effects.explanation: Prints the seconds 600 to 609 table and the average time and average final staircase length.

risks.explanation: Staircase length, steps behind and the running totals are loop-carried, so each increment is guarded by an explicit length cap that stops the trial with a visible 'limit exceeded' report instead of altering results.
The random index is taken modulo the staircase length, which is declared as a subtype starting at 100 so the divisor is provably nonzero.
Steps-behind must stay within the staircase length type, which needs a guard before each increment since no invariant can relate the two loop-carried values.
The linear congruential generator state is a modular type so wraparound is the defined arithmetic and the reduction to an index uses a bounded unsigned value.
The escape loop is a while loop inside a procedure, so no termination check is generated, but the run is only bounded by the length cap.

Long stairs.approach: A procedure-only program keeps the generator state, steps behind, staircase length and totals as ranged or modular scalars, with a deterministic linear congruential generator supplying the random step position. An outer for loop runs 10000 trials, an inner while loop advances one step per second and adds five steps, each counted as behind when the random index is below steps behind, with a cap guard before every increment. The first trial prints seconds 600 to 609 and the end prints integer averages built from 'Image text.
Long stairs.summary: Everything is simple integer simulation whose checks follow from subtype ranges and a length-cap guard, and no annotation is needed because the while loop lives in a procedure; the work is in keeping the many loop-carried values bounded by guards.

effects.explanation: Prints each long year found in the demonstrated range, one per line.

Long year.approach: Declare a subtype Year of 1 .. 9999 and a function Is_Long (Y : Year) return Boolean that computes the weekday index of Dec 31 for Y and Y-1 as (P + P/4 - P/100 + P/400) mod 7 with P a bounded integer, returning true when it is 4 or the previous year's is 3. The previous year's term is computed with a guard so that Y-1 is only used when Y > 1 (year 0 term is 0). Main loops with a for loop over Year 1900 .. 2100, calling Put_Line (Y'Image) for each long year.
Long year.summary: Every check follows from a bounded Year subtype, small integer arithmetic and a plain for loop, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: Each test case's longest common prefix is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Indexing both strings at First + I - 1 is safe because the for loop bound is the minimum of the current prefix length and both string lengths, computed just before the loop.
Computing A'First + I - 1 for an unconstrained String could in principle overflow, but I is bounded by A'Length so the sum stays at or below A'Last.

Longest common prefix.approach: The first string of each test set is kept as a constant, and a procedure Narrow (First, Other : String; Len : in out Natural) clamps Len to the minimum of Len and both lengths, then scans with a for loop and sets Len to I - 1 at the first mismatching character, exiting the loop. Main embeds the nine test sets as String constants, calls Narrow once per further string, and prints the prefix slice First (First'First .. First'First + Len - 1) via Put_Line; the empty set prints an empty line, and no input is read, so no validation is needed.
Longest common prefix.summary: The program is a bounded for-loop character comparison over constant strings, so every index and length check follows from the clamped loop bound computed just before use and no loop-carried fact needs an invariant. The only new surface is unconstrained String parameters, string indexing and slices, and Natural counters.

effects.explanation: Prints the LCS of the embedded example strings with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The table cell increment L(I-1,J-1)+1 depends on array contents that no invariant describes, so it is guarded by an explicit comparison against the capacity limit with Reject as the visible outcome.

Traceback indices I, J are subtype-ranged 0..Max and decremented only under I>0 and J>0 guards, and the result cursor K needs an explicit K<Capacity guard because only an invariant could relate it to the match count.
The traceback while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, while the table fill uses only for loops.
The output slice of the result buffer must be proven within bounds from the guarded cursor, and the string lengths are fixed capacities checked against the embedded inputs.

Longest common subsequence.approach: Embed the two example strings as constants, fill a (0..M)x(0..N) Natural-subtype dynamic-programming table with nested for loops (match gives diagonal+1 under a capacity guard, otherwise the max of left and up), then trace back iteratively in a procedure with a while loop into a fixed-capacity Character buffer. Print the collected characters with Put_Line, using guards before every decrement and buffer write and rejecting if a guard fails.
Longest common subsequence.summary: The iterative table-based dynamic program uses only for-loop indexes, subtype-bounded indices and guards, so checks should discharge without annotations, but loop-carried counters in the traceback require careful guards.

effects.explanation: Prints the longest common substring "test" with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Indexes Left(I+K) and Right(J+K) are discharged by guards in the while condition (I+K <= Left'Last and J+K <= Right'Last) placed just before use.

The loop-carried match length K and best length/start are bounded only by their subtype ranges, so each increment and slice bound needs an explicit guard (K < 11 before K+1; Start+Len-1 <= 11 before slicing or copying) that GNATprove cannot derive without an invariant.
Indices and lengths use small ranged subtypes so sums like I+K stay far below Integer'Last, discharged by types alone.
The inner while loop sits in a procedure (no termination check) and the function-style wrapper is avoided in favor of a procedure with out parameters.

Longest common substring.approach: Embed the two strings as constant String(1..11) and String(1..16); a procedure Longest_Common uses nested for loops over every start pair (I, J) and an inner while loop that extends match length K under guards K < 11, I+K <= 11, J+K <= 16 and character equality, updating Best_Len and Best_Start (ranged subtypes) when K exceeds Best_Len. It then copies the best substring into a fixed 11-character buffer behind a guard on Start+Len-1 <= 11 and prints the slice (buffer(1..Best_Len)) with Put_Line.
Longest common substring.summary: All indexing follows from for-loop ranges and while-condition guards, but the loop-carried best length/start and match counter need careful guards since no invariants exist, so discharge depends on program shape. No annotation, recursion or non-trivial arithmetic is required.

effects.explanation: Prints each test case's word list and its longest common suffix to standard output.

risks.explanation: Character reads from the end of each word use Data (Len - P + 1), which is discharged by for-loop bounds P in 1 .. K where K is a ranged count never exceeding the word's Len, plus an explicit guard just before the read.
The loop-carried common-suffix length is declared with the subtype 0 .. 16 and only ever assigned a value from a guarded for-loop index, so its range check follows from its type.

Longest common suffix.approach: Each word is a record holding a fixed-capacity String (1 .. 16) and a Length in 0 .. 16, and the test lists are constant arrays of these records embedded in the program with the task's example data. A procedure takes the list and a count, starts with the first word's length as the candidate suffix length, and for each further word uses a bounded for loop comparing characters from the end (guarded by P <= Len of both words) to shrink the length to the true common suffix length. Main prints each list and the resulting suffix via Put and Put_Line with slices of the Data field.
Longest common suffix.summary: All loops are bounded for loops over ranged subtypes and every index is guarded by a length comparison just before use, so the checks follow from types and guards without any annotation. The new needs are small: records, arrays of records, character indexing, slices and non-terminating Put output.

effects.explanation: Prints the two longest increasing subsequences as text lines.

risks.explanation: The length table Best(J)+1 is a loop-carried value that stays in range only with a guard against a documented maximum length, or via a Best subtype bounded by the array capacity.
The predecessor chain walk uses a loop-carried index Pred(Best_Idx) that may be 0 by type, so each Seq(Best_Idx) access needs an explicit guard Best_Idx >= 1 with a visible stop.
The output line is assembled in a fixed-capacity buffer sized for the maximum sequence length, with a visible rejection if it would overflow.
Assigning Pred(I) := J and Best_Idx from loop-carried values depends on subtypes of the index range, which discharges only with constrained subtypes.

Longest increasing subsequence.approach: Two constant Integer arrays are embedded, and a procedure computes Best and Pred tables with nested for loops over the array range (O(n^2) DP), then finds the best tail and traces back through Pred into an output array, with explicit guards on index zero and on length limits. The result is rendered into a bounded text buffer using Integer'Image and printed with Put_Line, or element-wise with Put and a final Put_Line.
Longest increasing subsequence.summary: All loops are for loops in a procedure so no termination or variant issue arises, and the only non-routine checks are loop-carried Best lengths and the Pred index chain, which explicit guards can discharge without annotations. Text building of the printed lists adds some bounded-buffer length checks.

effects.explanation: Prints the longest palindromic substring of the embedded sample string with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: S(I+K) and S(J-K) are discharged because K runs over 0 .. (J-I)/2 inside I .. J, which are loop ranges over S'Range, so both indexes stay within I .. J.

The best-start and best-length variables are carried through loops, so they are declared as subtypes bounded by the string's range and length and assigned only from loop indexes, making the slice S(Best_Start .. Best_Start + Best_Len - 1) provably in bounds.

Longest palindromic substrings.approach: Embed a constant sample String and use three nested for loops over its own range: candidate start I, end J, and an inner for loop over K comparing S(I+K) with S(J-K), clearing a Boolean flag on mismatch. When a palindrome is longer than the best so far, record its start and length in bounded subtype variables, then print the slice with Put_Line, with a guarded branch for an empty string.
Longest palindromic substrings.summary: Every loop is a for loop and all indexes derive from S'Range and the loop bounds, so the checks follow from types and loop ranges with no invariants or recursion; the only care needed is bounded subtypes for the loop-carried best start and length.

effects.explanation: Reads lines until end of file.
Prints each longest line.
Over-limit input (line too long or too many ties) is rejected with a specified failure status.

risks.explanation: Appending a tied line indexes the fixed table only after an explicit Count < Max_Ties guard, and over-limit input takes the Reject path.
Copying a line into a table slot slices by its length, which is a subtype bounded by the maximum line length and checked on read.
The loop-carried tie count and best length are subtypes bounded by their maxima, with the increment guarded just before use.

Longest string challenge.approach: A fixed table of up to 256 stored lines (each a 1..255 character buffer plus a length) holds the current longest lines, with a count and best length. A while loop in the Main procedure reads each line from stdin until end of file, rejects lines over 255 characters, then clears the table if the line is longer, appends it if equal and the table is not full (else rejects), and ignores it if shorter; at end of file it prints the stored lines. The restrictions on comparison and arithmetic are treated as the challenge's own puzzle, and the program uses ordinary integer comparison and a bounded table instead of exceptions.
Longest string challenge.summary: Every check follows from bounded subtypes and guards placed before table appends and slice copies, with out-of-limit input given a specified rejection; the only unknowns are stdin line-reading operations and slice-copy proof shape.

effects.explanation: Prints each test string and its longest repeat-free substring with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The window start and last-seen positions live in subtypes bounded by a documented maximum length, with an explicit length guard rejecting longer inputs, so the +1 and length arithmetic stay in range.

Indexing the per-character table by Character and slicing Item(Best_First .. Best_Last) follow from the Character-indexed array type and the loop-carried subtype ranges, with the empty case handled by a guard before slicing.

It is plausible rather than likely because the loop-carried length, the mod index and the successor step depend on careful guard placement.

effects.explanation: Prints the compressed code list and the round-tripped text.

risks.explanation: Dictionary lookups, the output code array and the decoder's reverse-expansion buffer are indexed by loop-carried counters, so each use needs a guard just before it (for example a capacity check on the next free entry and on the buffer length) that rejects when full.
The prefix-chain walk in decompression is a while loop, which is acceptable only because it lives in a procedure and is also bounded by an explicit buffer-length guard.
Codes are a subtype 0..4095 and the next-entry counter increments in a loop, so the program guards the increment against the capacity limit instead of relying on an invariant.
The dictionary arrays and the buffers must be fully initialized by loops or aggregates before use, which flow analysis tracks reliably for whole-array aggregate initialization.

LZW compression.approach: Embed the task's example string TOBEORNOTTOBEORTOBEORNOT in a constant; store the dictionary as two parallel fixed-capacity arrays (prefix code and last character) with 256 pre-seeded single-character entries, and compress by a for loop over the input that linearly searches the dictionary for the (current code, next character) pair, emitting a code and adding an entry when absent, with a capacity guard that stops adding entries when the table is full. Decompress in a procedure that expands each code by walking the prefix chain into a bounded reverse buffer under a length guard, handling the code-equals-next-entry special case explicitly and rejecting out-of-range codes, then prints the codes and the reconstructed text, which must equal the input.
LZW compression.summary: Every check reduces to bounded-array indexing and range-typed codes with capacity guards placed immediately before use, and the loops sit in procedures with no recursion, but several loop-carried counters and the decoder's chain walk need carefully shaped guards.

effects.explanation: The task requires querying an internet API (such as api.macvendors.com) to retrieve the manufacturer for a MAC address.
Results (vendor name or N/A) are printed.
The task advises pausing between calls to avoid API throttling.

MAC vendor lookup.summary: The task needs a network lookup of a MAC address, returning N/A for no match and a null result for network or API errors. No fixed Oracle rule is broken, so network is only an effect Silver lacks today, with a delay between calls and console output. A future admitted network library operation with specified failure outcomes could cover it.

conflicts.explanation: The task's central requirement is to poke raw opcode bytes into memory and execute them. That means turning an address into a subprogram access (an unchecked conversion), allocating executable memory through foreign calls such as mmap, and running machine code that cannot be verified. SPARK excludes all of this, so no future Silver can admit it.

effects.explanation: Prints the result (19) returned by the machine code.
Needs executable memory from the operating system, such as mmap with PROT_EXEC, then munmap to clean it up.

Machine code.summary: Excluded: the task requires writing machine-code opcodes into memory and executing them. That needs unchecked address-to-subprogram conversion, foreign calls to allocate executable memory, and running unverified machine code, all of which break the Oracle's ban on unsafe constructs.

effects.explanation: Reads the multiline story up to a blank line and then one replacement word per placeholder.
Prompts for each placeholder and prints the final story.

risks.explanation: Scanning for '<' and '>' and slicing lines uses loop-carried positions, so each access is guarded by a comparison against the stored line length just before use.
Replacing a placeholder can lengthen a line past the fixed capacity, so a guard computes the new length in a wide integer type and rejects the story with a visible message when it would not fit.
Line counts, lengths and shift offsets are bounded by subtype ranges (e.g. 0..200 lines, 0..1000 characters) so arithmetic on them cannot overflow.
All loops live in procedures, so no termination check applies, and the replace-all scan advances past each replacement so it still finishes in practice.

Mad Libs.approach: Store the story as a fixed-capacity array of lines, each a bounded String buffer plus a length, read from stdin with a while loop until a blank line or the line cap (over-long lines or too many lines are rejected visibly). Repeatedly scan for the first complete <...> placeholder, prompt for its replacement, read the word into a bounded buffer, then replace every occurrence in all lines by rebuilding each line in a bounded buffer after a capacity guard. When no placeholder remains, print every line with Put_Line.
Mad Libs.summary: Everything is bounded string and array manipulation in procedures with explicit capacity guards and visible rejection, so no annotations are needed, but index and length checks on loop-carried positions make careful program shape necessary.

effects.explanation: Prints the welcome text, the prompt and the chosen answer.
Reads the user's question as one line from standard input.

risks.explanation: The hash step multiplies a value of subtype 0..19 by a small constant and adds a Character position (at most 255), so the result fits Integer and a mod 20 returns it to the subtype, which types alone establish.
The for loop runs over the question buffer's own index range and the answer selector has subtype 0..19, so the case statement is complete and every index is in range.

Magic 8-ball.approach: The program prints a welcome and a prompt, reads one question line into a bounded fixed-capacity buffer with a length (an over-long or empty line takes a specified rejection message), then folds the question's characters with a for loop into a hash in a 0..19 subtype using (H * 31 + Character'Pos) mod 20. A case statement over that subtype prints one of the 20 classic answers with Put_Line, replacing system randomness with a deterministic generator.
Magic 8-ball.summary: Every check follows from the 0..19 subtype, the loop over the buffer's own range and the bounded multiply-add, with no loop-carried value needing an invariant; the only new work is stdin line reading and a case statement over 20 literals.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 20 constants, the 1000th constant and the orders for thresholds 10^1 to 10^10 line by line.

risks.explanation: n*(n*n+1) is nonlinear but n is a subtype bounded to 3..3000 so the result is at most about 1.4e10 and fits in 64 bits, which provers discharge from the type range.
The threshold 10**p with p in 1..10 has a static-range exponent and the search covers orders up to 3000, beyond the required 2715, with a visible not-found line if the loop ends without a hit.

Magic constant.approach: "Declare a subtype of Long_Long_Integer for orders 3..3000 and a Magic function computing N*(N*N+1)/2 with bounded operands. Use a for loop over 3..22 and a line for order 1000, each printing 'Image text concatenated into bounded output lines. For each power p in 1..10, a for loop over orders with an exit on the first constant greater than 10**p prints the order, with an explicit visible not-found line if the loop ends without a hit; the optional 10^11 to 10^20 stretch is omitted."
Magic constant.summary: "Every check follows from the bounded order subtype and static loop ranges, and the 10^10 search fits in 64-bit integers, so no invariant is needed."

effects.explanation: Prints the total count, the largest magic number, per-length counts and the pandigital numbers.

risks.explanation: The depth cursor of the iterative search is loop-carried, so it is typed as a subtype 1..25 and every increment is guarded by a depth check just before use, with the 26th digit rejected explicitly since none exists.

Prefix values exceed 64 bits, so the program never forms them and instead recomputes the prefix remainder digit by digit as (r*10+d) mod n with r below n at most 25, which a subtype range keeps within bounds.
Counters (total at most 20457, per-length counts) are loop-carried and typed with a generous range subtype so increments cannot overflow.
The depth-first search is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the real bound is the 25-digit depth limit.

Magic numbers.approach: Digits of the current prefix are held in a fixed array of 25 digit values with a depth cursor, and an iterative depth-first search in a procedure tries digits 0..9 at each depth, keeping a prefix only when its remainder modulo its length is zero (recomputed from the digits with small remainders). Each accepted prefix increments a total and a per-length count array, the deepest one is copied into a 25-character buffer for the largest, and length 9 or 10 prefixes are checked for pandigitality with a seen-digit Boolean array and printed through a bounded text buffer. Integers are converted to text by 'Image-style digit conversion and all depth and digit indexes are range subtypes guarded before use.
Magic numbers.summary: No big numbers are needed because only prefix remainders modulo at most 25 are tracked, and every loop is a procedure while loop over bounded subtypes, so checks follow from types and depth guards. The nonroutine part is the loop-carried depth cursor and counters, which need careful typing.

effects.explanation: Prints the 8x8 square one row per line, with an optional magic-sum header line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried counter and the complement 65 minus counter stay inside 1..64 because the counter is derived directly from the row and column loop indexes (8*(r-1)+c) rather than accumulated, so the type range and static loop bounds discharge it.

Each output row is built into a fixed 8-cell buffer with fixed-width 3-character fields, so concatenation lengths are static; the integer text is padded using a guard on whether the value is below 10.

Magic squares of doubly even order.approach: Declare a constant N = 8 and a 2D Integer array subtype range 1..64 indexed by 1..N; two nested for loops compute each cell from the row and column indexes, taking the number itself when exactly one of row or column lies in the middle band 3..6 and its complement 65 minus the number otherwise. A second nested loop appends each value as a fixed-width field via 'Image with a guard for single digits and prints each row with Put and Put_Line. All indexes come from the loops over the array's own range, so no guards beyond width padding are needed.
Magic squares of doubly even order.summary: The task is a fixed-size 8x8 fill by a closed-form formula with for loops over static ranges, so every index and range check follows from types and loop bounds with no loop-carried unbounded values. Only the new surface for 2D arrays, integer-to-text conversion and Put is missing.

effects.explanation: The square rows and the magic number are written to standard output.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried row and column positions are typed as a subtype 0..Max-1 and each step is guarded by an explicit wrap test against N, so every array index check follows from the type.
N is bounded to an odd value up to a documented maximum such as 15, so N*N and the magic constant N*(N*N+1)/2 stay within Integer without needing a loop invariant.
Computing the next position as 'if X >= N-1 then 0 else X+1' keeps the result inside the subtype, and the start column N/2 is within range given N in 3..15.

Magic squares of odd order.approach: Use a constant-capacity two-dimensional Natural array (e.g. 15x15) and a procedure taking an odd N, which rejects even or out-of-range N and otherwise fills the square by the Siamese method in a for loop over 1..N*N with guarded wraparound of row and column, moving down when the up-right cell is already nonzero. The main program calls it for embedded values such as 3 and 5, printing each row with padded integer images via Put and a line terminator, then the magic number N*(N*N+1)/2.
Magic squares of odd order.summary: Every check is an index or arithmetic bound that follows from subtypes, a small documented maximum N, and guards before each wraparound step, so no annotation is needed. The fill loop only needs the types of its carried positions, which are tight enough because the wrap tests are explicit.

effects.explanation: Prints the magic constant and the 6x6 grid as text lines.

risks.explanation: The Siamese-method cell position is carried across loop iterations, so it is kept in a subtype 0..2 and advanced with (p + 1) mod 3 and (p + 2) mod 3, which keeps indexes in range without an invariant.
Cell values are computed as base + offset*9 from loop indexes with small declared ranges, so the results stay inside the 1..36 element subtype by static range reasoning.
Each output row is assembled in a fixed 18-character buffer, padding each 'Image of a 1..36 value to width 3, so the bounded-string length checks follow from static bounds.

Magic squares of singly even order.approach: Fixed n=6 with a 6x6 array of subtype 1..36; build the 3x3 odd magic square by the Siamese method with a for loop over 1..9 and position held in subtype 0..2 using mod, then fill the four quadrants with offsets 0, 9*3, 9*2, 9*1 per the A/C/D/B pattern and swap the left and right column blocks (with the middle-row indent) using for loops. Print the constant 111 and each row as a padded text line via 'Image; the construction is deterministic so no input validation is needed, and the row and column sums are not rechecked at run time.
Magic squares of singly even order.summary: Everything is fixed-size for-loop and mod arithmetic over small declared ranges, so index and range checks follow from types, but the loop-carried Siamese position and swap indexes need careful subtyping, hence plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints the three requested groups of numbered magnanimous numbers, one per line.

risks.explanation: The candidate is a subtype capped at 999_999 and every split sum and trial-division square stays below 2_000_000, so all arithmetic is bounded by types.
The results array has 400 slots and the store is guarded by count < 400 inside the while loop, with a visible message if the candidate cap is reached first.
The unbounded search is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the primality function uses only a for loop.

Magnanimous numbers.approach: A function Is_Prime uses a for loop over divisors 2..1000 with an exit when d*d exceeds the value, and a constant array of powers of ten supplies the split points. A procedure runs a while loop over candidates (guarded by count < 400 and candidate < 1_000_000), treats 0..9 as magnanimous, and for larger numbers tests left + right sums for each power of ten not above the candidate, storing hits in a 400-element array. A final for loop prints the 1..45, 241..250 and 391..400 entries as index and value text.
Magnanimous numbers.summary: All values are bounded by declared ranges (candidates below 10^6, sums below 2*10^6), indexes are guarded and loops are for loops or sit in a procedure, so no annotation is needed. The 400th magnanimous number is 602081, which fits within the cap.

effects.explanation: The program prints the resulting 64-bit block as hexadecimal text for the embedded example data.

risks.explanation: Each nibble extracted from the 32-bit sum by division and mod 16 is converted to a 0..15 table index, which follows from the mod bound and discharges without loop-carried facts.
The hexadecimal output digit lookup uses a value reduced mod 16 into a 16-character constant, so the index bound is statically evident.

Main step of GOST 28147-89.approach: Represent the two 32-bit halves and the key element as a 32-bit modular type, the substitution table as a constant 8x16 array of 4-bit-ranged values, and apply the main step as a function: add the key modulo 2^32, loop over the eight nibbles with a for loop replacing each via the table, rotate left 11 using modular multiply and divide by powers of two, xor with the other half, and swap. A Main procedure runs the step on embedded example data and prints the two halves as hex digits using a constant digit string indexed by a value reduced mod 16.
Main step of GOST 28147-89.summary: All arithmetic is on a wraparound modular type with for loops over fixed nibble indexes, so no overflow, range or index check depends on a loop-carried value and nothing needs an annotation.

effects.explanation: Renames the existing target file to a backup name and writes new text to a new file under the original name.
Must resolve symlinks to their target and check that the file exists, so it needs file metadata and link resolution.
The file name to back up and rewrite is most naturally given as a command-line argument.
Reports the outcome, including a rejected missing file.

Make a backup file.summary: The task needs a file rename (not copy), symlink-target resolution, and writing new text, all doable through a specified file and directory library operation with defined failure outcomes. Nothing in it breaks an Oracle rule; it only needs file and directory effects Silver lacks today.

effects.explanation: Creates a directory and any missing parent directories, and must succeed quietly if the directory already exists.
The path string is naturally supplied as a command-line argument by a runnable program.
A Silver program needs to report success or failure of directory creation, including an invalid path or a failed creation, through its exit status.

Make directory path.summary: The task is to create a directory path with the same behavior as mkdir -p, succeeding if it already exists. This needs a directory-creation effect that Silver does not yet have, plus string handling to split the path, but it breaks no fixed Oracle rule. Bounded path length and a specified failure outcome (non-zero exit status) fit Silver.

effects.explanation: Prints the computed value for k = 10 (-67) with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Frame pool and explicit-stack indices are loop-carried in a while loop with no invariant, so each use is guarded by a capacity test just before it and exceeding capacity takes a visible Reject path.
Accumulated values are subtype-bounded and each addition is guarded by a range test just before it, with an out-of-range sum rejected visibly.
The driver is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and a step-budget counter bounds work and rejects when exhausted.
The Algol recursion is replaced by an explicit fixed-capacity stack and a frame pool so no input-dependent recursion depth exists.

Man or boy test.approach: Model each Algol activation record as an entry in a fixed-size array of records (k copy, five argument-thunk references, each a small tagged choice of constant 1/0/-1 or a B-closure bound to a frame index), standing in for the heap and closures. A procedure runs an explicit-stack state machine in a bounded while loop that evaluates A and B without recursion, guarding frame allocation, stack depth, step budget and sum ranges with explicit tests that Reject on exceed. Main embeds k = 10 and prints the result with Put_Line.
Man or boy test.summary: The program has no true closures or recursion, so the Oracle is not violated, but its iterative defunctionalised evaluator carries many loop-carried indices and values that each need hand-placed guards, making automatic discharge plausible but not routine. Fixed capacity (about 800 frames, depth about 1000) covers k = 10 where A is called 722 times, and larger k would be rejected visibly.

effects.explanation: The program emits the rendered set as lines of text art on standard output.

risks.explanation: Fixed-point integer arithmetic (scaled by 2**12 or similar) on loop-carried x and y is discharged by escape-test guards that stop iteration once x*x+y*y exceeds 4 and by operand types bounded to roughly +-4.0 scaled, so the products fit in 64 bits.

The new x and y values assigned inside the while loop must be proven within their subtype after each update, which needs a guard or clamp placed immediately before the assignment, and the clamp is safe because it only applies after escape, where the pixel is already classified as outside.
The scaling divisions use only positive constant divisors, so they discharge trivially.
The iteration loop is a while loop with an iteration counter bounded by a constant, which is allowed in a procedure since procedures get no termination check, and it is kept out of functions.

Mandelbrot set.approach: Render a fixed-size (for example 60x24) text-art picture of the set into console output using scaled-integer fixed-point arithmetic in place of Float, so that the overflow checks follow from bounded subtypes. For each pixel a procedure runs a bounded while loop (iteration count at most a constant maximum) that squares the complex value, exits as soon as the squared magnitude exceeds 4.0 scaled, and then selects '*' or ' ' for the pixel. Each row is built in a fixed-length String buffer and written with Put_Line, so no unbounded structures are needed.
Mandelbrot set.summary: The task only asks for the set to be generated and drawn, so text art satisfies it, and an integer fixed-point iteration with an escape guard and a constant iteration cap keeps every check dischargeable without annotations. The nonlinear arithmetic on loop-carried values makes it plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints each of the eleven source values with its mapped value, one line each.

risks.explanation: The mapping t = b1 + (s - a1)*(b2 - b1)/(a2 - a1) is discharged by declaring the operands in bounded Float subtypes (0.0 to 10.0 and -1.0 to 0.0) so no intermediate can overflow or be infinite or NaN, though float provers may need range guards.

The divisor a2 - a1 is a nonzero value that must be known to the prover, so the function either takes a ranged subtype that excludes equal endpoints or guards with an explicit a2 /= a1 test that rejects degenerate ranges visibly.

Converting the Float result back into the second-range subtype needs a bound on the result; with s inside [a1,a2] and the guard in place the result is within [b1,b2], but the prover must reason about rounding at the boundary, which may need a clamp-free guard on the computed value.
Each output line concatenates two Float'Image results with fixed text, so the bounded string buffer must be sized for the maximum image length.
