Nonogram solver.approach: The four embedded puzzles are stored as clue strings parsed (letter minus 'A' plus 1) into fixed-capacity run arrays for at most 25 rows and 25 columns, with a grid of an enumeration type Unknown, Filled or Empty. A procedure repeatedly line-solves each row and column with a for-loop dynamic program over positions and run indexes, intersecting feasible placements until no cell changes, and an iterative explicit-stack backtracking procedure picks an unknown cell and tries both values when propagation stalls. Each puzzle prints the grid as '#' and '.' rows or a "No solution" line, and invalid or oversized clues print a specified rejection message.
Nonogram solver.summary: Every check follows from fixed 25-by-25 bounds, small ranged subtypes and for-loop indexes, and the iterative solver needs no recursion or annotations, but loop-carried indexes in the line-solving dynamic program and the explicit search stack need carefully placed guards.

effects.explanation: Prints a header and one line per year 2020 through 2029 with the two Thanksgiving dates.

risks.explanation: The weekday-of-first computation uses a Sakamoto-style formula on ranged Year (1900..2100) and Month subtypes, so every intermediate is bounded and discharges from types.
Result day is computed as 1 + offset + 7*(N-1) in a small Integer range and returned as 0 when it exceeds the month length (a visible 'no such day' value), so no subtype check can fail.

Nth Particular Weekday of the Month.approach: Use ranged subtypes for Year, Month (1..12), Weekday (0..6) and N (1..5), a loop-free function giving the weekday of the first of a month, a Days_In_Month function with leap-year logic, and Nth_Weekday returning the day number or 0 when absent. A for loop over 2020..2029 calls it for October second Monday and November fourth Thursday and prints each line using Image with a leading-zero guard, so all arithmetic is bounded by types and no loop-carried state exists.
Nth Particular Weekday of the Month.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic on small ranged subtypes in a fixed for loop with no loop-carried values, so the checks follow from types and the error case is a visible zero result.

effects.explanation: Prints each root result line with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Float overflow and range checks on the loop-carried iterate are discharged only by a bounded float subtype (about 1.0 to 1.0e9), range-guarded inputs and a clamp before each store, since no invariant can carry bounds.
Computing A / x**(n-1) directly would overflow for the 125th root, so the program divides by x repeatedly n-1 times in an inner for loop while x stays at least 1, so the quotient only shrinks.
The divisor x is nonzero because its subtype has a lower bound of 1.0 and A below 1 is handled by taking the root of 1/A, with inputs outside the documented range rejected visibly.
Iteration uses a for loop with a fixed count (about 5000) instead of a convergence test, so no variant is needed and the result is exact to printed precision since Newton converges monotonically.

Nth root.approach: A function Nth_Root takes a bounded float subtype A (1.0 to 1.0e9) and N in a small integer subtype (1..200), starts at x = A, and runs a fixed-count for loop of Newton steps x := ((N-1)*x + A/x**(N-1))/N, computing the power quotient by an inner for loop of N-1 divisions so no overflow occurs. Inputs below 1.0 are inverted and the root reciprocated, and out-of-range inputs are rejected with a printed message; the main procedure embeds the four sample cases and prints each result via a float-to-text image.
Nth root.summary: Everything is bounded by float subtypes and fixed-count for loops with no annotations, but proving float range/overflow on a loop-carried iterate through nonlinear arithmetic depends on careful clamping, so it is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints whether the object equals null with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The pool-specific access variable is never allocated, so the ownership memory-leak check at scope exit discharges because the value is known to be null.

Null object.approach: Main declares a pool-specific access type to Integer and a variable of that type initialized to null, without ever allocating. An if statement compares the variable with null and prints "object is null", with an else branch printing "object is not null".
Null object.summary: In Ada, null exists only for access values, so the program needs an access type declaration, but with no allocation or dereference the only checks are initialization and the leak check on a known-null value, which discharge trivially.

effects.explanation: Each embedded sample number and its spelled-out English name is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Appending words to a fixed 300-character buffer in a loop has a loop-carried length, so every Append guards Length + Word'Length against capacity and sets a visible overflow flag that makes the caller print a rejection line instead of a silent truncation.

Dividing a number in 0..999_999_999 into triplets and tens/units uses div and mod by literals on a ranged subtype, so each quotient and remainder is bounded by its subtype and discharges, but the loop-carried remainder must stay in a declared subtype rather than Integer.
Converting a digit value 0..19 or 2..9 into a word relies on case statements covering the whole subtype range, so no table indexing by a computed value is needed.

Number names.approach: Words are returned by non-recursive functions using case statements over small ranged subtypes (0..19 and 2..9), and a procedure splits the number (range 0..999_999_999, covering the required one million) into three-digit groups with a for loop from the millions group down. It appends each group's words, the scale name and the separators to a fixed 300-character buffer with an explicit length, using an Append procedure that guards capacity and sets an overflow flag, then prints the number image and the buffer slice for an embedded list of sample values including zero. Negative numbers are left out as optional, and an out-of-range sample prints a visible rejection.
Number names.summary: All arithmetic is div/mod by literals on declared subtypes and the buffer appends are guarded, so checks follow from types and guards with no recursion or annotations, though careful loop shape is needed for the buffer length.

effects.explanation: Prints the list, the prompt and the final score.
Reads the player's reversal count one line at a time, with a specified outcome at end of input.

risks.explanation: The reversal counter is loop-carried, so it is a bounded subtype and the loop stops with a visible message at the cap, letting the increment discharge from the guard.
The swap indexes N+1-I are safe because N is parsed into a 1..9 subtype with invalid input re-prompted, and I runs only over 1..N/2.
The play loop is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the sortedness test is a plain function using a for loop.

Number reversal game.approach: The board is a constrained array of 9 digits of a 1..9 subtype, initialised from an embedded jumbled permutation that is not sorted, and a function with a for loop checks ascending order. A procedure loops while unsorted: prints the board with Put, reads a line, parses it with validation into 1..9 (invalid text prints a message and re-prompts, end of input ends the game), reverses the first N elements with a for loop over 1..N/2, and increments a capped counter. Finally it prints the board and the score via 'Image.
Number reversal game.summary: All checks follow from the array's static bounds, a validated 1..9 subtype for the player's count and a capped counter, and the only unbounded loop sits in a procedure, so no annotation is needed. The one faithfulness cost is a fixed starting permutation instead of a shuffle, which a deterministic generator could replace.

effects.explanation: Prints the text board, move count and win message each turn.
Reads move commands as lines of text in place of mouse clicks.

risks.explanation: Row and column come from parsed input, so each move is validated against the 5x9 subtype bounds and rejected with a printed message before any array access.
The deterministic generator and the move counter are kept inside ranged subtypes (counter saturating at a stated limit), so the arithmetic cannot overflow.
The input-reading game loop is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and it ends at end of input or a quit command.
Board arrays and selection state are fully initialized by an initialization loop before play, so data-flow checks are routine.

Number triplets game.approach: The 5x9 board is a two-dimensional array of cell kinds (blue, black, white, yellow, red) plus a parallel array of tile labels 1 to 4, initialized and shuffled in rows 3 to 5 by Fisher-Yates driven by a small deterministic generator. A procedure loops reading lines such as a select command or a move command, validates ranges and the rule that tiles move only onto yellow or blue cells, applies the move, and reprints the text board with the move count. After every move a win check compares each red row against 1,2,3,4 and prints the win message with the move count.
Number triplets game.summary: The task is a vague interactive tile-sliding puzzle whose mouse and window parts can be replaced by text commands on stdin and a text board, and all checks follow from bounded array subtypes and guards on validated input. It is plausible rather than likely because of the moderate amount of loop-carried state, text parsing, and move-rule logic that needs careful guards.

effects.explanation: Prints each qualifying number on its own line.

risks.explanation: Each mod by a digit or by the product is preceded by an explicit nonzero guard that returns false for zero digits, so the check follows from the guard.
Digits are subtypes 0..9 and N is 1..999, so the product of at most three digits stays at most 729 with no loop-carried accumulator.

Numbers divisible by their individual di.approach: A for loop runs N over 1..999 and splits N into hundreds, tens and units digits typed 0..9 with / and mod, treating leading zeros as absent digits by branching on N < 10 and N < 100. For each digit present it rejects the number if the digit is zero or N mod digit is nonzero, then checks that N mod (product of present digits) is nonzero, and prints qualifying numbers with Put_Line of the integer image.
Numbers divisible by their individual di.summary: All values are bounded by types (N <= 999, digits <= 9, product <= 729) and every division is guarded by a nonzero test, with no loop-carried accumulator, so the checks should discharge from types and guards alone.

effects.explanation: Prints each qualifying number on its own line.

risks.explanation: The digit counter is a loop-carried value, discharged by a subtype range of 0..32 plus an explicit guard before each increment.
Digit array accesses use the counter and mirrored indexes, discharged by the counter's range subtype and for-loop bounds derived from it.

Numbers in base 10 that are palindromic.approach: A function Is_Palindrome (N : Natural; Base : Positive range 2..16) fills a fixed 32-entry digit array with a for loop (instead of a while loop, so the function needs no variant), peeling digits with mod and / while the remaining value is positive and the counter is below 32, then compares mirrored digits in a for loop over half the count. Main loops N over 0 .. 24999 and prints N'Image via Put_Line when Is_Palindrome holds for bases 2, 4 and 16, joined with and then.
Numbers in base 10 that are palindromic.summary: All arithmetic is bounded by small constants (values below 25000, 32 digits suffice for base 2), and every loop is a for loop, so checks follow from types and guards without annotations.

effects.explanation: Prints each qualifying number with its hex form and a final count.

risks.explanation: Hex digit buffer writes use a position that decreases in a while loop, so a guard before each write (position >= 1) is needed, and the buffer is sized for 3 digits to cover the 499 limit.
The count is a loop-carried value, discharged by declaring it as a subtype ranged 0 .. 499 and incrementing it only inside the 1 .. 499 for loop, or by guarding it before increment.

Numbers in base-16 representation that c.approach: Loop over N in 1 .. 499 in the main procedure; a helper procedure copies N into a local, extracts hex digits with mod 16 and / 16 in a bounded while loop (at most 3 digits, guarded by an index check), and sets a flag false if any digit is below 10. Qualifying numbers are printed with a decimal image and a hex string built from a Character lookup into a constant 16-character table, and a final count line is printed.
Numbers in base-16 representation that c.summary: All arithmetic is on small ranged integers with constant bounds (n < 500, at most 3 hex digits), so every check follows from types and guards just before use, and the digit-extraction loop lives in a procedure so it needs no termination proof.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 50 qualifying numbers, the 1,000th to millionth qualifying numbers and the final-digit breakdowns.

risks.explanation: Loop-carried counters (qualifier count, per-digit counts, candidate k) are bounded by declared ranges and an explicit guard that ends the loop or rejects before any increment, since no invariant can be written.
The scan is a while loop inside a procedure (no termination check) or a for loop over a fixed range, and the letter-lookup functions are loop-free so they need no variant.
Letter lookups decompose a bounded number (below 100,000,000) with division and mod into subtype-ranged parts that index constant name tables, which discharges from the subtype bounds.
Output lines are built in fixed-capacity buffers sized for the largest value, with padding computed from 'Image lengths that the bounded number range limits.

Numbers k such that the last letter of k.approach: Compute the first and last letter of the English name of any n below 100,000,000 directly (without building the name) from constant Character tables for 0..19, tens, and the magnitude words, using a loop-free case/if decomposition by millions, thousands and hundreds. A procedure scans k upward with a bounded while loop, compares last_letter(k) with first_letter(k+1), records the first 50 values, bumps a 10-entry array of per-final-digit counts, and at 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000 qualifiers prints the number and the breakdown as bounded string lines. Counts and k are range-typed and guarded, with the loop exiting at the millionth qualifier.
Numbers k such that the last letter of k.summary: Every check follows from small constant tables, range subtypes and division/mod on a bounded k, but the carried counters and the 10-million-iteration scan need careful guard placement without invariants, so discharge depends on program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints the 50 members, one line each, with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The divisor-sum accumulator is loop-carried with no invariant, so each addition is guarded against a declared 64-bit-range cap, and exceeding the cap yields a visible rejection rather than a changed result.
The scan counter K and found count are bounded by an explicit search limit and a count limit checked in the loop condition, with a visible failure message if the limit is reached before 50 members.
The search uses a while loop inside a procedure (no termination check), while the divisor-sum function uses only a for loop, so no variant is needed.
The mod divisor is the for-loop index starting at 1, so it is statically nonzero.

Numbers k whose divisor sum is equal to.approach: A function Sigma(N) loops I in 1 .. N with trial division (N mod I = 0), adding I to a guarded accumulator typed as a range-bounded integer; a Main procedure scans K from 1 upward in a while loop bounded by a fixed search limit, comparing Sigma(K) and Sigma(K+1) and counting matches until 50. Each hit is printed with Put_Line using the count and K images; reaching the limit before 50 prints a specified failure line. The full trial-division loop over 1 .. N avoids the square-root bound, which needs floating point or nonlinear reasoning.
Numbers k whose divisor sum is equal to.summary: Everything is small integer arithmetic with for-loop indexes and a capped accumulator guard, so it should discharge with careful program shape, though the accumulator and search limit need explicit guards. No annotations, recursion, or exotic effects are needed beyond console output.

effects.explanation: Prints each non-representable positive integer and a final count with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The reachable-sum update reads Reachable (S - K*K) inside a reverse for loop over S in K*K .. Limit, and an explicit guard on S >= K*K just before the access keeps the index in range without an invariant.
K*K and S - K*K are bounded by declared subtypes (K at most the square root of Limit, S at most Limit), so the arithmetic cannot overflow or leave the index range.

Numbers which are not the sum of distinc.approach: Keep a Boolean array Reachable (0 .. Limit) with Reachable (0) true, where Limit is a documented fixed bound comfortably above 128 (the largest non-representable number), and run a 0/1 subset-sum pass over the squares K*K for K in 1 .. Root, with S iterating in reverse from Limit down to K*K and setting Reachable (S) when Reachable (S - K*K) holds. A final for loop prints every positive index that is still false, with a running count in a subtype-bounded counter, then prints the count. All loops are for loops, so no variants are needed, and the Limit is justified by a documented argument that every value from 129 up is a sum of distinct squares (verified for a run of consecutive values and extended by induction), so the output is complete.
Numbers which are not the sum of distinc.summary: Everything is bounded for loops over small ranged subtypes with a Boolean array, so each index and arithmetic check follows from types and the loop range; the only subtlety is documenting the fixed limit, which Oracle rule 7 allows.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 50 matching numbers and the 500th, 5,000th and 50,000th as text lines.

risks.explanation: The divisor count and match count are loop-carried, so each increment sits behind a guard against a small cap (the divisor count is capped at 9, since only exactly 8 matters), and the cap does not change which numbers match.
Candidate N is a for-loop index over a fixed range of 1..300000, and the divisor loop index runs over 1..512 with an I*I <= N guard, so I*I and N mod I stay within Integer.
Formatted output lines are built in a fixed-size buffer sized for 10 numbers of at most 6 digits plus padding, with a guarded write position before each append.
The program must give a visible failure outcome if fewer than 50,000 matches are found within the 300000 limit; the real 50,000th value is 223735, so this path is never taken.

Numbers which are the cube roots of the.approach: A procedure Divisor_Count takes N in a ranged subtype and loops I over 1..512 with a guard I*I <= N, adding 2 per divisor pair (1 when I*I = N) with a saturating cap. The main loop is a for loop over candidates 1..300000 that counts matches (N = 1 or divisor count = 8). It prints the first 50 in rows of 10 using Image and a fixed buffer, and prints the 500th, 5,000th and 50,000th when the match counter reaches them.
Numbers which are the cube roots of the.summary: All arithmetic is bounded by declared ranges and a fixed 512 trial-division limit, and every loop is a for loop, so checks follow from types and guards; the only care needed is saturating the loop-carried counters and bounding the text buffer.

effects.explanation: The qualifying numbers are printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: The digit-sum accumulator is loop-carried so GNATprove knows only its type, which is handled by declaring it as a wide ranged subtype and guarding the addition with a visible check that never changes the result, since at most 8 base-2 and 5 base-3 digits are summed.
Digit extraction uses for loops with fixed iteration counts (8 binary, 5 ternary digits, enough for n below 256), so the functions need no variant.

Numbers whose binary and ternary digit s.approach: A function Digit_Sum (N, Base) loops a fixed number of times, adding N mod Base to a ranged accumulator and dividing N by Base, and a function Is_Prime tests divisors 2 to 9 on sums of at most 10 with a for loop. The Main loop runs n from 1 to 199 with a ranged subtype and prints each qualifying n with Put_Line of its image, because a line-terminator-free Put may be unavailable.
Numbers whose binary and ternary digit s.summary: All values are small and bounded by declared ranges (n below 200, sums at most 10), and every loop is a for loop with a static bound, so the checks follow from types and one accumulator guard. No annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the qualifying numbers in rows of ten with Put_Line (and Put for padded columns).

risks.explanation: The sieve counter increment Counts(J)+1 is loop-carried through array elements, so it is guarded by an explicit comparison against the component subtype's upper bound with a visible Reject outcome otherwise.
The while loop's J := J + I is guarded by J < Limit before each use, and I and J are range-typed so J + I cannot overflow and Counts(J) is in range.
Each 6-character column is written into a fixed 80-character line buffer at a position guarded to stay within bounds, flushing every ten entries.
The stepping while loop lives in a procedure so no termination check arises, and the primality test uses for loops.

Numbers whose count of divisors is prime.approach: Build a Counts array indexed 1..99_999 of a ranged subtype by a sieve: for each I a while loop in a procedure steps J by I while J < Limit, incrementing Counts(J) under a bound guard. Then for each N from 1 to Limit-1 test whether Counts(N) is prime and not 2 using a for-loop trial division over 2..Counts(N)-1 with a Boolean flag, and print N right-justified in a fixed buffer, flushing a line every ten hits. Doing the n<1000 task first and the stretch bound as the constant Limit keeps everything fixed-size.
Numbers whose count of divisors is prime.summary: All arrays, indexes and counters have declared ranges and are guarded just before use, and the only non-for loop is a stepping while loop inside a procedure, so no annotation is needed; the loop-carried count increments and the text formatting require careful guard placement, hence plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 200 sequence numbers in rows of 20 and the 10,000,000th number.

risks.explanation: The Rises and Falls counters and the candidate Value are loop-carried, so each increment is preceded by an explicit guard against the type's upper bound, and the outer loop stops with a visible rejection if Value reaches its limit.

The digit scan is a for loop over a fixed 10 positions inside a function, so no variant is needed, while the unbounded candidate search with a while loop lives in a procedure with no termination check.
Only division and mod by the literal 10 are used, so no zero-divisor check arises.

Numbers with equal rises and falls.approach: A pure Boolean function copies the candidate into a local, then runs a fixed 10-iteration for loop that peels off the last two digits with mod and / 10, counting rises and falls in guarded counters and comparing them at the end. A procedure with a while loop on Count below 10,000,000 increments a ranged candidate (rejecting at the type's upper bound), prints the first 200 hits via Put and Integer'Image padded into rows of 20, and prints the 10,000,000th hit (41,909,002) with Put_Line.
Numbers with equal rises and falls.summary: Every check follows from ranged types, the fixed-length digit loop and small guards before each carried increment, and the roughly 42 million iterations are a runtime cost, not a proof issue; the main work is careful guard placement for the counters, hence plausible.

effects.explanation: Prints each matching number on its own line.

risks.explanation: The digit-sum accumulator is a subtype 0..13 and the addition is guarded by a test just before it, so the range check discharges without an invariant.

Numbers with prime digits whose sum is 1.approach: A for loop runs N over 1 .. 322222 (the largest possible answer, since seven digits sum to at least 14), and an inner fixed six-iteration for loop peels digits off a copy of N using mod 10 and / 10, accepting a digit only if it is 2, 3, 5 or 7 and the running sum stays at most 13 (guard before the add). Digits are tracked in a Natural-range remainder, a Boolean ok flag, and a 0..13 sum, and numbers with ok and sum exactly 13 are printed with Put_Line of the integer image.
Numbers with prime digits whose sum is 1.summary: Every check is a range or division-by-ten on bounded integer subtypes with for loops only and a guard before each accumulation, so the proofs follow from types and local guards with no annotation needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the matching numbers and the total count.

risks.explanation: The digit-extraction while loop is placed in a procedure that fills a Boolean array so no termination check applies, and a for loop over 0 .. 99_999 always terminates.
Set (Nn mod Base) is indexed by a value in 0 .. 15, which holds because Base is a constant 10 or 16 (or a subtype 10 .. 16) so the mod result is within the array range.

The Count increment is bounded because Count is a subtype of 0 .. 100_000 and is only incremented once per iteration of a 100_000-iteration loop, so a guard before the increment (Count < 100_000) is needed since the loop-carried value is otherwise unbounded in the prover's view.

Numbers with same digit set in base 10 a.approach: Two Boolean arrays indexed 0 .. 15 are filled by a procedure Fill_Digits (N, Base, Set) that uses a while loop with Nn mod Base and Nn / Base, and the main for loop over 0 .. 99_999 compares the two arrays element by element (or via array equality) and increments a bounded Count guarded by Count < 100_000. Output is each number via 'Image text built in a bounded String buffer with padding to fixed width, ten per line, followed by a total line, using Put_Line only if each row is assembled into a String first.
Numbers with same digit set in base 10 a.summary: Every check follows from small constant bases, a 0 .. 15 array range, a for-loop bound and a guarded counter, and the while loop lives in a procedure so no variant is needed; the main work is just the new integer, array and string-building surface.

effects.explanation: Prints the distance and its propagated error as a line of text.

risks.explanation: Every Float operation needs a no-overflow and finite-result proof, which the program obtains by declaring a bounded Float subtype (for example magnitude up to 1.0E6) and guarding operands before each multiply, square and divide.
Sigma/Value division requires Value /= 0.0, discharged by an explicit guard whose failure yields a visible rejection flag in the result rather than a silently altered number.

Sqrt requires a nonnegative argument, which the prover must infer from a sum of squares (nonlinear floating point), so the code guards the argument with an explicit check before calling the admitted Sqrt.
Result magnitudes after each operation must fit the bounded subtype, so each operation checks the result bound in a guard and reports an error outcome otherwise.

Numeric error propagation.approach: Represent an uncertain number as a record of Value, Sigma and a Valid flag over a bounded Float subtype, with straight-line functions for subtract, add, multiply, integer power and square root that guard operand magnitudes and zero divisors before each floating-point step. Main embeds the four example coordinates, computes d = sqrt((x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2) with no loops, and prints the value and error rounded to two decimals through a bounded string-building routine, or a visible rejection message if any guard failed.
Numeric error propagation.summary: The program is loop-free with bounded float operands, so each check follows from subtype ranges and guards just before the operation, but it depends on Float arithmetic and an admitted Sqrt with nonnegativity provable, which makes proof discharge depend on careful range guards.

effects.explanation: The program prints the description of the separator rules and the demonstrated values with Put_Line.

Numeric separator syntax.approach: The program prints String-literal lines stating Ada's rule (underscore only, single, between digits) and declares Integer constants written with separators such as 1_000_000 and 16#FF_FF#. It compares each with its separator-free literal using if statements and prints the 'Image of each value and an equal or differs line. All values are static constants within Integer, so no loop or guard is needed.
Numeric separator syntax.summary: Every value is a static literal constant and the output is fixed text plus 'Image of in-range constants, so no check depends on loop-carried values or annotations.

effects.explanation: Prints each input list line and its expanded result line with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Fixed-capacity decimal digit arrays carry through multiply-by-small-factor loops, so each digit-times-multiplier-plus-carry is kept in range by digit and carry subtypes bounded by the multiplier (at most 1728 or 10) and an explicit overflow check that rejects results exceeding capacity.

Digit positions for decimal-point shifts, exponent scaling and comma insertion are computed values, so each is guarded by a comparison against the buffer bounds before use, with a visible Reject-style outcome on overflow.
Exponent digits are accumulated in a loop and must be clamped by a guard (reject beyond a small limit) since no invariant can bound the accumulator.
All parsing and arithmetic loops live in procedures or are for loops over the buffer range, so no variant is needed.
Output lines are built in a bounded String buffer sized for the longest result (about 120 digits with commas and fraction), with length guards before each append.

Numerical and alphabetical suffixes.approach: Embed the 27 test strings in a constant array of bounded strings; a procedure scans each, strips commas, reads sign, mantissa digits and optional exponent into a fixed-capacity decimal digit array with a scale, then repeatedly applies suffix multipliers (named words matched case-insensitively with minimum abbreviations, metric letters with optional i, or counted factorial steps) via digit-wise multiply-by-small-integer and multiply-by-power-of-ten shifts. Results are printed exactly as comma-grouped integer part plus trimmed fraction, with every index and capacity use guarded and overflow producing a specified rejection message.
Numerical and alphabetical suffixes.summary: Exact arithmetic in fixed-capacity decimal digit arrays handles the 10^100 and 2^120 multipliers without floating point, and every check follows from digit and carry subtypes plus guards before each shift or append, though the many loop-carried positions need careful shaping.

effects.explanation: Prints the five method results for each of the four demonstration integrals.

risks.explanation: Float sums carried through loops of up to 6,000,000 iterations know only the type range afterwards, so each accumulation step is guarded against leaving a declared bounded float subtype and rejects visibly otherwise.
The 1/x integrand and the step-size division by N need a nonzero divisor, which is discharged by guarding x against a positive lower bound just before dividing and by N being a Positive subtype.
The x**3 and 4*sum1 style products need operand ranges small enough to stay within the float subtype, which declared bounds on a, b, n and the integrand domain provide.

Converting the loop index to a float and computing a + h*i produces a loop-carried value whose range is not known, so it is computed directly from the index and clamped by a guard to the interval before calling the integrand.
Printing floats needs a bounded float-to-text conversion that scales to integers with guarded range checks, whose proof depends on the admitted library or a carefully guarded scaling routine.

Numerical integration.approach: Real is a bounded Long_Float subtype and the integrand is selected by an enumeration (Cubed, Reciprocal, Identity) through a case-based function F rather than a function parameter or generic. Five procedures (left, right, midpoint, trapezium, Simpson) use for loops over 1 .. N with each x computed directly from the index, and each accumulation is guarded against leaving the bounded range, rejecting visibly if it would. A main procedure runs the four embedded test cases and prints results through a bounded float-to-text routine.
Numerical integration.summary: The task is plain numerical code with no Oracle conflict and loops that are for loops, but proofs for float accumulators over millions of iterations only discharge if each step carries an explicit range guard, which makes it plausible rather than likely. Float formatting and the 1/x domain guard add further care but need no annotations.

effects.explanation: Prints the integral estimate for sin(x) from 0 to 1.

risks.explanation: Every float operation must be shown finite, so all values live in bounded subtypes and each stored sum is guarded against leaving the range with a visible rejection outcome.
The recursion is replaced by an explicit fixed-capacity work stack in a procedure with a while loop, which gets no termination check, and a depth cap bounds the stack so push never overflows.
Stack pushes are guarded by a depth limit strictly below the array capacity, so the index check follows from the guard just before each push.

Accumulating the result across loop iterations loses all facts except the type range, so the accumulator is clamped by a guard that rejects out-of-range totals rather than silently altering the answer.
sin must come from a hand-written Taylor series over a bounded argument in 0..1 in a for loop, whose nonlinear float arithmetic discharges only because operands are range-bounded.

Numerical integration/Adaptive Simpson's.approach: Intervals are records of (a, fa, b, fb, tol, whole, m, fm, depth) held in a fixed-capacity array used as an explicit stack inside a procedure, replacing the recursion, with a while loop popping an interval, applying the Simpson test, and either adding to the accumulator or pushing two halves when depth and stack capacity allow. The integrand is a function computing sin by a fixed-term Taylor series on a bounded float subtype, and the result is printed with a float-to-text conversion. Guards on depth, stack index and value ranges lead to a specified rejection message.
Numerical integration/Adaptive Simpson's.summary: The task is plain bounded floating-point arithmetic with recursion convertible to an explicit stack in a procedure, so no annotation is needed, but float range proofs through loop-carried values need careful guarding. The expected output 0.459698 is a bounded computation with depth cap, so it is faithful under the Oracle.

effects.explanation: Prints the 5 roots, 5 weights and the integral estimate as text lines.

risks.explanation: Exp, Cos and the Newton iteration need operands bounded by a subtype such as Float range -1.0e3 .. 1.0e3, with the division by the derivative guarded against zero (visible fallback outcome) so no overflow or division check can fail.
The Newton loop is a while loop in a procedure with a fixed iteration cap (e.g. 100) and a convergence exit, so no termination check applies and no variant is needed.

Computed values stored back into range-limited Long_Float subtypes (the iterate x, the polynomial values) need clamping guards or wide subtypes, otherwise the loop-carried values only have type-range knowledge and each store checks against that range.
Legendre coefficient table indices 0..5 come from for-loops over the array's own range, but expressions like n-2 need loop bounds starting at 2 to stay in range.

Numerical integration/Gauss-Legendre Qua.approach: Fixed constant N=5 with arrays of Long_Float for the Legendre coefficients, roots and weights, built with nested for-loops and a bounded Newton iteration (while loop with an iteration cap inside a procedure); the integrand exp(x) is a function applied over the shifted nodes on [-3,3], and the results are printed via a fixed-precision float-to-text routine into bounded String buffers. Every loop-carried float is declared in a bounded subtype and guards precede each division, so the failure outcome is visible (a printed message) rather than silently altered.
Numerical integration/Gauss-Legendre Qua.summary: The task is bounded, uses a fixed 5-point rule and float arithmetic over small ranges, so it needs no annotations, but proving no overflow or division-by-zero through loop-carried floats and Newton updates depends on careful subtype bounds and guards. Float formatting and an admitted elementary-function library (Exp, Cos) are new surface that makes it plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The program prints the Romberg result for the integral of exp(x) from -3 to 3 with 5 steps.

risks.explanation: Every float add, multiply and divide needs a bounded operand range, which the program gets from a ranged Real subtype and from guards before each operation that reject (printing a visible failure) if a value leaves the range.

Loop-carried sums and the extrapolation values R(k) are known only by their subtype range, so each is guarded just before the update against a fixed bound far above the expected magnitudes (about 60).
The divisors (f-1) with f=4**k and the interval count are constants or loop-bounded positive values, so a guard or the subtype lower bound shows they are nonzero.
All loops are for loops over fixed small ranges and exp is a fixed-term Taylor series, so no variant or recursion is needed.
The Taylor terms term*x/k stay bounded only through a guard on the magnitude of each term, which must hold for x in [-3, 3] without changing the computed value.

Numerical integration/Romberg integratio.approach: Fixed-size arrays of a bounded Real subtype hold the previous and current Romberg rows (6 entries), and the integrand exp(x) is a function using a fixed-term Taylor series with range reduction avoided by the narrow domain [-3, 3]. The trapezoid refinement is nested for loops (intervals doubling via an integer counter bounded by 32), with guards before each accumulation that print a rejection if a value leaves the bounded range, and the final value is printed through float-to-text formatting.
Numerical integration/Romberg integratio.summary: All loops are bounded for loops and the data is small, but floating-point checks on loop-carried accumulators only discharge through declared range subtypes plus explicit guards, so success depends on careful program shape; Silver also needs float types and float formatting that it lacks today.

effects.explanation: Prints the two integral results as text.

risks.explanation: Sinh, Cosh and Tanh of a bounded t (|t| at most 3.2) stay finite only if the float type is range-constrained and the library functions carry range contracts, which the provers must bound through nonlinear products.

The integral accumulator ss is loop-carried with no invariant, so each addition must be guarded against the declared float range, with an overflow outcome that is a visible rejection rather than a clamp.
The index i from -n to n with n = 2**k - 1 and k at most 5 is bounded by a ranged subtype for k, so i*h stays within a declared range.
All loops are bounded for loops inside a procedure, so no variant is needed; the integrand is selected by an enumeration with a case-style if rather than a function pointer.

Numerical integration/Tanh-Sinh Quadratu.approach: Define a bounded Float type, an enumeration choosing the integrand (Sin or Exp) in place of a function parameter, and a procedure that runs the nested for loops over k in 1..5 and i in -n..n with h = 0.1, computing sinh, cosh, tanh from an admitted elementary-function library with range-bounded inputs. Early exit on accuracy is a visible stop test between iterations; results are printed through text formatting of the float to eight decimals via integer scaling.
Numerical integration/Tanh-Sinh Quadratu.summary: Control flow is just bounded for loops, but floating-point hyperbolic functions and a loop-carried accumulator need an admitted math library with range contracts and careful range subtypes, so discharge is plausible rather than routine.

effects.explanation: Prints each embedded sample name with its NYSIIS code via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Every look-behind, look-ahead and prefix or suffix test (MAC, SCH, DT, EV, the previous character) must be guarded by a length comparison just before the access, which is routine but needs care throughout.

The buffer holds 64 characters and each rewrite step (such as MAC to MCC, SCH to SSS, EV to AF) never lengthens the text beyond the bound, with an explicit guard before every append so the buffer cannot overflow.
The loop-carried logical length is a subtype bounded by the buffer capacity, so index arithmetic on it discharges from its type, but each increment needs a guard against the capacity.
The in-place rewrite passes use for loops, or while loops inside procedures, so no function needs a variant.

NYSIIS.approach: Embed the sample names as String constants in an array, and for each one copy its uppercased letters into a fixed 64-character buffer with a length counter, rejecting names longer than the capacity with a visible message. Apply the original NYSIIS rules as a series of procedures, each a for loop copying from one buffer to another with explicit length guards: prefix rules, suffix rules, vowel mapping, H and W handling, trailing S and A removal, and duplicate collapse. Print the name and the code with Put_Line; the optional suffix and multi-name handling is a small table of suffixes tested by length-guarded comparison.
NYSIIS.summary: The task is pure text processing over bounded character buffers, so every check follows from the buffer's declared capacity, for-loop ranges and guards before each look-behind or look-ahead. It is plausible rather than likely only because many loop-carried lengths need guards and many rewrite passes must be written carefully.

effects.explanation: Prints a heading and the sixteen O'Halloran numbers to standard output.

risks.explanation: The array write Areas (Area) is preceded by an explicit if Area <= 999 guard, so the index check discharges from the guard and the array's declared bounds.
Loop indexes are subtypes limited to 1 .. 249, so every product and sum of three products stays far below Integer'Last without any invariant.

O'Halloran numbers.approach: A Boolean array indexed 8 .. 999 starts all True; three nested for loops over 1 .. 249 (the largest side possible below 1000 since the other two sides are at least 1) compute Area = 2*(L*W + W*H + H*L) and, guarded by Area >= 8 and Area <= 999, clear that entry. A final for loop over the array's range prints each remaining True even index with Put_Line of its 'Image, after a heading line.
O'Halloran numbers.summary: Every check follows from loop-index subtype ranges and one guard before the array write, so no loop invariant is needed; the only cost is about 15 million cheap iterations of the triple loop, which is not a proof issue.

effects.explanation: Each object's print procedure writes its contents to standard output, before writing and after reading back.
The objects are written in binary form to objects.dat, which is then reopened and read back, with open, write or read failure and malformed content each giving a specified outcome.

risks.explanation: Rebuilding ranged integer fields from bytes read back from the file is guarded by an explicit comparison against the field's range, and a malformed record is rejected with a visible message.
Flow analysis of dispatching Print calls needs every overriding Print to touch the same globals (the output state) as the root's Print, which holds because they all write only through Silver_IO.

SPARK excludes stream attributes such as 'Class'Output and 'Class'Input, so serialization must be written by hand as a kind byte plus field bytes through an admitted binary file library whose failure outcomes are specified.

Object serialization.approach: A package declares a tagged root record (Message, with an Id field in a declared range) and two derived types (Sensor_Message and Control_Message), each extending it with integer fields and overriding a primitive Print, plus a class-wide Display that dispatches; Main builds one instance of each from embedded data and displays them. Each object is serialized to objects.dat as a kind byte followed by its fields split into bytes with / and mod, and a record count is written first. The file is read back with a for loop over that count, where at most 3 are accepted; each record's kind byte selects which concrete object to rebuild, and the program rejects an unknown kind, an out-of-range field or an I/O failure with a visible message.
Object serialization.summary: Every check is a byte-to-field range check guarded just before use, a for-loop index, or a static bound, and tagged types with dispatching procedures are supported by SPARK without annotations. Serialization uses hand-written byte encoding because SPARK has no stream attributes, and nothing else needs an annotation.

effects.explanation: Reads the source image from a named file in a simple uncompressed raster format such as binary PGM.
Prints each text line (or its recognized stand-in) and a placeholder or empty line at every detected gap.

risks.explanation: Pixel and row-band indexing is into fixed-capacity bounded arrays, with the header width and height validated against the capacity before any read and oversized images rejected visibly.

Row ink sums, band heights and the average-height gap threshold are accumulated in loops, so they are held in ranged integer types sized from the image capacity bound so that type ranges alone discharge them.
Loop-carried band counters must stay below the band array capacity, which needs an explicit guard before each band is recorded that rejects images with too many bands.

Real glyph recognition is far larger than gap detection, so the faithful program recognizes layout geometry only and a limited template match of the known glyph set would be needed to print the text itself.

OCR of text in image.approach: Read a bounded grayscale PGM image into a fixed two-dimensional pixel array after validating its header and dimensions, compute a per-row ink count, and group consecutive inked rows into line bands recorded in a bounded array. Compare the vertical gap between consecutive bands with a threshold proportional to the average band height, and print each line followed by an explicit blank-line placeholder wherever the gap exceeds it. Reading and loops are in procedures with while loops guarded by capacity checks, and unreadable or oversized input prints a specified rejection.
OCR of text in image.summary: There is no fixed Oracle conflict because the task allows geometric line-gap measurement, and the bounded-array row scan is mostly ranged integer arithmetic that types and guards discharge, though real text recognition is the hard, uncertain part.

effects.explanation: Prints the odd squares between 100 and 999 on one line.

Odd and square numbers.approach: Main loops over I in 11 .. 31. If (I mod 2) /= 0, Put writes Integer'Image ((I * I)); a final empty Put_Line terminates the row. The square is an expression, with no object or declared subtype.
Odd and square numbers.summary: The index covers every positive square root of a three-digit square. Modulo by 2 selects the eleven odd squares; the largest intermediate is 961 and the divisor is nonzero.

review.setting_evidence: Selected GPT-6.1 Sol High by the lead; runtime setting not independently exposed
review.method: Concrete sample and task reconciliation after independent arithmetic/native core review; subsequent delivery evidence and test-result scope are recorded in docs/integer-division.md#integrated-delivery-checkpoint

effects.explanation: Prints each odd squarefree semiprime below 1000, one per line.

Odd squarefree semiprimes.approach: A subtype Small_Natural range 0 .. 1000 and an Is_Prime function using a for loop over divisors 2 .. 31 with a guard d*d <= n (bounded so no overflow). The main procedure loops n over odd values 15 .. 999 and, for each smallest odd divisor p from 3 to 31 with p*p < n and n mod p = 0, checks that q = n / p is prime and differs from p, then prints n with Image via Put_Line. All arithmetic is on values bounded by 1000, so every check follows from types and for-loop ranges.
Odd squarefree semiprimes.summary: Everything is a small bounded for-loop computation over a declared range with no loop-carried accumulators and no termination checks needing variants, so all checks follow from types and static bounds.

effects.explanation: Characters are read one at a time from standard input with no peeking, and end of input must be detected.
The transformed stream is written one character at a time without line terminators, plus a final newline.
Malformed input (missing full stop, over-long word) is rejected through the existing Reject outcome.

risks.explanation: Reversal without a collection needs recursion of depth equal to the word length, so the program carries an explicit Depth counter and rejects words longer than a documented limit (e.g. 255), making stack use a fixed bound.
The Depth counter is a ranged subtype and a guard before each recursive call rejects when it would reach the limit, so the increment cannot fail.
Only procedures are used (loops and recursion in procedures get no termination check), and the reading loop is guarded by end-of-input rejection, so no variant is needed.
The out parameter carrying the delimiter character back to the caller is assigned on every path through the recursive procedure.

Odd word problem.approach: A Read_Char procedure fetches one character from stdin (with an end-of-input flag that triggers rejection), and a main loop alternates between echoing an even word directly and handling an odd word with a recursive procedure Reverse_Word(C, Depth, Next) that reads the following character, recurses while letters continue, prints C on the way back, and returns the delimiter in an out parameter. Depth is a bounded subtype, guarded before each recursive call, and the loop stops after printing the full stop and a newline; no array or string stores characters.
Odd word problem.summary: Every check follows from character comparisons and a ranged depth counter guarded before each recursive call, but the task's no-collection rule forces recursion, which is acceptable only with an explicit depth limit and rejection of longer words. This makes the outlook plausible rather than likely, since stack use rests on that documented limit.

effects.explanation: Reads the unixdict.txt word list named in the task, which needs a specified outcome when the file is missing or unreadable.
Prints each odd word with its derived word, plus a rejection message for invalid input.

risks.explanation: Odd-letter positions 1+2*(i-1) and the binary-search midpoint are nonlinear or loop-carried, so they discharge only because word length, count and the low/high cursors are ranged subtypes with a guard before each use.
Capacity limits (such as 32 characters per word and about 30000 words) are explicit, and a longer line or overfull dictionary is rejected visibly at load time instead of truncated.
The binary search and file-reading loops are while loops, so they live in procedures, which get no termination check.
Binary search is only correct if the list is sorted, so the load step checks ordering and rejects an unsorted file rather than assuming it.

Odd words.approach: Load unixdict.txt line by line into a fixed array of records, each holding a bounded character buffer and a length, rejecting overlong lines, overfull dictionaries and unsorted input. For each word, build the odd-index letters into a bounded buffer with a for loop, and if its length exceeds 4, binary-search the array with a while loop in a procedure and print the word and its odd word when found. Everything is in procedures with range-typed indexes and guards before each array access.
Odd words.summary: Every check follows from bounded types and guards, and no recursion, heap or annotation is needed, but the file-read, nonlinear odd-index arithmetic and binary-search cursors need careful shape, so the outlook is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The lyrics are written line by line with Put_Line.

Old lady swallowed a fly.approach: Animals are indexed by a subtype Animal_Index range 1..8 (fly to donkey), with small procedures that use case statements on the index to Put_Line each animal's opening line, its second line, and the "She swallowed the X to catch the Y" line using bounded concatenation of literals. The main body is a for loop over verses whose inner for loop (reverse) walks back down the chain, then the fixed closing "horse" verse is printed; all lyrics are embedded literals, no input is read, and every loop bound is static.
Old lady swallowed a fly.summary: Fixed embedded text, for loops over a static range 1..8 and case statements over a bounded subtype need no loop-carried values, so every check follows from types and static bounds.

effects.explanation: The unit name and the value are taken from the first two command-line arguments.
The conversion to each of the seven units is written line by line.
Invalid unit or value text is rejected with a specified nonzero exit status.

risks.explanation: Value times unit factor is discharged by capping the parsed value (at most 99999.99, stored as hundredths) in a ranged subtype so the 64-bit product and the later scaling by 100 cannot overflow.
Digit-by-digit parsing and output buffer filling use loop-carried positions, which need explicit length guards before each index and a rejection of over-long text.
The parse accumulator is a loop-carried value, so each step guards it against the cap before multiplying by 10 and adding the digit, rejecting input that exceeds the cap.
Division is only by constant nonzero unit factors held in a constant array indexed by an enumeration, so the divisor is statically nonzero.

Old Russian measure of length.approach: The program holds the seven unit factors as a constant array indexed by an enumeration, in units of 0.01 mm. It parses argument 1 as a unit name and argument 2 as a decimal value with at most two fractional digits through a guarded digit loop into a capped integer, rejecting bad input. A for loop over the enumeration converts to each unit by integer multiplication and division and prints each result as integer and fractional digits built in a bounded buffer.
Old Russian measure of length.summary: All arithmetic can be kept in capped 64-bit integers with constant nonzero divisors, so only the parsing and formatting loops need careful guards and nothing needs an annotation. Floating point is avoided by fixed-scale integer output, which still meets the task's linear conversion.

effects.explanation: OLE Automation is a Windows COM mechanism, an operating-system service the task requires for the server and the proxy-object client.
The server and client must run in separate processes and communicate across the process boundary.

OLE automation.summary: The task needs a COM/OLE automation server and an out-of-process client exchanging variant values. That is an operating-system service and inter-process effect that a future admitted library could specify, so it is an effect gap rather than a fixed-rule conflict. Variants can be modelled as a discriminated record, so no Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: The task is an on-screen (virtual) keyboard that is shown in a window and reacts to key presses or clicks. The task file has only a title, so this comes from the task name and the existing solution. A console text-art keyboard would not be a real on-screen keyboard.
The solution detects raw key presses and shows which key is down, which needs raw keystroke input.

On-screen keyboard.summary: The task file holds only the title, so the requirement is inferred from the name and the FreeBASIC solution. It is a virtual keyboard shown in a window and responding to input, which needs GUI and raw key input effects. Nothing in it breaks an Oracle rule, so it could be covered once Silver has such admitted library operations.

effects.explanation: The ten per-line counts are printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: The LCG step multiplies a state bounded below 2**31 by a constant below 2**31, so the product fits in 64 bits and is reduced with mod, which follows from the subtype ranges alone.

Each count is incremented in a loop with no invariant, so the program guards the increment with a comparison against the 1,000,000 cap and rejects visibly if it were reached, which cannot happen for the fixed run count.
The chosen line index is assigned from a for-loop variable over 1 .. N into a subtype 1 .. 10, so the array index check follows from types.

One of n lines in a file.approach: A procedure One_Of_N takes N (subtype 1..10) and an in out LCG state of a bounded integer subtype, loops I in 1..N advancing the state and setting Choice := I when (state mod I) = 0 (probability 1/I), and returns Choice in 1..10. Main runs a for loop of 1,000,000 simulations using a fixed seed, increments a Results array (1..10) of bounded counters behind a cap guard, then prints each count with Put and Integer'Image. The deterministic generator replaces system randomness and the repetition count is the task's full 1,000,000.
One of n lines in a file.summary: All loops are for loops with fixed bounds and every arithmetic value is bounded by subtype ranges or a visible guard, so no annotation is needed, though the LCG arithmetic and counter guard require careful shape.

effects.explanation: Prints ten generation lines of the automaton to standard output.

risks.explanation: Neighbour access Culture(I+1) and Culture(I-1) is guarded by looping I over 2..19 and handling cells 1 and 20 separately, so all indexes are statically within 1..20.
The output line buffer has fixed length sized for the 'Generation N ' prefix plus 20 cells, and each slice assignment uses constant-bounded indexes so lengths match.

One-dimensional cellular automata.approach: Use a constrained Boolean array of 20 cells initialised from the task's example aggregate, with a Step procedure that copies the old generation into a second array and computes each new cell from its left and right neighbours (off-end cells treated as dead via explicit boundary cases for the first and last cell). A for loop over generations 0..9 builds each output line in a fixed-length String buffer (prefix, generation digit, then '#' or '_' per cell) and prints it, then calls Step. All loops are for loops over static ranges, so no loop-carried value needs an invariant.
One-dimensional cellular automata.summary: Every index and length is determined by static array bounds and for-loop ranges over them, with Boolean-only cell arithmetic, so all checks follow from types and no annotation or while loop is needed.

effects.explanation: The task states the important part is true random pad data (e.g. from /dev/random), so a deterministic generator would not satisfy it.
Pad files (.1tp) are written, read and updated to mark used lines; encrypted and decrypted output is also stored in files.
The pad filename and length are user-specified, which a command-line solution takes as arguments.
Prints the results and status messages for the encrypt and decrypt operations.
The message text to encrypt can be read from standard input.

One-time pad.summary: The task needs true-random pad generation, file reading and writing, and letter-wise modular addition on bounded strings. None of that breaks an Oracle rule, because invalid or exhausted pads can be rejected with a specified outcome. The management sub-task is optional and is left out.

effects.explanation: Prints the 20 terms, one per line.

risks.explanation: Terms of 20 digits exceed 64 bits, so candidates are fixed-capacity digit arrays and the remainder step (rem*10+d) mod p is safe only because the divisor type is bounded so rem*10+9 fits in 64 bits.
The candidate search and divisor loop are while loops in procedures, which get no termination check, and each is bounded by a fixed count such as 2**n candidates and a divisor ceiling.
Candidate digit arrays are indexed by for loops over the array's own range, and the odometer increment uses guards on the digit index so carry never leaves bounds.

Trial division of 20-digit candidates up to about 1.5e10 is correct but slow, so a fixed-capacity big-number Miller-Rabin library would be needed to run fast and the stretch to 2000 digits is out of scope.

One-two primes.approach: For each length n from 1 to 20, enumerate candidates over digits 1 and 2 in increasing order with a binary odometer held in a fixed 20-digit array, and test each by trial division using long division of the digit array by bounded 64-bit divisors, stopping at the first prime. The program prints each term via a fixed buffer and Put_Line, with guards on carry and divisor bounds, and the stretch part is omitted as optional.
One-two primes.summary: Every check follows from array ranges and bounded remainder arithmetic, but 20-digit values exceed 64 bits so the work rides on digit-array or big-number handling in loops, which makes it plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The task says to display a smooth shaded triangle with OpenGL, which needs an OpenGL window or on-screen display.
The triangle is drawn on a display through OpenGL, so a text-art or image-file output would not meet the task.

OpenGL.summary: The task requires displaying a smooth shaded triangle with OpenGL, so a program needs a window and graphics display effects that Silver lacks today. Nothing in the task breaks a fixed Oracle rule, so a future Silver with admitted graphics library operations could cover it.

effects.explanation: The task is to render a triangle in an OpenGL window using a pixel shader, so it needs a window and an OpenGL rendering context. Text art or an image file does not meet it.
The required work is GPU rendering: a shader runs once per pixel of a triangle on a display.

OpenGL pixel shader.summary: The task requires an OpenGL pixel shader that colors each pixel of a triangle in a window. That needs the gui and graphics effects, which Silver lacks today. It does not break any fixed Oracle rule, so it is a candidate for future inclusion once admitted library operations for graphics exist.

effects.explanation: The task requires rendering the teapot through the OpenGL library, so the program needs an admitted OpenGL-style operation set to open a window, set up the view and draw line or triangle primitives.

risks.explanation: Bezier evaluation multiplies Bernstein weights in [0,1] by control coordinates declared in a subtype such as -4.0 .. 4.0, and writing each surface point as straight-line sums of 4-term rows avoids loop-carried float accumulators, so the overflow and range checks stay within what the provers can bound.
Patch index entries are declared as a vertex-index subtype matching the control-point array's range, so looking up control points by stored indices discharges from the types.

The parameter u = Float(K) / Float(N) for a for-loop index K in 0 .. N with static positive N stays in [0,1], which provers can establish from the static bounds before passing it to the basis functions.

OpenGL/Utah teapot.approach: The standard 306 control points and 32 bicubic patches (16 indices each) are embedded as constant arrays with ranged float and index subtypes. Nested for loops over the patches and a fixed tessellation grid evaluate each surface point with explicit straight-line Bernstein sums, and a procedure sends the resulting wireframe lines to the admitted OpenGL operations to draw one fixed rotated view. Rotation and animation are left out because they are optional.
OpenGL/Utah teapot.summary: Only the graphics effect goes beyond what the Oracle allows today, and it is an effect, not a conflict. The patch data and evaluation loops use static bounds, but floating-point overflow checks discharge only if coordinates use ranged subtypes and sums are written without loop-carried accumulators, so the outlook is plausible.

effects.explanation: Prints the computed reply line such as *#25280520## with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Converting each nonce character to a digit is guarded by a '0'..'9' test, and a non-digit nonce is rejected with a visible message.
All bit arithmetic is on a 32-bit modular type where wraparound is defined, and shift amounts are static constants less than 32.

OpenWebNet password.approach: The program embeds the password 12345 and the example nonce as constants, holds num1 and num2 in a 32-bit modular type, and runs a for loop over the nonce's own index range with a case statement on each digit character applying the shift, mask and or rules (Shift_Left/Shift_Right with static counts). Non-digit nonce characters are rejected with a specified message, and the final number is converted to text and wrapped as *#...## for Put_Line.
OpenWebNet password.summary: Every operation is on a wraparound modular type inside a for loop over the string's own range, so no check depends on a loop-carried fact beyond type ranges, and the only guard is the digit test on each nonce character.

effects.explanation: The program prints the precedence and associativity table and the parameter-passing statement with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Operator precedence.approach: A parameterless Main procedure with SPARK_Mode On prints one Put_Line per precedence row in descending order (highest-precedence operators such as ** abs not first, then multiplying, unary adding, binary adding, relational, and logical operators), each with its associativity. It finishes with lines stating that parameters of elementary types are passed by copy and that composite or tagged parameters are by reference or by copy as the compiler chooses. There are no variables, loops or inputs, so there is nothing to guard.
Operator precedence.summary: The program is a fixed sequence of Put_Line calls with String literals, which Silver already supports, so no check can fail and nothing needs an annotation.

effects.explanation: The program prints the embedded table after each call to the sort procedure with a different mix of default, positional and named parameters.

risks.explanation: The column parameter has a declared subtype equal to the row's index range, and the bubble-sort loops run over static subranges of the table's index type, so every index check follows from types.

Optional parameters.approach: The table is a constrained array of rows, and each row is a constrained array of fixed-length, space-padded String cells. A procedure Sort takes the table as in out, plus Order_By (an enumeration with Lexicographic as default and By_Length as the alternative, chosen with a case statement), Column (a ranged subtype, default 1) and Reverse_Order (Boolean, default False). It sorts with a simple bubble sort written as nested for loops over static bounds, because Silver has no admitted sort routine. Main calls Sort with defaults, with positional arguments and with named association, printing the table after each call.
Optional parameters.summary: All checks follow from declared ranges: indexes come from for loops over static bounds or from a parameter of the index subtype, and a cell's trimmed length is bounded by the cell size. No while loop or recursion is needed, so nothing requires an annotation.

effects.explanation: Prints the position and speed vectors as text lines.

risks.explanation: Sin, Cos and Sqrt must be admitted library operations, with the sqrt argument 2/R - 1/a guarded as non-negative and the sine and cosine arguments in a bounded range.
The divisions by L, by 1 + e*cos, by the speed magnitude and by a are each guarded explicitly, with a rejected-input outcome if the denominator is zero.
Floating-point operands are given bounded subtypes (for example a in 0.1..100.0 and e in 0.0..0.95) so no intermediate result can overflow or become infinite.
Formatting reals as fixed six-decimal text requires an admitted float-to-text operation with a bounded magnitude, as Float_IO is not available.

Orbital elements.approach: The program uses a bounded floating-point subtype Real, a 3-element array for vectors and a record holding position and speed, with procedures for rotation and for state computation. The example elements (a=1, e=0.1, rotation angle 355/678) are embedded as constants, Rotate uses admitted Sin and Cos, and guards on e, L, R and the speed magnitude reject invalid or degenerate input visibly. Output is formatted to six decimals through an admitted float-image operation and printed with Put and Put_Line.
Orbital elements.summary: The task is a short straight-line floating-point computation with no loops over carried values, so proofs depend on bounded real subtypes, guarded divisions and sqrt arguments, and admitted elementary functions. It is plausible rather than likely because floating-point range reasoning and float formatting need library support Silver lacks today.

effects.explanation: Prompts for each pair and the final ordered list are printed.
The user's answer to each pair comparison (less, equal or greater) is read as a line from standard input.
Invalid or missing answers are rejected with a specified nonzero exit status.

risks.explanation: Binary-insertion bounds lo, mid and hi are loop-carried, so they are declared in a ranged subtype 0..7 and mid is computed only under an explicit lo <= hi guard so the array index check discharges from types.
Updating hi := mid - 1 and lo := mid + 1 must stay within the subtype, which needs guards such as mid > 1 before subtracting and mid < 7 before adding.
The sorted array is fully initialized by an aggregate and the shift loop runs over the array's own range, so flow analysis is routine.

Reading each answer requires a specified outcome for end of input or an unrecognized response (reject with exit status), which depends on an admitted stdin library operation with a documented failure result.

Order by pair comparisons.approach: The seven colours are embedded as an enumeration (or index 1..7 with a case-based name printer) in the unordered input order, and a sorted array of at most 7 entries is built by binary insertion, which asks about ceil(log2(k+1)) comparisons per new item. Each comparison prints a prompt, reads one line from stdin, and maps it to less, equal or greater, rejecting anything else; an equal answer inserts next to the matching item, and elements above the insertion point are shifted with a reverse for loop. The binary-search loop is a while loop inside a procedure with ranged lo/hi indexes and explicit guards before every index and update.
Order by pair comparisons.summary: All checks come from small ranged subtypes, a fixed capacity of 7 and guards before each index update, and the while loop sits in a procedure so no termination proof is needed; the careful shape of the loop-carried binary-search bounds keeps this at plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Each of the seven required cases prints its M, N and resulting M' lines via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The write cursor for the output line and the next-N counter are loop-carried, so each gets a guard (capacity check and count check) immediately before its array or slice use.
The Count fields and N index live in subtypes bounded by the fixed capacity, and increments are guarded so the new value stays within the subtype.

Order disjoint list items.approach: Words are fixed-length 3-character padded Strings held in a record with a fixed-capacity array (capacity 16) and a count, with the seven test cases embedded as aggregates. A procedure Order_Disjoint marks, for each N word in order, the first unused equal M position in nested for loops (reporting a visible 'DomainError' outcome and leaving M unchanged if any N word is not found), then a second for loop over M copies successive N words into the marked positions using a guarded next-index counter. Another procedure builds each output line in a bounded buffer with explicit capacity guards and prints it with Put_Line.
Order disjoint list items.summary: All loops are for loops over fixed array ranges and all indexes come from subtype ranges or guards just before use, so no annotations are needed; only the loop-carried counters need routine guards.

effects.explanation: Each embedded test pair prints true or false through Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Order two numerical lists.approach: Lists are fixed-capacity Integer arrays (capacity 8) paired with a length of a subtype 0 .. 8, and a Boolean function Before takes both lists and lengths. It loops with a for loop over 1 .. the smaller length, returning True or False at the first differing element, and otherwise returns whether the first length is less than the second. A main procedure holds embedded example lists and prints true or false for each pair with an if statement.
Order two numerical lists.summary: Every index is bounded by the length subtype and the for-loop range, comparisons of Integer elements cannot overflow, and for loops terminate by themselves, so even inside a function no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the six partitions of (2,0,2) line by line.

risks.explanation: Next-permutation scans use K and L as loop-carried indexes, so each access to K+1 or L is guarded by a just-before test and the indexes are subtypes of the array range.
Output line text is assembled in a fixed-capacity buffer sized for the maximum 8 elements and 4 blocks, with a capacity guard before each append and a visible rejection if exceeded.
Block sizes and their sum are bounded by ranged subtypes so the running offset into the permutation cannot overflow.

Ordered partitions.approach: Embed the sizes (2,0,2) in a bounded array of at most 4 blocks with values 0..8, hold the permutation of 1..N in a bounded array, and loop in a procedure with a while loop that advances it by the standard next-permutation algorithm. For each permutation, emit a line only when elements are ascending within every block, which removes duplicates while keeping lexicographic order, and build each line into a bounded text buffer using scalar-image conversion for numbers before Put_Line.
Ordered partitions.summary: Every check is on small bounded index or length types with guards before each array access and append, and the only loops with carried state live in procedures, so no termination check or invariant is needed; the care needed is in the index guards and buffer capacity.

effects.explanation: The task requires reading unixdict.txt line by line, with a specified outcome when the file is missing or unreadable.
The ordered words of maximal length are displayed one per line.

risks.explanation: The stored-word count and the per-word length are bounded by declared subtypes and each append is guarded by a capacity test just before it, so no index check depends on a loop invariant.
Lines longer than the fixed word buffer are rejected with a visible outcome rather than truncated, so the length check follows from the guard before copying.
The running maximum length and word count are subtypes capped by the buffer and table capacities, so increments are guarded by a capacity test and discharge from types.
Word buffers and the table are fully initialized by aggregates and only the first Count entries are read, so the flow analysis is routine but must be shaped carefully.
The line-reading while loop sits in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the ordered test uses a for loop.

Ordered words.approach: A procedure reads unixdict.txt through an admitted file-input library operation into a fixed 64-character line buffer with a length, and a for loop over 1 .. Length-1 (guarded by Length > 1) tests that each character is not greater than the next. The ordered words are kept in a fixed array of 256 buffers with a count and the current maximum length: a longer ordered word resets the count to 0, an equal-length one is appended only if count is below capacity, and over-long lines or table overflow call Reject. Finally a for loop over 1 .. Count prints each stored word with Put_Line, and a missing file also ends in Reject.
Ordered words.summary: Every index, length and counter is bounded by declared subtypes and explicit guards before use, with the only loop being a procedure-level while that needs no termination proof, so no annotation is needed but the bounded-table and file-input library behavior must be carefully shaped.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 30 pairs and the count up to one million as text lines.

risks.explanation: Sieve indexes stay within 0..1_000_000 because every index is a for-loop variable over the array range or is guarded by j <= Limit - i before the update.

The digit-signature accumulator is a loop-carried value, so it is held in a 64-bit type and each add is preceded by a guard on its current value (or the digit loop is a fixed 7-iteration for loop over bounded per-digit counts).
The while loops live only in procedures, which get no termination check, and the prime scan is a for loop over a static range.
The count of pairs and the output line buffer are given bounds large enough (count well under 1000) so subtype range and length checks follow from declarations.

Ormiston pairs.approach: Sieve of Eratosthenes into a constant-size Boolean array of 1_000_001 entries, then a for loop over 2..1_000_000 tracks the previous prime and compares digit-multiset signatures, computed by a bounded digit-extraction loop with guarded accumulation. The first 30 pairs are output with Put_Line of bounded concatenated image strings, and a bounded count is printed at the end; the ten-million stretch is left out as optional.
Ormiston pairs.summary: All checks follow from fixed array bounds, for-loop indexes and guards before the sieve step and signature accumulation, with no annotation needed, but the loop-carried signature and sieve stride need careful guard placement.

effects.explanation: Prints the smallest members of the first 25 triples and the count of triples up to one billion.

risks.explanation: Digit-count signatures and sieve offsets are carried through loops, so they are held in Long_Long_Integer-ranged subtypes with explicit guards sized so 10 digits at weight 16 and offsets below 2**31 cannot overflow.
Segmented-sieve strike indexes are loop-carried, so each strike loop is a while loop in a procedure guarded by a comparison against the segment length just before each array write.
The digit-extraction and strike while loops live in procedures, which get no termination check, so no variant is needed.
