effects.explanation: Prints one ordinal word string per embedded test case with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Word tables are indexed by values from n mod 1000 and the like, which discharge because the quotient and remainder subtypes are bounded by division by constants, and each group loop uses a for loop over fixed scale indexes.

Appending words into a fixed buffer carries a loop-carried length, discharged by a Natural-ranged length subtype and an explicit guard before every append that sets a visible overflow flag (the buffer is sized above the longest 64-bit spelling, about 200 characters).
Group extraction divides a 64-bit value by constant powers of 1000, which is safe with a positive-range input type and no accumulation of the value.
Finding the last word scans backward in a while loop whose index is loop-carried, so it needs a guard (i greater than zero) in the loop condition before each string access.
Padded fixed-length word tables need per-entry length handling because Silver has no unconstrained strings, so entries are stored with a separate length array to keep slices in range.

Spelling of ordinal numbers.approach: Hold the test numbers in a constant array of a positive 64-bit range subtype; for each, a procedure fills a fixed-capacity character buffer with the spelling by walking six thousand-groups from most significant to least using a for loop over constant divisors, and spelling each 0..999 group with case statements on hundreds, tens and units into guarded appends. A second procedure finds the final word with a bounded backward while loop, replaces irregular endings (one, two, three, five, eight, nine, twelve) and y-to-ieth, or appends th, then prints the result with Put_Line.
Spelling of ordinal numbers.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic, constant tables and iterative buffer building with explicit capacity guards, so no annotations are needed, though the buffer-length and backward-scan loops need careful guarded shape. The optional alternate numeric forms (00123.0, 1.23e2) are skipped as optional.

effects.explanation: Prints the sphenic numbers below 1,000 and the sphenic triplets below 10,000 with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The factor counter is guarded (return False once it reaches 3) before each increment, and the remainder is a ranged subtype that only shrinks by division, so no check depends on a loop invariant.
The function uses only for loops over static ranges, which terminate on their own, so no variant is needed.

Sphenic numbers.approach: A function Is_Sphenic takes N in a ranged subtype (1 to 10_002). It loops P from 2 to N with a remainder and a factor count; a divisor increments the count and divides out P, and a count above 3 or a repeated factor returns False. A main procedure runs for loops over 1..999 and 1..9_999, printing each sphenic number and each triplet using Integer'Image concatenation, with the stretch counts (which would need million-scale trial division) left out as optional.
Sphenic numbers.summary: All checks follow from declared ranges, for-loop indexes and a guard before each counter increment, and no while loop or recursion is needed, so proofs should discharge without annotations. The required output is small and the optional million-scale stretch parts are omitted.

effects.explanation: Prints each spinner frame (| / - \) as text.
Each frame must clear the previous one, which needs cursor control or a carriage return or backspace overwrite on the terminal.
A 0.25 second pause is required between frames.

Spinning rod animation/Text.summary: The task is a looping or finite text spinner that cycles four ASCII frames with a 0.25 s delay and clears the previous frame, so it needs console output, terminal control and delay. Nothing in it breaks an Oracle rule, so it is a candidate once Silver gains those effects; a finite number of frames avoids any need for an endless loop or key-press polling.

effects.explanation: The 5x5 spiral is printed to standard output as five rows of aligned numbers.

risks.explanation: The per-cell ring and offset arithmetic is nonlinear (ring times side length) but all operands come from small ranged subtypes for N=5, so bounds follow from the types.

Each computed value must be shown to lie in 0..24 for the array element subtype, which the prover must derive from case-wise guards on ring and position and may need the ranged intermediate subtypes to make easy.

Spiral matrix.approach: Declare a constant N = 5, a 2-D array of a ranged subtype 0..N*N-1 indexed 0..N-1, and fill it with nested for loops that compute each cell directly from its ring (the minimum distance to an edge) and which side of the ring it lies on, so no loop-carried counter exists. Then print each row with nested for loops, formatting each value into a fixed-width text field using a small bounded buffer with Put, ending each row with a line terminator.
Spiral matrix.summary: Every cell is computed independently from its indices with small ranged arithmetic and explicit side guards inside for loops over the array's own range, so checks follow from types and guards without loop invariants.

effects.explanation: The program prints the split string to standard output.

Split a character string based on change.approach: Embed the example string as a String constant and run one for loop over its index range. For each position after the first, print ", " when the character differs from the previous one (guarded by an index greater than S'First), then print the character as a one-character slice, and end with a line terminator. No buffer or loop-carried value is needed, so every index check follows from the loop range and the guard.
Split a character string based on change.summary: The for loop indexes the constant's own range and the previous-character access is guarded by I > S'First, so all checks are routine and no annotation is needed. Output is a streamed sequence of Put calls, avoiding any bounded output buffer.

effects.explanation: Prompts, the computer's coin count and guess, and each round's result are printed.
The player's coin count and guess are read as lines of text for each round.

risks.explanation: The deterministic generator multiplies a state bounded to a 31-bit subtype by a constant, which fits in 64 bits by the declared range, though the nonlinear product needs the provers to cope.
Parsed player input is checked against 0..3 for coins and 0..6 for guesses before conversion to the ranged subtypes, with a Reject outcome on invalid or missing input.

Spoof game.approach: The program plays a fixed number of rounds in a for loop inside a procedure, keeping coin counts and guesses in small ranged subtypes and drawing the computer's choices from a bounded linear congruential generator seeded by a constant. Each round reads two lines from standard input, parses and validates them against their ranges (rejecting end of input or bad values with a specified message), then compares the guesses to the coin total with if/elsif to print draw, computer wins, player wins or no winner.
Spoof game.summary: Every check follows from small ranged subtypes, a bounded generator and parse-then-validate guards just before use, and the round count is fixed so no loop needs an invariant or variant. The task is under-specified, so a simple interactive round-based game meets it without recursion, heap or annotations.

effects.explanation: The task requires connecting to a MySQL database server and running queries against it.
Usernames and passwords for creating and authenticating users would be read from standard input.
Reports the outcome of connecting, creating a user and authenticating (success or rejection).
A database client interface (MySQL) is required, with specified failure outcomes. No admitted library operation provides this.

SQL-based authentication.summary: The task needs a MySQL connection, so it needs a network and database effect that Silver lacks today, and it needs an MD5 hash over a 16-byte salt plus the password. Nothing in it breaks a fixed Oracle rule, because bounded strings, a deterministic salt generator and iterative MD5 can be written in SPARK once a database library operation is admitted.

effects.explanation: Prints the 30 qualifying squares on one line.

risks.explanation: Square fits 1..1600 from Root in 1..40; each cube product fits Integer from Trial in 1..13; the direct Count<30 guard makes the increment fit 0..30.

Square but not cube.approach: The driver samples/rosetta_square_but_not_cube.adb computes Root*Root for Root in 1..40. It scans Trial in 1..13 and sets a Boolean Cube flag if Trial*Trial*Trial equals the square. When not Cube and then Count<30 it increments the bounded counter and streams the square with Put and Integer Image. A final empty Put_Line ends the line. It prints exactly the required first 30 values; the optional common squares and cubes are omitted.
Square but not cube.summary: All products fit the declared small Integer ranges, and the direct Count<30 guard justifies the increment. Cubes include every candidate cube up to 1600; scanning increasing square roots and stopping output after 30 qualifying values gives the required prefix through 1089. Independent expected output uses square/cube set difference. Scope and validation status are recorded in docs/boolean-objects.md and the linked assessment record.

review.setting_evidence: Selected setting through bounded subthread controls; runtime model and effort not independently exposed
review.method: Current source/task/scope reconciliation at tree 59cfd9c3dc, implementation/proof input b6aeb9f978; prior prepared-review and contingent-render provenance retained in the linked record; universal and native assurance tracked separately in docs/boolean-objects.md

effects.explanation: Prints each N and its factor pair or a fail line with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The reduction step's products and the c update are loop-carried, so with no invariant they need explicit guards (e.g. compare q against a bound divided by a) that reject or fail the attempt visibly, and nonlinear provers may struggle.
Form coefficients a, b, c must live in a wide subtype such as 0..2**62 and every update is guarded against leaving it, because only the type range is known after the first iteration.
Divisions by a, the multiplier and the queue entries are each preceded by an explicit nonzero guard.
All searches (cycle walk, ambiguous-cycle walk, integer square root by bisection) use for loops with fixed iteration caps, and a cap hit produces the reported fail outcome.
The 32-entry circular queue index is kept in range with mod and a ranged subtype, and the pro scan runs over the array's own range.

Square form factorization.approach: Embed the task's example Ns in a constant array of a 64-bit-range subtype, and run the four multiplier instances (1, 3, 5, 7, 11) sequentially in a procedure instead of threads, with the form (a, b, c) held in wide ranged variables. Integer square root is a bisection for loop over 32 bits, the principal-cycle search is a capped for loop with a fixed 32-entry circular queue of small coefficients, and the ambiguous-cycle walk is a capped loop that stops at the symmetry point and yields a factor via mod and division behind guards. Results print as "N = ..." and "f = ... N/f = ..." or "fail" via 'Image concatenation.
Square form factorization.summary: Everything is integer arithmetic with fixed-size arrays and loops that can be capped without changing the required outcome, so no annotation is needed, but the loop-carried 62-bit coefficient updates need careful range guards to avoid overflow checks the provers cannot bound.

effects.explanation: Each decimal digit of the root is written to standard output as it is generated.

risks.explanation: Remainder and 20*root are fixed-capacity base-10 digit arrays, and the multiply-by-small, add and subtract carry loops stay safe only because digit and carry subtypes bound every intermediate (digit <= 9, carry <= small constant).
Digit-array indexes are for-loop indexes over the array's own range, but the carry out of the top digit needs an explicit guard that rejects or stops when the fixed capacity would be exceeded.
The trial-digit search (largest d in 0..9 with (20p+d)*d <= remainder) is a bounded for loop over a digit subtype so d never leaves 0..9, and the Character conversion of d is safe by that subtype.
All loops are for loops or while loops inside procedures, so no variant is needed and the digit count is a fixed documented limit.

Square root by hand.approach: Implement the classic digit-by-digit (long-hand) square root of an embedded constant such as 2, bringing down two-digit pairs (zero pairs after the radicand ends), with the remainder and the running 20*root held in fixed-capacity digit arrays sized for a documented maximum digit count N (for example 50). Each step finds the next digit by a for loop over 0..9 using big-number multiply-small, compare and subtract procedures, then outputs the digit with Put and the decimal point at the right position. The requested digit count is a constant (or a validated first argument rejected when outside 1..N), so the loop runs a bounded number of times.
Square root by hand.summary: The spigot is a bounded loop of small digit-array arithmetic whose operands are all bounded by digit subtypes and guarded carries, so it should prove without annotations, but fixed-capacity big-number carry loops require careful shaping. The task's 'forever' option is met by a documented digit limit, which Oracle rule 7 allows.

effects.explanation: Prints the square-free lists in horizontal rows and the five counts.

risks.explanation: Values near 10^12 and d*d for d up to 10^6 need a 64-bit integer type, and the products and the sum 10^12 + offset are bounded by the declared ranges of d and offset.

The Boolean sieve of 1_000_001 entries is indexed by m*(d*d) with m limited to 1_000_000/(d*d), a nonlinear bound the provers may need help with, so the program instead uses a for loop over 1..1_000_000 testing n mod (d*d) = 0 against d in 2..1000, or guards idx <= 1_000_000 before each store.
The offset (d*d - 10^12 mod (d*d)) mod (d*d) is guarded by 'if off <= 145' before it indexes the 146-entry window array, which the provers discharge from the guard.
Every divisor d*d is at least 4 because d is a loop index over a range starting at 2.
All loops are for loops, or while loops inside procedures, so no termination check arises.

Square-free integers.approach: Two Boolean arrays are used, one of 1_000_001 entries for 1..10^6 and one of 146 entries for 10^12..10^12+145. Each is marked by looping d over 2..1000 for the small one and 2..1_000_000 for the window, computing the first multiple of d*d inside the window with mod and storing only when the offset is at most 145. A procedure prints the numbers in rows with Put and 'Image, and the counts at 100, 1000, 10_000, 100_000 and 10^6 come from a running count over the small array.
Square-free integers.summary: Every check follows from declared integer ranges, for-loop indexes over array ranges and a guard before each window store, but 64-bit nonlinear products and the string and 'Image output machinery make it depend on careful program shape. No annotation is needed because all loops are for loops or sit inside procedures.

effects.explanation: Prints each engagement and the stable or unstable verdict for the Gale-Shapley result and for every pairwise exchange.

risks.explanation: Partner entries are Guy_X including a no_guy sentinel, so every use as an index into the preference tables sits behind an explicit /= no_guy guard, and rank tables are filled by for loops over the arrays' own ranges.
The per-man proposal counter is a 0..10 range type incremented only after a guard that it is below 10, so the increment and the following Rank index both follow from the type and the guard.

The Gale-Shapley while loop lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed, though the loop-carried free and engaged flags are only typed, not bounded, so progress is never proved.
Output lines concatenate names from 'Image of enumerations whose maximum lengths are statically bounded, so the concatenation length checks need the bounded-concatenation support to discharge.

Stable marriage problem.approach: Guys and girls are enumerations with a sentinel value plus subtypes excluding it, and the ten-by-ten preference tables are constant arrays of arrays embedded as aggregates. A procedure precomputes rank tables with for loops, then runs Gale-Shapley with a while loop over free men, guarding the proposal counter and the sentinel before each index. A stability-check procedure uses nested for loops over men and women comparing ranks, and the main procedure prints the engagements, then swaps each pair of partners, rechecks and restores them.
Stable marriage problem.summary: Everything is fixed-size arrays and enumerations with index checks that follow from types and sentinel guards, and the only loop-carried state (proposal counters, free flags) is range-typed, so no annotation is needed. Plausible rather than likely because of the nested-array aggregates, the sentinel handling and the 'Image-based output strings.

effects.explanation: The demo prints pushed and popped values and the result of empty tests with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Pop reads Items (Top) only after testing Top > 0 and Push writes Items (Top + 1) only after testing Top < Capacity, so both index checks follow from guards just before use.
Pop assigns its out Item and Success parameters on both the empty and non-empty paths, and the stack record is initialized by an aggregate, so data-flow checks are routine.

Stack.approach: The stack is a record holding a fixed-capacity Integer array plus a Top count of subtype 0 .. Capacity, with Push and Pop as procedures that take a Success out flag. Push sets Success to False instead of writing when the stack is full, Pop returns False with a defined dummy value when it is empty, and Is_Empty is a Boolean function. Main pushes embedded values in a for loop, prints Is_Empty, then pops and prints values in a while loop until the stack is empty.
Stack.summary: All checks are index and range checks on Top that guards placed right before each array access discharge, and the only while loop sits in the Main procedure, where no termination check applies, so no annotation is needed.

conflicts.explanation: The task requires printing the program's actual current call stack, which is run-time introspection of program structure. SPARK cannot express it: the only Ada route is GNAT.Traceback, which works on raw code addresses and symbolic debug information and is outside SPARK. A shadow stack of names that the program keeps by hand would be a simulation, not the real call stack.

effects.explanation: The stack trace is printed to the console, and then the program carries on.

Stack traces.summary: Excluded. The task requires inspecting the real run-time call stack, including the function name in each frame. That is reflection on program structure, which SPARK cannot express (GNAT.Traceback relies on addresses and debug symbols outside SPARK).

effects.explanation: The simulation prints each climb or fall and the final level with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried pending-steps count and the level are bounded subtypes with an explicit guard before each increment, and hitting the bound gives a visible 'gave up' outcome rather than a silent change.
The pseudo-random generator uses a modular type so wraparound is by definition, avoiding any overflow check.
Step_Up is a procedure so no termination check applies, and the attempt loop is a for loop with a fixed maximum anyway.

Stair-climbing puzzle.approach: A Step procedure advances a deterministic modular LCG in an in out state, moves a bounded Level up or down, prints it, and returns a Boolean success. Step_Up is iterative rather than recursive: it keeps a bounded count of pending steps that starts at one, and on each attempt decrements it on success or increments it on failure (the iterative equivalent of the recursive scheme), looping until the count is zero. Guards before each increment and a fixed attempt cap produce a printed 'gave up' outcome when the documented limits are reached.
Stair-climbing puzzle.summary: The recursion in the task's pseudo-code can be replaced by an explicit pending-steps counter in a procedure, so no variant is needed and all checks follow from bounded subtypes and guards. The nonrecursive form is a faithful equivalent, and the only non-routine items are loop-carried counters that need explicit bound guards.

effects.explanation: The main procedure prints a line through Silver_IO.Put_Line to show it ran.

Start from a main routine.approach: A parameterless Main procedure with pragma SPARK_Mode (On) is the program's entry point, with no event loop or window. Its body prints one String literal with Silver_IO.Put_Line to demonstrate that startup goes straight to the main routine. There is no data, no loop and no guard.
Start from a main routine.summary: The task only needs a parameterless main procedure that runs at startup, which Silver already supports, and it has no run-time checks to prove.

effects.explanation: Writes an HTML file containing the processed address table so the browser can open it.
Launches the system web browser on the generated HTML file (start or xdg-open).

Starting a web browser.summary: The task needs a program that processes addresses (separates house number from street, using bounded strings and arrays), writes a colored HTML table to a file, and launches a browser on it. This is only a file-writing and process-launching effect, which a future Silver library operation could specify, so there is no fixed-rule conflict.

effects.explanation: Prints each matching pair of state pairs for the original and the extended lists.

risks.explanation: Letter counts and the unique-state counter are loop-carried values, so each is declared in a bounded range and guarded before it increments, and the summed counts stay within a small range type.
Mapping a character to a letter slot needs a guard that the character lies in 'a'..'z' before the position computation, and name offsets are bounded by explicit length guards.
Output lines are assembled in a bounded buffer sized for four names plus separators, with each append guarded by the remaining capacity.
Only for loops are used in procedures, so no variant is needed.

State name puzzle.approach: Embed the 50 states and the 5 fictitious names as padded fixed-length Character buffers with explicit lengths in a constant array, normalize each to lowercase letters only, drop exact duplicate normalized names with guarded appends into a bounded table, and give each remaining state a 26-entry letter-count array. Four nested for loops over the table enumerate pairs i<j and k<l with i<k and all four indexes distinct, compare the summed letter counts across the 26 letters, and print each match with Put_Line from bounded string-building buffers, once for the original list and once for the extended list. Table size, name length and count ranges are fixed constants, and each loop-carried count is guarded before it increments.
State name puzzle.summary: The task is bounded nested for-loop enumeration with per-letter counts over embedded data, so every check follows from declared ranges and local guards without annotations, though the amount of guarded buffer and counter handling needs careful program shape.

effects.explanation: Prints each sample size's mean, standard deviation and an ASCII histogram.

risks.explanation: Loop-carried sum, sum of squares and bin counters lose their bounds after the first iteration, so each addition is preceded by an explicit guard against the type maximum that rejects with a visible outcome, or sample counts and scaled values are fixed so the 64-bit range clearly suffices.
The LCG step multiplier times state is nonlinear, so the state is a bounded range type with a modulus small enough that the product fits in 64 bits, which provers handle from the type bounds.
The histogram bin index is computed as sample times 10 divided by the scale from a ranged sample value, so the index range follows from the sample type, with a guard on the top edge.
Mean and variance divide by the sample size, which is a nonzero constant or ranged subtype of the loop, so the divisor is provably positive.
The integer square root is a bounded for loop or a while loop inside a procedure, so no variant is needed.

Statistics/Basic.approach: A deterministic linear congruential generator over a ranged integer state yields samples as fixed-point integers scaled to 0..1_000_000, and one procedure accumulates count, sum, sum of squares and an 11-bin histogram array in streaming fashion for sizes 100, 1000 and 10000. Mean and standard deviation come from sum and sum-of-squares via the hint formula with integer arithmetic and a bounded integer square root, and are printed as scaled decimals built into a bounded string with 'Image digits. Histogram rows are built with a for loop of X characters and printed with Put_Line, with each accumulator addition guarded against its type maximum.
Statistics/Basic.summary: Streaming mean, variance and histogram over a deterministic integer fixed-point generator needs only integers, arrays, loops and text building, with all checks following from ranged types and a few overflow guards on loop-carried accumulators. It is plausible rather than likely because the accumulators and the nonlinear LCG and variance arithmetic depend on careful range sizing.

effects.explanation: Prints the pdf table, the cumulative and p-value table, and the airport chi-squared result.

risks.explanation: Exp, power and gamma on Double need operand-range guards (x in 0..32, k in 1..5) so no overflow or domain check fails, and float provers are weak.
The incomplete-gamma series is written as a for loop with a fixed term count (for example 200 terms) inside a function, avoiding a while loop that would need a variant.
Loop-carried accumulators and running terms lose bounds after the first iteration, so each must be clamped by an explicit guard before use, and the guard must not change the result.
Float-to-integer conversions used for fixed-decimal printing need guards on magnitude, and the elementary-function library must supply verified contracts for Exp, Log and Sqrt.
Divisions by x, k or the gamma value need explicit nonzero guards, with pdf at x = 0 returning a specified 0.0.

Statistics/Chi-squared distribution.approach: Embed the airport table as a constant 4x2 integer array and compute gamma at half-integer and integer arguments with a Lanczos-style fixed-size coefficient array, or by recurrence from Gamma(1/2) and Gamma(1). The incomplete-gamma series uses a for loop with a fixed term count, and the pdf and cdf functions are guarded on x and k ranges. Main loops over k = 1..5 and x = 0..10, prints the pdf table, the cdf and p values for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32, and the airport statistic with p value, formatting the floats into fixed-decimal text through bounded integer scaling.
Statistics/Chi-squared distribution.summary: Everything is bounded and loop counts are fixed, so there is no recursion or variant need, but the proof depends on floating-point library contracts for Exp and power, and on range guards for the float series. This makes it plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints the mean, standard deviation and a text histogram with Put_Line and Put.

risks.explanation: The Box-Muller transform needs log, sqrt and cos of values bounded away from zero, and each result must be shown finite, so the uniform draw is built from an integer in 1..2**16 divided by 2.0**16 and every float operand is range-guarded.

The sum and sum of squares over a few thousand samples stay within bounds only if each sample is clamped to a declared float range, which a guard can express as a visible out-of-range histogram bin without altering the statistics.
The deterministic LCG uses a modular type so wraparound is defined and cannot fail a check.
The histogram bin index is computed from a float, so a guard on the value range selects explicit under/overflow bins before conversion to the index type.

Divisions by the sample count and the square root of a variance need guards showing the count is positive and the variance is nonnegative, which a nonlinear sum-of-squares loop makes hard for provers.
All loops are for loops or live in procedures, so no variant is needed.

Statistics/Normal distribution.approach: Embed a fixed-size sample array of Float (say 1000), fill it with a modular-type LCG feeding a Box-Muller transform using a guarded uniform value in (0,1], then compute mean and standard deviation in for loops. Bin each sample into a fixed array of 12 counters via range guards with explicit under and overflow bins, and print mean, sd and star bars built in a bounded buffer with Put. The task's part 2 (native support) is satisfied by a comment-free note in the output text, since Ada has no native normal generator.
Statistics/Normal distribution.summary: Everything is bounded and loops are for loops in procedures, so index and termination checks are routine, but floating-point log, sqrt and cos with accumulated sums need careful range guards for the provers to discharge the float overflow and domain checks. Outlook is plausible rather than likely because of the float-heavy arithmetic and float-to-index conversion.

effects.explanation: Prints each steady square and its square, one line each.

Steady squares.approach: A for loop runs N over a subtype 1 .. 9999, computes the square in a ranged Integer subtype (at most 99_980_001), and picks the modulus 10, 100, 1000 or 10000 with an if/elsif chain on N. If Square mod Modulus = N, it prints N, "^2 = " and the square using Integer'Image concatenated into a bounded line via Put_Line.
Steady squares.summary: Every operand is bounded by the loop range, so the square cannot overflow, the modulus is a nonzero constant, and the for loop carries no values between iterations that need an invariant. Only integer arithmetic, 'Image output and a for loop are new.

effects.explanation: Prints one result line per initial estimate: no answer, spurious answer, or the intersection point.

risks.explanation: Every float operation in de Casteljau, the implicit equation and Aitken's step must be proved free of overflow, so the iterate is held in a bounded float subtype and the Aitken step is only taken when it is guarded to stay within that bound.
The Aitken denominator p2 - 2*p1 + p0 can be zero or tiny, so the program guards on its magnitude before dividing and reports no answer for that start, a visible specified outcome.

The loop-carried iterate p has only its subtype range after the first iteration, so a divergence guard (magnitude above a fixed bound reports no answer) keeps the cubic and quartic terms within float range, and the provers must handle the nonlinear products.

The Steffensen iteration is a while loop with an iteration counter, which is acceptable only because it lives in a procedure (no termination check), with the Aitken step as a function containing no loops.
Float-to-integer conversion for printing needs the scaled value range-guarded, and the tolerance comparisons must not hide NaN or infinity, which the bounded subtype and guards exclude.

Steffensen's method.approach: Use a bounded Long_Float subtype for the iterate, small functions for de Casteljau, the implicit equation, f(t) and one guarded Aitken step, and a procedure with a while loop (counter up to 1000, tolerance 1e-8) that returns a found flag and the value, treating a zero or tiny denominator or a diverged iterate as no answer. A for loop over 0..10 computes t0 = I/10, then prints no answer, spurious solution (implicit residual above 1e-6) or the point (x, y) formatted by scaling to integers and building the decimal text by hand.
Steffensen's method.summary: Everything is bounded floating-point arithmetic in a procedure-driven loop with explicit guards for the Aitken denominator and divergence, so no annotation is needed, but proving float overflow and division freedom through the loop-carried iterate depends on careful guard placement and float provers.

effects.explanation: The plot lines are written to standard output, with several items per line.

risks.explanation: The per-value count increment inside a loop has no invariant, so a guard just before the increment (reject if the count is at its subtype maximum) discharges it.
Converting stem and leaf digits to Character via 'Val is safe because the stem is declared 0..14 and the leaf 0..9, so the digit arithmetic stays within range.

Stem-and-leaf plot.approach: Embed the 120 data values in a constant array whose element subtype is 0..149, tally them into a counts array indexed 0..149 (a counting sort that avoids a sorting loop), then loop over stems 0..14 and leaves 0..9 printing each leaf digit as many times as its count. Each stem row is a two-character right-aligned stem, " |", then the leaves, built with Put of Characters and ended with a line terminator. Increments are guarded against exceeding the count subtype.
Stem-and-leaf plot.summary: Every index comes from a subtype-bounded element or a for-loop range, and the only loop-carried value (the count) gets a guard before its increment, so no annotation is needed. Output is plain text through procedures with only for loops, so there are no termination or recursion issues.

effects.explanation: Prints the first fifteen members, the first-occurrence indices for 1 to 10 and for 100, and the GCD check result.

risks.explanation: The generation loop sums two array elements whose values are only known by their subtype range, so a guard before each sum rejects the program with a visible outcome if it would exceed the element limit.
Writing positions 2*I-1 and 2*I for I in 2..1000 in a 2000-element array follows from the for-loop range, but the prover needs the linear index arithmetic bounded by the declared loop range.
Assigning the guarded sum into the bounded element subtype needs the guard to be the exact condition for the subtype, which is routine once written just before the assignment.
The Euclid GCD in a procedure uses mod with a divisor guarded by the while condition N /= 0, and loop-carried M and N are typed to a positive range so mod cannot fail.
The GCD and the search loops are while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, whereas making GCD a function would need a variant Silver cannot supply.

Stern-Brocot sequence.approach: Fill a 2000-element array of a bounded positive subtype with 1,1 and then, for I in 2..1000, set S(2I-1)=S(I)+S(I-1) and S(2I)=S(I) after a guard on the sum. Print results with Put and scalar 'Image text, find first occurrences of 1..10 and 100 with for loops over the array range and a found flag, and check consecutive-pair GCDs with a procedure using a while loop on bounded positive variables, reporting the outcome by printing text.
Stern-Brocot sequence.summary: Everything is bounded array and for-loop work with a single guarded addition, and the only while loop is in a procedure, so no annotation is needed, but the guard on the sum and the index arithmetic make it depend on program shape.

effects.explanation: The triangle of S1(n, k) up to n = 12 is printed as text rows.

risks.explanation: Table entries are loop-carried values known to GNATprove only by their type, so the recurrence is computed in a wider type and guarded against exceeding the entry subtype with a visible rejection outcome.
Row n-1 and column k-1 are safe because the loops run n from 1 and k from 1 with row 0 set separately, so the indexes follow from the loop ranges.
Padded output lines are built in a fixed-size buffer sized for 13 columns of width 12, with image lengths bounded by the entry subtype's range.

Stirling numbers of the first kind.approach: Use a 13x13 constrained array of a ranged subtype (unsigned Stirling numbers, noted in the output), zero-initialised by an aggregate, row 0 set to S1(0,0)=1, then fill rows 1..12 and columns 1..n with the recurrence in a wider type behind an explicit range guard that rejects on exceeding the subtype. Print each row with nested for loops, using 'Image to text and padding into a fixed buffer, emitted with Put and Put_Line. The optional n == 100 maximum needing big numbers is omitted.
Stirling numbers of the first kind.summary: Everything is a bounded nested for-loop over static ranges with a guarded recurrence, so checks should discharge, but the loop-carried array values need careful guard placement and the 'Image padding needs bounded buffers.

effects.explanation: The triangle of S2(n, k) for n and k up to 12 is printed as text rows.

risks.explanation: The recurrence k*S(n,k)+S(n,k-1) works on table entries known only by their type after the first loop iteration, so the sum is computed in a wider type and an explicit guard against a stated limit rejects before storing, which keeps the stored values in range.
Indexes n+1 and k-1 are safe because the for-loop ranges (n in 0..11, k in 1..12) are written to stay inside the 0..12 array bounds.
Padded output lines are built in a fixed-size buffer whose size must be shown sufficient for 13 columns of width 12 plus the row label, with each image's width guarded before copying.

Stirling numbers of the second kind.approach: Hold S2 in a 13 by 13 array of a ranged subtype, set the diagonal to 1, then fill rows with nested for loops using S2(n+1,k) = k*S2(n,k) + S2(n,k-1) computed in Long_Long_Integer and guarded against the element limit with a visible rejection. Print each row with Put of right-justified 'Image text and Put_Line at row end. The optional n==100 big-number maximum is omitted.
Stirling numbers of the second kind.summary: All indexes come from for-loop ranges over a fixed 13x13 table and the largest entry (1379400) is small, so the only non-routine checks are the loop-carried overflow guard and padded-text formatting, none needing an annotation.

effects.explanation: Prints the plaintext, the ciphertext digits and the decrypted text with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Decrypt's cursor into the ciphertext advances by one or two inside a while loop, so each read is preceded by an explicit bound guard and a truncated escape sequence takes a visible reject path.
Output buffers are fixed-capacity with an explicit used-length, and each append is guarded by a capacity check that rejects over-long input rather than truncating.

Mapping characters and digits to board positions needs the lookup tables typed as ranged subtypes and a guard that the character or digit is in the board, with unmapped input producing a specified rejection.
Decrypt's while loop sits in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the cursor strictly advances anyway.

Straddling checkerboard.approach: Represent the board as constant arrays: a 10-entry digit row for the first row, two 10-entry rows for the other two blanks, and a lookup table from Character to a code string held in a small fixed record-free pair of arrays (digit count and up to two digits). Encrypt walks the embedded plaintext with a for loop, upcases letters, emits the escape code plus the digit for numerals, and appends to a bounded buffer after a capacity guard; Decrypt walks the ciphertext with a while loop in a procedure, reads one digit or a blank digit plus a second digit, handles the escape by taking the next digit literally, and sets a rejected flag on any malformed or truncated sequence. Main encrypts the example message, prints it and the digits, decrypts, and prints the result, or prints a rejection message.
Straddling checkerboard.summary: Every access is into fixed arrays indexed by guarded or ranged values and the only loop-carried cursor is guarded before each use, so no annotation is needed, but the decrypt cursor and buffer lengths make the program shape-sensitive.

effects.explanation: Prints the strange numbers in 101..499 and the 10-digit count to standard output.

risks.explanation: The per-digit count table is a loop-carried array whose element bounds are unknown after the first iteration, so each sum guards against a documented cap and rejects with a visible outcome if it is exceeded.
The row-printing counter is loop-carried and is kept in a small ranged subtype reset to zero by a guard, so its increment is checked just before use.
Neighbour digit indexes (digit plus or minus a prime step) are guarded by explicit bounds tests before indexing the table.

Strange numbers.approach: Part one loops A over 101..499 and splits it into three digits by static division and mod, tests each adjacent absolute difference against 2, 3, 5 and 7 with plain comparisons, and prints matches ten per row using scalar images. The stretch goal uses a dynamic-programming table Ways(length, last digit) over a 2D array of digits 0..9 and lengths 1..10, seeded with one way per digit, extended by for loops over neighbour digits via guarded index offsets, then sums the length-10 row for leading digit 1 by tracking the table starting from digit 1 only, avoiding the brute-force 10^9 scan.
Strange numbers.summary: Every check comes from digit ranges, static loop bounds and guards, and the DP avoids while loops and recursion; the only non-routine parts are loop-carried count sums needing cap guards.

effects.explanation: Prints the qualifying numbers and their count to standard output.

risks.explanation: The qualifying-number counter is loop-carried, so it is typed 0..400 and incremented only under an explicit if Count < 400 guard to discharge the range check.

Strange plus numbers.approach: A for loop runs N over 101..499, splitting it into three digits with / and mod on a range-subtyped integer, and a non-recursive Is_Prime function trial-divides with a for loop from 2 to Sum-1 over digit sums bounded 0..18. Each N where both adjacent digit sums are prime is printed with Put of its Image plus a separator, with a line break every ten, and a final count is printed using a guarded bounded counter.
Strange plus numbers.summary: All values are bounded by the 101..499 loop range and digit sums of at most 18, every loop is a terminating for loop, and the only loop-carried value is a counter that a guard keeps in range, so checks follow from types and guards.

effects.explanation: Prints the 41 triplets below 30 and the count of triplets below 1000 to standard output.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried triplet counter has no invariant, so it is guarded by an explicit check against its type's upper bound with a visible Reject outcome before each increment.
The sum of three loop indexes, each at most 999, is at most 2997, which interval reasoning on for-loop ranges shows fits a prime table indexed 0..2999.

Strange unique prime triplets.approach: Fill a Boolean primality table over 0..2999 using trial division in a for loop with divisors starting at 2 (no division by zero), then use three nested for loops over p < m < n up to 999 with the primality table lookups. Count qualifying triplets in a bounded integer and print those with n below 30 as text built from 'Image concatenation, then print the final count.
Strange unique prime triplets.summary: All loops are for loops over static or loop-bounded ranges and every index and divisor is bounded by types and loop ranges, so only the counter needs a guard.

effects.explanation: Prints the product matrices computed by standard and Strassen multiplication.

risks.explanation: Strassen's sums and products of sub-matrix entries are bounded only by declaring a small entry range (for example -1000..1000) and fixed 4x4 inputs, so each intermediate stays well inside Integer.
Recursion is avoided by unrolling the levels into procedures for 4x4 (using 2x2 blocks) and 2x2 (using scalars), so no variant is needed.
Quadrant copy loops use for-loops over fixed constrained ranges with offsets of constant size, so index checks follow from static bounds.
Using exact Integer matrices (the task's inverse example D can be replaced by an integer permutation or identity pair) avoids floating point entirely.

Strassen's algorithm.approach: Represent matrices as constrained 2D arrays of a ranged integer subtype, with fixed 2x2 and 4x4 types and procedures that add, subtract, naively multiply, split into quadrants and recombine. A 2x2 Strassen procedure uses the seven products on scalars, and a 4x4 Strassen procedure splits into 2x2 blocks and calls the 2x2 procedure seven times, which unrolls the recursion into a fixed two-level depth; embedded example matrices are multiplied both ways and printed with Put_Line of integer images.
Strassen's algorithm.summary: Fixed-size integer matrices with unrolled two-level Strassen need only static bounds and a declared entry range for overflow, so all checks are routine for provers and no annotations are required. The main care points are the nonlinear products (bounded by the range subtype) and the task's recursion, which must be expressed as fixed-depth unrolling rather than a general recursive routine.

effects.explanation: The two input file names come from the command line.
Each input stream is a named file read line by line without loading it whole.
The merged sorted lines are written to standard output.
An unreadable file, missing argument or over-long line is rejected with a failure status.

risks.explanation: Each line is read into a fixed-capacity buffer with a length field, and a line longer than the capacity is rejected with a visible outcome, so slice and comparison bounds follow from the length subtype.
Comparing buffered lines uses only the prefix 1 .. Length of each buffer, which is bounded by the declared capacity, and the minimum-selection loop runs over the array's own range.

Stream merge.approach: Each stream is a record holding an open admitted file reader, a fixed-capacity line buffer with a ranged length, and an Has_Item flag; a procedure Fetch refills the buffer or clears the flag at end of file, rejecting over-long lines. A while loop in a procedure runs while either stream has an item, choosing the smaller buffered line (or the only available one) by guarded string comparison, printing it with Put_Line and refetching from that stream. Arguments are validated first (two readable file names), and the N-stream variant would be the same loop over an array of such records with a for loop selecting the minimum.
Stream merge.summary: All checks follow from bounded buffer types, a Has_Item guard before every comparison, and a while loop confined to a procedure, so no annotation is needed once Silver gains file reading, string ordering and extra arguments.

effects.explanation: The program prints the string after the append with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

String append.approach: Keep the text in a bounded buffer with a length counter: declare a Str buffer, a Len counter, and a literal to append. Guard on the length (Len plus the literal's length does not exceed the capacity), then copy the literal's characters into the buffer and print the first Len characters; if the guard fails, print a specified rejection message. Because the buffer's capacity is fixed and the guard precedes the copy, no index or length check can fail.
String append.summary: The task is one in-place append of a literal followed by one print, so every index and length check follows from a fixed buffer capacity and a guard just before the copy. Today's Silver only has fixed-length strings with bounded concatenation, so a bounded string buffer with an in-place append is the only missing piece.

effects.explanation: Prints the upper-case, lower-case and optional swapped-case forms with Put_Line.

String case.approach: Keep the constant "alphaBETA" and copy it into fixed-length String variables of the same length (9) for the upper, lower and swapped results. A for loop over 1 .. 9 inspects each character, and an if guard tests whether it lies in 'a' .. 'z' or 'A' .. 'Z' just before adding or subtracting 32 via Character'Pos and Character'Val, so the result is always a valid Character. Each result is printed with Put_Line.
String case.summary: Every check (string index within 1 .. 9, Character'Val argument within 0 .. 255) follows from the fixed loop bounds and the range guard immediately before the conversion, with no loop-carried state. No termination, nonlinear or floating-point issues arise.

effects.explanation: Each comparison result for the embedded string pairs is printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: The case-insensitive comparison indexes B at B'First + (I - A'First) for I in A'Range, which discharges because an equal-length guard immediately precedes the loop.
Lowercasing uses Character'Val (Character'Pos (C) + 32) only inside a guard C >= 'A' and C <= 'Z', so the result stays within Character.
Strings of arbitrary parameter length are printed piecewise with Put rather than concatenated, so no result-length check on unbounded concatenation arises.

String comparison.approach: A procedure Print_Comparison (A, B : String) prints the pair and then, through if statements, reports =, /=, <, >, <= and >= using Ada's built-in lexical String operators, with pieces written by Put and a final Put_Line. A Boolean function Equal_Ignoring_Case first returns False when lengths differ, then loops over A'Range comparing ASCII-lowercased characters of A and the corresponding offset index in B. Main calls it on embedded pairs including case variants ("THAT"/"That") and numeric strings ("10"/"9", showing they are compared lexically, not numerically).
String comparison.summary: Every check follows from String parameter bounds, an equal-length guard before the character loop and an 'A'..'Z' guard before the Character'Val shift, and the only loop is a for loop, so proof should discharge automatically.

effects.explanation: The program shows the content of both strings with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

String concatenation.approach: A parameterless Main declares a String constant S1 := "Hello" and a String constant S2 := S1 & " literal", with fixed lengths known statically. It then prints S1 and S2 with two Silver_IO.Put_Line calls; there are no loops, inputs or guards.
String concatenation.summary: The task needs only String constants, bounded concatenation and Put_Line, all of which Silver already supports, and every check is static, so proofs discharge trivially.

effects.explanation: Prints Mary had a little lamb after the admitted library operation replaces the marker with the value held in Little.

String interpolation (included).approach: Follow the captured Ada answer's library-based interpretation: declare Original as the constant String "Mary had a @__@ lamb" and Little as a String variable containing "little", then print Ada.Strings.Fixed.Replace_Slice (Original, 12, 15, Little). The fixed task text makes the placeholder positions static, so no search operation or application-written interpolation routine is needed.
String interpolation (included).summary: This future library candidate performs replacement in an existing template using a standard Ada operation, with fixed valid positions and a statically bounded result. It neither claims native interpolation syntax nor treats plain concatenation as interpolation; admission still requires the operation's complete contract and source-correspondence justification.

review.setting_evidence: Selected setting; runtime not independently confirmed
review.method: Targeted static task, captured-answer and fixed-specification review

effects.explanation: Prints the byte length and the code point length of the embedded example strings.

risks.explanation: The loop-carried code point counter has no invariant, so an explicit guard Count < Natural'Last before each increment is needed, with a visible Reject outcome if it fails.
Character'Pos of each indexed byte is bounded by the Character type and the loop index runs over the string's own range, so these checks are routine.
Building the output line from the 'Image of the lengths needs a bounded buffer sized for the largest Natural, which must be checked against the buffer capacity.

String length.approach: The example strings (such as "møøse" and the non-BMP Unicode example) are embedded as constant Strings holding their UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 characters, so the byte length is S'Length. The code point length is found by a for loop over S'Range that counts every byte except UTF-8 continuation bytes (Character'Pos between 128 and 191), guarding the counter before incrementing. Both lengths are printed with Put_Line using Natural'Image concatenated into short bounded strings.
String length.summary: Counting UTF-8 lead bytes with a for loop over the string's own range uses only types and a single counter guard, so the proofs should discharge without annotations; the grapheme count is optional and omitted.

effects.explanation: Prints the starts-with, ends-with and match-location results with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Slice bounds I .. I + S2'Length - 1 are discharged because the for loop runs I over 1 .. S1'Length - S2'Length + 1 with static constant lengths, and starts/ends slices are guarded by a length comparison with and then.
The output line concatenates fixed-length literals, constants and a short Integer'Image, so its bounded result length is statically known.

String matching.approach: Embed two constant Strings (for example a text with repeated occurrences and a pattern) in Main, and use a length guard with and then before comparing the leading and trailing slices for starts-with and ends-with. For contains, a for loop over the valid start positions compares the slice to the pattern and prints each match location via Integer'Image, handling multiple occurrences with no loop-carried accumulator; an empty pattern is excluded by a visible guard that prints a specified message.
String matching.summary: All indexing uses constant lengths and for-loop indexes over the string's own range with guards just before slices, and there is no loop-carried arithmetic, so the checks follow from declarations and guards.

effects.explanation: Prints the resulting string with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The result is built in a fixed-capacity buffer, so the program's literal sizes make the prepend fit statically and the length checks discharge from constants.

String prepend.approach: Keep the variable as a fixed-capacity buffer (a String of capacity 32 plus a length in a declared range), initialized to "World!". Prepend "Hello " by guarding that the combined length fits the capacity, shifting the old contents right and copying the literal in front, then print the used slice with Put_Line. If the guard fails, print a visible rejection message instead.
String prepend.summary: The task is one prepend and one print on embedded literal data, so every length and index check follows from constants and a single guard before the copy. Silver already has bounded concatenation, so only a buffer with a computed length and slice printing are missing.

effects.explanation: Prints the stripped result line with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The write position Last is a loop-carried counter, so it is declared as a subtype with range 0..Max and guarded by Last < Max before each increment, which discharges index and range checks.

Strip a set of characters from a string.approach: Embed the example text and the set "aei" as constants, build a Boolean Keep table indexed by Character (all True, then False for each set character), then copy kept characters into a fixed-capacity Character buffer sized to the input length with a guarded count. Print the buffer prefix as a String of computed length via Put_Line, using a procedure for the strip so the output length is returned via an out parameter and the loop-carried index is guarded.
Strip a set of characters from a string.summary: All loops are for loops over the constant strings' own ranges, and the only loop-carried value is the output count, which a bounded subtype and an explicit guard keep safe without any annotation.

effects.explanation: The stripped text is written to standard output with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Reading the character after the current one is guarded by a test that the current index is below Text'Last, and the loop index runs over Text'Range.
The output length counter is a subtype bounded by Text'Length and is incremented only after a guard that it is below that bound, with Reject as the visible outcome otherwise.

Strip block comments.approach: The sample program text is embedded as a constant String built by concatenating line literals with Character'Val (10) line feeds, and a single for loop over its indexes copies characters into a fixed output buffer while tracking Inside_Comment and a Skip_Next flag. On "/*" outside a comment it enters the comment and skips the next character, on "*/" inside a comment it leaves it and skips the next character (so the "/*/" case stays inside the comment), and line feeds inside comments are kept to preserve line structure as in the sample output. The buffer slice up to the counter is printed with Put_Line, and the delimiters are constants (the caller-specified delimiter extra credit is left out).
Strip block comments.summary: Every check is an index or counter bound that follows from the for-loop range, one lookahead guard and one capacity guard, with no loop-carried arithmetic beyond a guarded counter, so the proofs should discharge without annotations. The program needs only a few Character and String indexing constructs beyond today's Silver.

effects.explanation: The stripped result lines are printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The first and last kept positions are only assigned from for-loop indexes over Line'Range, so slice bounds stay within the string without an invariant.
Line'First and Line'Last arithmetic such as I - 1 is guarded by comparing I to Line'First, or avoided by using slices keyed to loop indexes.

Strip comments from a string.approach: The two example lines are embedded as String constants and passed to a procedure Strip_And_Print taking an unconstrained String. It uses a for loop over Line'Range to find the first '#' or ';' (recording the cut position, defaulting to the end), then a forward for loop to find the first non-blank and a reverse for loop to find the last non-blank within the kept prefix, and prints the slice if non-empty or an empty line otherwise. All loop-carried positions are assigned only from loop indexes, so slice bounds are always valid and no while loop is needed.
Strip comments from a string.summary: Every check is an index or slice bound derived from for-loop indexes over the string's own range, and there are no function loops, recursion or arithmetic beyond small index steps, so proofs should discharge unaided. The program must trim whitespace (the current task rules), which is done with simple for loops rather than a loop-carried while scan.

effects.explanation: Prints the original string and the two filtered strings with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The output count is a loop-carried value, so each increment must sit behind an explicit guard that the buffer has room, with a visible rejection otherwise.
Writing Out(Count) after the guarded increment discharges because Count is declared in 0 .. buffer length and the guard bounds it just before use.
The output buffers must be fully initialized (for example with spaces) before slices are printed, which a declaration initializer provides.

Strip control codes and extended charact.approach: Embed the sample as a constant String built from literals and Character'Val codes, then run one for loop over its range testing each Character against the printable range 32..126 (control codes stripped) and against above-127 (extended kept in the first output only). Characters are appended to fixed-size String buffers with a ranged Natural count, guarded before each increment, and the slices Buffer(1 .. Count) are printed with Put_Line.
Strip control codes and extended charact.summary: Everything is bounded character-by-character filtering in a for loop, so checks follow from types and one guard on the loop-carried count, with no recursion or annotations needed (the Ada solution's recursive function would be replaced by iteration).

effects.explanation: The three trimmed strings are printed with Put_Line, each wrapped in quotes.

risks.explanation: The scan indexes are subtypes ranging from 0 to N+1 and each Text(I) read is guarded by an and then bound test just before it, so slice and element checks follow from the loop conditions.
Each increment or decrement happens inside a loop whose condition keeps the index strictly inside the subtype range, so the type range alone discharges it.

Strip whitespace from a string/Top and t.approach: Embed a constant String with leading and trailing spaces and tabs (tabs built via Character'Val(9) concatenation), then in Main use two while loops with guarded indexes, treating any Character <= ' ' as whitespace, to find the first and last non-whitespace positions. Print the left-trimmed, right-trimmed and both-trimmed slices of the constant, each wrapped in quote marks, with an all-whitespace case producing an empty slice naturally.
Strip whitespace from a string/Top and t.summary: Every check is an index or range check on scan variables bounded by subtypes and guarded by and then tests, in plain procedure-level while loops, so no annotation is needed. The only new surface is Character comparison, String slicing and while loops.

effects.explanation: Prints the two lists of first strong and weak primes and the four counts to standard output.

risks.explanation: The sieve's inner while loop carries a multiple index j, which is discharged by putting the 'j <= Limit' test in the loop condition immediately before each array access.
Sums of neighbouring primes and the running counts stay within 32-bit Integer because values never exceed about 10,000,100, and the sieve step addition is guarded by the loop condition.
A Boolean sieve of several million entries (odd-only storage helps) is a large fixed object whose memory is an environmental premise that GNATprove does not check.

Strong and weak primes.approach: A constant Limit just above 10,000,000 sizes a fixed Boolean sieve array that a Main-level procedure fills with nested while loops (outer bound i*i <= Limit, inner step guarded by j <= Limit). A single for loop over the array's range then tracks the previous prime and current prime, classifying the current one as strong or weak when the next prime arrives by comparing prev + next against 2*cur, and records the first 36 strong and 37 weak primes and counts below 1,000,000 and 10,000,000. Results are printed with Put and Put_Line using Integer'Image, with all loop-carried values kept in bounded Integer subtypes.
Strong and weak primes.summary: Every check is an index or addition on values bounded by the Limit constant, and all loops live in a procedure so no variants are needed, but sieve loop-carried indexes and the large fixed array make careful guarding necessary.

effects.explanation: Prints each example polynomial followed by its isolated real roots, or a message that it has none or that a numeric limit was exceeded.

risks.explanation: Horner evaluation, polynomial long division and the negated remainders carry Long_Float values through loops, so each multiply and add needs a guard just before it that bounds the operands (for example |acc| and |x| at most 1.0E100), with any breach reported as an explicit 'numeric limit exceeded' outcome for that polynomial.

Dividing by a divisor's leading coefficient, and making the polynomial monic, is guarded by trimming coefficients whose magnitude falls below a small threshold, so the divisor is provably nonzero and the quotient cannot overflow.

Coefficient arrays, the Sturm sequence array and the explicit interval worklist that replaces recursive isolation all have fixed capacity, and each write is guarded by a count check before it that leads to a reported capacity failure.
The sign-variation counter and the root count are bounded by the sequence length and the degree, so they rely on declared ranged subtypes plus a guard before each increment.

Interval isolation runs in a procedure as a for loop capped at a fixed number of worklist steps, and bisection uses a for loop with a fixed iteration cap, so there is no while loop or recursion inside a function.

Sturm sequence.approach: Each polynomial is a record holding a degree in a ranged subtype and a fixed-capacity Long_Float coefficient array. The example polynomials are embedded as an array aggregate. For each one, a procedure builds the Sturm sequence into a fixed array of such records using a for loop bounded by the degree, with negated remainders from guarded long division. Roots are isolated over a Cauchy bound using an explicit worklist of intervals: Sturm sign-variation counts split intervals until each holds one root, and then a fixed-count for-loop bisection refines it. Magnitude guards placed before every floating-point operation, and capacity guards before every array write, lead to a printed rejection of that polynomial.
Sturm sequence.summary: The program needs only arrays, records, for loops and procedures, and it uses no recursion or annotations. Its outlook is plausible rather than likely because Long_Float overflow and division checks on values carried through Horner evaluation and polynomial division discharge only if magnitude guards are placed carefully before each operation.

effects.explanation: The Sturmian words for the embedded rational 13/21 and for the inverse golden ratio are printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: b*b*k*k*a and mid*mid are computed in a 64-bit range type whose declared bounds on a, b, m, n and k (k at most 32) keep every product within range, so guards at entry suffice.

Floor division of a possibly negative numerator (m is negative for the golden ratio) is made safe by adding a bounded non-negative offset before dividing, with a visible rejection if the numerator is out of range.
The integer square root uses a binary search while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and the other loops are for loops.
The output buffer index is a loop-carried value that is guarded by a capacity check before each append of one or two characters, since no invariant can be written.

Sturmian word.approach: Embed the data (m=13, n=21, and a=5, b=1, m=-1, n=2 with k=32) as constants of declared range subtypes; a procedure computes floor(k*x) exactly, using a bounded binary-search integer square root of b^2*k^2*a for the quadratic case and plain integer division for the rational case. A for loop over k appends '0' or "10" into a fixed-size Character buffer, guarding capacity before each append, and stopping when k*m is divisible by n for the rational case; x>1 is handled by swapping m and n and inverting the characters. The buffer slice is printed with Put_Line.
Sturmian word.summary: All arithmetic is bounded integer arithmetic with ranges set by declared limits, and the only loop-carried hazards (buffer position, search bounds) are covered by types and explicit guards, so no annotation is needed, but the nonlinear square-root search needs careful range shaping.

effects.explanation: Prints the sub-unit squares found, one per line.

risks.explanation: n is bounded by a declared range (for example up to 10**9) so n*n fits in 64 bits, and the repunit is built over at most 18 digits so subtraction stays in range.
The search is a while loop inside a procedure (no termination check), and the digit and square-root loops are for loops with fixed bounds, so no function needs a variant.
Loop-carried values (the shrinking quotient, the repunit, the bisection bounds) are typed with explicit ranges and guarded before each multiply or subtract, since no invariants can be written.
Finding more than the required five terms depends on the search limit chosen; the program prints the first five and stops, with the bound being a documented limit.

Sub-unit squares.approach: A procedure loops n from 1 with a while loop up to a documented bound, squares n in a 64-bit range type, and calls a function that walks the decimal digits with a bounded for loop, rejecting any square with a zero digit and accumulating the digit-reduced value by subtracting a repunit. A second function does a fixed-iteration bisection integer square root over a bounded range to test whether the reduced value is a perfect square, and the main procedure prints each hit with Integer'Image and Put_Line until five are found.
Sub-unit squares.summary: All arithmetic is bounded integer work with fixed-iteration for loops in functions and the only unbounded-looking loop in a procedure, so checks follow from range types and guards; the main care is keeping n*n and the repunit subtraction within 64 bits.

effects.explanation: Emulated output instructions write characters to standard output, plus a message when the machine stops abnormally.
The emulated input instruction (A = -1) reads one character from standard input, with end of input stored as -1.

risks.explanation: The subtraction of two 32-bit words is computed in 64-bit Long_Long_Integer and range-tested before storing, so the check follows from types and a guard just before the store.
Every memory access uses an address first tested to lie in 0 .. Size-1 (and PC+2 in range), with out-of-range addresses halting the machine with a visible fault message.
Character'Val on a memory word is guarded by a 0 .. 255 test, with out-of-range output words halting with a fault message.
The interpreter loop is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, and a documented step limit also stops runaway programs with a visible message.

Subleq.approach: The program holds memory as a constant-size array of a 32-bit ranged Word type initialized by an aggregate with the Hello world words and others => 0, then runs a procedure with a while loop over the program counter and a step counter. Each iteration guards that PC+2 is inside memory, then branches on A = -1 (read a character), B = -1 (write a character, guarded to 0..255) or subtract-and-branch (guarding A and B as addresses, computing the difference in Long_Long_Integer and rejecting results outside Word); negative PC halts normally, and every guard failure prints a specified fault or step-limit message and stops.
Subleq.summary: Every array index, character conversion and subtraction is protected by a guard just before use with a defined halt outcome, and the loop lives in a procedure so no variant is needed, so the proofs should discharge without annotations.

effects.explanation: The chosen words and their weights are printed as lines of text.

risks.explanation: The reach lookup at s-w and the backtracking sum index must stay inside the sum range, which is discharged by an explicit range guard before each lookup and a ranged subtype for sums.
Running sums are loop-carried, so they are kept in a ranged subtype and each update is guarded, with out-of-range cases skipped because no reachable sum can lie outside the bound.
The roughly 2M-entry Boolean table must be fully initialized by an aggregate or nested for loops over its own ranges before use.

Subset sum problem.approach: Embed the 31 words (fixed-width padded strings) and weights in constant arrays, then run a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program filling reach(i, s) = some non-empty subset of the first i words sums to s over sums -31000..31000. If reach(31, 0) holds, backtrack with a reverse for loop carrying the remaining sum, preferring exclusion, and print each chosen word with its weight and the total; otherwise print a specified no-subset message.
Subset sum problem.summary: The dynamic-programming formulation avoids subset enumeration and needs only bounded 2D Boolean tables and for loops, so index and range checks follow from ranged types plus explicit guards; the risk is only the guarded loop-carried sums and table size.

effects.explanation: Reads the source file and writes the encrypted file and then the decrypted file through admitted file operations.
The first argument selects encode or decode mode.
Reports usage, rejected input and completion.

risks.explanation: The alphabet lookup uses a for loop over the 52-character alphabet's own range and the key has the same fixed length, so the index checks are static.
The input is read into a fixed-capacity buffer with a reported length, and a file larger than the capacity is rejected with a visible message.

Substitution cipher.approach: Declare constant 52-character Alphabet and Key strings and a fixed-capacity text buffer with a length. A Translate procedure walks the buffer with a for loop, finds each letter's position in the source alphabet with an inner for loop over its range, and replaces it from the target alphabet, leaving non-letters unchanged. Main reads the input file with a status result, rejects oversize or unreadable input, writes the encrypted file, then reads that back and writes the decrypted file.
Substitution cipher.summary: All indexing is over fixed-length constant strings and a bounded buffer using for loops inside procedures, so checks follow from static bounds and one size guard; the only gap is that Silver needs file read and write operations with specified failure outcomes.

effects.explanation: Each of the five substrings is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Slice bounds computed from a found position and M are discharged by explicit guards just before each slice, with the loop-carried found position typed as a bounded subtype or recomputed under a guard.
Position plus M arithmetic stays far below Integer'Last because Str has a static length of 8 and M is a small constant.

Substring.approach: Embed the string "abcdefgh" as a constant with constants N and M, and print the first three cases as slices with static, guarded bounds. For the known-character and known-substring cases, use a for loop over the string's own index range that records the first match, then print the slice after a guard that clips to the string end and prints a visible 'not found' line when no match exists. The substring comparison compares slices Str(I..I+Len-1) only for I in a range that keeps the upper bound inside the string.
Substring.summary: All five cases use a short constant string with static bounds, for loops over the array's own range and guards placed just before each slice, so every index and overflow check follows from types and guards. No loop invariant, recursion or while loop is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints the nine qualifying primes (2 3 5 7 23 37 53 73 373) on one line or one per line.

Substring primes.approach: A subtype Small is range 0 .. 999 and a Boolean function Is_Prime(N) uses a for loop over 2 .. N - 1 with a test of N mod D = 0 (guarded so that N < 2 returns False first). A second function Is_Substring_Prime(N) checks N itself and, by guarded branches on N >= 10 and N >= 100, the substrings N mod 100, N mod 10, N / 10, N / 100 and (N mod 100) / 10 using Is_Prime. The Main procedure loops N over 2 .. 500 and prints each qualifying number with Put and an Integer image of N.
Substring primes.summary: Every check follows from the Small subtype range, nonzero loop divisors and for loops, so no loop-carried values or annotations are needed, and the functions terminate because only for loops are used. The task needs only integer arithmetic, bounded for loops and number printing.

effects.explanation: Prints the full string and the three trimmed variants with Put_Line.

Substring/Top and tail.approach: Declare a constant String "upraisers" (ASCII, an 8-bit encoding the task exempts from full Unicode handling) and print the original and three slices with literal bounds 2..9, 1..8 and 2..8, each concatenated into a labeled quoted line using the existing bounded concatenation and Put_Line. No loops or inputs are involved, so all index and length checks are static.
Substring/Top and tail.summary: The only new surface is slicing a String by static bounds, and every slice bound is statically within the constant's range so the index and length checks discharge without guards. There are no loops, arithmetic or input.

effects.explanation: Prints r220, r221 and r222 for the embedded seed 292929 with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Each difference of two elements typed 0 .. 10**9 - 1 lies in -(10**9 - 1) .. 10**9 - 1, and the guard "if D < 0 then D := D + M" just before storing brings it back into the element subtype by linear reasoning.

Ring-buffer and reorder indexes are computed fresh from the for-loop index as N mod 55, (N + 31) mod 55 and (34 * (N + 1)) mod 55, so each lies in 0 .. 54 from the mod alone with no loop-carried index.

Subtractive generator.approach: Main stores the 55 seed values S and the ring buffer R in arrays indexed 0 .. 54 whose elements have the subtype 0 .. 10**9 - 1, with seed 292929 embedded. One for loop fills S(2 .. 54) with the subtractive formula and a second sets R(I) := S((34 * (I + 1)) mod 55). A third loop over N in 55 .. 222 updates R(N mod 55) from R(N mod 55) - R((N + 31) mod 55), adding 10**9 when the difference is negative, and prints the value with 'Image whenever N >= 220.
Subtractive generator.summary: Every value is bounded by its element subtype, the only arithmetic is a linear subtraction followed by an add-m guard, and every index is a fresh mod 55 of a for-loop index, so all checks follow from types and local guards.

effects.explanation: Prints the first group, last group and count for each of the six difference patterns.

risks.explanation: Sieve strike index j is loop-carried in a while loop, so the loop condition j <= Limit is tested just before each array access and the increment j + i is bounded by that guard.

Group counters and the prime count are loop-carried and known only by type, so each increment is preceded by a guard against a declared maximum with a visible Reject outcome, and the 78498 prime count fits a declared capacity.
Pattern scan reads P(i+k) for k up to 3, so the for-loop upper bound is the prime count minus the pattern length, with an explicit guard that the count is at least the pattern length.
Group lines are assembled from scalar images of up to four 6-digit numbers into a bounded buffer sized for the worst case, so concatenation lengths are static.

Successive prime differences.approach: Sieve of Eratosthenes over a Boolean array 2..999999 using for loops for candidates and a guarded while loop for strikes, then compact the primes into an array of capacity 78498 with a guarded count. A procedure taking a difference table and its length scans consecutive primes with for loops, tracking first, last and a guarded count, and prints each result line from scalar images in a bounded string buffer.
Successive prime differences.summary: All arrays and ranges are static and every loop-carried value (strike index, counters) can be guarded just before use, with no recursion or functions needing variants, but several loop-carried guards and a large Boolean array make careful shape necessary.

effects.explanation: The program prints F_n(x, y) for a few embedded sample arguments with Silver_IO.Put_Line.
