The loop-carried area accumulator and interval-end values only have their subtype range after the first iteration, so each must be declared in a bounded float subtype wide enough to hold any sum of strip contributions and clamped by a visible guard.
Converting the float area scaled by 1e6 to an integer for printing needs a guard on the magnitude, which the bounded accumulator type provides.

Reaching six digits requires an exact per-strip union length with roughly 100000 midpoint strips, and the float rounding behavior of that sum is not provable but is only an accuracy concern rather than a check.

Total circles area.approach: Embed the 25 circles as constant arrays of centre x, centre y and radius in bounded float subtypes, then integrate the union's vertical cross-section length over x with many midpoint strips (exact, using only Sqrt, not grid sampling). For each strip a for-loop builds each circle's interval, sorts the intervals with a bubble sort made of nested for loops, and sweeps them with a running right end to sum the union length. The area is scaled to an integer, guarded, and printed with Put_Line using integer image and string building of the decimal point.
Total circles area.summary: Everything is for loops over fixed array ranges with bounded float subtypes, so checks reduce to range and guard facts, but float accumulation, Sqrt and the float-to-integer conversion need careful bounding for the provers.

The prime counter incremented across up to 100000 iterations needs a guard such as Count < 100000 with a visible Reject outcome, since without an invariant its bound is otherwise unknown.
I * I is avoided by looping I over the static range 2 .. 316 so that I * I <= 99856 is safe in Integer.
The inner while loop dividing N2 by I exists only in a procedure (totient as an out-parameter procedure), so no termination check is generated.

Totient function.approach: A procedure Totient (N : in Positive_Limit; Phi : out Natural_Limit) copies N into N2 and Tot, runs for I in 2 .. 316 with an if I * I <= N2 guard and an inner while N2 mod I = 0 loop dividing out the factor and setting Tot := Tot - Tot / I, then adjusts for a leftover prime factor N2 > 1. Main loops N in 1 .. 100000 with embedded constants, calling the procedure, counting primes where Phi = N - 1 under a bounded-counter guard, printing the first 25 rows with 'Image-built lines, and printing the count at 100, 1000, 10000 and 100000.
Totient function.summary: All checks come from subtype ranges, a static for-loop bound and guards, and the only while loop sits in a procedure, so no annotation is needed; the loop-carried Tot and counter arithmetic need careful range typing and guards, which makes discharge plausible rather than certain.

The Ndisks - 1 subtraction in each recursive call is guarded by the enclosing Ndisks > 0 test, so it discharges from the subtype range.

Main calls Hanoi (4, Left, Right, Center); all arguments are statically in range and the only subtraction sits under the Ndisks > 0 guard.
Towers of Hanoi.summary: This is a tiny recursive procedure whose only checks are a guarded decrement and concatenation of bounded image text, and procedures get no termination check, so proofs should discharge; the one soft spot is recursion depth, which the declared subtype bounds.

effects.explanation: Prints the prompt and one result or alert line per item.
Reads eleven textual numeric inputs from standard input.

Sqrt of abs(x) needs a nonnegative argument and a bounded result, which follows from the ranged float type and the verified library contract.
The eleven-element array is filled and read back with for loops over its own range, so indexes are routine.
Parsing decimal text into floats and formatting results depends on an admitted library with specified failure outcomes; unparsable or out-of-range input must be rejected visibly, not clamped.

Trabb Pardo\u2013Knuth algorithm.approach: Store eleven values in a Float array with a bounded range subtype, read each through an admitted parse operation that rejects invalid or out-of-range text with a visible message, then loop in reverse printing each item and either its f(x) result or a too-large alert. The function is guarded so that when x is above a small bound the alert is printed without computing the cube, otherwise f is computed within safe bounds and compared with 400.0.
Trabb Pardo\u2013Knuth algorithm.summary: The control flow is simple for loops and every check follows from ranged types and guards, but it depends on admitted floating-point parsing, Sqrt and formatting operations with verified contracts, so discharge hinges on careful range guards.

effects.explanation: Prints each transliterated line with angle-bracket Greek letter names, using the task's allowed ASCII fallback.

Advancing I by 1 or 2 is guarded by the I <= Text'Last loop condition and an I < Text'Last test before the two-letter step, so I + 2 stays within Integer.

Transliterate English text using the Gre.approach: Embed the task text as several String constants, one per output line, and pass each to a procedure Transliterate (Text : String) that scans with a while loop and index I. At each position it checks the next character through guarded lookahead (I < Text'Last) for the digraphs ch, kh, ph, ps, th, rh, ck, ee and oo, otherwise a case statement on the single letter, and it emits the angle-bracket Greek name with Put, using the capitalized name for upper-case letters. For s it looks ahead and emits sigma-final when the next character is absent or not a letter; any other character is passed through unchanged, and the line ends with Put_Line.
Transliterate English text using the Gre.summary: All checks are string-index bounds that the loop condition and an explicit lookahead guard establish, with no nonlinear arithmetic, and the loop sits in a procedure so no variant is needed; the only new surface is Character handling, string indexing, case statements and Put.

Cycle-search and basis-tree walks use computed row and column indices, which are discharged by declaring them in subtypes of the matrix bounds and guarding before each use.
Pivot updates of shipment quantities add and subtract the minimum along the cycle, so quantities are kept in a bounded subtype and each update is preceded by an explicit range guard.

The stepping loop, potential propagation and cycle search are all while loops inside procedures (never functions), so no termination check arises, and an iteration cap with a visible reject outcome bounds them.
The plan, potentials and visited-flag arrays are fully initialized by aggregates or for loops before the while loops read them.

Transportation problem.approach: Embed the 2x3 example (supply, demand, integer cost matrix) as constants in bounded arrays with a fixed maximum size plus room for a dummy row or column; build the initial plan with the north-west corner rule in for loops, then iterate a MODI loop in procedures: compute potentials over the basis by repeated sweeps, find the most negative reduced cost, trace the redistribution cycle with array-based index chains, shift the minimum quantity, and stop when no negative reduced cost remains. All indices and quantities use bounded subtypes with guards before every arithmetic update, and the final plan is formatted into bounded text lines and printed.
Transportation problem.summary: The task is plain integer array work with while loops confined to procedures and fixed bounds, so no annotation is needed, but many loop-carried potentials, indices and quantities each need a careful guard to discharge without invariants.

The nesting depth counter rises and falls through the loop, so it is declared with a bounded subtype and guarded (reject if above the maximum, ignore a close at depth zero) before every change.
Node names are copied into fixed-size name slots with a stored length, and each copy is guarded by the slot capacity and the node-count capacity.
All loops are while or for loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, so no variant is needed.

Tree datastructures.approach: Embed the example as a bracketed nest string such as RosettaCode(rocks(code,comparison,wiki),mocks(trolling)) in a bounded buffer, and hold the indent form as arrays of levels and fixed-capacity names with a node count. One procedure scans the nest text with a depth counter to fill the indent arrays; another walks the indent arrays, comparing each level with the previous one to emit open brackets, commas and close brackets into a bounded buffer. The program prints the initial nest, the indent lines, and the rebuilt nest, then compares the two nest strings with String equality.
Tree datastructures.summary: Only bounded arrays, bounded string buffers and while loops in procedures are needed, so no annotation is required, but loop-carried depth and buffer positions need explicit guards, which makes the outcome depend on careful program shape. Arbitrary trees are limited to documented node, depth and name capacities, with oversize input rejected.

effects.explanation: Prints the nested-list text for each of the seven example inputs.

The nesting depth variable is loop-carried and typed as a bounded subtype, with increments and decrements guarded by comparisons against the target level so the type range suffices.
Level values come from a subtype bounded to a small range in embedded data, so image and increment arithmetic stays within range.

Before each element it emits ']' while depth exceeds the level and '[' while depth is below, plus separators, appending characters into a fixed-capacity String buffer behind an explicit capacity guard that rejects on overflow, then prints the buffer slice with Put_Line. The output is the nested-list text, which meets the task's displayed results; the tree is not kept as a data structure.

effects.explanation: Prints the four labelled traversal lines to standard output.

Output counters and stack tops are ranged subtypes bounded by the guards, so increments are guarded just before use.
The iterative traversals are while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, so no variant is needed.
Output lines are built in a fixed-size buffer sized for 9 values plus label, with a guard before each append.

Tree traversal.approach: The tree is stored in arrays indexed by node number 1..9, holding Left, Right and Value, with 0 meaning no child, and filled with embedded constants. Preorder, inorder and postorder use iterative procedures with an explicit fixed-capacity stack, with postorder using a last-visited marker, and level order uses a fixed-capacity queue, all in while loops inside procedures. Every push, pop and append is guarded by a capacity or emptiness test that rejects on failure, and results are written into a bounded text buffer then printed with Put_Line.
Tree traversal.summary: The task has no conflicts, since recursion and pointers can be replaced by array-backed nodes and explicit bounded stacks and queues in procedures, and the checks are index and capacity guards on loop-carried tops. Plausible rather than likely because several loop-carried stack and queue indices need careful guards and the postorder state logic is delicate.

effects.explanation: The program prints the four 30-term tables and the three roots for each of the four integers.

Square roots and the cube-root formula need operands guarded to non-negative bounded ranges, and the cube root is computed by a bounded Newton or bisection loop in a procedure rather than a fractional power.
Root-finding iterations use for loops with a fixed iteration count or while loops inside procedures only, so no function needs a variant.
Converting the large integers and float results to text needs explicit range guards before 'Image or a hand-written digit-building routine.

Triangular numbers.approach: Keep a 31-element array of a 64-bit range subtype; build triangular, tetrahedral, pentatopic and then up to 12-simplex numbers by repeated in-place prefix sums with a guard before each addition, printing six per line. For the roots, embed the four integers as constants and compute each triangular and pentatopic root with a guarded floating-point square root and the tetrahedral root with a bounded fixed-iteration Newton loop, printing with a text-building float formatter.
Triangular numbers.summary: The tables are simple bounded integer prefix sums that discharge with range guards, but the real-valued roots need floating-point arithmetic and formatting that depend on careful range guarding, so the outlook is plausible rather than likely.

Tangent as sin/cos needs an explicit guard that cos is nonzero (or admitted library Tan preconditions), with a visible outcome when the guard fails.
Inverse functions need the argument guarded into -1.0..1.0 (Arcsin, Arccos) before the call, with the fixed example value 0.5 making this static.
If Taylor series replace library functions, loop-carried term and sum values must be bounded by a ranged subtype or a clamp, which GNATprove can accept but only with careful shape.

Inverse calls use a fixed argument in range, guarded explicitly, and results are converted to degrees and radians then printed as formatted float text lines through a small output procedure.
Trigonometric functions.summary: Nothing requires an annotation, a conflict or recursion since the task is a fixed set of float computations, but the proofs hinge on floating-point range and finiteness reasoning plus new float formatting output, so discharge is plausible rather than routine.

effects.explanation: Prints one line per qualifying n with Put_Line.

Sieve products I*K stay below about 36 million when I and K are ranged subtypes up to 6004, and a guard I*K <= 6004 precedes the array index.
Output lines are assembled from Integer'Image pieces whose maximum length is bounded by the ranged subtype, so concatenation lengths are statically bounded.

Triplet of three numbers.approach: Embed a Boolean array Prime (1 .. 6004) filled by a nested for-loop sieve (outer I over 2..77, inner K over 2..6004 with a guard on I*K) in a procedure, then loop N over 2..5999 testing Prime (N-1), Prime (N+3) and Prime (N+5) with and then. Each hit is printed with Put_Line from 'Image conversions of N and the three primes, padded to fixed width using small if comparisons.
Triplet of three numbers.summary: All indexes and arithmetic are bounded by static ranges and for loops over fixed limits, so no loop invariants or variants are needed and every check discharges from types and one guard. The only new work for Silver is integers, arrays, for loops and integer-to-text output.

effects.explanation: Prints each demonstrated identity and result line to standard output.

The loop-carried power accumulator is known only by its type after the first iteration, so the guard before each addition must be explicit and the exponent is a bounded positive subtype.

Representing real numbers by a bounded decimal fixed-point type with a separate negative-infinity flag is a documented resource limit that covers the task's example values (-0.001, 1.5, -0.5) exactly.

Tropical algebra overloading.approach: Represent a tropical value as a record holding a Boolean Is_Neg_Inf flag and a bounded fixed-point value (delta 0.001, range roughly +/-1.0E6), with Tropical_Add (max, with -Inf as identity) and Tropical_Mul (sum, -Inf absorbing, guarded against leaving the range) as expression functions or small functions. Power is a for loop over 1 .. B with B a positive bounded subtype, guarding each addition before performing it, and a procedure prints each required demonstration (2 times -2, -0.001 plus -Inf, 0 times -Inf, 1.5 plus -1, -0.5 times 0, 5 to the 7th, and the distributivity comparison) via Put_Line with 'Image text.
Tropical algebra overloading.summary: All arithmetic is on small bounded fixed-point values with explicit range guards before each addition and a for-loop power, so no annotation is needed, but fixed-point image formatting, the loop-carried accumulator guard, and the -Inf record make careful program shape necessary.

effects.explanation: Prints the largest left-truncatable and right-truncatable primes below one million.

Truncation arithmetic (N mod Power(K), N / 10) stays within 0..999_999 by subtype ranges, so Composite indexing is safe, with a guard to skip zero digits before use.

Truncatable primes.approach: A Boolean sieve array over 0..999_999 is filled using nested for loops (I in 2..1000, K in I..Max/I marking I*K), and the program scans N downward with a reverse for loop. For each prime it checks left truncation using a constant table of powers of ten (N mod Power(K) must be prime and the digit must be nonzero) and right truncation via repeated N/10 in a bounded for loop, recording the first success and printing both results with Integer'Image.
Truncatable primes.summary: Every loop is a for loop over static ranges with all indexes bounded by subtypes or guards, so no invariants or variants are needed and the sieve and truncation checks should discharge routinely.

effects.explanation: Reads the file name and the required length from command-line arguments.
Reads the source file as bytes and writes a binary temporary copy through admitted file operations with specified failure outcomes.
Deletes the original file and renames the temporary file over it, or deletes the temporary file on rejection.
Signals the error condition (missing file, length not less than file size, bad length) through a nonzero exit status.
Prints a message describing the rejection or success.

risks.explanation: The remaining-byte counter is only decremented inside a loop guarded by Count > 0, and the parsed length is a bounded natural type, so the subtraction check discharges from the guard.
The temporary name is the file name with a suffix appended, so the bounded name buffer must be capped and over-long names rejected with a visible outcome.
The copy loop is a while loop inside a procedure, which gets no termination check, so no variant is needed.
Admitted file operations must expose end-of-file, open, create, delete and rename failures as specified status results rather than exceptions, which depends on the library design.

Truncate a file.approach: A procedure takes the file name and a bounded-range length from the first two arguments, validating and rejecting a missing or unparsable length. It streams bytes from the source into a temporary file with a while loop that stops at end of file or when the remaining count reaches zero, then, if the count reached zero and the file had more bytes, deletes the original and renames the temporary file, otherwise removes the temporary file and rejects with a specified message and exit status. Every file operation returns a status that is checked before continuing.
Truncate a file.summary: The arithmetic is trivial and the copy loop's only carried value is a guarded counter, so proofs should discharge; the open work is the file, rename and delete library operations with status-based failure outcomes. The Ada solution's raised errors become specified rejections with an exit status, so no Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: The program prints the table header, separator line and one row per input combination.
The Boolean expression is taken from the first command-line argument, with embedded examples for the two- and three-variable demonstrations.
A malformed or over-long expression is rejected with a specified failure outcome and nonzero status.

The input position and output token count are loop-carried values whose bounds follow from their subtype ranges and a length guard on the input string rejecting expressions over the fixed limit.
The row count 2**N is computed with N capped at a fixed variable limit (for example 8), and the combination counter is a ranged subtype so the bit tests for each row stay in range.
All parsing and evaluation loops live in procedures (no termination check), and the evaluator is an iterative stack machine over postfix tokens, so no function needs a variant.
Stacks, token buffers and the variable table are fully initialized by aggregates before any loop reads them.

Truth table.approach: The program reads the expression from the first argument (defaulting to embedded examples), rejects it if longer than a fixed bound, and converts infix to postfix with an iterative shunting-yard in a procedure using fixed-size token and operator stack arrays guarded against overflow and underflow. It collects distinct variable letters into a bounded table (rejecting more than a fixed maximum), then loops over 2**N combinations, evaluating the postfix tokens with a bounded Boolean stack and printing each row with Put and Put_Line. Any syntax error, stack misuse or over-limit input leads to Reject with a visible message.
Truth table.summary: Everything is bounded arrays, ranged indexes and iterative stack loops in procedures, so checks follow from types and guards before each push or pop, but many loop-carried stack pointers and positions need careful guards. No annotation is needed, though the parser's shape makes automatic discharge plausible rather than certain.

effects.explanation: The 17 rows of 106 characters are printed as text art.

risks.explanation: The digit halving and bit-serial division carry values (carry 0..1, remainder 0..33) through loops without invariants, so each is a small ranged subtype and a guard subtracts 17 before the remainder is stored, which bounds every intermediate.

Bit position 17*column+row is computed from for-loop indexes with static ranges (at most 1801), so it fits the 1802-bit array bound by types, though this is nonlinear-looking arithmetic the provers must bound.

Each halving pass must reduce a 543-digit decimal array in place with a carry that stays a digit, which holds only if the digit elements are a 0..9 subtype and the 10*carry+digit expression is bounded by types.
All loops are for loops inside procedures, so no variant is needed.

Tupper's self-referential formula.approach: Embed k as a constant array of about 543 decimal digits (subtype 0..9), convert it to a 1802-element bit array by repeated halving with for loops, then bit-serially divide by 17 (remainder subtype 0..33, subtract 17 when at least 17) to get floor(k/17), reading y mod 17 as the row since k is a multiple of 17. For each of the 17 rows, build a 106-character String by testing bit 17*column+row of the quotient and writing a block or space character, then print each row with Put_Line.
Tupper's self-referential formula.summary: Every check follows from ranged digit and bit subtypes, for-loop indexes over static bounds and a guard before each remainder update, and no annotation is needed because all loops are for loops in procedures. It is plausible rather than likely because fixed-capacity big-number arithmetic with loop-carried carries and remainders is carried through nested loops.

effects.explanation: Prints the exact hits and the near-miss table to standard output.

risks.explanation: The truth counters in loops are loop-carried, so each increment is guarded by a test that the counter is below 12 (its subtype bound), which discharges the range check without changing results.
Statement indexes are constants 1..12 or for-loop variables over the table's own range, so every access is statically in bounds.
Decoding each assignment number 0..4095 into bits uses rem and division by the literal 2 on a loop-carried quotient, which stays in range only through its subtype bound.

Twelve statements.approach: Enumerate all 4096 truth assignments with a for loop over a ranged integer, decode each into a 12-element Boolean array using rem and division by 2 in an inner for loop, then evaluate the twelve statements with a counting function over array slices (guarded counters) and count mismatches against the claimed values. A procedure prints the true statement numbers with Put and Integer'Image for assignments with zero mismatches, and a second pass does the same for exactly one mismatch, adding the contradicted statement number.
Twelve statements.summary: Everything is bounded for loops over fixed ranges with small Boolean arrays and bounded counters, so checks follow from types and simple guards and no variants or invariants are needed. The only non-routine parts are loop-carried counters and quotients, which need guards or subtype bounds.

effects.explanation: The user-specified search size is read from the first command-line argument.
The twin prime pair count is printed as a line of text.
Rejecting an invalid or out-of-range search size should be reflected in the exit status.

risks.explanation: Parsing the decimal argument accumulates a value in a loop, discharged by a digit-count guard and a limit check before each multiply-add on a bounded subtype.
Sieve multiples J*I are computed in a loop with loop-carried values, discharged by a for loop over J in 2..Limit/I so the product is bounded, though nonlinear reasoning is needed.
The count is a Natural bounded by the fixed sieve capacity, so accumulating it in a for loop stays within its type.

Twin primes.approach: Parse the first argument into a Natural bounded by a documented maximum (for example 1_000_000), rejecting empty, non-digit or too-large input with a visible Reject outcome, then fill a fixed-capacity Boolean sieve array with for loops and a guard on I*I <= Limit. Finally count indices P in 2..Limit-3 where P and P+2 are both prime (so both are under the limit) with a for loop, and print the count with Integer'Image text. The extension (10^7 and 10^9 and timing) is optional and omitted.
Twin primes.summary: Sieve and count loops index a fixed array by for-loop ranges with guards, and parsing is the only loop-carried arithmetic, so no annotations are needed; the nonlinear multiple indexing is the main prover risk.

effects.explanation: Prints one line per qualifying twin-prime pair.

risks.explanation: D*D in trial division is bounded because D is a subtype range of at most 3163 and candidates stay under 10,000,001, so Integer cannot overflow.
Only for loops are used (with exit), so functions need no variant.

Twin primes whose sum is square number.approach: Since p+(p+2)=2(p+1) is a square only when p=2M^2-1, the program loops M over a subtype range 1..2236 and tests 2M^2-1 and 2M^2+1 for primality with a for-loop trial-division function (D in 2..3163, exit when D*D exceeds N). Qualifying pairs are printed with Put_Line and Integer'Image pieces, and the M bound is a static range keeping every product within Integer.
Twin primes whose sum is square number.summary: All arithmetic is bounded by static subtype ranges and every loop is a for loop, so checks follow from types and no variant or invariant is required. Only integers, for loops, a Boolean function and integer-to-text output must be added to Silver.

effects.explanation: Prints the four scenario labels with their death percentages.

risks.explanation: The LCG step multiplies a state bounded by a ranged subtype by a small constant so the product fits in 64-bit Integer, and the result is reduced with mod, and the trial and death counters are bounded by the fixed trial count.
Cylinder positions are a 0..5 subtype and rotation uses mod 6 arithmetic, so every array index is within range by type.
The load while loop skips occupied chambers and lives in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and a guard on the bullet count keeps it from spinning on a full cylinder.

Two bullet roulette.approach: The cylinder is a six-element Boolean array rotated by one position per step with a mod-6 copy; a deterministic LCG with a ranged state supplies the spin of 1 to 6 rotations. Four procedures (or one procedure taking a scenario number) unload, load, spin and fire in each scenario's order for 100000 trials, counting deaths in a bounded counter. Results are turned into a whole or one-decimal percentage with integer division and printed through a bounded text buffer.
Two bullet roulette.summary: Every check follows from ranged subtypes, fixed array bounds and a bounded counter, and the only loops are for loops plus a small while loop in a procedure. The only care needed is keeping the LCG arithmetic within 64-bit range, which types and mod make routine.

effects.explanation: Prints one line per matching integer with its decimal and binary forms.

risks.explanation: Slice bounds First..First+Len/2-1 and First+Len/2..10 depend on a loop-found First, discharged by a guard that First is in 1..10 and Len is even and positive just before slicing.
Concatenating the Integer image, a space and the slice has a bounded length because N is at most 999 and the slice at most 10 characters, within the output string's fixed size.

Two identical strings.approach: Loop N over 1..999 in Main; for each N, fill a 10-character buffer with its binary digits via a reverse for loop using mod 2 and division on a copy bounded by a Natural subtype, then locate the first '1' with a for loop that records the position in a bounded index variable. If the digit count is even and the two half-slices are equal, print the decimal image and binary slice with Put_Line, so every index and length is guarded by a test just before use.
Two identical strings.summary: All loops are bounded for loops over constant ranges with small-typed carried values, and slice indices are guarded just before use, so no annotation is needed and the only gap is Silver's missing arrays, slices and integer-to-text support.

effects.explanation: Prints the found index pair, or an empty list, to standard output.

Two sum.approach: The program declares a bounded integer subtype for values (for example -1000 .. 1000), a constrained five-element array type indexed by 0 .. 4, and embeds the example array plus a no-solution case. A procedure takes the array and the target sum and uses nested for loops, with the outer index over 0 .. 3 and the inner index over the outer index plus one .. 4, to test each pair. It records the first matching pair in a Boolean flag and two index variables, then prints "[i, j]" with Put and 'Image, or "[]" if no pair was found.
Two sum.summary: Every check follows from declared value ranges that keep the sum of two elements within Integer, and from for-loop indexes over the array's own range, so no loop invariant is needed. The loops live in a procedure and terminate on their own, and the output uses only simple image conversion.

effects.explanation: Prints a line stating whether the computed two's complement negates the original value.

Two's complement.approach: Declare a 32-bit modular type, a constant A of 42, a constant B computed as not A + 1, and a Boolean constant testing A + B = 0. Then use an if statement to print a literal line reporting the result with Silver_IO.Put_Line. There are no loops, no input and no guards needed.
Two's complement.summary: Modular arithmetic wraps by definition and so raises no overflow check, and the program is straight-line code over constants, so every proof is routine.

effects.explanation: The procedure prints each block of text with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Type detection.approach: A tag enumeration (Literal_Text, Buffer_Text) describes the source, and a procedure Process_Text takes the tag plus a String and uses a case statement on the tag to print a source label and then the text via Put_Line. Main calls it twice, once with a String literal tagged Literal_Text and once with a fixed-length String variable tagged Buffer_Text, with no loops, arithmetic or indexing.
Type detection.summary: The task is a tagged-dispatch print demo with no arithmetic, loops or recursion, so every check is trivially routine and no annotation is needed. It only requires enumerations, case statements and a procedure with a String parameter beyond today's Silver.

effects.explanation: Print the longest repeated digit string(s) and positions for each of the three sizes, plus timing figures.
The task requires timing each run to demonstrate roughly linear scaling.

Ukkonen\u2019s suffix tree construction.summary: The task needs Ukkonen suffix tree construction over a bounded alphabet. This fits arrays of node records with integer indices and iterative loops, with no recursion or pointers. It also needs pi digits to 100000 places, which needs fixed-capacity big-number arithmetic (or an embedded or file-read digit source), console output and a clock for timing. No fixed Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: Prints the Ulam numbers for the sample indices (10, 100, 1000) as text lines.

risks.explanation: Indexes into the Ulam list and the membership array are loop-carried, so each is guarded just before use (count below capacity, candidate minus element within 1..Limit) with an explicit rejection outcome when capacity would be exceeded.
The representation counter is stopped at 2 by a guard and candidates are bounded by a declared Limit subtype, so additions stay inside Integer ranges.
The generator is a procedure (no termination check) and its candidate loop is a for loop over 3..Limit with a flag for completion, so no variant is required.
Candidate values and list contents are held in a ranged subtype, and subtraction results are tested to lie in that range before conversion or indexing.

Ulam numbers.approach: A procedure keeps an array of the first Max_N Ulam numbers and a Boolean membership array over 1..Limit (about 13000 for n up to 1000); for each candidate from 3 upward it counts, with a for loop over the found numbers, the pairs u_i+u_j=c using the membership array and stops counting at 2. A candidate with exactly one pair is appended; if the requested n is not reached within Limit or Max_N the program prints a visible rejection line instead of a result. Main loops over embedded sample indices and prints each result with Image-based text.
Ulam numbers.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic and array indexing with guards placed immediately before use, in a procedure so no loop variants are needed, but several loop-carried indexes and counters need careful guarding and the nested loops make the proof shape delicate. Larger sample indices (10000, 100000) only raise the fixed capacity, not the proof difficulty.

effects.explanation: The spiral rows are printed as text lines of dots and spaces, which also satisfies the terminal-filling demonstration.

risks.explanation: The closed-form cell number (L-1)**2 + D is nonlinear, so it is computed in an Integer type with small constant Size, where the bounded operands make overflow checks routine for the provers.

Proving the cell number lies in 1..Size*Size needs nonlinear reasoning, so the program guards the value before indexing the sieve and treats an out-of-range value as not prime, which is never reached.
Sieve marking of I*J relies on J being at most Max/I, so a guard before the store keeps the index within the array.

Ulam spiral (for primes).approach: Embed a fixed Size (for example 29) and compute a Boolean sieve array over 1..Size*Size using nested for loops, then for each row build a fixed-length String buffer by assigning a dot or space per cell, where the cell number comes from the closed-form spiral formula in a ranged subtype. Each finished row is emitted with Silver_IO.Put_Line, with explicit guards on the computed number before each array index. All loops are for loops over static ranges and everything sits in procedures or simple functions.
Ulam spiral (for primes).summary: Everything uses static bounds, for loops and a small fixed grid, so only the nonlinear spiral index formula and sieve index arithmetic need guard-shaped code, with no annotations required.

effects.explanation: Prints the first ten sequence elements on one line.

risks.explanation: Limb products and column sums are carried through loops, so limbs are subtypes of 0..65535 held in 64-bit integers and each partial sum is reduced by carry propagation within a bound that the types alone establish.

Schoolbook multiplication and folding reduction index limb positions i+j and shifted offsets, which discharge only if loops run over the arrays' own ranges and each computed index is guarded just before use.
The search for k and the Miller-Rabin square loop are while loops, so they are placed in procedures (no termination check) and bounded by a explicit cap on k that yields a visible failure outcome.

Reduction modulo 2^N - k uses folding (2^N is congruent to k) instead of long division, but the repeated fold count is a loop-carried quantity that needs a fixed iteration count rather than an invariant.

Ultra useful primes.approach: Represent numbers as fixed arrays of 16-bit limbs (64 limbs for the 1024-bit case, 128 for products) in 64-bit integers, and for each n from 1 to 10 search odd k upward, testing 2^(2^n) - k with a Miller-Rabin test using a few fixed small bases and modular exponentiation done by square-and-multiply with folding reduction. Control flow is for loops over array ranges inside procedures, with a capped k search and a printed failure message if the cap is hit, and the ten results are printed with Put and Integer'Image.
Ultra useful primes.summary: Everything is bounded fixed-capacity big-number arithmetic in procedures with limb types that bound all intermediate values, so no annotation is needed, but the multi-precision multiplication, folding reduction and fixed-base Miller-Rabin demand careful program shape for the provers.

effects.explanation: For each N from 3 to 6 the program prints the counts of ones and zeros from randN and from the unbiased generator.

risks.explanation: The count accumulators are loop-carried, so each increment needs a guard such as Count < Natural'Last; the guard's else branch can never run with 10_000 samples, so required behavior is unchanged.
The Von Neumann retry loop is a while loop with no variant, so it must sit in a procedure (Unbiased with an in out generator state and an out bit), where GNATprove performs no termination check.
Converting the modular LCG state to a bit uses mod N with N in a declared subtype 3 .. 6, so the result and the zero-divisor check follow from the types.

Unbias a random generator.approach: A modular 32-bit LCG state, passed in out, drives a procedure Rand_N that returns 1 when the scaled state mod N is zero (N in a subtype 3 .. 6), and a procedure Unbiased that draws pairs in a while loop until they differ and returns the first. Main runs a for loop over N in 3 .. 6 and an inner for loop over a fixed sample count, increments guarded Natural counters of ones for both generators, and prints the counts with 'Image.
Unbias a random generator.summary: Every check follows from modular wraparound, a ranged N and guarded counter increments, and the unbounded retry loop needs no variant because it lives in a procedure; it is plausible rather than likely only because the loop-carried counters need explicit guards.

conflicts.explanation: Exercising Ada's undefined-value mechanism means creating and reading a variable whose value is undefined (uninitialized or invalid) and testing it with 'Valid. SPARK's Bronze level (initialization and data flow), which the Oracle requires every program to pass, rejects any read of an uninitialized variable, so a variable with an undefined value can never be observed.

In Ada, reading an uninitialized scalar is a bounded error. Getting an invalid value that 'Valid can detect needs a configuration pragma (Normalize_Scalars or Initialize_Scalars), Unchecked_Conversion, or invalid external data. The task asks for this undefined state to be observed, so it requires observing an erroneous or bounded-error condition.

effects.explanation: Prints whether each variable is valid or undefined, and its value once it is assigned.

Undefined values.summary: The task asks a program to exercise the language's notion of an undefined value, which in Ada means reading uninitialized or invalid scalars and testing them with 'Valid. SPARK Bronze flow analysis rules out reading uninitialized data, and producing an invalid value needs a configuration pragma or unchecked conversion, so no Silver program can do this.

effects.explanation: Prints the lists, the 600th number, the count and the largest for bases 10 and 7.

risks.explanation: Building a d-digit number from digit pairs accumulates a loop-carried value, so the program guards each step against a declared 64-bit-safe maximum (sums stay below 10**17) and takes a visible stop path otherwise.
Counters for the running ordinal and the 1125 total are loop-carried, so they get types sized well above the true maximum and guards before each increment.
Output text buffers and result lists are fixed-capacity arrays, so each store is preceded by a capacity guard or indexed by a for-loop over the array's own range.
Base conversion to base 7 divides only by the constant 7 and loops a bounded number of times over a fixed digit array, so no zero divisor arises.

Undulating numbers.approach: For each base in {10, 7} and each digit count 3..16, nested for loops over a in 1..base-1 and b in 0..base-1 (skipping b = a) build the number from a table of powers of the base using guarded accumulation, in numeric order. The program prints the 3-digit and 4-digit lists, tests 3-digit values for primality by a for-loop of trial divisors up to 31, tracks the ordinal to capture the 600th, and counts and records the largest number below 2**53 (a constant 9007199254740992) in a Long_Long_Integer-sized range type. Numbers are formatted into bounded text buffers via a digit loop, and base-7 renderings come from a fixed-capacity digit array.
Undulating numbers.summary: Every number is generated by bounded for loops from a small set of digit pairs and fits in 64 bits, so checks follow from types and guards before additions, with only the loop-carried accumulation needing careful shape. No annotations, recursion or variants are required because everything is in procedures with for loops.

effects.explanation: Each test input and its unescaped result or an error message is printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: The scan index advances by 1, 2, 6 or 12 positions in a while loop with no invariant, so every Input(I+k) read and every Output write is preceded by an explicit bound guard (I+5 <= Input'Last, Out_Len + 4 <= Output'Last) with the failing case rejected as an error.

Hex accumulation and the surrogate-pair formula 16#10000# + ((H-16#D800#)*1024) + (L-16#DC00#) are nonlinear loop-carried arithmetic that discharges only if each hex digit is range-checked to 0..15 and the accumulator is a subtype 0..65535, which the program does by guarding each digit.

Character'Val conversions of UTF-8 bytes computed with div and mod by constants need the code point constrained to 0..16#10FFFF# and each byte to 0..255, which holds after the surrogate and control-character guards.
The while loop sits in a procedure so no termination check applies, and the index strictly increases on every path.
Output is a fixed-capacity buffer with a separate length, and capacity exhaustion is a specified error outcome rather than a silent truncation.

Unescape a string.approach: The program embeds the 14 test strings and calls one procedure per string that scans a String parameter in a while loop, writing decoded bytes into a fixed 128-byte output buffer and returning a length and an Ok flag. A case statement handles the eight two-character escapes, while \u escapes use a hex-digit helper with range-checked values, surrogate-pair combination, and a UTF-8 byte encoder using division and mod by constants. Every lookahead is guarded by an index bound and every invalid case (truncated, bad hex digit, lone or mismatched surrogate, unknown escape) sets Ok to False and prints a specific error message.
Unescape a string.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic and character handling in a procedure-based while loop, so each check can be discharged by explicit guards placed before each lookahead and by range-typed hex digits, with no annotation needed. The risk is the careful guard shape for index and arithmetic bounds across many loop-carried values.

effects.explanation: Each embedded test polynomial and its normalised form are printed as UTF-8 text.

risks.explanation: Rational coefficients with decimal scaling, exponent shifts, duplicate-term summation and fraction normalisation are loop-carried in 64-bit numerator/denominator pairs, so each step needs a guard just before the operation that rejects the input with a visible message when the limit would be exceeded.
Divisors from '/' and the fraction slash may be zero, and gcd reduction divides by a loop-carried value, so each is guarded by an explicit nonzero test with a rejection outcome.

The scan position into the compacted UTF-8 byte buffer and the exponent-indexed coefficient table are loop-carried, so every lookahead tests the position against the length and every exponent is range-checked before indexing, rejecting out-of-range exponents.

Multi-digit and signed exponents (including 007, scientific e-notation and negative superscripts) are accumulated in loops, so digit counts and magnitudes are capped by guards before each accumulation step.
All parsing and gcd loops are while loops, which is acceptable because they live in procedures and not in functions, so no variant is needed.

Unicode polynomial equation.approach: Embed the test polynomials as byte strings, strip spaces into a bounded buffer, and parse with a while-loop scanner over UTF-8 byte sequences (written with Character'Val codes) into terms holding a rational coefficient (Long_Long_Integer numerator and positive denominator) and an exponent. Accumulate terms into a fixed array of rational coefficients indexed by a bounded exponent range, then print nonzero terms from highest exponent down, mapping exponent digits to UTF-8 superscript bytes and reducing coefficients to mixed or vulgar fractions. Every arithmetic step is preceded by an overflow, range, zero-divisor or index guard that rejects the input with a printed message.
Unicode polynomial equation.summary: The task needs only bounded integer parsing, arrays and string building, but a hand-written rational parser with many loop-carried values needs careful guards at every arithmetic step, so discharge is plausible without annotations rather than routine.

effects.explanation: The program prints a short discussion of Unicode support and a few UTF-8 demonstration strings to standard output.

Unicode strings.approach: The program holds fixed String constants for the discussion text and for sample words in several scripts, with the non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes spelled as Character'Val values joined by bounded concatenation so the source stays plain ASCII. It prints each line with Silver_IO.Put_Line and uses a 'Length comparison to show that byte length differs from code point count, with no loops or input.
Unicode strings.summary: The task asks only for a discussion plus a demonstration, so a straight-line program of constant strings and Put_Line calls needs no loop-carried values, and every check follows from static string lengths.

effects.explanation: Prints the incremented value of the object whose identifier contains the Unicode delta character.

Unicode variable names.approach: Declare Δ : Integer range 1 .. 2 := 1, increment it with Δ := (Δ + 1) inside if Δ < 2 then, and print Integer'Image (Δ). Accompany the source with the admitted encoding and Unicode identifier documentation; the guard makes the increment fit its range under delivered scalar guard refinement.
Unicode variable names.summary: The bare-name/static-threshold increment fits the delivered scalar-guard-refinement fragment. Unicode identifiers are permitted by inherited Ada/SPARK but remain excluded by Silver ASCII source rules, so this task still requires explicit Unicode identifier support. No Unicode admission or task delivery is claimed.

review.setting_evidence: Selected setting; runtime model/effort not independently exposed
review.method: Static comparison with selected bare-name/static-threshold rules; Unicode admission remains excluded

effects.explanation: Prints the unique characters, separated by spaces, to standard output.

risks.explanation: The per-character counter is incremented in a loop with no invariant, so it is only incremented under a guard (count below 2) or its type is bounded, which keeps the 'exactly once' result unchanged because counts of 2 or more are all equivalent.

Unique characters.approach: Hold a constrained array of small-range counters indexed by Character, initialized to zero, and a procedure Count taking an unconstrained String that loops over its own 'Range and increments each character's counter only when it is below 2 (saturating). Call Count on the three embedded strings, then loop over every Character in order and Put the character and a space for each counter equal to 1, ending with a line terminator.
Unique characters.summary: Every index is a Character-typed array index or a for-loop index over a string's own range, and the only loop-carried value (the counter) is bounded by its type plus a saturating guard, so nothing needs an annotation. Silver mainly lacks arrays, Character indexing, procedures with String parameters, for loops and Put.

effects.explanation: Prints the characters unique in every string, space separated, on standard output.

risks.explanation: The per-character count is capped at 2 by a guard just before the increment, so the increment cannot overflow its small range subtype.
Counts are indexed by Character over an array whose index type is Character and the string is walked with for loops over its own 'Range, so every index check follows from types.

Unique characters in each string.approach: Embed the three strings as constants and keep a Count array indexed by Character with a small range subtype (0..2) per string, filled by a procedure that loops over the string's own 'Range and increments only when the count is below 2. Then loop over every Character in order (which is alphabetical order) and print it followed by a space when all three counts equal exactly 1. All loops are for loops and nothing is recursive or heap allocated.
Unique characters in each string.summary: Every check follows from the Character-indexed array type, a capped counter guarded just before the increment, and for loops over the arrays' own ranges, so no annotation is needed. The only missing pieces are arrays, Character indexing, for loops, procedures and unterminated character output.

effects.explanation: The test driver prints a PASS or FAIL line per test case, a summary, and a line stating that the testing support is external to the compiler.
The driver reports overall test failure through a nonzero process exit status, as unit-test runners conventionally do.

risks.explanation: The function under test multiplies values of a declared small range whose result subtype is sized for the maximum product, so the nonlinear multiplication is bounded by types alone.

Unit testing.approach: The program defines a small pure function over a declared integer range (for example squaring a bounded value) and a Check procedure that compares an actual result with an expected value, prints PASS or FAIL with the case name, and clears an in out Boolean All_Passed flag on failure. Main runs a straight-line sequence of embedded test cases, prints a summary plus a statement that Ada's unit testing support (such as AUnit) is external to the compiler, and sets a nonzero exit status if any case failed.
Unit testing.summary: A hand-written test driver needs only bounded integer arithmetic, Boolean flags, straight-line calls and if comparisons, with no loops or loop-carried values, so every check follows from declared ranges. Assertions and contracts are not needed because failures are detected by explicit comparisons with visible outcomes.

effects.explanation: The BLC program bits or bytes and its input are read from standard input.
The machine's output bits or bytes are written to standard output.
The -b flag selects bit mode over the default byte mode.

risks.explanation: Term-array, environment-node pool and stack indices are loop-carried and must each be guarded against the fixed capacity, with exhaustion producing a visible out-of-resources outcome.
The reduction loop and the parser loop run in procedures, which get no termination check, and a step budget makes non-halting BLC programs end visibly.
Fixed pools of nodes, term cells and stack must be fully initialized before use, which is routine with aggregate initialization but sizeable.
Reference counts and bit accumulators are bounded by pool capacity or masked into small ranged types so guards suffice.

The existing design uses heap cells and a reference-count free list, so the program must replace them with index-based array pools and an explicit capacity limit, and stack or heap exhaustion becomes a specified rejection.

Universal Lambda Machine.approach: Read the input into a bounded buffer, parse the BLC term into a fixed-capacity array of tagged term cells (lambda, application, variable index) via an explicit stack in a while loop inside a procedure, and evaluate it with a call-by-need environment machine whose closures and environments are index-based records in fixed pools. The evaluator loop runs in a procedure with a step budget and capacity guards before every pool or stack access, and the output list of bits or bytes is decoded and written as it is produced, rejecting visibly on exhaustion or malformed input.
Universal Lambda Machine.summary: The interpreter needs only bounded arrays, records and procedure loops with explicit capacity guards, so no annotation is needed, but the many loop-carried pool indices and the pointer-to-index redesign make careful program shape necessary. Non-halting or oversized programs end through a specified resource-limit outcome rather than a hidden failure.

effects.explanation: Prints the final tape and head marker for the incrementer and the three-state busy beaver with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The head position is loop-carried, so each move is guarded (left only when head is above 1, right only when below the tape capacity) and an off-tape move halts with a visible 'tape limit' outcome.
The step counter is incremented only inside a loop condition that tests it against a declared maximum, so the increment cannot overflow.

Universal Turing machine.approach: A generic-free procedure Run takes a rules table (2-D array indexed by ranged state and symbol subtypes, each entry a record of new state, movement enum and new symbol) plus a fixed-capacity tape array of ranged symbols with a start head position and a step limit. A while loop in a procedure steps until the halt state, with guards on step count and head bounds that end the run with a printed outcome (halted, step limit, or tape limit); the final tape is rendered into a bounded String via a symbol-to-Character map and printed with a caret line. The incrementer and busy beaver are embedded as constant rule tables and run in sequence; the 47-million-step bonus machine is left out as optional.
Universal Turing machine.summary: All indexes and values come from ranged types and bounded tapes with explicit guards before each head move, and the loops live in procedures so no termination check or variant is needed. The only care needed is the guarded head and step counters, which need no annotations.

effects.explanation: Lists the entries of the current directory.
Prints the sorted entry names, one per line.

Unix/ls.summary: The program lists the current directory and prints the names sorted. That needs an admitted directory-listing operation with specified failure outcomes, plus a bounded sort over fixed-capacity name storage, so no Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: Prints the top card, the human player's visible hand, bot actions, uno calls, penalties and scores as text.
The human player reads a menu choice per turn, plus color declarations and challenge decisions, as lines from standard input.

risks.explanation: Deck top, discard count and each hand count are loop-carried across turns, so every draw, play and removal is guarded by an explicit count and range test (reshuffling the discard pile when the deck is empty) before indexing fixed 108-card arrays.

Scores, hand counts and the deterministic shuffle generator use bounded ranged types with a small multiplier and mod, and score sums are capped by the 500-point game end, so each addition is range-guarded.
Parsed human menu input is validated against the current hand size and invalid input gets a visible re-prompt, so no unchecked index reaches an array.
The turn and round loops are while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, so none is required, though a turn cap may be needed to bound play.
The deck, hands and discard arrays must be fully initialized by loops before use, which flow analysis can miss for partially filled arrays unless whole-array aggregates are used first.

Uno (card game).approach: The program uses a record per card (color and kind enumerations), a 108-card deck array, a 4-by-108 hand array with per-player counts, and a linear-congruential shuffle with fixed bounds. A procedure-based round loop deals seven cards, handles skip, reverse, draw-two, wild and wild-draw-four effects, uno calls, the draw-four challenge penalty and reshuffling, with the human choosing from validated stdin lines and the bots using a fixed deterministic policy. Rounds repeat, scoring the remaining hands, until a player reaches 500 points.
Uno (card game).summary: Nothing requires an annotation because all state lives in bounded arrays and ranged counters guarded before each use and all loops are while loops inside procedures, but the large amount of loop-carried game state means careful guard placement is needed.

effects.explanation: Prints a title line, the first 35 unprimeable numbers on one line, and the 600th.

risks.explanation: Digit replacement computes N - digit*place + d*place on a subtype bounded to 0..9999, with the place restricted to 1, 10, 100 or 1000 and at most N, so the result stays within 0..9999 by type ranges and a guard.
The array of 600 results is indexed by a count that is guarded to be below 600 before each store, which is needed because the count is loop-carried and has no invariant.
Primality uses a for loop over divisors 2..99 (since 99*99 exceeds 9999) inside a function, so no variant is needed, and the outer search is a for loop over 1..9999.

Unprimeable numbers.approach: Declare a subtype Num 0..9999, a function Is_Prime using a for loop over divisors 2..99, and a procedure that, for each N in 2..9999, tries replacing each decimal digit at places 1, 10, 100, 1000 (only those not exceeding N) with 0..9 and records N in a 600-element array when no variant is prime, guarding the count before each store. The main body then prints a title, the first 35 entries with Put, and the 600th entry via 'Image; the search limit 9999 covers the 600th value 5242, and a visible message is printed if fewer than 600 were found. The optional per-last-digit minima are omitted because some exceed 1,000,000 and would need a much larger bound.
Unprimeable numbers.summary: Every check follows from small bounded subtypes, for-loop-only primality testing in a function, and a count guard before array stores, so no annotations are needed. The nonlinear digit arithmetic is bounded by subtypes and the place guard, making discharge likely.

effects.explanation: The grid of untouchable numbers up to 2000 and the counts are printed to standard output.

risks.explanation: Each aliquot-sum accumulator element is loop-carried through the nested sieve, so the program saturates it at a cap just above 2000 (which cannot change any result since only sums up to 2000 matter) so the addition is guarded and provably in range.
The multiple index i*k is nonlinear, so the loop runs k over 2 .. Limit/i and the bound i*k <= Limit must be dischargeable by the provers from that range, with a guard before indexing as fallback.

A sieve bound of about 4 million (sufficient since any aliquot sum v needs n <= v*v) makes a large static array and a harmonic-sum loop count that only terminates trivially because for loops are used, so counts beyond 1000 or 2000 must be dropped as impractical.
All loops are for loops or while loops inside procedures, so no variant is needed.

Untouchable numbers.approach: Keep a constrained Boolean array Touched over 1..2000 and a sieve array of saturating aliquot sums over 1..4,000,000, built with nested for loops (for each i, for k in 2 .. Limit/i add i to the sum at i*k, capped at 2001). Then mark Touched(sum) for every n whose capped sum is at most 2000, and print the untouchable numbers in a 16-column grid using integer-to-text into a bounded buffer, followed by the total count and the counts up to 10, 100 and 1000 computed with a running counter in a single for loop.
Untouchable numbers.summary: Every check follows from fixed array bounds, for-loop indexes and a saturating cap on the accumulator, so only the nonlinear index i*k and the large sieve size need careful shaping; no annotation is needed, but counts at 10,000 and above are impractical and are treated as optional.

effects.explanation: The untrusted input being demonstrated is the first command-line argument.
The program reports whether the input was accepted, and echoes it only if accepted.
Rejected input ends with the specified failure outcome through Silver_Arguments.Reject.

Untrusted environment.approach: Main reads the first argument with First_Or_Default, rejects it through Input_Is_Valid and Reject when malformed, and rejects it when its 'Length is outside a documented limit. A for loop over the argument's own index range sets a Boolean flag if any character falls outside an allowed set (letters, digits, space), tested with plain character comparisons. Only input that passes every check is echoed with Put_Line, and anything else gets a visible rejection message. The prose explanation covers what the Oracle guarantees: no eval or dynamic code, no exceptions, no unchecked conversions, external effects only through admitted operations, and every check proven.
Untrusted environment.summary: The demonstration only validates a bounded argument: it checks lengths against literals and indexes characters in a for loop over the string's own range, so every check comes from static bounds and guards. "Untrusted code" needs no program construct, because Silver has no way to evaluate code at run time and the prose explanation says so.

effects.explanation: Each of the ten embedded scans prints its decoded 12-digit number, a reversed marker, or an invalid message.

risks.explanation: The checksum accumulator is kept in a 0..9 subtype by taking mod 10 after each weighted add, so the loop-carried addition cannot overflow without an invariant.
Slice bounds are computed from the for-loop variable over fixed 1..6 ranges on constrained 95-character strings, so each start and end index is statically within 1..95.
Digit characters come from a lookup that returns a value in 0..9 or a not-found flag, with the guard tested just before the Character'Val conversion.

UPC.approach: Embed the ten 95-character scans as constants in an array of constrained Strings, and hold the left and right 7-character digit patterns in constant arrays indexed by a 0..9 subtype. A procedure Decode checks the start, middle and end markers, then loops over the 12 digits taking fixed-offset 7-character slices and matching each against the pattern table with an inner for loop, setting a found flag. If any marker or digit fails it retries once on a reversed copy built with a for loop; otherwise it applies the mod-10 checksum, and prints the result, a reversed note, or an invalid message with the line number.
UPC.summary: Every index is fixed-offset on constrained 95-character strings inside for loops, the checksum accumulator is bounded by mod 10, and no recursion, while loop or variant is needed, so all checks follow from types and static bounds.

effects.explanation: The embedded sample file is rewritten in memory and the revised file is printed line by line with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Scanning for the option word, trimming whitespace and copying parameter text use loop-carried positions, so each access sits behind an explicit bounds guard or a for loop over the buffer's own range.
Output lines are built in fixed-capacity buffers with a length counter, so every append is guarded by a capacity check that rejects over-long lines visibly rather than truncating.
Line counts and buffer lengths are declared ranged subtypes with a capped line count, and the forced values 1024 and 62000 are constants, so counters cannot exceed their ranges.
All loops run in a procedure, using for loops or while loops over bounded positions, so no variant is needed.

Update a configuration file.approach: The sample file is embedded as a fixed-capacity array of line records (a bounded character buffer plus a length), and one procedure walks the lines, passing lines that start with a hash through unchanged. For other lines it strips semicolons and whitespace and drops control or non-ASCII characters, upper-cases the option word, and compares it with the four known options, keeping only the first occurrence of each. It emits the updated entry (NEEDSPEELING disabled with a semicolon, SEEDSREMOVED enabled, bananas 1024), appends any missing entry such as NUMBEROFSTRAWBERRIES 62000, and prints the result with Put_Line.
Update a configuration file.summary: The task only needs bounded line buffers, character scanning and Put_Line output over embedded data, and every index and length check can be guarded in procedures with bounded loops, but many loop-carried positions make careful guard placement necessary.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 50 numbers and the 500th and 5000th upside-down numbers as text lines.

risks.explanation: Loop-carried remainders and digit choices (k, count, digit in 1..9) lose bounds after the first iteration, so each is clamped by a guard that rejects out-of-range values visibly, or avoided by an odometer over fixed Digit-typed arrays.
Dividing by a loop-carried block count needs a guard that the count is nonzero immediately before the division.
Building the output line in a bounded buffer needs a guard on the write position before each character is stored.
Values up to 56546545 fit in Integer, but the accumulated value in a loop needs a type range or guard to bound it.

Upside-down numbers.approach: Treat the 1st, 2nd, ... Nth number as a selection by length (counts 1, 9, 9, 81, ... up to 8 digits, covering 5000) and then fill an array of at most 8 digits (subtype 1..9) pair by pair, with the mirror digit 10 - d placed at the opposite end and a 5 in the centre of odd lengths. A procedure takes N (guarded to 1..8200 with a visible reject otherwise) and returns the digit array and length; a second procedure copies the digits into a bounded String buffer for Put_Line. The main program loops 1..50 building one comma-separated line, then prints the 500th and 5000th; the stretch targets (millions, 14 digits) are optional and are omitted.
Upside-down numbers.summary: Every check follows from small fixed bounds and digit subtypes, but loop-carried block counts, quotients and string buffer positions each need a guard placed just before use, so discharge depends on careful program shape rather than being routine. No annotation is needed since the work is done in procedures with for loops.

effects.explanation: Each decoded test string is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The write index into the bounded output buffer is loop-carried, so a guard before each store rejects input that would exceed the buffer capacity, and a guard that Position+2 does not pass the last index precedes reading the two hex digits.
Position and Filled are declared as ranged subtypes with spare headroom and guarded before each increment, so Position+3 and Filled+1 cannot overflow.
Hex digits are converted by explicit comparisons to values 0..15 so Hi*16+Lo lies in 0..255 and Character'Val cannot fail, with a non-hex digit giving a visible reject outcome.
The while loop sits in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and Position strictly advances on every branch.

URL decoding.approach: A procedure Decode takes an input String and fills a fixed-capacity output String buffer plus a ranged length, scanning with a while loop that maps '+' to space, '%XX' to the byte from two hex digits, and anything else to itself. Guards reject truncated or non-hex escapes and buffer overflow with a visible reject message, and the three test strings are embedded constants whose decoded results (including the UTF-8 bytes for 'á' and the %25%32%35 to %25 case with a single pass) are printed with Put_Line.
URL decoding.summary: All checks come from ranged subtypes and guards placed just before each index or conversion, and the loop is in a procedure so no variant is needed; the loop-carried indices need careful guarding, hence plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: Prints the encoded example string with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Output buffer writes are guarded by a capacity check before each append (each input character adds at most 3), and the for loop indexes the input over its own range.
The Character'Pos value (0..255) is split into two hex digits by /16 and mod 16 on a bounded subtype, so the digit lookup index is statically within a 16-entry constant table.

URL encoding.approach: A procedure encodes an embedded constant input string such as "http://foo bar/" into a fixed-capacity Character buffer with a length counter, using a for loop over the input's own range. Each character is classified by comparisons (0-9, A-Z, a-z are copied; all others become '%' plus two digits from a constant hex-digit string indexed by Pos/16 and Pos mod 16). A capacity guard before each append rejects input that would overflow the buffer, and the main program prints the result with Put_Line.
URL encoding.summary: Everything is a single for loop over a fixed-length string with bounded byte arithmetic and a capacity guard before each append, so all checks follow from types and guards without any invariant. The only care is keeping the output length counter's growth safe, which the pre-append guard handles.

effects.explanation: Each embedded URL and its parsed components or an error diagnostic are printed line by line.

risks.explanation: Component boundaries are found by for loops recording delimiter positions in loop-carried variables, so each slice is guarded with explicit start and end comparisons against the string's bounds just before use.
Position variables use a bounded Natural subtype and the input length is rejected above a documented limit (for example 256), so index arithmetic like pos + 1 cannot overflow.
Printed output is built from slices with guarded bounds, and any concatenation is limited by the length cap, so no length check can fail.

URL parser.approach: Embed the task's test URLs as string literals and pass each to a procedure that rejects input longer than a fixed cap or lacking a valid scheme (letters then ':'), printing a specific diagnostic. It scans with for loops over URL'Range to record the first positions of ':', "//", '@', '/', '?' and '#' in bounded Natural variables, then derives scheme, userinfo, domain, port, path, query and fragment as guarded slices and prints each non-empty one with Put_Line, treating bracketed IPv6 hosts as a single domain.
URL parser.summary: Every check is an index or range check on slice bounds from loop-found positions, which can each be protected by explicit guards before use, and there are no while loops, recursion or floating point, so no annotation is needed. Discharge depends on careful guard placement across many loop-carried positions, hence plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The task requires an HTTP API: a POST / endpoint that accepts JSON and returns a short URL, and a GET /:short endpoint that redirects to the original URL.
A server-less form of the task would print the short URL and the redirect target as text.

URL shortener.summary: The task is an HTTP service with a POST endpoint that shortens a URL and a GET endpoint that redirects, so it needs network access, which Silver lacks today. The rest is in-memory bounded string and array handling with a deterministic key generator, which fits Silver once admitted library operations for bounded strings, tables and networking exist. No Oracle rule is broken.

effects.explanation: The task requires HTTP GET and POST requests to the Meetup.com REST API.
The API key is read from api_key.txt.
Responses and failure outcomes are printed as text.

Use a REST API.summary: The task needs generic get and post functions over HTTP, with the API key read from a file. That requires a network effect that Silver lacks today, plus files and console output, and nothing in it breaks a fixed Oracle rule. A bounded-string solution can handle the details and URL, validate the response, and report failures through specified outcomes.

conflicts.explanation: The task requires a Query function that a C program links against and calls. The function must use C convention and be exported (Export/Convention C) and take a raw char* buffer and a size_t* by pointer. That is foreign-language interop with unchecked C pointers, and the C caller, which is outside SPARK, controls the buffer's real size and aliasing. A program limited to SPARK's own checks could not prove it free of run-time errors.

effects.explanation: The Silver code has to be linked into a foreign C program and called from it through a C ABI entry point. The C main does the printing.

Use another language to call a function.summary: Excluded: the task's whole point is to export a C-convention Query function that writes through a raw char* and a size_t* passed in by a C main program. That needs foreign-language interop and unchecked pointer access, which the Oracle's rules (no foreign-language calls, no unrestricted aliasing) rule out for good.

effects.explanation: The program prints its demonstration and explanation lines with Silver_IO.Put_Line.

Useless instructions.approach: The program names a redundant built-in (elsif, which nested else-if statements make redundant) and demonstrates it with a String constant selector classified once by an if/elsif chain and once by nested if/else, printing both results and a line stating they are identical. Everything uses existing Silver constructs (String constants, equality tests, if/elsif/else, Put_Line), with no loops, arithmetic or input.
Useless instructions.summary: The task only asks to showcase a redundant language feature, which fits entirely inside today's Silver surface with no loops or arithmetic, so every check is trivial and nothing needs an annotation.

effects.explanation: The program prints the Pioneer line to standard output.
tee writes ALGOL_pioneers.lst and the_important_scientists.lst as named files.

risks.explanation: Substring matching for grep slices a fixed-width line at a computed offset, which is discharged by a for loop bounded by the pattern and line lengths so every slice stays in range.

Head, tail, uniq and sort insert into fixed-capacity record arrays with loop-carried counts, which are discharged by count subtypes bounded by the capacity and an explicit capacity guard before each append.
All loops live in procedures or are for loops, and the pipeline stages are procedures with no recursion, so no variant is needed.

User defined pipe and redirection operat.approach: The 22 scientist records are embedded as a constant array of fixed-width lines held in a record with a length, and each filter (head, tail, grep, sort, uniq, tee) is a procedure moving records between fixed-capacity bounded stream buffers, with the Unix operators replaced by the alternate procedure names since Ada cannot overload the pipe symbol. Records are passed on one at a time where the filter allows and sort buffers only as sort inherently requires, with explicit capacity guards that reject overflow visibly. Tee writes the two named files and the final grep on 'aa' prints the Pioneer line.
User defined pipe and redirection operat.summary: Every check follows from fixed array bounds, for-loop indexes and capacity guards, and no recursion or annotation is needed, though the loop-carried buffer counts and substring search need careful shape. Needing file output is an effect Silver lacks today, not a conflict.

effects.explanation: The task requires taking a string and an integer from a graphical user interface, so a window with text entry widgets and an event loop is needed.

User input/Graphical.summary: The task asks for a string and the integer 75000 to be entered through a graphical user interface, so the GUI is an effect Silver lacks, not a conflict. Nothing in the wording requires exceptions, assertions, or other fixed-rule violations; the GtkAda solution's exception handler and callbacks are incidental to how it was written. A Silver-friendly version would validate integer text with explicit character loops and a specified rejection outcome for invalid input, so the features are integers, characters, string operations and loops.

effects.explanation: The program must read a string and the integer 75000 from the text console.
Prompts and the echoed string and integer are written to the console.

risks.explanation: Parsing the integer line is discharged by an admitted validating parse operation that reports failure, and invalid input is rejected visibly rather than raising Constraint_Error.
Input lines longer than the fixed buffer are rejected or reported by the admitted line-reading operation, so the bounded string never overflows.

User input/Text.approach: A procedure Main prints a prompt with Put, reads one line into a fixed-capacity bounded buffer through an admitted stdin line operation that returns a status, then prompts again and reads a second line which it parses into a bounded Integer subtype through a validating parse operation. On any read or parse failure it prints a specified rejection message and stops, otherwise it echoes the string and the number (75000 is just a valid input) with Put_Line using the integer-to-text conversion.
User input/Text.summary: The task is plain console input of a string and an integer, and with an admitted bounded line reader and validating integer parser every check is a type or guard, so no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: The text is displayed, and each word is printed as it is spoken. The task allows this when highlighting is not possible.
The task requires spoken audio output from a speech engine.
Producing speech means invoking an external speech engine or command, as the existing solution does with a shell command.
Each word's output has to be paced to match its speech, either by waiting for the speech engine to finish that word or by sleeping.

Using a speech engine to highlight words.summary: The task needs a fixed text split into words, each word printed (the permitted fallback to cursor highlighting) and then spoken through an external speech engine. That requires sound and process effects Silver lacks today, but no Oracle rule is broken. Word splitting can use bounded strings and iteration.

effects.explanation: Prints a table of characters, code points and UTF-8 hex bytes, plus decode results.
