The write cursor into the 11-letter message and the placed-word count are loop-carried and are each guarded by an explicit test against their capacity before use.
The retry and placement loops are while loops in procedures, which get no termination check, and each is also bounded by an explicit attempt counter so the program ends with a specified outcome.

Packing at least 25 words and leaving exactly 11 free cells depends on the deterministic search succeeding, so the program must reject or report failure in a visible way after its attempt budget is spent rather than shrinking the requirements.

Word search.approach: The program embeds about 40 lowercase words of 3 to 9 letters taken from unixdict as records holding a fixed buffer and a length, keeps the grid as a 10 by 10 Character array, and draws positions and directions from a deterministic modular pseudo-random generator. A procedure with bounded while loops tries random start, direction and word candidates, tests that the word fits and agrees with the cells it crosses before writing, and records each placement; once 25 or more words are placed and exactly 11 cells are empty, a for loop fills them with ROSETTACODE in row-major order. It then prints the grid and the word list with coordinates, and prints a failure message if the attempt budget runs out.
Word search.summary: Every access is a bounded grid cell or fixed-capacity buffer slot that can be guarded just before use, and no recursion, heap or annotation is needed. The risk is the nonlinear generator and the loop-carried placement cursors, so careful guard placement is needed but no invariant.

effects.explanation: The dictionary unixdict.txt must be read line by line from a named file.
Each matching word is printed on its own line.

risks.explanation: Letter counts are indexed by Character'Pos minus 'a', which is discharged by a guard that the character lies in 'a'..'z' before each use, with non-lowercase words treated as non-matches.
The per-letter available count is a subtype 0..9 and is decremented only after a guard that it is greater than zero, so the loop-carried counts stay in type range.

Dictionary lines are read into a fixed bounded buffer with a reported length, and lines longer than the buffer are rejected as non-matches since they exceed nine letters, so no truncation changes a result.
The counts array is rebuilt from the wheel string for every word by a full for loop over the array's own range, and the file-open failure has a specified rejection outcome.

Word wheel.approach: Embed the wheel string as a constant and, for each dictionary line read into a bounded 64-character buffer by a while loop in the Main procedure, reset a 26-entry array of letter counts from the wheel. A for loop over the word's characters decrements counts under explicit guards (lowercase letter, count above zero), tracks whether the central letter k was seen, and prints the word via a slice of the buffer if it has 3 to 9 letters, all consumed, and contains k. A missing or unreadable file produces a specified rejection message; the optional nine-letter grid search is omitted.
Word wheel.summary: Every check follows from small array bounds, a 0..9 count subtype and guards placed immediately before each decrement or index, and the while loop is in a procedure so there is no termination obligation; the only new needs are line-by-line file reading and character-indexed arrays.

effects.explanation: Wrapped lines of the embedded sample paragraph are printed with Silver_IO.Put_Line at two wrap columns.

risks.explanation: Word-scanning indices are loop-carried in while loops, so each Text(I) access and each Text(Start .. Stop) slice is preceded by an explicit guard such as I <= Text'Last and Start <= Stop.
Index and line-length arithmetic stays within Natural bounds because the text is a fixed-size constant and the width parameter is a small ranged subtype, though loop-carried sums need guards.
The scanning loops live in a procedure, which gets no termination check, and each iteration advances an index.
A word longer than the wrap width is placed alone on its own over-long line, which is the specified visible outcome rather than a truncation or error.

Word wrap.approach: Embed the task paragraph as a String constant and write one procedure Wrap(Text, Width) that implements the greedy algorithm by index arithmetic: skip spaces, find the end of the next word, and either extend the current line or print the slice Text(Line_Start .. Line_End) and start a new line. Main calls it at two widths (for example 72 and 40), with guards before every index or slice and an over-long word emitted alone on its line; no line buffer or Unbounded strings are needed. The Knuth-Plass extra credit is omitted and stdin reading is not required.
Word wrap.summary: The greedy wrap is plain index scanning over a constant string inside a procedure with while loops, so checks follow from guards before each index and slice, but several loop-carried indices need careful guard placement without invariants. No annotation-only facts, recursion or heap are needed, so discharge is plausible rather than certain.

effects.explanation: Prompts, the first word and the loss message are written to the console.
Player names and each turn's word are read as lines from standard input.

risks.explanation: Comparing words character by character across lengths differing by one needs every index guarded by a length test just before use, which is expressible with explicit guards.
Input lines and names are copied into fixed-capacity buffers with a stored length, and over-long or empty lines are rejected with a visible message.
The deterministic generator is seeded from a constant and reduced with mod by the dictionary size so the chosen index stays in range.
The turn loop is a while loop inside a procedure and the scans are for loops, so no variant is needed.

Wordiff.approach: The dictionary is an embedded constant array of bounded word records (a character buffer plus length) holding a modest word list, with a fixed-capacity history array of used words and two player-name buffers. A procedure reads names and then loops per turn: read a line, validate length and characters, check dictionary membership and history by for-loop scans, and check one-edit difference (substitution, insertion or deletion) with index-guarded comparisons. Any failed check ends the game with a printed outcome naming the losing player, and the initial 3 or 4 letter word is picked using a small deterministic generator reduced by mod.
Wordiff.summary: Every check follows from fixed-capacity buffers, for-loop scans and length guards placed before indexing, and the game loop lives in a procedure so no termination annotation is needed; the main work is careful guarding of the one-edit comparison and the bounded history. The timing stretch goals are optional and omitted, and the embedded dictionary replaces file reading.

effects.explanation: Prints each answer/guess pair and its per-letter green, yellow or grey marking.

Wordle comparison.approach: Define a constrained subtype Word as String (1 .. 5) and a Color enumeration (Grey, Yellow, Green), then a procedure Score that takes answer and guess Words and fills an out array of Color plus a local array of Boolean flagging answer letters already consumed. Pass one marks greens with a for loop over the shared index range, and pass two uses a nested for loop over answer positions to mark each remaining guess letter yellow against the first unused equal answer letter, otherwise grey. Main embeds the ALLOW/LOLLY test and a few further 5-letter pairs as constants and prints each result with Put and a case statement per letter.
Wordle comparison.summary: Every index is a for-loop variable over the arrays' own constrained range and the loops carry only Boolean flags and enumeration values, so all checks follow from types and no invariant or variant is needed. The fixed 5-letter bound is a documented resource limit and the task's same-length assumption is met by the Word subtype.

effects.explanation: Reads the dictionary file unixdict.txt line by line, with a specified outcome when it cannot be opened.
Prints each found word and a final count to standard output.

risks.explanation: The substring scan indexes Line(I..I+2) only for I in 1 .. Len-2 after a guard Len > 11, so bounds follow from the loop range and the admitted line reader's Length postcondition.
The found-word counter is incremented only under an explicit guard against its declared capacity, with an overflow outcome of stopping and reporting rather than wrapping.
Lines longer than the fixed 40-character buffer are reported by the library reader as a specified outcome (reject or truncate-flag) and handled by an explicit branch rather than silently dropped.

Words containing \"the\" substring.approach: A procedure opens unixdict.txt via an admitted file-reading library, reads each line into a bounded 40-character buffer with a returned length in a while loop, and an explicit failure branch handles an unopenable file or over-long line. For each line with length above 11, a for loop over start positions 1 .. Length-2 compares three characters to 't','h','e'; matches are printed with Put_Line and counted in a range-guarded Natural counter, and a final count line is printed.
Words containing \"the\" substring.summary: Every check is a loop-index or guard-based bound on a small fixed buffer and the while loop sits in a procedure, so no annotation is needed; the only new ingredients are bounded line reading from a file and character indexing.

effects.explanation: Reads the dictionary file unixdict.txt line by line, with a specified outcome if it is missing or unreadable.
Prints each matching nine-letter word on its own line.

risks.explanation: Word storage and the n+k-1 row lookups are safe only because the loop bound is Count-8 and a guard rejects the file when more than the fixed capacity of words arrives, which is a visible outcome.
Each line is read into a bounded buffer with an explicit length guard, and over-long lines are rejected visibly rather than truncated.
The word counter and output counter are typed ranges bounded by the capacity, with a guard before every increment, so no loop-carried value needs an invariant.
The line-reading and lookup loops are while loops inside procedures (no termination check), and the lookup is a for loop over the fixed word table.
The word table and result list must be fully initialized by aggregate or loop before reads, which is routine but costs a nested initialization loop that flow analysis must accept.

Words from neighbour ones.approach: Read unixdict.txt in a procedure with a bounded line buffer, keeping only words of length 9 or more as a 2D Character table of their first nine characters plus a flag for exactly nine, rejecting input beyond the fixed capacity. For each n up to Count-8, build the nine-character diagonal word by indexing row n+k-1 column k, then scan the table for an exact length-9 match using a for loop, skipping repeats of the previously printed word, and print matches with Put_Line.
Words from neighbour ones.summary: Every check follows from fixed-capacity typed ranges, for-loop indexes over the table and guards before use, with all while loops in procedures, but file reading, bounded line handling and the 2D table add shape-dependent work. No annotation is needed, so it is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The histogram table of counts per place and points is printed line by line.

risks.explanation: Per-team point sums and histogram counts are loop-carried, so each increment is preceded by a guard (for example the value is below a cap) that cannot trigger for real inputs but must be written visibly.
Indexing the count table by a team's total points needs the total bounded to 0..9 or the table sized to the type's range, since no invariant can state the true maximum of 9.
Decoding the outcome number into base-3 digits with div and mod must stay within 0..2 per game, which follows from mod 3 on a bounded non-negative loop index.
Formatting counts into fixed-width columns needs bounded string building with padding computed from digit counts.

World Cup group stage.approach: A for loop over outcome numbers 0..728 decodes six base-3 digits into win/draw/loss per game and adds 3/1/0 points to four team totals held in a small array, with guarded increments. The four totals are sorted by a fixed bubble-sort procedure with for loops, then a 4x10 count array indexed by place and points is incremented. Finally a procedure prints a header and four rows, formatting each count to a fixed width using bounded string building.
World Cup group stage.summary: All loops are for loops over fixed ranges inside procedures, so termination is free and the checks reduce to guarded accumulator increments and bounded array indexes. The nonroutine parts are loop-carried sums and counts plus text formatting, which need careful shape but no annotations.

effects.explanation: The table is printed as text lines to standard output.

risks.explanation: The product of frequency, shaved seconds and five years reaches about 8e9, so it is computed in a declared 64-bit range type whose constant array elements bound every operand.
Each cell is built in a fixed 13-character buffer with a padding procedure that guards the number's digit count before copying, so no slice can exceed the buffer.

Worthwhile task shaving.approach: Constant arrays hold the nine shaved-seconds values, the six per-five-year frequencies (using integer 365-day-year constants) and the unit labels; a nested for loop over the array index ranges computes t and picks a unit via an if/elsif chain with constant divisors. Each cell is formatted into a fixed 13-character buffer by a procedure using 'Image of a small bounded count plus pluralised unit text, and rows are emitted with Put and Put_Line. Blank cells are emitted as spaces for the over-a-year cases.
Worthwhile task shaving.summary: Every operand is bounded by constant tables and a wide declared integer range, loops are for loops over array ranges, and output is plain text, so all checks follow from types and static bounds. The only care needed is the 64-bit product range and fixed-width cell buffer lengths.

effects.explanation: The program must create or overwrite a named file so that it contains a string.
A rejection or failure message is printed when the file cannot be written.
A write failure should be reported through a nonzero exit status.

Write entire file.approach: Main holds a fixed file name constant and an embedded String constant (the task text), then calls an admitted library procedure that overwrites the file with that string and reports a success flag. An if statement on the flag prints a visible failure message and sets a nonzero exit status when the write fails, so no exception handler is needed.
Write entire file.summary: The task is a single library call with constant data and no loops or arithmetic, so every check is trivial and the only missing piece is an admitted file-writing operation with specified failure outcomes. The Ada solution's exception handler for Name_Error is replaced by the library's status result.

effects.explanation: The program creates and writes the two-column text file, and a failure to create or write it needs a specified outcome.
The output file name is taken from the first command-line argument, with Input_Is_Valid and Reject for a missing or unusable name.
A short status or rejection message is printed with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: Sqrt needs a non-negative operand and results must stay finite, which the program discharges by declaring a constrained non-negative float subtype for x (1.0e11 is far below the overflow bound) and guarding before each call.
Precision values 3 and 5 must be valid digit counts for the admitted float formatter, which constrained integer subtypes for the precisions discharge.
Each formatted line must fit a fixed-size bounded buffer, which is sized for the two formatted columns (about 40 characters) and checked against the formatter's specified maximum length.
Scientific notation such as 1e+011 for large values depends on a specified admitted float-to-text operation with precision and exponent behavior, which Silver does not yet provide.

Write float arrays to a text file.approach: The program holds x and y as constrained four-element arrays of a non-negative float subtype, with x embedded as an aggregate and y filled by a for loop that calls an elementary-function Sqrt after the range is established by the subtype. A procedure opens the file named by the first argument (rejecting a missing or unusable name), then for each index formats x with 3 digits and y with 5 through an admitted float-image operation into a bounded buffer and writes the line through an admitted file-output operation. All control flow is for loops over the array's own range inside procedures, with explicit visible outcomes for open or write failure.
Write float arrays to a text file.summary: Everything is a fixed-size loop over constrained arrays, so index and initialization checks are routine, and the only non-routine parts are float range guards for Sqrt and the specified contracts of admitted float-formatting and file-writing operations, none of which need an annotation.

effects.explanation: Prints the nine lines of 3D ASCII art of the language name to standard output.

Write language name in 3D ASCII.approach: The program embeds the nine pre-indented lines of the slanted-shadow "Ada" banner as String literals and emits each with Silver_IO.Put_Line in a straight statement sequence. There are no loops, variables, arithmetic or inputs, so no guards are needed; backslashes are ordinary characters in Ada string literals.
Write language name in 3D ASCII.summary: The task is fixed text output, which today's Silver (String literals and Put_Line) already expresses, and there are no run-time checks to prove.

effects.explanation: Writing a status entry to the Windows Event Log is a Windows operating-system service; Silver has no admitted library operation for it.

Write to Windows event log.summary: The task only asks to write a script status to the Windows Event Log. That needs an OS-service effect Silver lacks today. It does not break any fixed Oracle rule, because an admitted library operation could specify the call and its failure outcomes.

effects.explanation: The anti-aliased pixel grid is written as text art (grayscale characters) with Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The gradient and intersection y are held as fixed-point integers (scaled by 256) within a small canvas, so every product and sum is bounded by the declared ranges.
Each plotted y and y+1 is guarded against the canvas bounds before the array write, and out-of-canvas pixels are skipped as a visible specified outcome.
The gradient division by dx is guarded by a dx = 0 branch that plots the single point.
Loop-carried intersection y has no invariant, so it is typed with a wide fixed-point subtype and clamped by guards before conversion to a row index.

Xiaolin Wu's line algorithm.approach: Use a constant-size 2D array of intensity values 0..255 as a canvas, with line endpoints embedded as constants in a bounded coordinate range. Implement Wu's algorithm in integer fixed-point (scaled by 256) instead of floating point, with a procedure that swaps for steep and reversed lines and a for loop over x updating intersection y. Print the canvas as rows of shade characters chosen from the intensity, using Put_Line with a fixed-size line buffer.
Xiaolin Wu's line algorithm.summary: The task has no required I/O beyond drawing, so text art from an integer fixed-point version needs only bounded arithmetic, for loops and guarded array indexing, which should discharge without annotations. The main care is bounding the loop-carried intersection value and keeping the plotted rows in range, so the outlook is plausible rather than likely.

effects.explanation: The program prints whether the embedded XML document is valid against the embedded XSD schema, naming the first violation found.

risks.explanation: The scanner cursor into the XML and XSD text is a loop-carried value, so every character read needs a guard of the form Pos <= Text'Last just before it, with end of text reported as a malformed-document outcome.

Node, child and stack indices into the fixed-capacity tree and work-stack arrays come out of while loops, so each store must be guarded by a count-below-capacity test that rejects documents that exceed the documented limits.
Occurrence counters compared with minOccurs and maxOccurs (unbounded) are bounded by the node capacity, and an explicit guard placed before each increment keeps them inside their declared range.
Copying element names and text values into bounded name buffers needs a length guard before each slice assignment, and any name that is too long is rejected visibly.
All scanning and tree walking happen in while loops inside procedures, which get no termination check, while the helper functions use only for loops.
Nested element validation uses an explicit array stack in place of recursion, so stack depth is fixed and does not grow with the input.

XML validation.approach: The W3Schools shiporder XML and XSD are embedded as String constants, and each is parsed by a hand-written scanner into a fixed-capacity array of node records (name buffer, kind, attributes, parent, first-child and next-sibling indices). The program validates against a defined XSD subset: element, complexType, sequence, attribute with use=required, minOccurs/maxOccurs including unbounded, and the simple types xs:string, xs:decimal, xs:integer and xs:positiveInteger, which are checked lexically. It walks the schema and document trees together using an explicit work stack inside procedures, and every limit or malformed-input case prints a specified rejection message.
XML validation.summary: No Oracle rule forbids the program, but it is a fairly large one. Its many loop-carried cursors, tree indices and counters each need a guard just before use, since no invariant can be written. That makes discharge depend on careful program shape, though no annotation is needed.

effects.explanation: The serialized XML text is written to standard output.

risks.explanation: Appending into the fixed-capacity output buffer is guarded by a length check against the capacity, with an overflow outcome of rejecting the document, and child and node indexes come from for-loops over the arrays' own ranges.
The buffer length counter is loop-carried, so each append checks remaining capacity just before writing so the counter stays within its subtype.

XML/DOM serialization.approach: Represent the DOM as a fixed-capacity array of node records (kind, parent index, bounded name or text held in a fixed-size String with a length field) built by a procedure that adds root, element and text nodes. A non-recursive serializer procedure walks the nodes in document order using a for loop over the node array and the stored depth, appending the XML declaration, indented tags and text into a bounded buffer with a capacity guard before each append, then prints it with Put_Line per line.
XML/DOM serialization.summary: The task is a tiny fixed three-node tree serialized to console, which needs only bounded arrays, records and guarded for-loop appends with no annotations, so proofs should discharge routinely.

effects.explanation: Each extracted student name is printed on its own line, with non-ASCII characters emitted as UTF-8 bytes.

risks.explanation: The scanner advances a position through the embedded XML text in a while loop inside a procedure, so every lookahead (tag name, Name=" prefix, closing quote, entity terminator) needs an explicit bounds guard just before the indexing.
Each name is copied into a fixed-capacity buffer (for example 64 characters), so a guard must check capacity before every append and give a visible outcome such as reporting an over-long name.

Decoding the numeric character reference É accumulates a code point in a bounded integer and encodes it to UTF-8 bytes, which needs digit-count and value guards so the accumulator and Character'Val arguments stay in range.
The loops sit in a procedure so no variant is required, but the scan must be written so the position visibly advances and no function contains a while loop.

XML/Input.approach: Embed the XML fragment as a String constant and scan it with a position index in a while loop inside a procedure. Detect a start tag named Student, locate its Name attribute, copy the quoted value into a bounded buffer while decoding numeric character references to UTF-8 bytes, then print the buffer with Put_Line. Every lookahead is preceded by a bounds guard, and a malformed or over-long name produces a specified rejection message.
XML/Input.summary: The task is plain string scanning of fixed embedded data with no recursion, annotation or dynamic construct, so it fits Silver once string indexing, loops and bounded buffers exist. It is plausible rather than likely because the scanner has several loop-carried indices that each need a guard just before use.

effects.explanation: The XML document is printed line by line to standard output.

risks.explanation: Writing escaped text into a fixed buffer uses a loop-carried length, so each append is preceded by an explicit capacity guard and the buffer is sized at six times the longest input.

The loop-carried length is declared with a subtype bounded by the buffer capacity and checked against remaining room before each increment, with overflow giving a visible rejection message rather than truncation.
Printing the escaped slice Buffer (1 .. Length) needs Length to be known within the buffer bounds, which its declared subtype provides.

XML/Output.approach: A procedure Escape_Text copies an input String into a fixed-size Character buffer, replacing the five XML entity characters (&, <, >, " and ') with their entity strings, using a for loop over the input's range and a case statement. A procedure Emit_Character takes a name and a remark, escapes both, and prints one Character element line with Put_Line. Main prints the CharacterRemarks opening tag, calls Emit_Character for the three embedded name/remark pairs, then prints the closing tag.
XML/Output.summary: Every check follows from array bounds, a bounded length subtype and a guard before each append, with no while loops or recursion, though the loop-carried output length needs careful guarding.

effects.explanation: Prints the first item element, each price text and each name element to standard output.

risks.explanation: Every slice or character access during tag matching is preceded by an explicit guard that the tag length fits within the remaining document, and the scan position is a for-loop index over the document's own range.
Positions are subtype-bounded to the document length so the arithmetic computing end offsets stays within the declared range.
All scanning is in a procedure using for loops, so no variant is needed and no function contains a while loop.

XML/XPath.approach: The XML document is embedded as a constant String, and a Find_Tag-style helper procedure scans it with a for loop over the string's own index range, comparing a guarded slice against an open tag and then locating the matching close tag. Three scans print the first item element (from the first open tag through its close tag), the text between each price tag pair, and each name element, using Put_Line for output and Put for inline text. A missing close tag is handled by an explicit visible outcome of stopping the scan with an error message.
XML/XPath.summary: The task reduces to substring search over a fixed embedded document with a handful of bounded scans, so every index check follows from for-loop ranges and explicit length guards. Plausible rather than likely because the careful position arithmetic across several scan phases needs guards on each loop-carried offset.

effects.explanation: Prints a header per redaction target and one labeled redacted sentence per option combination.

risks.explanation: Word-boundary scans and pattern-window comparisons use loop-carried positions, so each access is preceded by an explicit bounds guard (Pos <= Len and then ...) and positions live in a subtype 0 .. Len + 1.
Position increments and Start + Pattern_Length - 1 sums stay safe because the sentence and pattern are fixed-length subtypes with small bounds and loop positions are range-typed.
Lower-casing a letter through 'Pos and 'Val is guarded by an explicit test that the character is in 'A' .. 'Z' just before conversion.

XXXX redacted.approach: The sentence and the two targets are embedded fixed-length String constants, and a Redact procedure copies the sentence into an out String of the same length and overwrites ranges with 'X'. It scans words with while loops bounded by Len, trims non-letter edges to get the core, then handles whole-word equality, partial-match windows (for loops over start positions with case folding via a small function) and overkill by overwriting the whole core; main loops over the two targets and Boolean option combinations printing labeled lines. The optional grapheme stretch is left out and the text is ASCII.
XXXX redacted.summary: Everything is bounded string and index arithmetic over fixed-length strings, inside procedures so no termination check applies, and every index is guardable by explicit tests. The nested scan loops with several loop-carried positions need careful guard placement, so discharge is plausible rather than routine.

conflicts.explanation: The task requires defining a stateless Y combinator, a higher-order function that takes a function and returns its recursive fixed point. This needs first-class functions, lambda expressions and closures that capture arguments of enclosing functions, plus self-application. Ada/SPARK cannot express these: there are no anonymous functions or closures, and SPARK limits access-to-subprogram values, so a function cannot build and return a new function at run time.

effects.explanation: Prints the factorial and Fibonacci values computed through the combinator.

Y combinator.summary: Excluded. The task asks for a stateless fixed-point combinator that turns non-recursive functions into recursive ones, which requires first-class functions and closures. Ada/SPARK cannot express those, and the FreeBASIC entry gets around this only by not implementing a real combinator.

effects.explanation: The program has to send HTTP requests to Yahoo! search and fetch the result pages, including the next page of results.
It prints the URL, title and content read from each search result.

Yahoo! search interface.summary: The task needs a search object, which can be a package with a record or tagged type. It also needs a Next Page operation and parsing of the returned HTML into bounded URL, Title and Content strings. None of that breaks an Oracle rule; the only thing Silver lacks is an admitted network (HTTP) library operation, so the task is a future candidate.

effects.explanation: Prints the first 30 Yellowstone numbers, space separated, on one line.

risks.explanation: The Used array is indexed by the candidate, so the search loop tests Candidate < Limit in its condition before every access and rejects visibly if the table is exhausted.
The candidate increment and the Euclid remainder values live in a bounded subtype with a Limit guard, so the types alone bound them even though the loop carries no invariant.
GCD is a procedure with a while loop (no termination check is generated), and the search loop is also in a procedure, so no variant is needed.
The mod operation sits inside a while loop whose condition is B /= 0, which is the guard placed just before the operation.

Yellowstone sequence.approach: Keep a Boolean array Used (1 .. 200) and a 30-element array of the sequence values, both in a bounded positive subtype; seed a(1..3) = 1..3, then for each n from 4 to 30 scan upward from 1 with a while loop (condition guarded by Candidate < Limit) for the smallest unused value whose GCD, computed by an Euclid while-loop procedure, is 1 with a(n-1) and greater than 1 with a(n-2). If no candidate is found within the limit the program rejects visibly; otherwise it marks Used and prints each value with 'Image via Put, ending with a newline.
Yellowstone sequence.summary: Everything is bounded integer arithmetic and array indexing in procedures with guards before each access, and the extra plot is optional, so no annotation or function variant is required. The only non-routine point is the candidate search limit, which a visible Reject branch handles; the actual maximum in the first 30 terms is 51, well within the table.

effects.explanation: The two symbols are drawn as text art on standard output.

risks.explanation: Squared-distance tests on coordinates are discharged because the radius is a small ranged subtype (for example 1 .. 20) and the loop indexes are bounded by it.

Yin and yang.approach: A function Cell (R, X, Y) returns a Character ('#', '.', or ' ') using integer circle tests on squared distances (outer circle radius R, half-radius lobes, small eyes of radius R/5 or so) with R/2 computed on a ranged subtype. A procedure Draw (R) uses nested for loops over Y in -R .. R and X in -2*R .. 2*R (doubled width for character aspect), emitting each cell with Put and ending each row with Put_Line. Main calls Draw with two small constant sizes (for example 6 and 12).
Yin and yang.summary: Text art meets the task's picture requirement, and every check is integer arithmetic on small ranged subtypes inside for loops, so proofs follow from types and loop bounds with no loop-carried state.

effects.explanation: Prints the five houses with their drink, nationality, colour, smoke and pet, ending with who owns the zebra, via Put_Line.

risks.explanation: The permutation table is filled by nested for loops with a loop-carried row counter, so each write is preceded by an explicit guard that the counter is below 120, and the later search indexes the table only with for-loop variables over its own range.

Zebra puzzle.approach: Houses are a subtype 1..5 and each of the five attributes (colour, nationality, drink, smoke, pet) is one row of a 120 by 5 permutation table, built once by five nested for loops that skip repeated values. Five nested for loops over table rows test each clue as early as its attributes are chosen, using integer comparisons and abs differences on house positions, and the solution is printed once found through fixed-length name strings. The search uses only for loops in a procedure, so the only loop-carried value is the table counter and there are no termination checks.
Zebra puzzle.summary: Every check follows from subtype ranges, for-loop indexes over array ranges and one counter guard, with no recursion, no while loops and no annotations, so proofs should discharge automatically. The brute-force search cost is a run-time cost and not a proof obligation.

effects.explanation: Prints the Zeckendorf results of the addition, subtraction, multiplication and division examples as digit strings.

risks.explanation: Carry and borrow propagation move loop-carried digit indexes left and right, so each access is guarded explicitly against the array bounds before use.
Results exceeding the fixed digit capacity must take a visible outcome (reporting overflow and leaving the value unchanged) via a guard before carrying past the top digit.
Normalization is written as while loops inside procedures only, which get no termination check, and any function uses for loops only.
Every digit array is fully initialized by aggregate or a for loop before use, and out parameters are assigned on all paths.

Zeckendorf arithmetic.approach: A Zeckendorf number is a fixed-capacity array of 0..1 digits (about 40 positions) with the task's examples embedded as constant digit strings. Add, subtract, multiply (doubling table of shifted values and adding) and divide (greedy subtract of table entries) are procedures that apply digit-wise operations then normalize 11 to 100 with guarded while loops, with explicit capacity checks that report overflow. Output converts digit arrays to a String via a bounded buffer and Put_Line.
Zeckendorf arithmetic.summary: All checks are index and capacity bounds on loop-carried positions that can be guarded explicitly in procedures without invariants, but carry/borrow normalization and the multiplication and division tables need careful shaping, so discharge is plausible rather than routine.

effects.explanation: Prints the table of numbers 0 to 20 with their Zeckendorf strings to standard output.

Zeckendorf number representation.approach: Embed a constant array of the Fibonacci numbers 1,2,3,5,8,13 and loop N over 0 .. 20; for each N, a for loop walks the array from largest to smallest, subtracting a Fibonacci number from a remainder of subtype 0 .. 20 only when the remainder is at least that number (greedy gives the unique Zeckendorf form). It prints each digit with Put, using a Boolean flag to drop leading zeros and printing a single "0" when N is zero, then ends the line with Put_Line.
Zeckendorf number representation.summary: Every check follows from a bounded remainder subtype, a guard comparing it to the array element just before each subtraction, and for-loop indexes over the array's own range, with no loop-carried value needing an invariant. The only added surface is basic integers, a constant array, for loops, integer-to-text conversion and non-newline output.

effects.explanation: Prints the computed result of 0**0 to standard output.

Zero to the zero power.approach: Declare an Integer variable X := 0 and a Natural variable Y := 0, compute Z : Integer := X ** Y, and print "z=" concatenated with the image of Z using Put_Line. There are no loops, no input and no guards, because the operands are fixed and the result is statically in range.
Zero to the zero power.summary: The program is a single exponentiation of small constant-valued integers with one image conversion, so every check follows from declared types and the values 0 and 1 cannot overflow. Silver only lacks integer ** and 'Image output formatting today.

effects.explanation: Prints the input image and the thinned image as rows of text art.

risks.explanation: Neighbour accesses at x-1, x+1, y-1 and y+1 are safe because the pixel loops run over the interior subranges 2..Rows-1 and 2..Cols-1 of constant bounds.
The neighbour count and transition count are small counters of a range 0..8 type incremented in straight-line code at most eight times, so the provers bound them without an invariant.

Zhang-Suen thinning algorithm.approach: Store the embedded 10-by-32 image as a two-dimensional Boolean array filled from constant row strings, with a second array for the next generation. A procedure loops while a Changed flag is set, running step 1 and step 2 as nested for loops over interior pixels only, computing B and A with fixed straight-line if statements, noting deletions in a marker array and then clearing them after each pass. Output builds each row in a fixed 32-character String buffer and prints it with Put_Line before and after thinning.
Zhang-Suen thinning algorithm.summary: All array indexing is over constant interior ranges and all counters are small ranged values, so every check follows from types and loop bounds; the only unbounded loop is a while loop in a procedure, which gets no termination check.

effects.explanation: The 5 by 5 array is printed as rows of numbers on standard output.

risks.explanation: The carried row and column cursors are known only by their 1..5 subtype after the first iteration, so every step such as I+2 or J-1 needs an explicit guard just before use, with an unreachable fallback that leaves the cursor unchanged.
The counter is a for-loop index bounded by 24 and stored in a 0..24 element subtype, so the store discharges from declared ranges.
Walking anti-diagonals with nested for loops and computing the cell from the diagonal and offset avoids loop-carried state but needs range guards on the computed row and column.

Zig-zag matrix.approach: Use a constant Size of 5 and a 5 by 5 array of a 0..24 subtype, filled in a Main procedure by a for loop over the elements 1..24 that moves guarded row and column cursors of subtype 1..5 along the anti-diagonals. Every cursor move is preceded by a bound test so each index stays in range. Nested for loops over the array's own ranges then print each row with Integer'Image and Put, followed by a line terminator.
Zig-zag matrix.summary: All checks come from the 1..5 index subtypes, the 0..24 element subtype and guards before each cursor step, with no recursion or functions with while loops, but the loop-carried cursors need careful guard placement. The program is plausible rather than likely for that reason.

effects.explanation: Prints the permutations for n from 1 to 5 and the counts for m from 1 to 30 as text lines.

risks.explanation: A(30) is about 4e26, beyond 64 bits, so counts use a fixed-capacity two-limb base-10^18 number whose limb sums stay below 2*10^18 and carries are 0 or 1, which follow from the limb subtype ranges.
The next-permutation scan loops decrement an index in while loops, so each decrement is guarded by an explicit index-greater-than-first test before the array access.
Entringer-table row and column indexes come from for loops over the array's own ranges, but the loop-carried big-number cells are only bounded by their limb types, which suffices for the additions.
Rendering a two-limb number into a decimal text buffer needs a fixed 27-digit buffer with padded limb digits so slice lengths are static.

Zigzag numbers.approach: Permutations of 1..n (n at most 5) are enumerated in lexicographic order with an iterative next-permutation procedure over a fixed 5-element array, printing those with the up-down pattern; n of 1 prints the single permutation. Counts for m from 1 to 30 come from the Seidel/Entringer triangle built with for loops using only additions on a fixed-capacity two-limb big number held in a two-dimensional array, and are printed by converting limbs to digit text.
Zigzag numbers.summary: Everything is iterative with bounded arrays and for loops, and the only unusual parts are the add-with-carry big number (A(30) exceeds 64 bits) and guarded while-loop scans in procedures, none of which needs an annotation.

effects.explanation: Prints each radix pair's first 20 Zsigmondy numbers as text lines.

risks.explanation: Computing a**m by repeated multiplication in a loop-carried accumulator needs an explicit guard (acc <= Limit / a) before each multiply, with Limit above 7**20 so all required terms fit in 64-bit integers and larger input is rejected visibly.
Dividing z by gcd g in a loop needs a guard (1 < g and g <= z) so the quotient stays within a positive subtype without an invariant.
Euclid's gcd and the divide-out loop use while loops, so they must be procedures (which have no termination check) rather than functions.
Divisors in gcd and the divide-out step are guarded nonzero just before use; a^m - b^m is positive because a > b >= 1 is a subtype constraint.

Zsigmondy numbers.approach: Embed the 10 radix pairs in a constant 2D array and, for each pair and n = 1..20, compute p = a^n - b^n by a guarded multiply loop in a procedure. Then for each m < n compute q = a^m - b^m and, while gcd(z, q) > 1, divide z by that gcd (Euclid in a procedure), which yields the greatest divisor of p coprime to all earlier terms without any factorization. Print each result with scalar image and Put, one line per radix pair.
Zsigmondy numbers.summary: Every check follows from subtype ranges and guards just before each multiply, divide and gcd step, and the divide-out method avoids divisor enumeration, but loop-carried accumulators in nested while loops make discharge depend on careful guard placement. The largest value, 7**20, fits in 64 bits, so the required 10 terms per radix set need no big numbers.

effects.explanation: Prints the 220 Zumkeller numbers, the 40 odd ones and the 40 odd ones not ending in 5 as text lines.

risks.explanation: The divisor sum is a loop-carried accumulator, so it is held in a 64-bit type and each addition is preceded by a guard that rejects the candidate (a visible outcome) if it would exceed a documented cap far above any sigma(n) needed.

The subset-sum table is indexed by the running target minus a divisor, so each access is guarded by a comparison immediately before it and the table size is a fixed capacity checked against sigma(n)/2 before use.
Divisor count is a loop-carried index into a fixed-capacity divisor array, so it is guarded against the capacity before each store, with overflow of the capacity reported as a rejection.
All searching, divisor enumeration and subset-sum work is done in procedures using for loops or while loops over bounded counters, so no function needs a variant.

Search limits (n up to roughly 10^5 to 10^6 for the odd lists) are documented resource bounds, and the main search loops must stop with a specified outcome if a limit is hit before the required counts are found.

Zumkeller numbers.approach: Enumerate divisors of n with a for loop into a fixed-capacity array, sum them with a guarded accumulator, and reject odd sums; for odd n use the abundance parity shortcut, otherwise run an iterative boolean subset-sum table (iterating sums downward over a bounded array) for target sigma/2. A while loop in the main procedure scans candidates (step 1 or 2) counting hits until 220 or 40 are found, formatting each number into a text buffer and printing in rows.
Zumkeller numbers.summary: Everything is bounded iteration over fixed arrays with guards before each loop-carried addition or index, and no recursion is needed because the subset-sum is a table; the difficulty is only the guard discipline and the integer-to-text output.
